title: I hiked 100 miles to find the best walking poles, here are my favourites | Walking | The Guardian
description: Trekking poles can improve balance on uneven terrain and reduce stress on joints. Our seasoned adventurer put 10 to the test to find the best
Author: Sian Lewis
Headline: Trekking poles can improve balance on uneven terrain and reduce stress on joints. Our seasoned adventurer put 10 to the test to find the best
Content: Poling station: Sian Lewis testing walking poles in the countryside.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPoling station: Sian Lewis testing walking poles in the countryside.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterWalkingReviewI hiked 100 miles to find the best walking poles, here are my favouritesTrekking poles can improve balance on uneven terrain and reduce stress on joints. Our seasoned adventurer put 10 to the test to find the best‘I’d never head out without one’: 10 hiking essentialsSian LewisTue 29 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOh, I would walk 500 miles – with the help of a trusty pole. A walking pole – or two – makes a surprisingly handy addition to your hiking kit, helping with balance on uneven terrain, taking strain away from your legs and knees, and making going up and down hills much easier. I first tried walking poles when I went trekking in the Himalayas – now, I wouldn’t be without one on rugged terrain, but they can be just as helpful on a casual stroll.Hiking poles are typically used as a pair, and the idea is to swing each pole in time with the opposite foot as you move forwards: right foot and left pole, then left foot and right pole, in a rhythm. You can also use poles singly to keep a hand free or to take the weight off one side of your body.Walking poles are available in fixed lengths or as adjustable models, and there are ones you can fold up and stick in a rucksack when not in use. There’s more variety out there than you may think – but we’ve narrowed it down to eight of the best walking poles for all kinds of hikers.At a glanceBest walking poles overallBlack DiamondPursuit Carbon Z poles£115.18 at DeporvillageBest budget walking poleVangoAnnapurna£28.95 per pole at LiGoBest adjustable walking polesSilvaCarbon trekking poles£89.95 at Outdoor ActionBest lightweight walking polesGossamer GearLT5 Carbon trekking poles£214.99 at Ultralight Outdoor GearWhy you should trust meI’m a seasoned adventure travel writer and gear-tester, and I’ve been putting outdoor kit through its paces for more than a decade. I’ve hiked thousands of miles with walking poles – everywhere from the summit of Mount Kenya to my favourite local trails in the Cotswolds. I’ve also been working on two UK walking guides – a great excuse to grab a hiking pole and go exploring.How I testedView image in fullscreenOn the right track: the poles were tested on a range of terrains.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianThe only real way to test a walking pole is to get out and walk with it. For this roundup I hiked at least 10 miles with each model I’ve recommended, covering a mix of trails, inclines and surfaces, including mountain tracks in the Lake District and more relaxed rambles on theCotswold Way.I tested 10 different individual models or sets of poles in these real-world conditions to find my favourites, using them in warm weather to see if the grips stayed comfortable when my hands were hot and sweaty, and in cold, wet conditions to assess traction and confidence on slippery terrain.When trying out adjustable poles, I checked how easy they were to extend, fold and stash on the go. Durability was another focus: I paid attention to locking mechanisms, handles and materials to see if they seemed built to last. On longer hikes, I checked if each pole felt light and comfortable to carry, mile after mile.Where not returned to the manufacturer, any poles sourced for this article were donated to charity after testing.The best walking and trekking polesView image in fullscreenField work: the walking and trekking poles tested for the guide.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianBest walking poles overall:Black Diamond Pursuit Carbon Z polesBlack DiamondPursuit Carbon Z polesfrom£115.18£115.18 at Deporvillage£170 at Black DiamondWhat we loveComfortable; sturdy; can cope with all conditionsWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need to spend more for an adjustable versionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£115.18 at Deporvillage£170 at Black DiamondBlack Diamond makes kit specifically for climbers, runners and hikers, so it’s no surprise that it knows a thing or two about poles. The Pursuit Carbon Z were brilliant when I hiked with them, whether on slick rock surfaces in Cumbria or chilled-out walks in the Cotswolds. They’re lightweight, have great grip and are easy to snap into shape to fold away and carry with you.Why we lovethemThe Pursuit Zs combine my favourite walking pole ingredients – cork and carbon. The cork grips are comfy, prevent sweat from pooling and dry fast if you do get caught out in the elements. At 191g at the shortest length, the 100% carbon body of each pole is lightweight, but feels sturdy when I put weight on it, adding confidence on uneven surfaces. Their carbide tips also grip the ground well when you need extra support. I’ve used these poles on dozens of hiking adventures, including taking them to the French Alps on a trekking holiday, and their durability seems to match their build quality.These poles fold up into three sections in a Z-design, so they’re easy to carry, but they’re not adjustable. That means you’ll need to order a height that suits you from between 110cm and 130cm. If you’d rather change the height of a pole on the fly, the good news is that the brand’s newDistance Carbon FLZ polesoffer full adjustability. I’ve been able to test this more premium new version, and while I recommend the original Pursuit Zs for the average user, you could spend the extra £30 if adjustability is a big priority for you.It’s a shame that …you’ll need to spend extra for an adjustable versionWeight:191, 196, 200, 205, 209g, dependent on length?Height:110, 115, 120, 125, 130cmMaterial:carbon and corkTelescopic:noFoldable:yesAdjustable:noBlack DiamondPursuit Carbon Z polesfrom£115.18£115.18 at Deporvillage£170 at Black DiamondWhat we loveComfortable; sturdy; can cope with all conditionsWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need to spend more for an adjustable versionBest budget walking pole:Vango AnnapurnaVangoAnnapurnafrom£28.95£28.95 per pole at LiGo£32.95 per pole at Outdoor ActionWhat we loveSuperb priceWhat we don’t loveProbably too flimsy to hike its Himalayan namesakeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£28.95 per pole at LiGo£32.95 per pole at Outdoor ActionCarbon walking poles needn’t cost you a packet – Vango has proven you can grab a great pair of poles for far less than £100 with the Annapurna. Nice and light at 190g per pole, and folding down to a respectable 62cm for easy transport or for tying to your backpack, I think this functional pole punches above its price – just note that it’s not sold as a set.Why we love itThe Vango Annapurna strikes a good balance between weight, comfort and price. Built from a 50% carbon fibre shaft, it’s lightweight but still feels solid when leaned on, making it a reliable choice for varied terrain. The pole is collapsible via aluminium quick locks – they worked well during my tests, even with most of my body weight leaning on them, but didn’t feel as durable as the most high-performing (and expensive) poles I tested.The foam grips are solid, even when wet, and long enough to be held at different heights on the go. I think they’re flimsy for a tough trek at altitude, despite being named after a Himalayan mountain, but for weekends exploringBritish hiking trailsor for your first walking holiday, they’re a bargain and allow you to adjust pole height and grip position on the go.It’s a shame that …thelocks seem a little flimsy.Weight:190gHeight:62-135cmMaterial:carbon, foamTelescopic:yesFoldable:noAdjustable:yesVangoAnnapurnafrom£28.95£28.95 per pole at LiGo£32.95 per pole at Outdoor ActionWhat we loveSuperb priceWhat we don’t loveProbably too flimsy to hike its Himalayan namesakeBest adjustable walking poles:Silva Carbon trekking polesSilvaCarbon trekking polesfrom£89.95£89.95 at Outdoor Action£112.99 at DecathlonWhat we lovePractical, comfortable and long-lastingWhat we don’t loveThe wrist straps could be widerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£89.95 at Outdoor Action£112.99 at DecathlonI’ve been testing Swedish brand Silva’s popular carbon poles for more than a year, so I can vouch for their longevity as well as their good first-day performance.These poles combine comfy cork and foam handles with lightweight carbon, and they’re sturdy without adding excessive weight. The flick locks are easy and intuitive to use, and mine are still going strong after miles of adventures.Why we love itThese no-nonsense poles tick all the boxes. They’re easy to hold thanks to long cork and foam grips, so you can quickly change your hand position on varied terrain. The quality flick locks allow you to adjust pole height during a walk – without breaking your stride and even while wearing gloves. There are centimetres marked on both adjustable sections, too, so you can easily find the height you’re after.These poles collapse to 65cm when you’re not using them, so they’re small enough to stick in a bag or to carry one-handed, and the carbide tips dig nicely into the ground when you need extra grip, offering extra confidence on mud and scree.If I’m being really picky, I’d have preferred comfier, wider wrist straps, but these are great all-rounders for high- and low-land hikes.It’s a shame that …the wrist straps are a touch thin.Weight:178gHeight:65-140cmMaterial:carbon, corkTelescopic:yesFoldable:noAdjustable:yesSilvaCarbon trekking polesfrom£89.95£89.95 at Outdoor Action£112.99 at DecathlonWhat we lovePractical, comfortable and long-lastingWhat we don’t loveThe wrist straps could be widerBest lightweight walking poles:Gossamer Gear LT5 carbon trekking polesGossamer GearLT5 Carbon trekking poles£214.99£214.99 at Ultralight Outdoor GearWhat we loveLight; may convert walking pole scepticsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and lack an extended gripView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£214.99 at Ultralight Outdoor GearGossamer Gear reckons its LT5s are among the lightest poles on the market – the brand claims they weigh 151g per pole. But when I weighed them, they were even less, at 139g. They feel delightfully light and freeing to handle but are still sturdy on tougher hikes, so if you think walking poles are too clunky to carry over long distances, these featherweights might just change your mind. They split into three sections and have twist locks that I found intuitive and efficient on test.Why we love itThe ultralight LT5 Carbon Poles are popular among minimalist hikers, and for good reason. They feel surprisingly lightweight, even if you’re walking all day. I also thought their grip was the comfiest in the test, despite being made from foam, rather than my normally favoured cork. This allows sweat to evaporate quickly in hot conditions – I took them hiking in the jungle in Belize, and they performed brilliantly – and are comfy in cold or wet conditions, too.The grip isn’t as long as the grips on other poles on test, so you can’t hold this pole at a different height without changing its setup. The three-section carbon design has a simple twist-lock adjustment, which I usually don’t rate over flick locks, but Gossamer Gear has managed to create good-quality twist locks that stay put, allowing me to fine-tune the length fast and without excessive fiddling.The minimal pack size makes them easy to strap on to a backpack or stow in your luggage, so they’re ideal for fast packers or thru-hikers who count every gram and need poles that perform day after day. Casual hikers can choose something cheaper.It’s a shame that …they’re expensive, and there’s no extended grip.Weight:139gHeight:60-130cmMaterials:carbon, foamTelescopic:yesFoldable:noAdjustable:yesGossamer GearLT5 Carbon trekking poles£214.99£214.99 at Ultralight Outdoor GearWhat we loveLight; may convert walking pole scepticsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and lack an extended gripThe best of the restView image in fullscreenAn affordable lightweight option: the OEX Duralumin.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianOEX DuraluminOEXDuraluminfrom£31£31 at Blacks£35.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredibly good value and pleasingly lightWhat we don’t loveComparatively poor gripView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£31 at Blacks£35.99 at AmazonBest for:lightweight on a budgetAluminium doesn’t offer carbon’s magic combo of lightweight and sturdiness, but it still does a great job on the trail – and it’s far more affordable. OEX’s Duralumin champions its high-grade 7075 aluminium build, and I was impressed by how lightweight each pole was at just 244g – there are lighter options out there, but you’ll have to spend a lot more.I thought the Duralumin’s grip performed less well during testing – the foam is unforgiving and not as ergonomic in the hand as the grips on some pricier models. It does extend down, though, which is handy for adjusting where you hold these poles, and the flick locks work well and stay in place all day once adjusted.It didn’t make the final cut because …the grip isn’t great.Height:105-135cm;weight:244g;material:aluminium, foam;telescopic:yes;foldable:no;adjustable:yesOEXDuraluminfrom£31£31 at Blacks£35.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredibly good value and pleasingly lightWhat we don’t loveComparatively poor gripLeki CressidaLekiCressidafrom£90£90 at Nevisport£113.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLightweight and easily adjustableWhat we don’t loveOnly suited to shorter peopleView image in fullscreen£90 at Nevisport£113.99 at AmazonBest for:shorter people and smaller handsDo women need to choose female-specific walking poles? In general, no – but shorter women and teenagers may prefer a lightweight design tailored to their height rather than a unisex model.Leki’s Cressida trekking pole is fully adjustable, and the aluminium shaft feels rugged and stable in all terrains. Each pole weighs 237g, so while carbon would be lighter, you won’t feel weighed down. The clips are quick and easy to lock and unlock, allowing you to adjust your pole on the fly, and the breathable strap and comfortable cork grip, designed for smaller hands, keep hands cool even in hot weather.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’ll only suit shorter people and smaller hands.Height:100-120cm;weight:237;material:aluminium;telescopic:yes;foldable:no;adjustable: yesLekiCressidafrom£90£90 at Nevisport£113.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLightweight and easily adjustableWhat we don’t loveOnly suited to shorter peopleCraghoppers Venture T GripCraghoppersVenture T Gripfrom£28£28 per pole at Next£35 per pole at CraghoppersWhat we loveHandle is comfortable and satisfying to holdWhat we don’t loveIt’s weighty, so not ideal for longer treksView image in fullscreen£28 per pole at Next£35 per pole at CraghoppersBest for:a T-grip poleA T-grip pole looks as it sounds, with an ergonomic, elongated handle like those you might find on old-fashioned wooden walking sticks. T-shaped handles offer a wider surface for support on uneven ground, and are easier to lean on than a regular pole.If you’re after a single pole, Craghoppers’ affordable option might suit you to a T. It has a foam handle that I rated for its comfort and satisfying feel. This pole has a twist-lock system, which I don’t find as reliable as flick locks, but it’s still sturdy enough for more casual country walks or exploring a city. At 270g, this isn’t a lightweight model, so I wouldn’t trek all day with it, but you can stuff it in a rucksack when you don’t need support.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not lightweight and is best used singly.Height:100-135cm ;weight:270g;material:aluminium, foam;telescopic:yes;foldable:no;adjustable: yesCraghoppersVenture T Gripfrom£28£28 per pole at Next£35 per pole at CraghoppersWhat we loveHandle is comfortable and satisfying to holdWhat we don’t loveIt’s weighty, so not ideal for longer treksMountain Warehouse BowfellMountain WarehouseBowfell£22.99£22.99 per pole at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveA decent first walking pole at a competitive priceWhat we don’t loveA touch flimsy, especially considering its weightView image in fullscreen£22.99 per pole at Mountain WarehouseBest for:a basic poleNot sure if walking poles are for you, or just want to snap up a design you can use now and then without having to splash cash on something fancy? Mountain Warehouse’s Bowfell is a no-fuss, simple model that’s still adjustable, folding into four sections. Just be sure to buy two if you want a pair, as it’s sold individually. Its fast-locking mechanism performed well and made it a good choice for travel. The foam grip is comfortable enough and suitable for cold weather.The fibreglass body of the pole feels flimsier than expensive models, and it isn’t a featherweight option at 255g per pole. But for weekend walkers, holiday hikers, or anyone wanting a dependable backup pole, the Bowfell offers good value, solid adjustability and decent functionality on unchallenging terrain.It didn’t make the final cut because …it feels cheaper and flimsier than more expensive models.Height:100135cm;weight:255g;material:fibreglass;telescopic:yes;foldable:no;adjustable:yesMountain WarehouseBowfell£22.99£22.99 per pole at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveA decent first walking pole at a competitive priceWhat we don’t loveA touch flimsy, especially considering its weightWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPole position: the grip and length can make all the difference on the trail.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianWhat are the key factors to consider?A good walking pole should feel like an extension of your arm, not an awkward bit of kit you’re forever adjusting. The first choice is material. Aluminium poles are durable and affordable; carbon fibre models tend to be lighter but more expensive. The lighter the pole, the less weight you’ll have to carry.Next, get a grip: cork handles mould nicely to your hand and prevent sweat from pooling, while rubber and foam offer solid comfort in cold or wet weather.Adjustability is useful on varied terrain, allowing you to lengthen poles on descents, shorten them on climbs and set them to suit your height. Collapsible or adjustable poles either telescope down or fold up in sections, and can usually be adjusted to any length within a given range with a locking mechanism. Flick locks (similar to those found on camera tripods) are generally more secure than twist locks.Benefits of using a walking pole – and when to use themWalking and trekking poles aren’t just for mountain-goers. Wherever you walk, they can reduce strain on knees and hips, improve balance, and help spread effort across your upper body. They’re especially handy on descents on rocky ground.Poles can also boost your rhythm and pace, turning a trudge into a stride. Use them on steep or uneven ground, or long-distance walks where fatigue might set in. For short city strolls, you can probably leave them behind.How to choose your walking polesThink about where and how often you walk before you pick up a pole. Occasional hikers can get by with mid-range aluminium poles, while regular trekkers may want to invest in carbon poles with ergonomic cork grips. Collapsible or telescopic designs will fit in a daypack or suitcase, so they’re better for travel and trekking abroad.In general, your elbow should be at a 90-degree angle when holding the pole by its hand grip, so either make sure you choose a fixed pole that’s the right length for your height, or buy an adjustable model.Ordering poles online can be tricky, especially if you’re unsure about what length to buy. According to Adam Simpson, climbing specialist at Bigstone, the best way to overcome this is to “stand straight and raise your elbow to 90 degrees, so your forearm is parallel to the floor, and make a fist like you’re holding a trekking pole”. It’s important to do this while standing on flat ground. “Measure from the floor to the top of your fist for your ideal trekking pole size,” he says. “For walking, hiking, and backpacking: stability and support matter most. Size up if you’re right on a size cusp.”Walking poles vs Nordic walking polesWalking poles are made for support and stability, while Nordic poles are designed to help with propulsion when you’re practising Nordic walking (a full-body exercise that involves walking to engage the upper body and to boost fitness compared with regular walking).The latter are lighter and used with a specific arm-swing technique for brisk walking. If your goal is upper-body exercise, go Nordic. If it’s hillwalking or rough terrain, stick to traditional poles.How to use walking polesWalking poles are designed to be used as a pair, with one in each hand to help redistribute the load as you walk. The idea is to swing each pole in time with the opposite foot moving forwards: right foot, left pole, in a rhythm.You can also use them singly – for example, for extra balance and joint support while keeping one hand free for navigation or carrying gear. After a few miles, you’ll wonder how you ever walked without them.For more hiking inspiration, read the Filter’s guides tothe best walking boots for menandthe best walking boots for womenSian Lewis is an award-winning freelance outdoors and travel journalist and author who loves putting adventure kit through its paces while hiking, swimming and wild camping. She discovered how great walking poles are in the Himalayas and has never looked back. She also shares her adventures at@sianannalewisandthegirloutdoors.comExplore more on these topicsWalkingThe FilterFitnessHobbiesHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stop press: why are garlic presses so out of fashion? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?
Content: Sometimes, a press can helpful, especially if the garlic is going in a sauce, stew or braise.Photograph: JoeGough/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenSometimes, a press can helpful, especially if the garlic is going in a sauce, stew or braise.Photograph: JoeGough/Getty Images/iStockphotoKitchen aideChefsStop press: why are garlic presses so out of fashion?It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?Anna BerrillTue 29 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy are garlic presses suddenly a no-no? Recipes nowstipulate gratinginstead, but who wants lumps of garlic in theirdinner?Sally, by emailPeople sure do love to hate on the garlic press, not that that’s anything new: in her aptly titled essayGarlic Presses Are Utterly Useless, Elizabeth David called them “both ridiculous and pathetic”, whileAnthony Bourdainwrote in Kitchen Confidential: “I don’t know what that junk is that squeezes out the ends of those things, but it ain’t garlic.” Fighting talk, indeed.Christina Soteriou, recipe writer at Ottolenghi Inc and author ofBig Veg Energy, however, takes a more balanced approach: “A garlic press is not necessarily a no-no, and there can definitely be a time and a place for it,” she says. “It’s definitely quicker [than chopping], but I’d use it only when said garlic is going into a sauce, stew or braise.” Which is to say, in a dish where those lumps that concern Sally will cook down and dissolve almost entirely.For Jenny Chandler, author ofThe Capsule Kitchen, meanwhile, there’s no “abhorrence and disgust at the idea of anybody using a garlic press, it just seems to add extra work to your cooking”. First, you’ve got to fumble around in a drawer to find it, then “half the garlic just squeezes up around the sides of the press, so I’ve got to do it twice to get all the garlic out”. That’s especially irksome given that Chandler is more often than not crushing multiple cloves. “So, in the time it takes me to locate my press and load it with, say, four cloves, I could have just crushed them with a bit of salt on a board under a heavy blade,” she says. And you’ll sure need extra time for cleaning the damned thing, Chandler adds: “That’s an absolute pain.”Soteriou usually minces her garlic with flaky sea salt “for the absolute best garlic flavour”, otherwise she “almost always” uses a Microplane grater or pestle and mortar. “The flavour is more consistent and mellow,” she explains. “Without getting too science-y, a pestle gently breaks down the garlic cells and releases a rounder, more even flavour, whereas a garlic press gives a slightly more bitter and uneven flavour because of how the cells are sharply broken down.” A Microplane falls somewhere between the two, and of course doing that by hand can be a sticky business. “People think a garlic press stops you from getting garlicky fingertips,” Chandler says, but there’s another solution: “When I worked on a boat many years ago, the owner gave me a bar ofstainless-steel soap, which turned out to be miraculous at getting rid of garlic smells.” The sulphur compounds in garlic bind to the metal molecules and wash away under water, and the same works if you brush those garlicky digits against a stainless-steel sink.As with most things in life, Sally should just do her, though Soteriou does suggest sticking to one rule: “A garlic press for anything that’s going to be slow-cooked, and a Microplane, pestle and mortar, or minced for anything where it will be raw or cooked very quickly.” Just “never, ever buy ready-crushed garlic”, Chandler says. “That’s another business altogether and it tastes awful.”Got a culinary dilemma? title: Why am I obsessed with China’s ancient golden age? I took my daughter on a trip to find out | China | The Guardian
description: The long read: I felt a duty to write about the Tang dynasty and its incredible social and cultural sophistication – but also to connect my Chinese past with my child
Author: Xiaolu Guo
Headline: The long read: I felt a duty to write about the Tang dynasty and its incredible social and cultural sophistication – but also to connect my Chinese past with my child
Content: Visitors surround a clay warrior from the Qin-era terracotta army at the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang. Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.I felt a duty to write about the Tang dynasty and its incredible social and cultural sophistication – but also to connect my Chinese past with my childByXiaolu GuoTue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTangDuringthe Tang dynasty, which lasted from the seventh to the early 10th century, Vikings were raiding the coasts of what today is called Europe. In the small archipelago now known as Britain, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms flitted by. Meanwhile, in Mesoamerica, after 3,000 years of flourishing, the Mayacivilisation was collapsing. In the east, China had been united for nine centuries and the Tang dynasty was already a proverbial high point of world culture.The Tang dynasty achieved an incredible level of social and cultural sophistication. Advances in science and medicine, sublime poetry, mystical paintings, high fashion in women’s clothing beyond the palace walls, exquisite ceramic and pottery arts, the invention of gunpowder and printing, highly elaborate cuisine, creative urban design and much more. It was a truly cosmopolitan empire with dynamic diplomatic relations with the neighbouring kingdoms.When I ponder this, an urge arises in me: a kind of duty, if you like, to write about this era. The Tang contrasts sharply with the image of a self-enclosed, inward-lookingChina, one that the west has long liked to promote. An open, cosmopolitan melting pot, it was the eastern centre into which flowed the riches of the silk roads that stretched all the way to the Byzantine empire.But still, why the Tang? And why learn about the Tang from me? I have my own story to tell, which has no pretence to objectivity. My story involves a specific, passionate reconnection with my own heritage. I wanted to return to China after a long absence. The last time I was there had been a decade before, along with my then three-month-old child, Moon. My desire to go back was in part for her, now 11 years old. So she and I set off on a journey back to the cultural womb from which I had emerged and had left behind. I had to explain the Chinese past not only to the child, but to myself.Xi’anOur journey began in Xi’an, thecapital of the Tang dynasty. A high-speed train had brought us from Beijing on a searingly hot day in July. On the road, the tarmac glistened and oozed out its black heat, while the city roared in full force with an immense river of traffic.I had booked a traditional-looking hotel, thinking we should taste more of the old China. When we reached the hotel, we had to squeeze ourselves in between a gang of businessmen all wearing black suits with alcohol-flushed faces. They spoke at high volume, while coughing and hawking. Was it a gathering for people with respiratory illnesses? I could smell their strong cigarettes from several metres away. With “no smoking” signs in the lobby, they stood by the hotel gate puffing away while cracking loud jokes. They spoke Shanxi dialect and I could vaguely make out that their laughter was to do with food and women. How familiar all this was; men in suits, chain-smoking, looking for girls – the kind of stuff that came with the recent wealth from the “Chinese miracle”. Where were the women, though? As usual, women worked. The receptionist and the manager were women. They gave us the room key after taking our money.Our room reeked of smoke; even the white bedding. We wanted to venture out immediately. We jumped into an air-conditioned taxi and set off to find some famous landmarks.An hour later we were standing by theGiant Wild Goose Pagoda. Moon hid under a nearby pomegranate tree, sucking an ice lolly, her chestnut-coloured hair tangled with sweat. Beyond the deafening sound of cicadas high up in the tree, the heat formed a shimmering layer of pink fog above the pagoda. Sweat was dripping from my eyebrows, obscuring my vision.View image in fullscreenThe Big Wild Goose Pagoda in Xi’an.Photograph: Sergio Azenha/AlamyEveryone in China knows that Xi’an is one of the oldest cities in the country. It’s our Rome or Athens. Over a 2,000-year period, it served as the capital for several dynasties, though it was called Chang’an back then. Traces of the Tang are everywhere. Like many other old monuments, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda of today is not original. Built at the beginning of the Tang in the seventh century, it was restored in the eighth century, then rebuilt in the 16th century after an earthquake. Constructed of brick and wood, the facade displays elaborate sculptures and carvings on the eaves. We joined a swirl of tourists around the tall tower, but we were not allowed to enter because it is too fragile for crowds.Moon was born and brought up in England. She had never experienced this climate, nor such crowds massed around her. There was not a single puff of wind. I feared she might get sunstroke. Hopping from the shadow of one tree to another, we managed to exit the park.Once outside, we leaned on the ancient city walls, enjoying the small respite offered by the shade. The wall, I read, was 14km in length, mainly built in the Ming dynasty in the 14th century. But the original was Tang. Xi’an is a great palimpsest on which many cultures have written their lives. This is very different from Rome or Athens, which are full of original ruins. Nothing in China can remain as ruins – the government either recreates the supposed original or builds something totally new. Ruins cannot exist under communism.NumbersWe wandered around a street market looking at all kinds of Chinese vegetables. We were eating stir-fried potato strips with vinegar and chilli.‘What’s this, Mum?’ Moon prodded a plate of white vegetables with her chopsticks.‘They are lotus root slices. Try it!’Embarking on this trip led me to think about my own relationship to China, but also about my daughter’s. Such an immense past. I wondered how I could educate her. What importance could it hold for her? Moon was English, or British: her first language was English, despite my ongoing efforts to fill her ears with my native tongue. These efforts have resulted only in the most moderate success. Moon could understand my Chinese, but it was as though the language had not penetrated beneath her skin. In England, at the end of a school day, she would say to me: “I find history difficult to enjoy.” I would respond: “If you do not know your history, you won’t know who you are!” And I heard myself say to her: “We can learn from the brilliance of the past, and one of these is the Tang.”But what did I really mean by that? Was I trying to convince myself as much as I was trying to convince my daughter?We spent the evening in one of the city squares, eating a half watermelon. We squatted by the flowerbeds and watched elderly couples dancing under the street lamps. The music, very kitsch 1980s Chinese songs, blasted in our ears. So at the top of my lungs I screeched at Moon about the ancient past, sounding not unlike the way the lectures were delivered in a re-education camp.“In the beginning, Xi’an was a stone-age village. Then a long, long time ago, like 3,000 years ago, it became the centre of a kingdom. Didn’t you learn about the Trojan war in ancient Greece? So that was around the same time.”I was already flailing, but I went on. “One of those earlier dynasties, the Zhou, was the founding dynasty of this area.” Moon started to look around, displaying her boredom. I paused, feeling a rising anguish.“The Qin emperor – Shi Huang – decided todesign his capital. It was called Xian-yang then, north-west of Xi’an. He built many palaces and unified the Chinese writing system. That was 2,000 years ago. You know he was the same one who started building theGreat Wall of China.”View image in fullscreenPortrait of Emperor Qin Shi Huang, in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesMoon spat out a few watermelon seeds. I searched desperately for something more dramatic.“But he also burned a great number of books and buried the scholars alive … Can you believe that?”“Horrible! Poor scholars!” Moon cried. “Why did he do that?”“Well, because he wanted to control people’s thoughts. Many emperors or dictators have done similar things. Anyway, the Qin empire only lasted for a short time. Then, around 202BC, a new dynasty came, one called the Han. The first emperor was Liu Bang.”I stopped, now frowning myself.“What’s wrong, Mum?”“Well, I really don’t like talking about Chinese history using western ways of counting years!”“You mean BC or AD. I don’t like those either!”“Yeah, what has China got to do with some man, Jesus Christ, being born so far away, who meant nothing to the emperor Liu Bang! We have our own way of dating different periods.”Now Moon turned to look at me: “What is your Chinese way?”I thought for a while, but I found myself fumbling. I could not translate the Chinese calendar in a simple way to an 11-year-old. The Chinese dynasty calendar is based on the name of the emperor followed by the name of the dynasty, along with a number to signify the year within that dynasty. Each new dynasty starts again from year zero.“Just give me an example, Mum,” she said, swallowing a piece of watermelon.“OK. We say: ‘唐高祖 12 年’, meaning the 12th year of the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang. Or, in your western equivalent, AD630.”As seemed to be so often the case, my speech to Moon was a mix of Chinese and English words. I went on, feeling like a schoolmistress. “You know, in the beginning of the Tang, in the early seventh century, Xi’an was one of the world’s largest and most populous cities.”It is estimated that about 1 million people lived within the city walls. By the dynasty’s end, in the ninth century, the country’s population had grown from 50 million to 80 million.For a contemporary Chinese person, numbers are essential to measure things, since we grew up in a populous country and under a governing party that was obsessed with numbers and numerical record-keeping. The Chinese Communist party would always describe a place with wording such as “the village used to have 38 Communist party members, which has expanded to 380, occupying an area of 32,000 sq metres”. We Chinese children grow up reciting numbers. Moon nodded, vaguely. Numbers are difficult for a British kid in this context.Silent armiesContemporary Chinese tourism is about rediscovering the country’s wondrous past, often in a banal and highly commercial fashion.History, it seems, can be a place for solace and the temporary forgetting of the stresses of contemporary Chinese life. I keenly felt that “history” was packaged as a touristic spectacle during this trip. Even so, I was confident that our travels would allow me to reassess my relationship to a past which had been entirely denied during the Cultural Revolution. I felt this intensely, and I believed that many in China felt the same way.Once you are in Xi’an, you cannot avoid passing the site where theterracotta army was buried. The warriors are not from the Tang dynasty, but from the earlier Qin, about 2,200 years ago. After waiting in an enormously long queue outside the Qin tomb site, a great throng of tourists pushed its way into the tomb like a host of locusts. By then we were already exhausted and our water bottles were empty.View image in fullscreenVisitors look at the terracotta warriors exhibition in Xi’an.Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesInside the vast hall where the terracottas were displayed, the eager tourists pressed on top of one another – not unlike the statues themselves. Beneath us, on the brown earth, headless figures, broken arms and body parts were neatly laid out. Most of them bore the uniform of a Qin dynasty warrior. They were ethereally still, as though waiting, or listening, but outside of time. I felt that we ourselves had come here to be temporarily buried along with these effigies of imperial power, a living host of terracotta tourists.These are not the traces of the Tang, though the Qin led to the Tang by way of a great tangled knot of dynastic struggle.“If there had been no Qin dynasty, then there would be no Tang,” I said to Moon.“So it’s like if there had been no Greeks, there would be no Romans?” she responded, boldly. She knew much more about Greek gods and Roman goddesses than I did.I pondered what the child had said while I gazed down at the broken statues. I asserted, and she agreed, that ancient Chinese culture was as rich and advanced as ancient Greek culture. But what did it mean really? I tried to breathe better. The air inside the hall was musty and thick with dust while the army of tourists pushed us this way and that in a vortex of human interaction. At one point, my child and I were desperate to get out from under the oppressive weight of all thishistory.The court diary and the sistersVery similar to theAnglo-Saxon Chronicle, or eventhe Domesday Bookfrom 1,000 years ago, there is theOld Book of Tang, comprising 200 chapters that chronicle the events during the Tang era as recorded by court ministers. The book is difficult to understand as it is written in classical Chinese.The difference between the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Old Book of Tangis that the former was written by monks living in monasteries, while the latter was written by mandarins living in the imperial court. Church culture was surely very different from court culture. The western church was a sanitised place peopled by men only, whereas the palace court was a luxurious and sensual inner city full of cultured courtesans and powerful women.“It was a tradition during those times that the palace diary, or any official record, was kept by the ladies of the palace,” I said to Moon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long ReadLose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crimeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe had just arrived at the Huaqing hot springs, 20km from Xi’an, a site where the Tang emperors and their wives would spend their leisure time. Now it is a major tourist destination.“But I thought women were badly treated back then, and they could not read or write,” Moon said.“Not during the Tang! From the Tang dynasty onwards, women were celebrated for their literary and artistic skills, not just because of their beauty.”Indeed, around the eighth century, there werefive famous sisters, whose key responsibility was to keep the court diary. The sisters were the granddaughters of a well-known poet, Song Zhiwen, and were educated not only in classical poetry, but also in politics. All five became accomplished writers and thinkers, and they made a pact never to marry but to devote themselves to literature and art. Together they wrote the Analects for Women, a counterpart of the Confucian Analectsfrom a female perspective, which became a classical text in women’s education in the Ming and Qing dynasties. In AD788, these sisters were recommended by a local official to Emperor Taizong, a great devotee of literature, who personally examined their work and recruited them all into the palace service asxueshi– masters of learning. The emperor held them in the highest esteem. It was during the Tang that, for the first time, literate women became important court ministers, calledshangshu.“That’s pretty amazing,” Moon said. “You told me that in ninth-century England, there were just Vikings raiding villages, and most people were illiterate.”“That’s right. And if Alfred the Great had not promoted literacy, no one would be able to read except the monks.”During the Tang, one of the areas in which women assumed an increasingly significant role was as artists, and some courtesans were famed singers and dancers, as well as being known for their extravagant clothing and hairstyles. Before the Tang, women in China were mostly veiled, and almost never in public service. The women of the Tang changed that tradition with the support of an enlightened court. They became fashion-makers, inventing elaborate makeup and sporting lavish dresses.Would it be too pretentious, too pompous, to call the Tang era one of the earliest feminist eras in ancient history? I thought of the Anglo-Saxon women during that period, or the wives of the Vikings and Romans. I was not convinced that they had achieved such power.The Grand CanalIn Britain, I have always lived by Regent’s Canal, around east London. After I left China, more than two decades ago, my daily routine revolved around that rusty urban English water. I would pass by the narrowboats along the winding waterways and often I thought of theGrand Canal in China. The Grand Canal is the longest and oldest artificial waterway in the world. The most ancient part was built in the fifth century BC. Later, in the seventh century AD, Emperor Yang of Sui undertook an ambitious project to connect the south and the north by a waterway. Then the Tang emperors expanded its scale and perfected its usage.I first saw the canal in 1993 when I left my southern home town and travelled to Beijing to study. The Beijing Film Academy is located right next to the canal, by the gate of the old Yuan dynasty ruins, and a park had recently been built along the waterway, with willows hugging the banks. After the day’s classes, I would leave the campus and sit by the water, reading or eating a takeaway. The water was motionless. I always wondered how such great quantities of rice and tea had been transported on this water in olden days.Often, on a cold sunny afternoon after snow had fallen, with one hand holding a translation of Pier Paolo Pasolini’s poetry, I would throw little stones on to the frozen surface to see if the ice would break. It was by that canal, dare I say, that I became a young intellectual, however arrogant and pretentious that may sound. I could even say that I was part of the historical landscape, stoic but everlasting, regardless of the destruction of ancient culture in China since the Cultural Revolution. For me, the Tang is the exact opposite of the Cultural Revolution. The former is rich and culturally diverse, whereas the latter is poor, unimaginative and functional in all aspects of life and thought.When we briefly visited Beijing, I wanted to show Moon the canal and the park near the Beijing Film Academy, but I never managed to venture to that part of the capital. Beijing was too big to get around. The six massive ring roads and countless highways surrounding it seemed larger than the orbits in our solar system.LuoyangOne might complain about the quality of water or air in China, but one can only admire the public transport: roads and railways lead to every possible destination. This is a very recent phenomenon. When I left China some 20 years ago, the infrastructure was very poor. The train from Shanghai to Beijing took two days: today it takes less than five hours.We were on a high-speed train from Shanxi to Henan province. The landscape was lush and mountainous; the vegetation was emerald green and luminous under the sun after a rainstorm.We arrived in Luoyang at noon, hoping the day would be cooler than the 39C we had suffered through in Xi’an.During the Tang dynasty, Luoyang was called Dongdu (東都), the eastern capital. When Wu Zetian became empress, she constructed the tallest palace in Chinese history in Luoyang, of which there is now a duplicate in the old town, to the east of the city.We stayed in a brand new Hyatt hotel in the new town of Luoyang. So new, in fact, that the hotel lobby was still filled with the large bundles of fresh flowers brought in for the opening celebration. From the 16th floor, I gazed down. On my left was the huge campus of the Luoyang Institute of Science and Technology; on my right was the jigsaw-like People’s Park, with sports facilities; on the horizon, skyscrapers stood in a bland, uniform line, like a monoculture forest. Where was the history? I longed for old sights and sounds.From Luoyang, we visited the nearbyLongmen Grottoes, one of the largest Buddhist sites in the world, which has survived more than 1,500 years. What a monumental sight to see countless statues of Buddha! Their elaborately sculpted details were once painted in gold. Now, all of them stood bare and colourless and most of them were missing body parts.View image in fullscreenThe Longmen Grottoes, Luoyang, Henan province.Photograph: VW Pics/Universal Images Group/Getty Images“Mum, do you know that there are 100,000 statues on these hills?” Moon said, reading a signpost.“That’s a lot,” I said. “What else does it say?”“It says there are more than 2,345 caves, some are little more than small holes, some are as large as 17 metres in height.”As always, the Chinese fanatically list numbers when referring to any historical artefact, but anyone who visits these grottoes hardly needs to learn them. Like me, they can experience a dizzying feeling of disbelief, even as our feet stand firmly on these old rocks. Like Stonehenge in England, or the Egyptian pyramids, these monuments induce a feeling of the sublime.As we descended toward the riverbank, I looked back at the blurred faces and figures of the Buddhist caves on the hill. How much more history could I take in one afternoon? Must we see 10,000 Buddha statues to come to the conclusion that there is a Buddha? Must we erect 20m Jesus on the cross statues to prove he died for us? Why are we so wedded to the materiality of spiritual life? Isn’t the sky vast and awesome enough to be pondered upon? Emptiness is where the richest possibility lies.Weary and drowsy, we abandoned the sumptuous spectacle. Flagging down a taxi by the gate, we wanted to hurry back to the hotel before the rush hour, where we would deal with the small and ungodly things in our daily life, such as paying our bills, charging our phones, ordering a meal and brushing our teeth.The Qianling Mausoleum and theafterlifeWe travelled over great distances on high-speed trains. From the northern plains we crossed over the Yangtze River and then zoomed down to southern regions, before going north again, entering the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. Moon had been tasting all sorts of strangely flavoured food and learning local dialects and could almost have passed as a native Chinese kid.At the very end of our trip, to draw a full circle, I wanted to pay a visit to the place where the Tang emperors and empresses were buried, so we returned to Shanxi province and arrived at Qing Xian, 85km north-west from Xi’an.Here, along the highways, even the ginkgo trees are newly planted, all trimmed, standing straight and of even height, like an obedient army waiting to be summoned to action. Even though this place was very much part of the royal centre of Chang’an during the Tang, visually there is nothing much to see now. Because of its peripheral location, its past has been totally paved over to make way for its new industrial purpose. One can see only some traces of the old ways of life half-hidden in a street corner: a tiny shoe repair place, an old tailor’s shop or a grandmother selling tea-brewed eggs by the roadside. Otherwise, large trucks carrying steel and cement rushed through streets, horns blasting.Qianling Mausoleumis where some of the most important imperial families of the Tang dynasty are entombed. After a long, stifling ride, the bus finally dropped us in front of a large complex.The scale of the mausoleum was something I had never seen in my life. A labyrinth to confuse anyone. Once we entered, we had to take another bus inside the vast complex, again with crowds of tourists. The bus took you up to the hills to get to the different burial sites. It was like travelling into an ancient settlement, with pavilions and waterways and inner gardens. There was even a busy street full of restaurants inside the Number Four Mausoleum site.View image in fullscreenTang court ladies in a fresco painting at Lady Li Xianhui’s tomb, the Qianling Mausoleum.Photograph: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesIt was difficult to correlate the tomb numbers on the map with the actual sites. There seemed to be a lot of tombs, but few were open to the public. The sound of cicadas faded away while the noon heat was rising. Under the burning sun, we felt like two roasted ducks. We staggered towards a mausoleum that promised some air-conditioning.We arrived at two tomb sites, one belonging to a princess and another to a prince. From the gate, we could see a sloping tunnel stretching into a darkening underground world. Cool but sepulchral air coming from the tunnel gate enticed us inside.We followed a group of perspiring tourists, walking into the narrow tunnel. It was the tomb ofPrincess Yongtai. She was the seventh daughter of Emperor Zhongzong and the second daughter of his wife, Wei. She died when she was 15, apparently while giving birth.“Oh, she died so young!” exclaimed Moon.There were elaborate murals around us, depicting palace ladies and officials in an enchanted garden. The colours were faded and the walls full of holes and patches. As we entered further, the air became musty and heavy.As we approached the end of the tunnel, we came upon a chamber with frescoes, and the mausoleum revealed itself. It was a miniature wooden house with carved windows and inscriptions on the surface. Inside, there was the actual coffin.What was life like for Princess Yongtai 1,300 years ago? I could not decipher the obscure inscriptions, but what I had read earlier from the New Book of Tang told me a different story of how she died. Since the all-powerful Empress Wu was her mother-in-law, Princess Yongtai did not have an easy life. An animosity persisted between the two women. It was well known that Empress Wu led an unconventional sexual life; even in her old age, royal family members, as well as ministers, were well acquainted with her exploits. As a result, indignation and resentment accumulated in the court, and when the princess was found to be disloyal, punishment immediately ensued. According to the New Book of Tang, it was said that the princess was caned to death, though elsewhere it was recorded that she was forced to kill herself.We did not visit the next tomb – we wanted to go straight to the most mysterious site, Empress Wu’s tomb. After much inquiry, we learned that it was impossible: no one would be allowed to enter the mausoleum of the emperor and the empress. In fact, we were told, the two main tombs were not even excavated.So we wandered on the hills of this sacred place, sucking on our ice lollies in the shade of pine trees. We imagined a curious dark world inside the uncovered tombs, barred to modern people. Time to leave, but still we lingered on: we suspected we would never return to this place.Along the road was a procession of statues, some headless and some armless. We walked past these ancient figures and sometimes stood before them, as if waiting for speech, a command or a bow. They stood like sturdy sentinels, without acknowledgment of our presence, their stone minds, far beyond the doings of the passing parade of tourists. I thought of John Keats’s “cold pastoral”, and felt a shiver and prickling of skin in the heat. Was that a slight puff of wind, or time itself touching our all too fragile bodies?Adapted from Everyday Tang, published by Notting Hill Editions (£9.99). To support the Guardian, buy your copy atguardianbookshop.com. P&P may apply.Xiaolu Guo is a novelist, memoirist and film-maker. title: The Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunity | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/PAView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/PAOpinionManchester CityThe Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunityJonathan LiewWhen transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealthTue 29 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.52 EDTShareThe cache of leaked emails and documents that would eventuallylead to the crisis in which Manchester Cityare now embroiled waspublished by Der Spiegel in 2018, and often it was the tone of the club’s communications that was as startling as their content. Of City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a trusted adviser to the royal family of the United Arab Emirates,it was said that he would“rather spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue [Uefa] for the next 10 years” than accept a fine.In the same tranche of documents,City lawyer Simon Cliff assertsthat “Uefa doesn’t respond to anything other than aggression”, and threatens the governing body of European football – who were pursuing City over alleged financial irregularities at the time – with “the destruction of their rules and organisation”.All of which feels like a rather extreme way of ensuring that your football club has the right tosign Jack Rodwell from Everton. And, yes, this is one of those stories in which the deeply serious and the deeply trivial, the universal and the parochial, are not always easy to tell apart. From a safe distance, the news that one of English football’s most successful clubshas been found guilty of more than 100charges of financial irregularity, including “sham” payments totalling around £900m, may feel like so much so-what, a thicket of sporting arcana that even devoted fans occasionally struggle to parse. But, of course, the City case goes deeper than one club, one league, even one sport. Fundamentally, it is a parable of power.After all, this is not simply a football club but a beloved cultural asset that happens to be majority-owned by the billionaire Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the UAE and brother of the president. Since the Premier League announced thecharges against City in 2023, the case has been discussed not merely at boardroom level but at a diplomatic level. Just last month,Bloomberg reported UAE officialswarning that an adverse verdict against City could threaten billions in Emirati investment in the UK.Bilateral trade between the countriesnudged above £25bn in 2025.Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney RonayRead moreAnd perhaps the logical starting point here is to observe just how ridiculous it is that this country’s foreign relations are effectively being negotiated in a football tribunal. That the UK’s clean-energy transition is somehow contingent on whether a panel decides whetherRoberto Mancini’s coaching contractwas fair or not. This was one of the reasons why it was such a bad idea for the Premier League to allow entire states to invest in football clubs. Over time it was inevitable that questions of sporting merit and integrity would become entangled with questions of diplomacy and hard power; that footballing warfare would increasingly come to resemble the real thing.We caught a glimpse of this in the bellicose statement City releasedin response on Tuesday evening, obliquely questioning the Premier League’s ability “to behave as an independent, impartial and fair- minded regulator, free from partisan influence”. In 2024, in a separate case against the Premier League, City tried to discredit the league’s basic governance model, arguing that the two-thirds majority required for motions to pass represented “the tyranny of the majority”, which gives you a good idea of what Abu Dhabi thinks of basic democracy.View image in fullscreenVincent Kompany lifts the Premier League trophy as Manchester City win the title after drawing 0-0 with Huddersfield Town at the Etihad Stadium, Manchester, 6 May 2018.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAt this point we should probably recall that this is a football club majority-owned by a country that, according to the UN’s own reports, is defying arms embargos inSudanandLibya, and that, according to Human Rights Watch, is responsible for widespread acts of political repression and rights abuses. From the years of warlike rhetoric, veiled threats, legal challenges and poisonous off-record briefings, City’s approach appears to consist, in part, of discrediting the very idea that anyone is fit to regulate it.In one respect, this stems from a genuine belief that football’s financial regulations – largely nonexistent in the decade after the Premier League’s foundation in 1992 – were designed to protect elite wealth while extinguishing new-money challengers such as City and the Chelsea of Roman Abramovich. But to follow this thread to its logical conclusion is essentially an argument for a world in which there are no legitimate checks on power – where you can do what you want, however you want, for as long as you want, for whatever purpose you want; where the only meaningful rules of the game are power and leverage; where you would rather destroy your enemies than accept even the slightest curb on your volition.And, of course, there is little sense in singling out City or Abu Dhabi here. From City and the Saudi-run Newcastle United to the opaque private-equity funds that now run most of their rivals, the top end of English football is essentially owned by bored men given more money than they can possibly know what to do with and more power than it is ever advisable to invest in a single human being.For Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia you might just as easily read Jeff Bezos, part of a consortium thatnow owns almost 40% of Liverpool FC. Or Meta, or Elon Musk, or Benjamin Netanyahu, or Donald Trump: an entire class of men who recognise no authority beyond their own, for whom politics and business and sport and culture are essentially the same basic substance – a game to be brought to heel by any means necessary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is the broader significance of the City verdict, beyond the interminable debate over whether the club should be forcibly relegated, stripped of titles and trophies. In a world where the UN is neutered, where transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, it offers an alternative vision to a world increasingly aligned along axes of brute power and wealth. It articulates the increasingly outmoded idea that there is a shared set of values and rules by which all must abide.And clearly this case is not over yet. City continue to deny any wrongdoing. Doubtless there will be appeals upon appeals, perhaps even ending in the high court many years hence. Doubtless there are diplomatic representations to be made, high-level deals to be brokered, realpolitik to be waged. After all, geopolitics, like football, is very much a results business.But it is in the interests not just of City’s rivals and not just of football itself, but of everyone with an interest in the rule of law that they do not succeed.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.This article was amended on September 29 2026. title: To the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button? | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guy, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guy, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Nigel Farage at a Reform UK press conference in Kirkcaldy, 15 January 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage at a Reform UK press conference in Kirkcaldy, 15 January 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionNigel FarageTo the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button?Marina HydeThe Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guyTue 29 Sep 2026 07.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTShareAnother week, another chance for Nigel Farage to demonstrate his literally hysterical leadership inabilities. For a guy who supposedly valorises the wartime British spirit, Nigel would genuinely have had to have been interned during that conflict on account of his serial predilection for spreading panic and unverified information at any given chance. The weekendincident near RAF Fairfordwas simply the latest in a long line of occasions that make you suspect the poster on the wall at Reform HQ reads simply: “Lose Cool and Start Shitposting.”Despite its popularity now, the famous “Keep Calm and Carry On” poster from the second world war was almost certainly never displayed in that conflict. Although more than 2m copies of it were printed, it was in factheld in reservein case a really serious crisis hit. Which, when you consider even the blitz apparently didn’t clear the bar, it is almost impossible to conceive of in our era where comparatively minuscule incidents force certain party leaders into more than 24 hours of madly irresponsible and emotional online incontinence.Many of you may find you have a low tolerance for shrieks of “We have the right to know absolutely everything, immediately!” from a congenitally secretive guy who notoriously declined to declare the £5m he was given from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and, since that weird “gift” has been uncovered, has been in a prolonged tantrum that has caused him to snap at any attempts to discover more about what might have motivated it. “None of your business,” ran one particularly ill-judged attempt by Farage to put the issue to bed. “What’s it got to do with you?”I do find my finger hovering over the “What’s it got to do with you?’ button with increasing regularity when Farage appears on screen to insert himself into moments of obviously active sensitivity. The clearly nuanced and potentially complex Fairford investigation – still ongoing, despite the release on bail of the five men arrested – was a case in point, although on Monday Nigel did attempt to set it out in a madly precipitous video on what he called “the Fairford plot”, captioned: “Fairford proves my pointon Iran and the IRGC.” Does it? OK, thanks Jack Ryan.Anyone who judges that this intemperate psychological liability should have access to the nuclear codes and other top-level information must have a subconscious wish for their answer to the question “where do you see yourself in five years’ time?” to be “living in Britain’s catacombs and distilling drinking water from my own urine”. It’s unclear whether a Prime Minister Farage would just bottle everything or shoot first and ask questions later, but the most likely metaphorical outcome in any given scenario may well be him shooting the wrong person first, then refusing to answer questions later.Furthermore, as always with Nigel, it’s worth highlighting his insistence on rising to only the occasions from which he feels he might personally benefit. And so it is that he will have an awful lot to say about the horrific murder ofHenry Nowak, but nothing or next to about those of Jo Cox or Sarah Everard. Whatever may or may not have happened at Fairford feeds into what we have to call, with heavy irony, his two-tier approach to public life. After all, for a guy who supposedly worries about illegal activity that could bear the hallmarks of foreign sponsorship, Farage strangely didn’t have a lot to say about the Ukrainian and Romanian nationals who were recruited via a Russian-speaking pseudonymous Telegram user tocommit arsonon property connected to Keir Starmer and on a car he had previously owned, back when Starmer was prime minister. Even after they were found guilty, the Reform leader didn’t seem to find this sort of darkly intriguing activity worthy of comment. Things he did find worthy of comment that same month included disputes over flying the St George’s cross flag andAI scam videos.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDon’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John HarrisRead moreThe thing about attaining the very highest office in the land is that you have to be prime minister of all the things, all the time. It is difficult to see how someone as cynically selective as Farage could somehow become the sort of leader able to speak for a nation. Or, just as importantly, the sort of leader able to realise when it’s time to shut up for a nation.Far more troubling still is the gathering sense that Farage is too mentally weak for the role, and would go to pieces in very short order once plunged into the realities of life in Downing Street. Perhaps hisdeclining poll ratingsmean worrying may be unnecessary. But he’s increasingly a set of walking psychological red flags: emotional, quick to temper, incapable of rising above the self-serving.Amazing that there is apsychological screening testto determine whether you are up to appearing on a reality TV show these days, but you could ascend to the office of prime minister without submitting to anything similar. At least 20% of would-be Big Brother contestants are deemed mentally unfit to participate during the casting process each year. And looking at the five main party leaders this week, you’d think a similar percentage had the potential to absolutely implode were they to enter the Downing Street house. Perhaps our politics needs new duty-of-care guidelines, so that the office of British prime minister is psychologically guardrailed to the same level as, say, a dating show like Love is Blind.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist. title: The Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: With the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck president, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: With the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck president, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘The powerful seem to get away with everything’ … Trump’s base has shifted.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The powerful seem to get away with everything’ … Trump’s base has shifted.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/EPAOpinionUS politicsThe Maga cult is finally crumblingArwa MahdawiWith the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck presidentTue 29 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTShareIt took a dead child sex offender and a disastrous war to do it, but it looks as though the Maga faithful are slowly beginning to lose confidence in dear leader. As Donald Trump’sapproval ratings dropto record lows, some of his most fervent supporters are turning on him.See, as exhibit one, Trisha Hope, who was once a proud member of the Front Row Joes, a group of Trump superfans who follow the president to rallies around the country. They havecustom-made T-shirts! They have branded baseball caps! They even have the attention of Trump himself, who frequently shouts out the group. He did once accidentally call them the “front row Jacks and Joes”, but who can expect a man of his calibre to pay attention to the plebs, eh?During Trump’s first impeachment, in 2019, Hope stationed herself in Washington DC for weeks, trying to drum up support for the president. But she’s not doing that again. In aninterview with Politicopublished on Monday, Hope declared: “If we do lose the midterms and [Trump] is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment.”What caused this change of heart? Hope cites the Iran war and the Epstein files as significant factors. So too does Rick Frazier, another defector from the Front Row Joes interviewed by Politico. “Epstein crimes and feeding the industrial military complex … those are big nos for me,” Frazier said.Hope and Frazier are just two people with limited influence, but there’s another, much more powerful, Joe who has soured on Trump. Earlier this month the podcaster Joe Rogan, whose endorsement of Trump in 2024 is widely credited withhelping him win the election, distanced himself from the president and his “rabid” supporters. “Trump supporters are fucking nuts, man,”Rogan said on his podcast. In the same episode, Rogan admitted that “I did kind of help Trump”, but insisted it was because he thought he’d drain the swamp. “Obviously, it’s not been ideal in that regard,” Rogan added.It’s very satisfying to watch people wake up to the fact that the convicted felon in the White House is out for himself and nobody else. But Trump is a lame duck now. With the end of his very lucrative reign in sight, does it really matter that people like Hope are calling him “a fraud and liar”?In the long term, the answer to that question is complicated. But growing disgust with the president certainly matters for the November midterm elections. Trump has asked voters to“pretend I’m on the ballot”and many have taken that advice to heart. A recentPBS News/NPR/Marist pollfound that 45% of voters overall said their largest motivating factor for the midterms was voting against Trump. While he still has a loyal following, the midterms are likely to be a rebuke to his presidency, with Democrats now on a path to flipping the Senate as well as retaking the House.Trump’s desperate gimmicks and grandiose assurances aren’t landing the way they used to. This month, the president promised a $5,000 (£3,775) “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress after the midterms. According to one poll,only 13% of voters believed him.If Trump is worried about the midterms – and the possibility ofa third impeachmentthat comes with a Democratic victory – he’s not letting it show. But Republicans more broadly are clearly stressed, not just about the midterms, but also about what sort of trouble they may be in when Trump 2.0 comes to an end. “After the first Trump administration, my family spent money we did not have on lawyers because of multiple partisan Democrat-led investigations into President Trump,” Katie Miller, the podcasting wife of Trump’s right-hand man, Stephen Miller,tweeted earlier this month. “You can’t convince me Democrats won’t do this again.”I hope they do. And this time I hope they do it properly, so that Trump and his enablers are at last held accountable. People who are finally leaving the Maga cult are angry at Trump, certainly, but they’re also angry at a world in which the powerful seem to get away with everything. To stop that anger from propelling another Trump-like figure into the White House, there needs to be a reckoning with the systems that created him. Let’s make Maga’s legal bills high again.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Cutting immigration to the UK means billions less for the Treasury. Can the country really afford that? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: ‘Taking back control’ turns out to be staggeringly expensive. That’s something to mull over as budget day approaches, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: ‘Taking back control’ turns out to be staggeringly expensive. That’s something to mull over as budget day approaches, writes Zoe Williams
Content: What price for securing our borders?Photograph: Gary E Perkin/AlamyView image in fullscreenWhat price for securing our borders?Photograph: Gary E Perkin/AlamyOpinionMigrationCutting immigration to the UK means billions less for the Treasury. Can the country really afford that?Zoe Williams‘Taking back control’ turns out to be staggeringly expensive. That’s something to mull over as budget day approachesTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTShareEvery 100,000 immigrants lost to the UKcosts the treasury £7bn, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. That figure is unsurprising if you’ve been concentrating at all – the calculation was made in 2024 – but at the same time completely staggering. Nobody ever says, “The chancellor’s going to be in trouble because of all those lost immigrants”; few people remark on, let alone decry, the very large numbers of migrants who have been lost due to policy decisions.And then, as budget day approaches, brute facts and mathematical realities assert themselves: migration numbers have been falling faster than anticipated. And if you take all the measures you can to discourage international students, skilled workers, all imaginable young, mobile people who work and don’t get ill, while at the same time preventing with all your might any legitimate employment opportunities for asylum seekers, you will suffer a hit to the national coffers.That’s another word I haven’t seen in a while. We used to talk about coffers all the time, these metaphorical chests of cash that would be added to, in the good times, by a bustling economy in which people worked and made and sold things. If these things were good enough, other countries might even want to buy them.It probably slipped out of usage around the time of Brexit, when we decidedby that overwhelming majoritythat money wasn’t important any more – or, at least, not as important as taking back control of our borders. If we had to poleaxe our export industries in order to prevent the arrival of healthy people who might contribute to the economy, then so be it – coffers be damned.If this were working in the other direction, it might almost be charming. If money were no object in the matter of human dignity, if no price were too high for functioning social care because that was the society we wanted to live in, then it would be beautiful, although there would definitely still be people saying: “Guys, money actuallyisan object. It’s both a trust metaphoranda real thing.”But we’re only prepared to jettison practicality in the interests of a particular set of higher objectives: securing our borders; assuaging formless anger (but only of a certain kind, from certain people); sending a message to the rest of the world – you might think this looks like a good place to live, but think again.I’ve never been especially attracted to rational economic arguments in politics: they usually seem to serve the interests of the establishment. But now that the establishment has become so emotional, I realise I miss the days when it could, at least, count.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
