title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?
Content: Manchester City celebrate winning the Premier League in 2018. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters after the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City celebrate winning the Premier League in 2018. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters after the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersManchester CitySham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severeJonathan WilsonHow can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTShareHow bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation thatManchester Cityhad been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.Manchester City’s ‘sham’ seasons: how they fared and who was in chargeRead moreCity continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that thePremier LeagueBoard and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.View image in fullscreenThe Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19.Photograph: Carl Recine/ReutersThe verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’Read moreHaving been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFinancesPremier LeagueFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Alexander-Arnold proves his worth to England with trademark assist against Czechia | England | The Guardian
description: The full-back is one of the best passers England has produced: Thomas Tuchel must find a place for him
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The full-back is one of the best passers England has produced: Thomas Tuchel must find a place for him
Content: The consensus is that Alexander-Arnold cannot defend. Andy Robertson took issue with that, saying his former teammate has shut down Kylian Mbappé.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenThe consensus is that Alexander-Arnold cannot defend. Andy Robertson took issue with that, saying his former teammate has shut down Kylian Mbappé.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandAnalysisAlexander-Arnold proves his worth to England with trademark assist against CzechiaJacob Steinbergat the Fortuna ArenaThe full-back is one of the best passers England has produced: Thomas Tuchel must find a place for himTue 29 Sep 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.53 EDTShareIt was the question nobody was asking: couldTrent Alexander-Arnolddo it against 10 game but limited Czechs on a mild Tuesday night in Prague? The answer was a resounding yes.Alexander-Arnold played well after starting for the first time under Thomas Tuchel, demonstrating his value to England by helping them work out the dreaded low block with a trademark assist for Anthony Gordon to settle the nerves in a game coloured byCzechialosing Pavel Sulc to a debatable red card midway through the first half.Gordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man CzechiaRead moreThe cross for Gordon to make it 1-0 early in the second half was a classic Trent moment. He was smart after a broken passage of play, adjusting quickly when a loose Czechia pass reached him on the right. The situation did not call for Alexander-Arnold to wait for support or check back and look inside for a pass. England needed decisiveness against a defence bent out of shape after losing possession and Alexander-Arnold provided it, taking the opposition out of the equation by getting the ball out of his feet and displaying his unrivalled vision by crossing for Gordon to put England on the way to their first win inNations LeagueGroup A3.“I always feel I can see things others can’t see,” Alexander-Arnold once said, and here was timely proof of those lock-picking skills. It is unlikely, after all, that Jarell Quansah would have had the imagination to pick out Gordon. Quansah is a good, quick defender but his crosses did not hit the mark when he started at right-back duringEngland’s defeat by Spain on Saturday. Alexander-Arnold, an unused substitute against the world champions, even when England were chasing an equaliser and could have done with better service from the flanks, does not tend to miss the target with his crosses.Yet the Real Madrid defender has not had many opportunities to express himself in an England shirt. Alexander-Arnold turns 28 next week and made his international debut eight years ago but this was only his 35th cap. He has endured a lot of false dawns at this level.Injury ruled Alexander-Arnold out at Euro 2020and successive managers have found it hard to find a place for him.View image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon and Trent Alexander-Arnold after the first England goal against Czechia.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PASir Gareth Southgate could never unlock Alexander-Arnold’s talent. He left him out at times. Trust was fleeting. Southgate was reluctant to use him at right-back and anexperiment as a midfielderat Euro 2024 was swiftly aborted.The general consensus is that Alexander-Arnold cannot defend. Andy Robertson took issue with that view last week, telling the Stick To Football podcast that his former Liverpool teammate has shut down Kylian Mbappé in the past. Tuchel, though, has often seemed ambivalent about Alexander-Arnold. England’s manager has questioned his defensive knowhow and it was not a surprise when heleft him out of his World Cup squad.Alexander-Arnold’s only previous minutes for Tuchel had come during a cameo in midfield against Andorra in June 2025. Eight players featured at right-back before his return here. Even then there was a sense that Alexander-Arnold was only in this squad because others were unavailable. It remains to be seen if a corner has been turned in his relationship with Tuchel.The problem is that this game told us little about Alexander-Arnold’s defending.Englandwon 2-0, Gordon’s header followed by another Harry Kane goal, but they made a ropey start. An unfamiliar back four struggled but the game changed after Sulc’s dismissal for catching Anderson’s achilles. Czechia moved into a 5-4-0 system and Alexander-Arnold spent little time in his own half.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe weirdness with Alexander-Arnold is that he remains an enigma for England even when his contribution is an obvious highlight. He looked rusty at first. He had little chemistry with Bukayo Saka and some of his touches were loose. A wayward crossfield pass that could have started a Czechia counterattack will be noted by Tuchel.But his game is about risk. He unbalances opponents, keeps them guessing. Tuchel felt a tweak in Alexander-Arnold’s position at half-time helped. Perhaps it is time to focus less on the weaknesses and more on the upside. Alexander-Arnold, who recorded 86 assists in 354 appearances for Liverpool, is not going to fix England’s lack of control in possession on his own. Those flaws are collective, not individual. But he is one of the best passers England has ever produced. Tuchel has to find a place for him in future squads.The former Liverpool man is a threat in multiple scenarios. Southgate not bringing him on when England were 2-1 down to France at the 2022 World Cup was an oversight. He is a wildcard option. He can create and score from set pieces. He can open up a deep defence. His defending will be tested against better opponents, but England needed Alexander-Arnold’s ingenuity against Czechia.Explore more on these topicsEnglandTrent Alexander-ArnoldNations LeagueCzechiaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Switzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after Hendry’s early red card | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Ricardo Rodríguez’s free-kick after Jack Hendry’s 11th-minute dismissal inspired Switzerland to a 3-0 Nations League victory against Scotland
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Ricardo Rodríguez’s free-kick after Jack Hendry’s 11th-minute dismissal inspired Switzerland to a 3-0 Nations League victory against Scotland
Content: Ricardo Rodríguez curls home Switzerland’s 12th-minute opener.Photograph: Alan Rennie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRicardo Rodríguez curls home Switzerland’s 12th-minute opener.Photograph: Alan Rennie/ShutterstockNations LeagueSwitzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after Hendry’s early red cardEwan Murrayat Hampden ParkTue 29 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwitzerland have responded exceptionally well after allegations ofcapers involving vaccination certificatesthat threatened to overshadow this international window. Make that six points out of six for Murat Yakin’s stylish team. Switzerland look comfortably capable of breezing out of Group B1 in the Nations League. They have not even played at home yet. Granit who?Sébastien Pocognoli, conversely, has been left to ponder one step forward and umpteen back.Scotland’s second half in Sloveniaat the ­weekend provided hope to the new manager and a supporter base who want to enter a brave new world. Age old, troublesome flaws remain.Scotland 0-3 Switzerland, Spain 4-1 Croatia, and more: Nations League – liveRead moreJack Hendry’s red card meantScotlandplayed almost 80 minutes of this encounter with 10 men. They were, however, outclassed in every department. Scottish patterns of play were not immediately obvious. The upcoming trip to North Macedonia carries importance as Pocognoli seeks to win hearts and minds. This was all pretty grim for anyone of a Scotland persuasion.“The red card of Jack is all of our red card,” said Pocognoli. “We stay together. We put this moment in our DNA today and hopefully it can be helpful for the future.”Scottish expectancy heading into a World Cup where theysubsequently took tedium to new levelsfeels a long time ago. They have scored only once in five games. Impotence can only concern Scotland’s Belgian manager, whose bow at Hampden Park was over as a contest long before full-time. A penny for the thoughts of Steve Clarke, Pocognoli’s immediate predecessor and a coach much-maligned in certain quarters. Were Clarke in charge of this ragged display, the public response would have been ferocious.Judgment of Pocognoli on this occasion requires appropriate context.Switzerlandhad control of the early exchanges without creating anything until a slick move saw Dan Ndoye sent through on goal from the halfway line. It was quickly apparent ­Hendry did not have the pace to halt his ­opponent. Initially, the referee Nenad Minakovic booked Hendry and awarded a penalty for the clear pull on Ndoye which ­toppled the Swiss forward. Following a video assistant referee check that was unnecessarily lengthy, the official corrected his decision to a free-kick and sending off. Up stepped Ricardo Rodríguez to crack the ball beyond Angus Gunn from 19 yards.Pocognoli’s immediate response was to withdraw Kieron Bowie, one of two strikers. The introduction of ­Stephen Welsh retained Scotland’s three-man backline. A noticeably subdued Hampden crowd feared a long evening. This is, after all, a Switzerland team that followed up a strong World Cup performance with a comfortable win in North Macedonia on Saturday.John McGinn appealed in vain for a penalty after claiming he was held at a Scotland corner. The blunt truth is Scotland have needed more from McGinn than the seeking or winning of fouls for some time.McGinn’s Aston Villa teammate Johan ­Manzambi was unsurprisingly lively; he fired just wide of Gunn’s right-hand post moments after a delicious cross that found no Swiss takers. With half an hour played, the Scots were gasping for air against opponents who looked physically and technically superior. When in possession, far too much of the hosts’ play was sideways or backwards. Gunn denied Ndoye nine minutes before the break.View image in fullscreenNico Elvedi celebrates after doubling Switzerland’s lead from close range in the second half.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAThe half ended with a yellow card for Pocognoli, who protested a little too vociferously after McGinn was fouled. All the episode did was sum up Scottish frustration. There had been needle in the game but the coherent football had been played by those in red.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManzambi had irritated the home support by embellishing fouls and entering into a verbal spat with Oli McBurnie. His play, though, was a compelling watch. Manzambi’s movement unnerved Scotland. His willingness to drop deep or wide to get involved in the game emphasised his versatility. His touch and dribbling ability set him apart; all at the age of 20. Scotland’s lack of anything approaching such emerging talent is glaring.Switzerland’s second came from a more unlikely source. Scotland only partially cleared a corner, with the ball funnelled wide right to Ndoye. The cross was pacy and low, with the central defender Nico Elvedi striding forward to flick home. Two nil was a more appropriate reflection of events to that point.Pocognoli now made a triple change. McBurnie’s 18th cap had passed without the ending of his international scoring wait. As on Saturday, the alterations were like-for-like in positional nature. ­Pocognoli’s level of tactical flexibility remains open to question. Yakin withdrew ­Manzambi, in what could be classed as a humanitarian act towards Scotland.Not that Switzerland had stopped dishing out punishment. The ­closing stages resembled an attack ­versus defence training exercise. A third from the Swiss was inevitable as they toyed with the Scots.Gunn was pitifully weak in attempting to deal with Zeki ­Amdouni’s strike, which flew into the roof of the Scotland net via the goalkeeper. Cue a mass exodus from the stands. Pocognoli has been served a strong, painful reminder of the scale of task he chose to inherit.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueScotlandSwitzerlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: England can take vital lessons from worst defeats into Rugby World Cup, says Johnson | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Martin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at the Rugby World Cup in Australia next year
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: Martin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at the Rugby World Cup in Australia next year
Content: Martin Johnson believes some of England’s most painful defeats, such as their 42-21 loss to Ireland at Twickenham, will help them.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMartin Johnson believes some of England’s most painful defeats, such as their 42-21 loss to Ireland at Twickenham, will help them.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersEngland rugby union teamEngland can take vital lessons from worst defeats into Rugby World Cup, says JohnsonFormer captain says losses can benefit team next yearJohnson refuses to comment on Henry Pollock hypeLuke McLaughlinTue 29 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at theRugby World Cupin Australia next year.England endured some disastrous moments during the Six Nations this year, most notably the42-21 defeat by Ireland at Twickenham, and finished the tournament with a solitary win against Wales. Summer Nations Championship fixtures began with an away defeat by the world champions, South Africa, before victories against Fiji and Argentina.Why England are yet to reap rewards of £264m deal with Rugby World Cup only a year away | Gerard MeagherRead moreWith a year until the tournament – England’s opener is scheduled for 2 October against Tonga in Brisbane – Johnson acknowledged the Six Nations was “up and down” under Borthwick but said vital lessons must be taken from the defeats.“The bad experiences, the losing, it’s not wasted experience,” said Johnson, who captained England to the Rugby World Cup in 2003, and was head coach from 2008 to 2011. “You always want to win and they’re horrible at the time, but it shouldn’t be a wasted experience. All experience, good or bad, should go into your memory bank as a player.“The emotional side: ‘We can’t let this happen again because it’s too painful,’ and the technical side: ‘This is why it happened … We now have that as a memory, as something to use.’ All your experiences go in that memory bank. You try to delete the emotional hurt of them, but sometimes that’s quite good to have there.”Speaking as patron of theJoe Humphries Memorial Trust, which is calling for everyone in sport to get free, life-saving sudden cardiac arrest training duringSADS week, Johnson said England’s concluding Six Nationsdefeat by Francein March was “one of the best games of rugby I’ve ever watched”.Regarding England’s prospects of matching the fearsome French and South African forward packs in Australia next year, he said: “I think we’re starting to develop some guys, front row, back row. The back five has probably been our strongest area in the last couple of years.View image in fullscreenJamie Osborne on his way to scoring Ireland’s fifth try against England at Twickenham in this year’s Six Nations.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA“If everyone’s fit you’ve got some pretty good depth there. It would be great to go to the tournament with all those guys firing. You’re going to need them at some point, the way the game is now, guys coming off benches is vitally important.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAsked if he sees parts of himself in the powerful Saracens lock, George Martin, Johnson said: “I think he’d give me a good kicking. He is a presence, isn’t he, when he’s there? I remember watching him ramming an All-Black through the ruck and into the No 9. That was a beautiful piece of rugby.”On whetherHenry Pollock’s ability justifies the considerable hype, meanwhile, Johnson said of the Northampton and England back-rower: “I don’t get involved in the Henry Pollock chats that go on. I always say for any young player, if you just keep improving and getting yourself to be a world-class player, that’s always a good thing. That’s what you need to do. Get yourself into the position where you’re a top-drawer player, and when they talk about the best in the world, your name gets mentioned. That’s never a bad place to be.”Regarding the buildup to the tournament next year and increasing interest in the media, the former Leicester second-row said: “You always get asked about it as a player, and it used to annoy me a bit … most things annoyed me a bit, really. But it does start to loom and these [Nations Championship and Six Nations] games are all part of your collective memory, as a team and a player.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamMartin JohnsonSteve BorthwickRugby World Cup 2027Rugby World CupSix Nations 2026Rugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s summer far from perfect but they head towards winter in upbeat mood | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: New red-ball coach Stephen Fleming and captain Joe Root can capitalise on side’s recent form and create a new identity
Author: Mark Ramprakash
Headline: New red-ball coach Stephen Fleming and captain Joe Root can capitalise on side’s recent form and create a new identity
Content: Stephen Fleming (right) with Kevin Pietersen (left) and the white-ball captain Harry Brook at Old Trafford before the third ODI against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Fleming (right) with Kevin Pietersen (left) and the white-ball captain Harry Brook at Old Trafford before the third ODI against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAEngland cricket teamEngland’s summer far from perfect but they head towards winter in upbeat moodMark RamprakashNew red-ball coach Stephen Fleming and captain Joe Root can capitalise on side’s recent form and create a new identityTue 29 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTShareJust a few weeks ago I was so demoralised. The England team was a mess, a shambles. The management was terrible.One red-ball coach had just been sackedand the otherwasn’t going to turn up for ages. The Test captain, whose skillset as a high-class batter who bowls at an elite standard was so important for the team’s balance,had abruptly retired. The squad seemed ill-disciplined and better atmanufacturing scandals than victories. And now here I am, heading into the winter full of optimism.The second half of the summer brought a series of outstanding Test and white-ball performances. There is a group of really talented cricketers, a coaching unit that has strong individuals and combinations across formats, and I feel we’re well placed to take on South Africa, who are always going to be tough and competitive, in our next Test series, and to go into next summer benefiting from a sensible, consistent approach.The Hotspot | Stumped for wood, bamboo bats offer cricket a substitute to leather on willowRead moreIt has been a long way from the perfect summer, but it is obvious that England are in a stronger position now than they were at the start. From the madness that followedBen Stokes’s and Gus Atkinson’s night outafter a promising win over New Zealand at Lord’s, England have rebounded and refined. The Kiwis, in the first red-ball series of the summer, played extremely well and actually exhibited a lot of the attributes England talk about adopting – resilience, adaptability, doing the basics really well. But against Pakistan we saw a more grownup style of play, leaning on a group of four pace bowlers, all different in their own ways and excellent as a combination.The removal of Brendon McCullum as red-ball coach felt necessary, and the appointment of Stephen Fleming as his replacement seems astute. It took a while for him to get here, but he seems to have had a series of really good conversations with people in the game, and I believe he and Joe Root will forge a really good partnership.WhenFleming spoke to the media last weekthe word identity came up a lot, as it does often in modern sport. When I joined Middlesex in 1987 they had just won six trophies in six years, they were an elite team, and that word was never mentioned. In the other successful dressing room I experienced, at Surrey in the early 2000s, we had individuals who were highly motivated and highly skilled, we challenged each other every day – but nobody spoke of identity. But I happened to hear an interview with Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, afterhis team beat Arsenal in the Premier League, and he also spoke about it, and how you can make a big impact from changing small habits. He wants players to be accountable to each other, to give them a say and make sure they’re invested in the team and how they play.Modern sportspeople thrive off being given more clarity than anybody provided me with in my career, on being given that sense of identity. McCullum arrived with an idea of what that word meant to him, and for a while it helped England thrive, but to me, judging from the messaging that came out in public, it was always a bit one‑dimensional. I believe Fleming and Root will create a more satisfying and lasting identity for the Test team.View image in fullscreenSonny Baker looks to have changed the angle of his run-up. He reminded me a little bit of Brett Lee and that is high praise.Photograph: Nigel French/PAFleming alluded to standards of behaviour. He wants people to relax and play with freedom, but to combine that with smart cricket and adaptability. He wants to focus on leadership and strategy. And he wants to take England to No 1 in the world, with an ambition to win the World Test Championship. As a lover of Test cricket and all it brings, how it challenges you as a player and as an individual, I was very pleased with what I heard.England end the summer with a much stronger, more multifaceted coaching team than they had at the start. Kevin Pietersen has come in to help prepare, challenge and mentor the white-ball players and the potential of his relationship with Harry Brook in particular is very exciting. McCullum seems to be in his element in white-ball cricket, and England have had some marvellous results in the shorter formats.I really enjoyed what I saw in theone-day series against Sri Lanka. Sonny Baker, taking the new ball at the Oval, looked to have changed the angle of his run-up and got the ball to swing away late, at 89mph. He reminded me a little bit of Brett Lee and that is high praise. I remember seeing him earlier in his county career and feeling he was a bit two-lengths, everything was either short or full, with not a huge amount of craft. That has certainly changed. Success as a fast bowler ultimately comes down to skill and making the ball move laterally, and that is why I have found some of his recent performances sensational.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the Sri Lanka series and the Tests against Pakistan, there was evidence of real competition for places, which should drive performance.In the recent past there has not been enough of that, and people seemed to have incredibly long runs in the side irrespective of their results.When players such as Jordan Cox, who has shown great temperament, character and technique and delivered outstanding performances in Test and one-day cricket, and Tom Banton are delivering as they are, nobody can rest on their laurels. England’s four seamers shone against Pakistan, but if Baker keeps improving he has to come into the mix.There are, of course, concerns and questions, particularly around the Test side’s best spinner and probably also the best opening partnership, but there is also huge excitement for the future. From where we were just a couple of months ago, that has to be something worth celebrating.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamCricketcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at Infantino | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Aleksander Ceferin condemned FFE and Balogun affair, and told club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to Fifa
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Aleksander Ceferin condemned FFE and Balogun affair, and told club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to Fifa
Content: The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferinin (right), has launched a scathing takedown of Gianni Infantino’s conduct.Photograph: Mark Pain/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferinin (right), has launched a scathing takedown of Gianni Infantino’s conduct.Photograph: Mark Pain/AlamyUefa‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at InfantinoAleksander Ceferin condemns FFE and Balogun affairTells club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to FifaNick Amesin CopenhagenTue 29 Sep 2026 15.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has attacked his embattled Fifa counterpartGianni Infantinoin a scathing takedown of the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and other recent scandals, saying “the emperor is naked” and declaring “it is time to say ‘enough’”.In a pointed address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin did not mention Infantino by name but made clear his view that Fifa’s leadership must change. He drew on the event’s location, Copenhagen, to make a comparison to Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes inassessing Infantino’s conduct, making clear reference to the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump and last summer’s FolarinBalogun affair along with the FFE scheme.Fifa accuses Uefa of ‘harassment’ and ‘misinformation’ in push against InfantinoRead more“An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see,” Ceferin said. “His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities.“Selling part of football’s future does not become development because you call it development. Putting afait accompliin front of national associations does not become democratisation because you call it democratisation, however big the cheque is. And secrecy does not become consultation because you call it consultation.”Ceferin suggested to the ­hundreds of club representatives present that ­Infantino’s behaviour would not be tolerated at one of their organisations. “Imagine one of your senior executives secretly negotiating away control of your club’s crown jewels,” he said. “You didn’t know. Your board didn’t know. Your players and fans didn’t know. And by the time you find out, the deal is almost done. What would your board do?“Imagine that he creates a peace prize for a political leader, without his own board having any say over its creation or its recipient. Then, that same political leader calls during the biggest competition in the world to complain about a decision on the pitch. The rules say one thing. The phone rings. Then the decision changes.“How many times would this have to happen at your club before the board says: ‘enough’? I think it is time to say ‘enough’. No office, no title and no amount of power gives anyone the right to sell the future of football.”The ongoing war of words between football’s biggest governing bodies had already intensified on Tuesday when Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency,urging a US court to reject Uefa’s requestto receive documents for use in a planned criminal complaint against Infantino.Senior figures within Uefa remain adamant that a candidate to oppose Infantino in theFifaelection next March must be found before the 18 November deadline for nominations. The EFC chair, Nasser al-Khelaifi, has been mooted in the past as a future contender but conclusively ruled himself out of the Fifa presidency in the Danish capital.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I have zero interest in Fifa, zero agenda or ambition to be there,” al-Khelaifi said. “I don’t think I’m the right guy for this position. I’m enjoying what I’m doing, having fun. Fifa, not for me.”Al-Khelaifi has designs on expanding the scope of his own organisation. In his speech to the general assembly he said “now is the time to create World Football Clubs”, explicitly stating that a representative body including those beyond Europe should be formed. “We are more than proud and happy if we can help and contribute outside of Europe for our colleagues from different clubs in the world,” he said later.Explore more on these topicsUefaFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ferrari say team has ‘made its choices’ and there’s no vacancy for Christian Horner | Ferrari | The Guardian
description: Marque reaffirmed its commitment to Fred Vasseur after Christian Horner had expressed interest in joining Ferrari
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Marque reaffirmed its commitment to Fred Vasseur after Christian Horner had expressed interest in joining Ferrari
Content: Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner told the Times leading Ferrari would be his ‘dream’ job.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFormer Red Bull team principal Christian Horner told the Times leading Ferrari would be his ‘dream’ job.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockFerrariFerrari say team has ‘made its choices’ and there’s no vacancy for Christian HornerMarque reaffirms commitment to Fred VasseurHorner had expressed interest in joining FerrariGiles RichardsTue 29 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFerrari have reaffirmed their backing for their team principal, Fred Vasseur, in an effort to end speculation thatChristian Hornerwas being considered as a potential replacement for the Frenchman.Horner gave aninterview in the Times last weekin which he stated that leading Ferrari would be his “dream” job and the only one he would consider without having part-ownership of the team. His comments provoked debate that he could replace Vasseur, given the Scuderia’s underperformance this season.Lando Norris targeted by online abuse after calling for Franco Colapinto banRead moreOn Tuesday,Ferraritook the unusual step of holding an unscheduled media call in an effort to close down the chatter, with the team’s chief communication officer, Maria Conti, speaking on behalf of the chair, John Elkann, and the chief executive officer, Benedetto Vigna.“Ferrari’s position is clear, has not changed, and Ferrari has made its choices already. We have confidence, full confidence, in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so,” she said.“Everybody, they are still ­creating a lot of different stories around Fred and this is not useful. We do not intend to fuel speculation or ­comment on assumptions coming from outside the company.“It is not just related to the story in the Times of Mr Horner but in general, there was other speculation also.”Ferrari had hoped the new ­regulations this season would ­present a chance to once more compete for the title but while they are second in the constructors’ championship they are 160 points off the leaders, Mercedes.Vasseur, who joined the team in 2023 and had his contract extended in July of last year, made it clear after the last round in Baku that speculation about his future was not helping the team. “We are not working in the perfect serenity,” he said. “But it is what it is, it’s not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job – that everybody knows – everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team.”Conti noted that Horner’s interest in the position was indicative of the enduring appeal of Ferrari. “Ferrari has always attracted extraordinary interest, and it is only natural that many professionals aspire to be part of it,” she said. “It is a reflection of the strength of what Ferrari really represents.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElsewhere on Tuesday Aston Martin confirmed their driver lineup for 2027 will remain the same with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. Alonso’s decision to remain in F1 ends conjecture that the 46-year-old double world champion was contemplating retirement from the sport as Aston Martin endure a dismal season with an underperforming car and engine. Next year will be Alonso’s 24thtfull season in F1.“It took me a little bit of time to make my decision. But now I have things very clear on my mind,” he said. “I will retire from F1 … But not yet. I still feel fast and motivated and a huge passion for F1 and for the sport. It is my life.”Explore more on these topicsFerrariChristian HornerFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: American exodus: why do so many US NHL stars want out of Canada? | NHL | The Guardian
description: Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respect
Author: Colin Horgan
Headline: Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respect
Content: Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck is one of several American players who sought moves out of Canadian markets this offseason.Photograph: Panayiota Good/NHLI/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWinnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck is one of several American players who sought moves out of Canadian markets this offseason.Photograph: Panayiota Good/NHLI/Getty ImagesNHLAmerican exodus: why do so many US NHL stars want out of Canada?Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respectColin HorganTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in September 1925, Frederick Wilson, sports editor at the Globe, explained the fear among hockey fans that Canadian teams might not be able to compete for players against the new US teams like New York or Boston that were entering the pro league. “Will it be a matter of money?” Wilson headlined his piece. And for about a century, money was the recurrent nexus of the Canadian hockey panic, proven by franchise departures and depleted buying power.At the time, Wilson reassured everyone that, no matter the big US cash, everyone on the ice would be Canadian anyway. “It will be some years before the [US] will be in a position to furnish players,” he wrote. He was right about that. It took a long time for the US to catch up to Canada in on-ice talent. But now that it has, should we expect Americans to want to play anywhere else than the US? For 100 years Canada has worried that the US would just buy all the best hockey players. But now it makes its own and, as the newNHLseason gets underway on Tuesday night, they want to go home.Alex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the oppositeRead moreIt’s difficult to pinpoint where this all started. But the general feeling, given the timing, is that something happened around this year’s Olympics that prompted US-born players to turn their backs on Canada. Maybe it started earlier, in 2025, afterthe 4 Nations Face-Off. Or maybe it was just in the wind, given the new geopolitical tensions between the two countries. In any event, as the 2026-27 NHL season kicks off Tuesday, the divide is back – or at least seems to have deepened.Quinn Hughes was the first to jump, leaving Vancouver for Minnesota last December after making it clear he wouldn’t re-sign. In April, Jim Rutherford, the Canucks’ president of hockey operations,was blunt about what underpinned it. “Some people think Quinn left here because the team wasn’t any good. He was leaving anyway,” Rutherford said, pointing to Matthew Tkachuk, who had left Calgary in 2022. “He wanted to go back to the US, and he went.” And, Rutherford noted, Hughes wouldn’t be the last.Rutherford was right. As the 2025-26 season ended, Tkachuk’s brother, Brady, captain of the Ottawa Senators, asked to go. Sure enough, he got his wish and landed in Florida with his brother. “Blood is thicker than water, and let’s just say that his father and his brother got in his kitchen,” Senators owner Michael Andlauersaid earlier this month. “Ultimately, the decision was made to go and play with his brother. It’s a decision that was out of our control to a certain degree.”Detroit’s now-former captain Dylan Larkin also wants out. And while it’s a US city he’s leaving, his reported potential destinations don’t include any Canadian teams – including the one who’s been asking about him for a while, Montreal, who have plenty of cap space and an exciting young roster built on fresh contract extensions. But it’s all moot. According to TSN, Larkinwon’t considerany Canadian team at all.View image in fullscreenMatthew Tkachuk, left, and Brady Tkachuk both left Canadian teams to play for the Florida Panthers.Photograph: Charles Krupa/APWhich brings us to Connor Hellebuyck, whose story is a little more complicated. Last month, the Winnipeg Jets goaltenderrevealedhe’d requested to be traded “several months” earlier. It came as a surprise. When Hellebuyck signed a seven-year contract worth $59.5m in 2023,he saidthat he was “ready to be a Jet for life and bring a Cup to this city”. But things changed. For one thing, the Jets have faltered and a Cup looks unlikely soon. Then there were the Olympics. Hellebuyck wasn’t the only reason the US beat Canada in the gold-medal game, but he was a big one (he made 41 saves) – good enough, anyway, for Donald Trump to award Hellebuyck the Presidential Medal of Freedom. That, and theWhite House visitthat came with it, soured some fans and, according to Hellebuyck, led to threats and online abuse aimed at his family.Hellebuyck is reportedly open to a competitive US team, and talks with Buffalo stalled over Winnipeg’s asking price. It’sbeen suggestedthat Hellebuyck would accept a move to Edmonton or Montreal, so it’s possible he’s swayed less by anti-Canada bias than he is by wanting to win, but who knows? For now, he’s beensuspendedfor failing to report to training camp, and will sit in limbo – presumably somewhere between Manitoba and his home state of Michigan – until it’s resolved.In fairness, none of these players has publicly decried Canada. There are legitimate reasons to go, including family ties and better tax rates. Nor is it a universal exit. Toronto Maple Leafs captain Auston Matthews is staying put for now, likely influenced by the team’s management overhaul and offseason additions. Ultimately, these are hockey players. They have the right to play where they want, contract allowing.But rights and respect are two different things, and that second one is tricky. Rutherford’s prediction echoed throughout the summer because it plucked a chord deep in the Canadian psyche. For a long time, the problem seemed to be one of money. But money problems can be fixed – and largely were. Since the salary cap was introduced in 2005, Canadian teams have been able to move and manipulate the numbers to compete with their US peers.But what they can’t manufacture is desire. “You have to want to play for Ottawa,” Andlauer said of Tkachuk’s departure. Lots of players still do want to play in Canada. The worry now is that the best American ones don’t.Explore more on these topicsNHLUS sportsIce hockeyUSA ice hockey teamCanada ice hockey teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump agrees to end court fight against $5m verdict in E Jean Carroll case | E Jean Carroll | The Guardian
description: The verdict stems from Carroll’s 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against Trump
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: The verdict stems from Carroll’s 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against Trump
Content: E Jean Carroll, and Donald Trump.Composite: AFP via Getty Images, APView image in fullscreenE Jean Carroll, and Donald Trump.Composite: AFP via Getty Images, APE Jean CarrollTrump agrees to end court fight against $5m verdict in E Jean Carroll caseThe verdict stems from Carroll’s 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against TrumpVictoria Bekiempisin New York CityTue 29 Sep 2026 17.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 21.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas agreed to stop fighting in court the disbursement of E Jean Carroll’s $5m verdict in her 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against him, a procedural development as the funds had already been distributed to her.While the decision does not change anything about Carroll’s receipt of the payout, its revelation effectively means that Trump will no longer oppose the monetary outcome he had long fought.This decision was revealed Tuesday by the United States court of appeals for the second circuit.Trump’s second circuit fight had already been made moot by a supreme court decision not to reconsider his opposition, so this morning’s filing marked a formality.“The parties stipulate to dismiss this appeal with prejudice … and [Trump] withdraws his motion for a stay pending appeal,” the second circuit said in a mandate. “The stipulation is SO ORDERED. The stay motion … is deemed WITHDRAWN.”“He’d previously given up in district court. Now he’s given up in circuit court,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor, of the money-related order. “It’s a final nail in the coffin. There’s absolutely no way Trump can go after Carroll for this five million plus dollars.”Trump in July unsuccessfully asked the second circuit to postpone disbursement of the money while he appealed a lower court’s decision mandating its distribution. The money was held in a court-administered fund pending Trump’s appeal of the 2023 verdict.Manhattan federal court judge Lewis Kaplan on 8 Julyordereddisbursement of the money after the US supreme court’s 29 June decision not to review Trump’s appeal. Less than an hour after the decision, Trumpaskedthe second circuit to grant him a stay so he could fight Kaplan’s mandate.The second circuit rejected the request. The court-held funds, which totalled $5.8m due to accrued interest, were released on 9 July, court records dated 14 Julyindicate.The supreme court in Augustrejectedfor the second time Trump’s efforts to overturn the jury verdict, denying his request for a rehearing. Trump isaskingthe US supreme court to throw out a second, much larger payment of $83m awarded against him for defaming Carroll in her January 2024 civil trial.Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said: “The American People stand with President Trump as they demand an immediate end to all of the Witch Hunts, including the Democrat-funded travesty of the Carroll Hoaxes.”“President Trump will keep winning against Liberal Lawfare, as he continues to focus on his mission to Make America Great Again,” the statement added.Explore more on these topicsE Jean CarrollTrump administrationUS politicsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: England’s national museums to remain free to overseas visitors | Museums | The Guardian
description: Government decision comes in response to Margaret Hodge review that proposed charging international tourists
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Government decision comes in response to Margaret Hodge review that proposed charging international tourists
Content: Hintze Hall in the Natural History Museum in London, which drew 7.1 million visitors in 2025.Photograph: E Westmacott/AlamyView image in fullscreenHintze Hall in the Natural History Museum in London, which drew 7.1 million visitors in 2025.Photograph: E Westmacott/AlamyMuseumsEngland’s national museums to remain free to overseas visitorsGovernment decision comes in response to Margaret Hodge review that proposed charging international touristsCaroline DaviesTue 29 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOverseas visitors will continue to enjoy free entry to England’s national museums after ministers decided against charging them after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders.Ministers said in March that “charging international visitors at national museums could provide significant benefits” as they promised to explore options including examining whether making overseas tourists pay could boost the institutions’ finances.They were responding to an independent review published in December by former Labour ministerMargaret Hodge, who said a charging model for international tourists “would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore, that charge an entry fee to international visitors while retaining free entry for citizens and residents”.The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) confirmed on Tuesday that free admission would remain in place for everyone.It said: “The government believes that charging overseas visitors could deter domestic visitors and that the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector and therefore will not introduce charges for overseas visitors.”Universal free admission to museums was introduced by Tony Blair’s Labour government in 2001.National museums contribute more than £1bn a year to the economy and attract visitors from around the world, the DCMS said, with the Natural History Museum and the British Museum drawing 7.1 million and 6.4 million visitors respectively in 2025.The government highlighted £760m in funding for museums through its £1.5bn Arts Everywhere Fund, as well as £600m in infrastructure funding for national museums.It said the £13.6m museum transformation programme would help organisations move towards more sustainable business models, while ministers would work withArts Council Englandand the sector on a long-term strategic plan for museums, with further details to be announced.London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said: “It’s great news that the government has committed to continuing to keep museums free for everyone.“London’s museums and galleries are the envy of the world, drawing millions from across the globe and an embodiment of our belief that access to culture is a right, not a privilege.“By keeping these important venues open to all, we will continue to educate and entertain generations to come and show why we are the culture capital of the world, as we build a fairer, more inclusive London for everyone.”Explore more on these topicsMuseumsArts policyArts Council EnglandArts fundingLondonEnglandMargaret HodgenewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concerns | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificially intelligent agent Muse
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificially intelligent agent Muse
Content: Sam Altman announcing new AI agents named ‘dots’ during OpenAI’s developers conference in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSam Altman announcing new AI agents named ‘dots’ during OpenAI’s developers conference in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesOpenAIOpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concernsCompany’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificially intelligent agent MuseDara KerrTue 29 Sep 2026 17.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 21.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLess than 24 hours afterOpenAIannounced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools.During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday,Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”.“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, to loud applause from the developers attending the event. “In the future, if you like, you can work with a whole team of dots.”OpenAI’s dots are colorful little blobs, donning berets or glasses, that appear on people’s phones or laptops, can be integrated into other apps and can follow commands. The agents can perform tasks without supervision such as schedule a meeting, book a flight or dole out assignments to colleagues. OpenAIsaysthe “dots are an extension of you” and describes the tool as “frontier intelligence”.Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s latest model. OpenAI said the previous evening it would halt the release of GPT-6.1 Astra because the updated modelshowed deceptive behaviorduring testing.OpenAI’s dots will compete with Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released two weeks ago. Meta’s product is aimed at everyday consumers more so than business customers, as OpenAI’s is, thoughMetaannounced a small business offering Tuesday. The agent’s app, available in the US, has been downloaded more than 3m times.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his houseRead moreOpenAI alsoapologizedon Monday for one of its AI agents going rogue andhacking an Australian government website. The apology came after the company has been plagued by reports and admissions that its AI systems have been acting independently and gaining access to various company and government websites.During OpenAI’s event on Tuesday, Altman touted the power of Astra and introduced similar potent AI tools. One model, called GPT-6.1 Sol, is cheaper and “smarter than Astra in many ways”, the CEO said. Altman also previewed a new “Ultrafast” mode for its AI coding models, which can generate outputs up to eight times faster than what’s available now.“People often talk about AI as a new industrial revolution, I find that quite off-putting,” Altman said at the end of his presentation. “There are some parts of life that we cannot and should not automate. I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be more like a new Renaissance than a new industrial revolution.”Explore more on these topicsOpenAISam AltmanAI (artificial intelligence)MetaChatGPTnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cherise Saywell wins national short story award for ‘tender’ tale of a child facing violence – read an extract here | National short story prize | The Guardian
description: The Edinburgh-based writer takes £15,000 prize for Ditto, a ‘beautifully told’ story about domestic abuse in a small Australian town
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Edinburgh-based writer takes £15,000 prize for Ditto, a ‘beautifully told’ story about domestic abuse in a small Australian town
Content: ‘Full of vivid descriptions, mounting tensions, and a compelling character’ … Ditto, by Cherise Saywell.Photograph: Julie Tinton PhotographyView image in fullscreen‘Full of vivid descriptions, mounting tensions, and a compelling character’ … Ditto, by Cherise Saywell.Photograph: Julie Tinton PhotographyNational short story prizeCherise Saywell wins national short story award for ‘tender’ tale of a child facing violence – read an extract hereThe Edinburgh-based writer takes £15,000 prize for Ditto, a ‘beautifully told’ story about domestic abuse in a small Australian townRead an extract from Ditto belowEmma LoffhagenTue 29 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEdinburgh-based writer Cherise Saywell has won this year’s BBC national short story award for a “tender” and “taut” story about a young boy caught in the midst of domestic violence.Saywell was announced as the winner of the £15,000 award, run in collaboration with the University of Cambridge, at a ceremony held at BBC Broadcasting House on Tuesday evening.Set in an isolated Australian town inspired by the place where Saywell grew up, the story follows a boy nicknamed Ditto as he grapples with what to do when his mother is threatened, eventually finding the courage to use a public telephone box to call the police.“Taut and beautifully crafted, tender and deeply rooted in one dusk evening and one small town, Saywell’s story writing is assured and true and we are absolutely delighted that Ditto is this year’s winner,” said Di Speirs, chair of the judging panel.Saywell, who was born and raised in Australia and has lived in Scotland since 1996, said she wanted to explore “how children experience violence, when they have no words for the things they are experiencing”.“They feel love and fear and responsibility all at the same time, but have no name for what’s happening around them,” she said.Saywell is the author of two novels, Desert Fish and Twitcher. Her short fiction has won the Pindrop short story award, the Mslexia short story prize and the VS Pritchett prize, and she has also been shortlisted for the Bristol prize and Asham award. She works for the Royal Literary Fund.Saywell beat an all-female shortlist that included Irish writer Caoilinn Hughes, Lucy Caldwell, who won the award in 2021, biographer and novelist Laura Beatty, and Merryn Glover. Each of the authors shortlisted for the short story award receives £600. Their stories appear in an anthology published by Comma Press, and are available to listen to on BBC Sounds.“Full of vivid descriptions, mounting tensions, and a compelling character, Ditto is a moving reminder of how much life a short story can hold and what’s simmering beneath the surface. It really is beautifully told,” said Dr Yvonne Battle-Felton, academic director for creative writing at the University of Cambridge.Speirs was joined on the judging panel by 2022 winner Saba Sams and two former shortlisted writers, Tahmima Anam and Will Eaves, and Costa best first novel award winner, Andrew Michael Hurley.The BBC national short story award is one of the UK’s major prizes for a single short story. Previous winners include Sarah Hall, Jonathan Buckley, Lucy Caldwell, Ingrid Persaud and Saba Sams. Last year’s award was won byColwill Brown for You Cannot Thread a Moving Needle.The winner of the young writer’s award, open to 14 to 18-year-olds, was also announced at the ceremony. Eloise Barrett, a 17-year-old sixth former from Birmingham, won for Bloodshed in Rafah, a “heartwrenching” story about the reality of a childhood affected by war.DittoAfter he made the call, Ditto ran from the public phone booth at the top of the street, past all seven houses, including his own, until he reached the place where the road ran out – the dead end, his father called it. He slowed there, as if he’d arrived somewhere he was expected. Beyond him, concealed by the night, was a sort of no man’s land – scrub and then a rocky embankment, and after that the railroad tracks. The sun was gone nearly an hour and lights had come on in houses and along the streets. Beneath Ditto’s sandshoes, the bitumen was gritty and loose, so he shifted his feet with great care, picked his way beyond the verge to where there was a patch of lantana. Crouching, he tucked himself into it and put his hand to his watch. It was his best thing, won in a competition. He slid his finger over the button that would illuminate its face but did not press for fear that this small light might reveal him. Instead, tensing his muscles, he listened to the night for a brief, frightened moment, then plugged his ears with his fingers and looked east, in the direction from where the police car would approach, if it came at all. The train would emerge from the same patch of blackness at 7.32pm. It passed by every night at the same time, on its way to Sydney.“Twenty minutes,” the woman had told him at the booth. It was the last thing she’d said before she left him there. “Twenty minutes, I reckon, if you call now and say what I told you. They’ll turn up before the train goes past.”The first thing she’d said (after she’d rapped on the glass door) was his birth name, not “Ditto”. “Your mother’s Lonnie, right?”Ditto hadn’t replied right away. He knew the woman lived directly opposite the phone booth, but he’d never seen her speak to his mother, not on the street, nor in the corner shop, nor anywhere else. He was aware it looked as if he was up to no good, mucking about in the booth. It could be a novelty, especially if you didn’t have a phone at home, and sometimes even if you did. There were numbers you could dial, some for free, just for the fun of it. Indeed, an automated voice had been chanting in his ear –at the third stroke, it will be… Only, he’d not been mucking about. It was none of her business anyway. He’d adjusted his stance and stared at the dial, willing her to walk away. Instead, she’d hoisted the door open, and he’d almost dropped the receiver; in his panic, he’d banged his head on the glass. But then she’d put her hands up, palms out, and something about the way she did that made him want to fall into her arms. It was an awful feeling.“Shhh,” she’d said, as if he was a wild thing trapped in that cramped space. “Shhh.” He’d remained perfectly still, clutching the receiver in his left hand, holding it away from his face, the automated voice now an articulated buzz –at the third stroke … at the third stroke…. She’d have heard it. Oh, the shame, and something else, indecipherable, a knot of it deep inside himself, a wave of heat rising from his neck and into his face; he’d looked away from those eyes of hers – had he not, they might have burned through his skin and exposed the ugly inside of him.“She gave it to you, didn’t she,” the woman had said, indicating his now-closed fist, the coin. “Your mother.” He’d watched his feet, pulling the receiver to his chest, saying nothing. But she was unperturbed. “I’ve seen you here. I’ve seen you here plenty of times with a coin in your hand.” She’d pointed at the phone. “But I don’t reckon you make the call.”Hunched in the lantana, Ditto’s stomach grew tight now, thinking of it, and his mouth watered like it had in that moment, when he was certain he would be sick.A full audio recording of Ditto isavailable on BBC Sounds.In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org. Use the following endnoteif a story is about suicide after domestic abuse or a murder/suicide: In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and thedomestic abuse helplineis 0808 2000 247. In the US, thesuicide prevention lifelineis 988 and thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis on 13 11 14 and the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. title: Former American Idol contestant found guilty of killing wife during affair | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Caleb Flynn convicted of aggravated murder in shooting of Ashley Flynn, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Caleb Flynn convicted of aggravated murder in shooting of Ashley Flynn, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach
Content: Caleb Flynn (left) and Emily Smith, one of his attorneys, on 28 September in Troy, Ohio.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenCaleb Flynn (left) and Emily Smith, one of his attorneys, on 28 September in Troy, Ohio.Photograph: APOhioFormer American Idol contestant found guilty of killing wife during affairCaleb Flynn convicted of aggravated murder in shooting of Ashley Flynn, a schoolteacher and volleyball coachUwa Ede-OsifoTue 29 Sep 2026 17.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaleb Flynn, the former Ohio music pastor and one-time American Idol contestant accused of killing his wife to pursue a lover, was convicted of her murder on Tuesday.As a judge read the guilty verdict, 40-year-old Flynn cried, shaking his head and closing his eyes at times. He faces up to life in prison.In February, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old teacher and volleyball coach, was found dead at the couple’s home with two gunshot wounds to the head. Caleb Flynn told police his wife was the victim of a deadly burglary. The couple’s two daughters were in the home when police arrived.Prosecutors argued the home invasion was fabricated, saying Caleb Flynn altered the crime scene to back up his narrative.While Caleb Flynn claimed to be asleep during Ashley’s murder, his electronic devices showed movement, according to evidence shown at trial.The state also presented evidence last week about Caleb Flynn’s years-long affair and fantasies of murdering his wife.“At first it was: I want her dead. I wish she was gone. And then it was: if I could kill her and not go to jail, I would. And one night, he was up really late – he told me he was thinking about ways to kill her,” his former girlfriend, Alleigha Botner, testified.The night before Ashley Flynn’s death, Caleb had also sent Botner a text saying: “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow, February 16, a day I’ll never forget.”Caleb Flynn’s defense team focused on casting doubt over the state’s case.They argued that some of Caleb Flynn’s texts where he spoke of hating his wife may have been to appease Botner. They also said the state lacked physical evidence to prove Caleb Flynn was the gunman, such as a recovered murder weapon.“His being unfaithful doesn’t equal murder,” defense attorney Patrick Mulligan said.Standing outside the courthouse after the Tuesday verdict, Mulligan told reporters: “While we respect the system certainly, we’re disappointed. I fully anticipate there will be a notice of appeal filed.”Caleb Flynn’s murder trial brought his American Idol past into the public eye. He appeared briefly on the show’s12th season, saying his wife whom he “loved more than anything”, urged him to try out.He will be sentenced on 5 October.Explore more on these topicsOhioUS crimeAmerican IdolnewsShareReuse this content

title: The night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels like | Environment | The Guardian
description: If more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creatures
Author: Tove Danovich
Headline: If more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creatures
Content: The Milky Way is seen in the western night sky near Mount Pinos, California, in 2026.Photograph: Raul Roa/Los Angeles Times via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Milky Way is seen in the western night sky near Mount Pinos, California, in 2026.Photograph: Raul Roa/Los Angeles Times via Getty ImagesEnvironmentThe night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels likeIf more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creaturesTove DanovichTue 29 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery night, I can turn off the lights in my room – but I can’t do anything about the outdoor lights in the walkway or parking lot that leak through the curtains.Living in Portland, where the night is still illuminated by street lights, porch lights and parking lot glare, I forgot what it actually feels like to sleep in darkness.I was excited when I realized my travels to a residency in south-east Oregon would show me a sky I hadn’t experienced in decades. In the Oregon outback, part of theInternational Dark Sky Placesnetwork, I would be surrounded by 2.5m acres of unpolluted night in every direction.I sent out a note to the other residents asking if anyone wanted to look at the stars with me. Everyone said yes. Thirty minutes after sunset, we trekked through the tall grass and out on to the dry lakebed. Those of us with headlamps set them on red so we wouldn’t destroy our night vision. We laid down our blankets and looked at the night sky together. There, just over the hills, was Venus. Vega shone overhead. So did numerous satellites which we could tell weren’t natural by their movement. They were so bright my eye was constantly drawn to them.As it got darker, more stars and constellations seemed to materialize: Ursa Major and Minor, Cygnus, Cassiopeia. By the time the Milky Way appeared, a band of light rising out of the night, we fell silent. We saw one shooting star and then another. I lay on my blanket and looked up until I felt small.Every year, the night sky is becoming10% brighter.Eighty per centof people live under light-polluted skies. And while the UN declared a healthy environment – clean air, clean water – to be a human right, I believe we also all have a right to darkness as well.View image in fullscreenLights across downtown Portland, Oregon, in 2014.Photograph: Wolfgang Kaehler/LightRocket/Getty ImagesThis doesn’t mean turning off every streetlamp. But do we really need bright white floodlights at the front of every garage? Replacing lights with ones that are bright enough to do the job – and no brighter – might make it so I wouldn’t have to get in my car and drive for hours to see the night sky as it actually shines above us.To preserve the darkness would mean rules and enforcement around the warmth of the lights, where they point, and how bright they can be. It would mean not putting in three lights when one would do. If we recognized that darkness is something we need, we’d become more careful about chasing it away.double quotation markIn our urbanizing world, the night sky is out of reach for those who don’t have the time or resources to find itSome communities have already done this. Flagstaff, Arizona, was the first city to have outdoor lighting rules, adding them in 1958. In 2001, Flagstaff became the first recognized Dark Sky City. Their rules regulate how much light can be used, what type, and where it can shine.Other cities and towns in the US and abroad have followed. New York state is now considering a Dark Skies Protection Act, which would add restrictions on outdoor lighting – including some that would affect the city that never sleeps. All it takes to preserve the night near you is the desire to protect it with a new zoning law or, perhaps, a rule for how bright car headlights can be.Access to darkness is about more than stargazing. The night is its own habitat. Artificial lights confuse animals who use the moon to navigate, whether they’re baby sea turtles navigating toward a parking lot instead of the ocean or moths who fly in circles around a lightbulb. Lightning bugs and frogs need darkness to complete their courtship rituals. Migrating birds get thrown off course by the bright lights of big cities.But the effects of light pollution linger even after it’s daylight again, becoming visible. Research has shown light pollution is breaking the relationship betweenplants and pollinators, changingthe time of yeartrees break into flower, and disrupting circadian rhythms for all living creatures. This includes humans. Whether it’s artificial lights indoors or creeping in through the window at night,studies have foundthat we need darkness in order to rest, recover and stay healthy.View image in fullscreenPeople spend time in a brightly lit park in New York City, in 2026.Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesMost light pollution comes from street lights, buildings, parking lots and sports courts left lit all night but increasingly there’s a threat of light pollution coming from the sky itself. Even if the rules of theDark Sky Sanctuarylet me see the Milky Way that night on the lake, it couldn’t stop the growing number of satellites from mixing in with the starry night.Is light pollution making darkness a luxury? | Emma BeddingtonRead moreDark-friendly practices such as making sure nightlights are targeted and shielded won’t do anything about the more than11,000 Starlink satellitescurrently in orbit, or a company who wants to provide artificial sunlight on demand, using satellites to illuminate areas of the Earthas large as three miles.Things we launch into space aren’t required to have an environmental review even when they affect life back on Earth.The stars hold our history. They have been maps, calendars, omens and landmarks. When it was dark, the constellations helped people find their way home. Now the night sky is an attraction people travel to. In our urbanizing world, the night sky is out of reach for those who don’t have the time or resources to find it.Darkness is becoming another luxury, but it can belong to all of us again. A right to darkness doesn’t mean every city would look like the ruralOregonoutback but it might make a few more stars visible after dark, let a few more creatures rest, give all of us a reason to look up again – no matter where we are.Tove Danovich is a journalist and the author of Under the Henfluence: Inside the World of Backyard Chickens and the People Who Love Them. She runs the newsletterA Little DetourExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentOregonWest CoastPollutionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New English homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva boss | Insurance industry | The Guardian
description: Amanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budget
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Amanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budget
