Content: Flooding in Retford, Nottinghamshire, after Storm Babet battered the UK in 2023.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenFlooding in Retford, Nottinghamshire, after Storm Babet battered the UK in 2023.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAInsurance industryNew English homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva bossAmanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budgetBusiness live – latest updatesJulia KolleweTue 29 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 05.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of Britain’s biggest insurer has said that homes being built now in Englandcould become uninsurablein the future because they are sited in flood-risk areas.Amanda Blanc, the chief executive ofAviva, said the flooding threat was “absolutely increasing”.Shetold the BBC: “You’ve seen a very dry summer, and what happens if you then get heavy rain on very dry surfaces is you get more surface water flooding.”She said 110,000 homes had been built in flood areas in the past 10 years, and if that continued, a further 115,000 new homes would be built in flood areas in the next decade. “That doesn’t seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built,” she said.Blanc told the BBC’sBig Boss Interviewpodcast that England was “for sure” building properties that might become uninsurable in the future.“If you think that there’s an inevitability of something happening, that’s not what insurance is, right?Insuranceis a pool where you know there’s a risk that something happens for some people and not for others. When there is an inevitability, it makes it very difficult for it to be insured.”She added: “It’s very well known where these flooding areas are. Let’s think very carefully about homes that are being built,” she told planners and housebuilders. “It’s dangerous.”Legal & General to cut 1,000 jobs by mid-2027Read moreAbout6.3m homes and businesses in Englandare at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. It has said this could increase to about 8m, or one in four properties, by the mid-century as the climate crisis worsens.If a property cannot get insurance cover or it is prohibitively expensive to insure because it is prone to frequent flooding, the homeowner would have to foot the bill, with knock-on effects on their ability to get a mortgage or sell the property. Some townsmay have to be abandonedas climate breakdown makes many areas uninsurable, a Guardian investigation found last year.Blanc said a lot could be done to mitigate damage, such as using bricks with self-closing air vents, having stainless steel kitchens instead of wooden furniture and creating plug points halfway up the wall rather than near the floor.“You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood.”According toAviva’s research, more than a quarter (26%), or 101,657 new homes, have some risk of flooding now, and one in seven will be at medium to high risk of flooding by 2050.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the very wet and stormy winter in the UK in 2023-24,the Met Office estimatedthat such winters had gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.Blanc also called on the government to avoid policy “kite flying” before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.Aviva is a leading private pension provider, andspeculation about changes to pensionsled to ajump in withdrawalsin the run-up to the budget in the last two years.“Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can’t put it back in,” she said.Blanc has come under criticism over her role as BP’s senior independent director in which she led the search for a new chair twice in a year, after the controversialousting of Albert Manifold. She will stand down next year after five years on the board.She said: “It’s been a tough gig, right? There’s no doubt about that, and there’s been a lot thrown at BP. But if I look at it today and the combination of a new chair, new CEO, I think that’s a good combination to take BP forward … it’s time for me to move away.”Explore more on these topicsInsurance industryAvivaHome insuranceInsuranceHousing marketPropertyFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Food and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priority
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Food and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priority
Content: More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded.Photograph: luoman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded.Photograph: luoman/Getty ImagesTrees and forestsUN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forestsFood and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priorityJonathan WattsTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, aUnited Nationsreport has warned.More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority.The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments.Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.”Graph showing annual rate of forest expansion and deforestation from 1990 to 2025Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods.Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources.Graph showing forest area restoration commitments by continent“This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states.It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQu Dongyu, the FAO director general, said the report “makes clear that forest and landscape restoration is more than an environmental priority – it is a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development”.He said: “The window for action is narrowing, and delayed or poorly designed restoration will increase long-term costs, exacerbate inequalities and risk locking landscapes into unsustainable trajectories. Given the continued loss and degradation of forest ecosystems, as well as growing global demand for land-based products and services, there is an urgent need to scale up effective restoration.”Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsDeforestationConservationBiodiversityUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: South West Water fined £8m for hundreds of sewage spills in Cornwall and Devon | Pollution | The Guardian
description: District judge orders record fine for region and says incidents of pollution cannot be tolerated
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: District judge orders record fine for region and says incidents of pollution cannot be tolerated
Content: Polperro in Cornwall, where in 2019 untreated sewage gushed through a harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPolperro in Cornwall, where in 2019 untreated sewage gushed through a harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianPollutionSouth West Water fined £8m for hundreds of sewage spills in Cornwall and DevonDistrict judge orders record fine for region and says incidents of pollution cannot be toleratedSteven MorrisTue 29 Sep 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA water companyhas been ordered to pay a record fine of almost £8m for hundreds of sewage spillsat popular bathing spots and sensitive habitats in Cornwall and Devon.On one occasion, untreated sewage gushed through a harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend but South WestWater(SWW) engineers took 10 hours to attend.Sewage was also discharged into the River Camel, which is home to otter and Atlantic salmon and is popular with birdwatchers and sailors.Fining SWW £7,867,733 at Plymouth magistrates court – the largest fine for environmental offences in the region – District Judge Matson said incidents of pollution could not be tolerated.The judge repeatedly found the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks.In August 2019, untreated sewage gushed through the harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend at Polperro harbour on the south coast ofCornwall.Between January 2016 and July 2021, there were 231 illegal sewage discharges at Harlyn on the north coast of Cornwall, not far from the foodie hotspot of Padstow.In another case, SWW failed to provide a permanent fix for a sewer that entered a creek in Plymouth, despite multiple formal warnings from theEnvironment Agencyover several years.The company pleaded guilty to 18 charges, 17 for illegal water discharge activities and one for failing to take reasonable remedial measures after a failure at a pumping station.View image in fullscreenSewage was discharged into the River Camel, which is home to otters and Atlantic salmon.Photograph: Environment AgencyMatson described the offences as “horrendous, very significant incidents of pollution” and said they should never happen again.Despite the company pleading guilty, the judge found that SWW had tried to minimise its role in the offending rather than being remorseful and accepting full responsibility.Clarissa Newell, area environment manager at the Environment Agency, which led the prosecution, said: “Hundreds of pollution incidents occurred at some of the most scenic locations in Cornwall andDevon, including bathing waters, a designated special area of conservation and a priority habitat. We hope this record fine will influence a new approach for South West Water.”The fine came as the prime minister, Andy Burnham, described water as a symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain and promised to reverse Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on the public ownership of water companiesResponding to the fine, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said: “For six years, South West Water repeatedly broke the law. That’s why we’re overhauling the water system to give the public control, with tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.”The Liberal Democrat MP for North Cornwall, Ben Maguire, criticised the punishment. He said: “Yet again, the response is essentially another slap on the wrist fine, which a company of this size can absorb as simply the cost of doing business. The hard-working South West Water technicians and other staff I meet are being completely let down by rotten executives.“I strongly believe we urgently need much tougher penalties for repeat offenders, including prison sentences for those responsible for overseeing serious and illegal sewage dumping.”SWW described the offences as “historic” and said: “The majority of the charges concerned the use of overflows in storm conditions. We’re investing £760m to tackle storm overflows and have reduced spills by 17% in the last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%. Significant improvements have been made across the sites concerned. We apologise for what happened in the past, and we remain focused on the future as we deliver record levels of investment.”The water company was ordered to pay £329,993 costs.Explore more on these topicsPollutionWaterDevonCornwallRegulatorsEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Dale Vince plans London-wide news operation to take on ‘rightwing bias’ in the media | Dale Vince | The Guardian
description: Green energy entrepreneur plans rescue package for the group behind the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Green energy entrepreneur plans rescue package for the group behind the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra
Content: Dale Vince.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDale Vince.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockDale VinceDale Vince plans London-wide news operation to take on ‘rightwing bias’ in the mediaGreen energy entrepreneur plans rescue package for the group behind the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster ExtraMichael SavageMedia editorTue 29 Sep 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe green energy entrepreneur and Labour donorDale Vinceis planning to launch a London-wide news operation, as part of a “rescue” of one of the capital’s most highly regarded local newspapers.Vince, who has vowed to take on what he sees as rightwing bias in the UK media, said he would invest “whatever it takes” to support the loss-making group behind the Camden New Journal (CNJ), Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra.He told the Guardian he was already looking at expanding the Westminster edition to cover London-wide issues, in an attempt to serve a city in which a series of major newsrooms have closed or drastically shrunk over the past 20 years.“We’re going to go forward together to put the CNJ on a better financial footing and take it digital – properly digital,” he said. “At the same time, [we will] get behind the Westminster edition and make that an edition for the wider London area.“I think London is missing a local paper now, with the demise of a couple that have gone before. It’s quite a bold plan, that we might morph the Westminster edition.“We might call it the north, south, east and Westminster edition, in a kind of nod to our intended larger audience.”Vince’s rescue package for the titles, which has not been formally finalised, is one of several attempts being made to revitalise local journalism in London. Despite its 9m population, media outlets have struggled to support large London-focused newsrooms.The Evening Standard, which has been published for almost 200 years,shut down its daily newspaperin 2024. It was replaced with a weekly edition renamed the London Standard, with a greater focus on arts and culture.Other attempts to run daily freesheets failed. The London Paper, launched by Rupert Murdoch’s News International, now News UK,closed in 2009after just three years. Its rival, London Lite, published by the owner of the Daily Mail,closed later that year.Meanwhile, Metro, a national freesheet distributed in UK cities including London, is undergoing major structural changes to put it on a “sustainable footing”.However, journalism focused on London has been boosted in recent years by the arrival of small, subscription-based operations.Jim Waterson, a former Guardian journalist who founded theLondon Centricnews site that now has more than 5,000 paying subscribers, said Vince had chosen to help a local group that had resisted “the disastrous choice in the 2010s to abandon quality for chasing clicks at all costs”.However, he said the success of his own “back-to-basics local journalism” outlet was still “only enough money to support a tiny operation that’s still run from a kitchen table”.“Vince has also realised that London is also one of the UK’s worst local news deserts,” Waterson said. “The challenge that we all face is how to get the funding to grow our audience without becoming financially unsustainable.”While not large, the Camden New Journal group still employs 18 people, according to recent financial records. It spent a chunk of its cash reserves in the last year.Vince said he was not supporting the Camden New Journal and its related titles “for business reasons”.“I’m motivated by the impact of local journalism,” he said. “I’m motivated by the bias of media in our country more broadly – the rightwing bias – and trying to do something about that.”Vince has already launched an online publication, Babelfish. He said he would consider writing comment pieces for the London titles, but would generally be a “hands-off” investor.“Big picture-wise, I’ve got a view of the world and how things should be, and the Camden people already fit within that,” he said. “There’s no kind of culture clash and I write op-eds for all kinds of people already. I would absolutely write op-eds for the Camden [New Journal], but it wouldn’t be a requirement.”Explore more on these topicsDale VinceRegional & local newspapersNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests | Facial recognition | The Guardian
description: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert
Content: More than half a million faces were scanned in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the trial.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than half a million faces were scanned in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the trial.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesFacial recognitionTrial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrestsFreedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alertPhoebe Davis andDaniel BoffeyTue 29 Sep 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests.More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British TransportPolice(BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders.A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive.Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations. British Transport Police said that since the extension there had been three positive confirmed alerts of people who were subsequently confirmed to be complying with sexual harm prevention orders or other imposed court conditions.Met to expand use of live facial recognition into central London by ChristmasRead moreWhen Transport for London announced its support for the extension of the trial, it said LFR technology “will target and identify people on police watchlists at key stations chosen for maximum impact” and would “specifically tackle violence against women and girls, whose travel behaviours are shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”.Fraser Sampson, a former biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner for the UK, said the police needed to show that the use of the technology was proportionate. “There many variables and all need to align: the choice of location, times of day, make up of the watchlist and likelihood of people being present and many more.”Sampson, who is now a non-executive director of Facewatch, a company that operates facial recognition systems in shops, added: “We know the technology works, but using it in supermarkets to deter shoplifters and prevent attacks on staff is very different from deploying it to catch people on a public transport network.“Success in a shop means no such people coming in. Success for the police trying to catch people means people being caught. In that respect the trial doesn’t appear to have been very fruitful.“Everything depends on the police watchlists; if you’re not on a watchlist, the live FRT cameras do not ‘see’ you and they don’t retain your image in the same way as CCTV cameras.“However, they are processing special category personal data and the technology must be used in a way that is appropriate, proportionate and necessary. It’s for the police to show how any deployment meets those criteria and – as the ICO [information commissioner’s office] has recently reported – for their oversight boards to hold them firmly to account in doing so.”More than half of police forces inEnglandand Wales have now deployed LFR on British streets, according to an analysis by Liberty Investigates.The Metropolitan police and London mayor’s office announced this summer that fixed LFR cameras would be installed in the capital’s West End. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has since confirmed the technology will be used on the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street.A recent report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights, which called on the government to introduce a law to address the threat of artificial intelligence to human rights, identified the rollout of live facial recognition technology as a “particularly clear example of risk”.Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Labour MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “Live facial recognition technologies are a serious invasion of our privacy. The government should be suspending their rollout until there are stronger safeguards in place, including a proper legal framework.”A BTP spokesperson said it had launched the LFR pilot “to understand how the technology could most effectively support the identification of wanted offenders and individuals who may pose a risk to passengers and staff”.They added: “During these deployments, officers have made a number of associated arrests, including for assault, theft, possession of an offensive weapon, breach of a criminal behaviour order and public order offences, as well as locating individuals wanted by the courts and other police forces. As these arrests did not result directly from an LFR alert, they are not included within LFR performance data.“Throughout the pilot, we have continued to refine how the capability is deployed within the railway environment. This has included developments to deployment locations, operating procedures, equipment and watchlist construction.“A particularly important point is that watchlist growth has been deliberate, controlled and aligned to BTP policy. We began with a more limited watchlist whilst ensuring data quality, governance and safeguarding arrangements were robust.”Explore more on these topicsFacial recognitionLondonPoliceCrimeEnglandWalesSurveillancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Former snooker world champion Graeme Dott jailed for child sexual abuse | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Dott, 49, receives seven-year sentence after abusing a boy and a girl in what judge says was ‘gross violation of trust’
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Dott, 49, receives seven-year sentence after abusing a boy and a girl in what judge says was ‘gross violation of trust’
Content: Graeme Dott arriving at the high court in Glasgow for his trial in August.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersView image in fullscreenGraeme Dott arriving at the high court in Glasgow for his trial in August.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersScotlandFormer snooker world champion Graeme Dott jailed for child sexual abuseDott, 49, receives seven-year sentence after abusing a boy and a girl in what judge says was ‘gross violation of trust’Patrick Greenfieldand agenciesTue 29 Sep 2026 06.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former snooker world champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years at the high court in Edinburgh after being convicted of sexually abusing two young children.In August, Dott was found guilty of sexually abusing a boy and a girl after a five-day trial at Glasgow high court. The court heard that the 2006 world champion inappropriately touched and exposed himself to both children. He denied the charges but was convicted of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour by a majority verdict.Dott appeared at the high court in Edinburgh on Tuesday, where the judge, Lord Harrower, told him he had “robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood”.Imposing a backdated sentence of seven years, he said the 49-year-old’s behaviour had involved a “gross violation of trust” that carried “the hallmarks of grooming”.Using pseudonyms for the boy and girl, Harrower said: “In both cases the abuse included penetrative sexual activity and in the case of Jane behaviour that would now be classed as rape.”Dott has continued to maintain his innocence, the court heard. Between 1993 and 1996, Dott – starting when he himself was still a child aged 16 or 17 – targeted a girl on multiple occasions. The woman, now in her 40s, told the trial that the abuse began when he started “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggyback.She told the court that Dott had told her not to tell anyone that he was sexually abusing her, describing incidents when he had suggested playing a “guessing game”. He would expose himself to her, she said, and began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis.The second victim, a man now in his late 20s, was targeted between 2006 and 2010. He said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts. He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.“He would … come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court. “While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.”He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place. The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”. The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips and “push himself up against me”.Harrower remanded Dott in custody and his name was added to the sex offender register indefinitely. Euan Dow, Dott’s lawyer, told the court in mitigation that his client had longstanding mental health issues, adding that his personal and professional reputations had been destroyed. The 49-year-old has separated from his wife but she remains supportive of him, the court heard.Dott, who turned professional in 1994, won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, defeating Peter Ebdon in the final at the Crucible in Sheffield. He reached the final in two other years but was beaten by Ronnie O’Sullivan in 2004 and Neil Robertson in 2010.Following his conviction, Dott’s name was removed from World Snooker’s hall of fame.Explore more on these topicsScotlandSnookerRape and sexual assaultnewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas charged with assaulting an officer | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Garcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive away
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Garcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive away
Content: Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a food delivery driver, after he was shot by a federal immigration agent, in Austin, Texas, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Austin Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenWilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a food delivery driver, after he was shot by a federal immigration agent, in Austin, Texas, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Austin Police/ReutersUS immigrationVenezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas charged with assaulting an officerGarcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive awayAssociated PressTue 29 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 21.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal prosecutors on Tuesday announced an assault charge against a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent inTexas, accusing the man of striking an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint. Garcés Pérez, whose attorney has said still has a bullet lodged in his back from the 20 September shooting, made an initial court appearance in anAustinfederal court on Tuesday, according to the US attorney’s office in the western district of Texas.Venezuelan shot by ICE in Austin needs surgery to avoid losing feeling in body, supporters sayRead moreA nine-page affidavit from a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent amounts to the government’s fullest public account to date of the shooting in the Texas capital, which has set off protests and outrage from Democrats over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The document includes photos taken from body-worn cameras but no video was released, and the complaint did not say whether the agent allegedly struck by the side mirror sustained any injuries.The accusations against Garcés Pérez were reminiscent of previous claims made by immigration agents after high-profile shootings, in which officers have similarly accused drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, those allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, and have renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.Garcés Pérez was in the custody of US marshals after being removed from a federal detention center in south Texas, according to court documents filed by federal prosecutors. Separately, Garcés Pérez’s attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop his removal from the US.If convicted, Garcés Pérez faces up to 20 years in prison.An attorney for Garcés Pérez declined to immediately comment on Tuesday. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Department of Justice.According to an affidavit signed by a DHS agent, officers first saw Garcés Pérez’s car parked outside a restaurant with its emergency flashers on. They decided to pull him over after conducting a database check that showed the car was registered to Garcés Pérez, who had a final order of removal from the US.The agents said that they turned on their lights to execute the stop, but in the same filing, Garcés Pérez told investigators that an unmarked SUV followed him and then abruptly cut him off on the side of the road.Garcés Pérez, who was making a DoorDash delivery, provided his driver’s license through a crack in the window, but ignored agents’ requests to step out of the car, the complaint said. Garcés Pérez told investigators that he declined to exit because he had asked for officers to wait to apprehend him until his wife could come retrieve his car. Court documents describe the interaction as initially conversational, with a tone that was “pleasant and not aggressive”.About a minute later, according to court records, Garcés Pérez “abruptly” closed the window and drove off. One of the officers, who is referred to only by his initials, was struck in his torso with the driver’s side mirror when Garcés Pérez tried to drive away, the documents say.The unnamed officer who shot Garcés Pérez wasn’t wearing a body camera. The other officer involved in the chase was wearing a camera, but only caught up to the chase after Garcés Pérez had been shot, according to the affidavit.ICE has previously said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September.The affidavit included screenshots from previously unreleased body-worn camera footage of the officer’s initial interactions with ICE agents. The first of three photos appear to show the officer standing in front of Garcés Pérez’s driver’s door mirror; the second shows the officer resting his hands on the hood and side of Garcés Pérez’s car, with the mirror close to or touching the officer’s abdomen; and the third shows the car pulling away.The Austin police department last week released video from its officers but that footage did not show the shooting or the moment that Garcés Pérez allegedly tried driving away.The affidavit includes Garcés Pérez providing his account to federal investigators, which paints a contrasting picture of the lead-up to the shooting than what federal prosecutors described.According to the affidavit, Garcés Pérez said that a law enforcement SUV struck his car after a brief chase and caused it to spin before an agent opened fire, shooting him in the back. By contrast, US attorney Justin R Simmons said in a statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol”.Garcés Pérez entered the US in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under Joe Biden that allowed immigrants to make appointments with US authorities to be considered for asylum.Donald Trumpended the program on his first day in office.Garcés Pérez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garcés Pérez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.The shooting occurred amid a surge in ICE enforcement across the US during Trump’s second term. ICE reported more than 50,000 monthly arrests in July and August – a first for the agency.Immigration officers have come under intense scrutiny for shootings that have occurred since Trump took office in January 2025 – at least 10 of which have been fatal. On a few occasions, federal law enforcement has charged the person shot by immigration officers with assault.A woman shot several times by border patrol officers in Chicago and a man shot in the leg by an ICE agent in Minneapolis were both accused of assaulting officers, but in both cases the charges were dropped. The ICE officer in Minneapolis has since been charged with lying about getting assaulted before shooting the man in the leg.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsTexasAustinnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back
Author: Cecilia Nowell
Headline: ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back
Content: ‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 December 2025.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreen‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 December 2025.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APLos Angeles‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming backCecilia NowellTue 29 Sep 2026 19.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering theLos Angelesneighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home.“Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday.Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower.Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LARead more“I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said.Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next.“Yellow 2120”made headlines last yearwhen he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months.In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns.“He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson toldthe Orange County Registerat the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute. Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.”After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at leasttwo 500-plus-pound black bearssought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings aregrowing more common. In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455.This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters,told the Guardianthat human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population isestimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000, with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesWildlifeAnimalsCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis
Content: Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (left), the UAE vice-president, and Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince, meeting in Riyadh.Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (left), the UAE vice-president, and Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince, meeting in Riyadh.Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenSaudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in YemenRelations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by SaudisPatrick WintourTue 29 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with theUnited Arab Emiratesover Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.Relations between the UAE andSaudi Arabiain Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen.But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to thenarrow Bab al-Mandab straitagainst pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.The future role of the UAE inYemenwas discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.2:34Why the civil war in Yemen has world governments on edgeNetanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat theHouthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice-president.It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.Following the Houthis’ push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, their forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city, trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front.“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”Yemen mapThe STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi,fled into exileafter the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.The former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provided some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.The STC has urged the Giant Brigades to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.“The UN-recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is, so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”The White House has been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done in the past in Yemen, sometimes to brutal effect.Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.The World Health Organization said 838 people had been killed and 3,643 others injured due to the escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday they published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war was existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis were not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine  | Estonia | The Guardian
description: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
Content: Margus Tsahkna at a meeting with the Finnish foreign minister, Elina Valtonen (not pictured), on Tuesday.Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPAView image in fullscreenMargus Tsahkna at a meeting with the Finnish foreign minister, Elina Valtonen (not pictured), on Tuesday.Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPAEstoniaEstonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying UkraineEuropean and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in TallinnEurope live – latest updatesJon HenleyEurope correspondent and agenciesTue 29 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia andUkraineafter the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services.Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry.Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said.Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign acrossEuropeaimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said.Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure onRussia. We will not be intimidated.”Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending.Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”.Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”.Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in RussiaRead moreLithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”.The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said.France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media.Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEstoniaRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays softens return-to-office plans for UK staff after backlash | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Bank allows employees to delay being in workplace at least three days a week until 2027, if permission granted
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Bank allows employees to delay being in workplace at least three days a week until 2027, if permission granted
Content: Barclays had said in the summer that the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenBarclays had said in the summer that the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersBarclaysBarclays softens return-to-office plans for UK staff after backlashBank allows employees to delay being in workplace at least three days a week until 2027, if permission grantedKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentTue 29 Sep 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays has watered down its return-to-office plans after amajor staff backlash, with the bank allowing some employees to wait until next year before having to be in at least three days a week.The bank this summer announced the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October, with more senior employees expected to come in for at least four days. That compares with current rules requiring staff to come in for two days.Now Barclays has offered a reprieve after thousands of bank staffsigned an open letterdrafted by the Unite union, calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work.The bank will allow staff to delay complying with the order until 2027. However, they will need to ask and receive permission to do so from their line manager by the end of this week.In a memo emailed to staff, Barclays’ executive committee announced: “We are extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition … We are also reviewing our flexible working policy.”The extension, first reported by the Financial Times, could give unions more time to request further concessions. Barclays andUnitesaid they would continue discussions on the issue, which has become a flashpoint across the banking sector.Banks ranging from JP Morgan toRevolut have clamped downon remote working after the Covid pandemic, arguing it harms the training of younger staff.Unite have said that while they recognise face-to-face working can support collaboration, team development and relationship building: “We do not accept that this requires a blanket, one-size-fits-all increase in mandatory office attendance.”The union has requested a series of concessions, including:Automatic exemptions of in-office attendance rules during school holidays and Christmas.Capping in-office requirements at one day a week for any carers or people with disabilities.Flexible start and finish times to allow for cheaper off-peak travel costs and to accommodate school pickup and drop-offs.Subsidised onsite meal costs.A single, consolidated payment made to all staff to make up for the costs of coming into the office, before March 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson said: “Unite is continuing to engage with Barclays on its proposals relating to colleagues’ working arrangements.”In an emailed statement, a Barclays spokesperson said: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned.“We have continued to listen to colleague feedback to ensure colleagues have the right support while enabling us to deliver the benefits of working together in person. This includes transitional measures for those whose personal circumstances currently prevent them from meeting the new arrangements.”Explore more on these topicsBarclaysBankingWorking from homeTrade unionsUnitenewsShareReuse this content

title: M&S links up with Sephora to lure younger shoppers | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: Beauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s website
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Beauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s website
Content: Sephora has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market.Photograph: Dave Benett/Tracey Welch/Getty Images for Sephora UKView image in fullscreenSephora has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market.Photograph: Dave Benett/Tracey Welch/Getty Images for Sephora UKMarks & SpencerM&S links up with Sephora to lure younger shoppersBeauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s websiteBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerTue 29 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarks & Spencer has signed a deal with Sephora to open areas under the beauty brand’s name within its stores, in its latest tactic to attract younger shoppers.The French retailer is to launch branded areas staffed by Sephora employees in 100 M&S stores and sell through the British retailer’s website in spring next year.Sephorarelaunched in the UK in 2023with huge fanfare and now has about 18 stand-alone British stores. The company is owned by LVMH, the luxury goods group led by Bernard Arnault, who with his family is among the world’s richest people with a $171bn (£129bn) fortune, according to Forbes.Aldi to invest £900m in UK and open 40 more stores next yearRead moreThe company has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market after closing a handful of stores in 2005, having failed make a dent in a competitive sector. The deal with M&S marks a new strategy in its expansion plans.Analysts havesaidSephora’s work with up-and-coming brands and collaborations with high-profile influencers on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube has helped the company reach its target female audience of 24- to 36-year-olds.John Lyttle, the managing director of M&S’s fashion, home and beauty division, said: “Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often.”“Combining Sephora’s specialist expertise with the strength of the M&S brand, our store estate and our growing digital platform,” Lyttle said. “Alongside this, we will continue investing in our own-label beauty categories where we have established strength and customer trust.”View image in fullscreenA jointly branded Marks & Spencer and Sephora shopping bag.Photograph: Marks & Spencer/PARetailers have been battling to grab a share of the beauty market after the disappearance of many department stores. In recent years a swathe of UK department stores have closed, including Debenhams, Beales and about half the House of Fraser chain.Sephora’s self-service model – which allows consumers to touch and test makeup and perfume without the help of shop staff – is seen to appeal to younger shoppers, who may test in store and buy online. The tie-up could provide increased competition for the specialist health and beauty chains Boots and Superdrug.Lyttle said the deal was part of M&S’s wider transformation plan, which involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening with the aim to have 200 full-line stores in the UK.M&S’s food arm is expanding rapidly, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas.Sarah Boyd, the managing director of Sephora UK, said: “Together, we can redefine what high street beauty means for customers across the UK, bringing the very best curated brand and beauty experience to the M&S stores.”She said the group would introduce its beauty advisers to M&S stores to “provide a truly personalised experience, and to reach customers in more communities where they already live, shop and spend their time”.Explore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerRetail industryMakeupnewsShareReuse this content

title: It was a ghost town of three people. So how did Luckenbach rival Nashville as the heartland of country music? | Country | The Guardian
description: In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American life
Content: Hondo Crouch in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonView image in fullscreenHondo Crouch in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonCountryIt was a ghost town of three people. So how did Luckenbach rival Nashville as the heartland of country music?In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American lifeLauren SneadeTue 29 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 1973, the US country singer Jerry Jeff Walker was in the middle of nowhere, recording his soon-to-be-classic album ¡Viva Terlingua!. A crowd was packed to the rafters in an old dancehall 70 miles west of Austin, in Luckenbach,Texas. An extension lead ran from the hall to a recording truck outside. After everyone had gone home that night, Walker stood in the street and said to Hondo Crouch, Luckenbach’s self-appointed mayor: “I wonder what we just did.”View image in fullscreenJerry Jeff Walker, left, and Hondo Crouch, right, in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonWhen Crouch had bought the town two years prior, its population was just three people – and according to the most recent census in 2021, it’s back at the same number. But in the 1970s, this ramshackle town thrived as Walker and his peers headed there, and Luckenbach became one of the most improbable yet important centres for country music.Hondo Crouch, who died 50 years ago this month, was a goat-rancher, writer and champion swimmer. A contradiction of white hair and a mischievous, boyish face he’d sing Mexicanrancheras– ranch songs – wherever he went. His business card read “Imagineer, authorised distributor”. In 1971, he clubbed together with two friends to buy Luckenbach, which had become a ghost town since its creation in the late 1800s and its population high in 1904. They paid $30,000 for an old dancehall, general store, bar and a few outhouses. With Crouch as the town’s self-appointed mayor, the Luckenbach Dance Hall became a gathering place for outlaw country musicians; a freer, rural alternative to Nashville.Country star Gary P Nunn remembers him as a “pied piper”, leading musicians and eccentrics to a simpler life. In Walker’s case, Crouch’s daughter Becky Patterson met him at an open-mic night, and brought him back to the family ranch. “He had on these little Coke bottle blue glasses,” Patterson remembers, “and Hondo said, ‘I knew he was a musician because he asked for seconds and ate so much. He was starving!’”View image in fullscreenHondo Crouch, left, and Gary P Nunn.Photograph: Becky PattersonAt the time, Nashville’s country industry was chasing the urbane, pop-friendly sound of countrypolitan, heard in stars like Patsy Cline and Charlie Rich. Musicians like Walker andWillie Nelsonwere tired of being told to clean the rust out of their music, and wanted their steel guitars and fiddles back. Going up into the country, they found Luckenbach, Texas.Away from the eye of studio producers, ¡Viva Terlingua! sounded like the communal, unpolished life it celebrated. Gary P Nunn’s song London Homesick Blues appears on the record and Nunn spent that summer in Luckenbach sleeping in a teepee with his wife and baby. “My wife didn’t think much of it, everyone else was staying in hotels,” he chuckles. “But Jerry Jeff used to say you can’t get that magic in the studio.”The atmosphere in the dancehall is palpable: you can hear crickets during the lulls between the crowd’s stamping and hooting. Two years later, ¡Viva Terlingua! even reached space when the song Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother was played to wake the Apollo–Soyuz astronauts in July 1975.Rolling Stone covered the ¡Viva Terlingua! sessions, which drew hippies from across the country. By the mid-70s, the life expectancy of Luckenbach road signs was reportedly about four hours; visitors stole them so frequently that the highway department stopped replacing them.View image in fullscreenInterior of rustic bar in Luckenbach, Texas, US.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesBut a haunt for hippies and country fans was catapulted to even greater renown when in 1977, Waylon Jennings released Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love). Guy Clark, who had been involved in ¡Viva Terlingua!, had told Nashville songwriters Bobby Emmons and Chips Moman about Crouch. They wrote the song the next morning. Willie Nelson joined Waylon on the final chorus and the song hankers after leaving metropolitan riches for a simpler life in Luckenbach: “Baby, let’s sell your diamond ring / buy some boots and faded jeans, and go away.”That yearning for rural life resonated so much that the song spent six weeks at No 1 on the country chart, then crossed over to pop radio. “It was like the whole world were like, where’s this Luckenbach, Texas?”, Nunn says. Folk came by the busload to get back to basics. Willie Nelson famously lost a game of dominoes against the town’s elderly champions, and returned in 1995 to host his Fourth of July Picnic festival in Luckenbach for five years running.There is a “picking tree” at Luckenbach, where country musicians have passed guitars around since Crouch’s day. Contemporary star and Yellowstone actor Ryan Bingham honed his trade there and organised an annual festival, The Western, in the hall. Kit Patterson, Crouch’s grandson, remembers Bingham and other musicians sitting round the picker circle. “It was this beautiful, intimate moment around the fire, reliving life before all the fame.”Crouch’s family still runs Luckenbach through Luckenbach Texas, Inc. Protecting its name has meant taking legal action, including against a whisky brand trying to piggyback on the town’s cultural capital. “Lawsuits are the antithesis of what Luckenbach is about,” says Kit, the company’s president. “But at the same time, if the integrity of what Luckenbach is isn’t protected, it becomes diluted.”View image in fullscreenHondo Crouch, self-appointed mayor, Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonCrouch preached a kind of backyard mysticism – a characteristically American devotion to ordinary things. In surviving footage filmed outside the hall he twinkles at the camera, “I love this town. I love every rotten board in it.” He liked to say Luckenbach had a bigger moon than any other town, and he says as much on Walker’s 1977 album A Man Must Carry On, also recorded in Luckenbach. On Luckenbach Moon, Crouch crows his poem over a stumbling guitar line.double quotation markWe try to tell folks who come by here to look at our townWhat a big, mean moon we haveBut nobody’ll believe it.Elsewhere on the record, poet Charles John Quarto remembers Crouch as “like some song you can’t unlearn” and Walker sings My Buddy: “I miss the way your eyes saw things upon the land … the grey days I miss you most of all.”‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generationRead moreCrouch never heard A Man Must Carry On or Waylon Jennings’s hit. He died suddenly of a heart attack on 27 September 1976. When Patterson phoned Walker to tell him her father had died, he dropped the receiver and never came back to the call. The church overflowed at Crouch’s funeral. Willie Nelson arrived but didn’t get out of his truck, unwilling to draw attention from Crouch.I asked his youngest daughter, Cris Crouch Graham, whether the moon really was bigger in Luckenbach. She laughed. “The moon’s the same moon as everywhere else. But he made it bigger, and so it is.”Explore more on these topicsCountryTexasWillie NelsonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re broken | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: From a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasures
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: From a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasures
Content: Less of the lip … a fragment of a statue of 14th-century BC ruler Akhenaten.Photograph: © The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Art Resource/Scala, FirenzeView image in fullscreenLess of the lip … a fragment of a statue of 14th-century BC ruler Akhenaten.Photograph: © The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Art Resource/Scala, FirenzeExhibitions‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re brokenFrom a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasuresPhilip OltermannTue 29 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nose of Cleopatra VII was supposed to have been so beautiful that it changed the course of history: if it had been shorter, French philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote, “the whole face of the earth would have changed”. A visit to the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence, however, will leave you convinced that Cleo’s conk was only the second most stunning feature to ever grace the face of an Egyptian pharaoh. Among the more than 80 objects on display at an exhibition that opened last week is an astonishingly lifelike sculpture showing off the lips of Akhenaten, from the 14th century BC: a seagull shape resting on a pillow of lush flesh, at once both stern and sensuous, almost uncomfortably kissable.It was Thomas Aquinas who first came up with the theory that we perceive things to be beautiful when they are intact and whole, but the Akhenaten sculpture is so striking precisely because it has a major blemish. Like all the objects shown in Florence, it is only a fragment: a shard of polished limestone found in the dumps south of the Great Aten Temple in the city of el-Amarna, showing only the ruler’s nose and mouth.View image in fullscreenHeads up … fragments of sculptures that feature in the Broken show.Photograph: Roberto Serra/Iguana Press/Getty Images“One of the unique qualities of fragments is that they focus your attention on details,” says CD Dickerson, an expert in Renaissance and baroque art. “You wouldn’t have considered the subtle way that the lip has been crisply carved in this stone if it had been part of a bigger statue with a bunch of other features. Fragments make you think about objects in a different way.”Entitled Broken: The Power of Fragments, the show that Dickerson has co-curated for the Palazzo Strozzi and the National Gallery ofArtin Washington DC, explores why people throughout history have gone to great lengths to damage or destroy carefully crafted sculptures and statues. But along the way, it raises an even more intriguing question: why it is that some works of art have a more powerful emotional pull in a broken state than when whole?Many of the objects shown here speak of fault lines in history. There is a decapitated lifesize statue of a kneeling prior from Romainmôtier in Switzerland, likely beheaded during the iconoclastic frenzy of the Protestant Reformation. The dismembered left foot and right hand of King Louis XIV are all that remains of an equestrian monument to the French royal after the revolution rolled across Paris’s Place Vendôme and put up a guillotine instead. Modernist sculptor Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini was adorned with a simple bullet through the forehead after the fall of the fascist regime.The vandals were following an age-old tradition, says co-curator Andrew Sears. “Across the ancient world it was a common practice during regime changes or religious transformations to destroy images of the previous one because it was believed that the images contained some kind of life force of the ruler.”In some cases, these defaced sculptures would stay on as a deterrent. “They were made to be displayed in that way,” says Sears. A 19AD bust representing Germanicus, heir to Tiberius, had its nose expertly hacked off, upper earlobes cut and forehead adorned with a cross by Christians who protested against the deification of Roman emperors. The past, we are reassured, was a foreign country with cruel rituals.View image in fullscreenFallen fascist … Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini, 1923.Photograph: Collezione Carlo EleuteriBroken starts to get more surprising and interesting where it explores brokenness as more than a result of historical fractures. A section called Sculpting the Fragment opens with an intriguingdogūfigurine from ancient Japan. Little is known about these small, fired-clay statuettes with bulging coffee-bean eyes other than that they have been found in pieces all over burial sites in Japan.Current research indicates that the function ofdogūfigurines may have been akin to modern-day birthday pinatas: smashed to celebrate not just the end of the old but also the start of the new. “It’s very clear that the culture was to make these sculptures to intentionally break them, and for communities to share pieces with each other,” says Dickerson. “Our contemporary perception of ancient cultures being more violent is not always accurate.”Dickerson and Sears’ rummage through the darker corners of museum storage rooms has yielded little evidence of Aquinas’s equation of breakage with ugliness. Often, the opposite held true. From the early 15th-century Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, they present a statue of a reclining figure that was intentionally decapitated, as part of a campaign to rebuild a temple. Modelling their approach on the ruinous state of their surroundings, the Mexica seem to have understood completion to be unattainable. A broken artwork was proper because it revealed the true state of the world.View image in fullscreenThe Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed jeans … Michelangelo’s Model of a Nude Woman, from around 1533.Photograph: © Photo Giusti Claudio Firenze/Archivio Fotografico, Fondazione Casa BuonarrotiWe may think of the cult of ruined buildings and broken statues as an obsession of the Romantics, of the paintings of Caspar David Friedrich or the “colossal wreck” ofPercy Shelley’s Ozymandias. But Dickerson says ruin lust was already embedded in the art and literature of the Renaissance from the 13th century onwards. One of the most striking displays in Florence is a Michelangelo terracotta model of a headless and armless woman. Dated around 1533, it looks damaged but isn’t. Instead, it was the Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed grunge-wash jeans: recent technical analysis of the torso’s breakage points suggests Michelangelo deliberately sculpted a fragment, in homage to the awe-inspiring antiquities that were being excavated in Rome at the time.View image in fullscreenBroken bodies on the big screen … Charlize Theron (on knees) in 2015’s Mad Max: Fury Road.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyThe exhibition culminates with contemporary artistic takes on broken sculptures, such as a Louise Bourgeois foot in a leg brace and German artist Julius von Bismarck’s collapsable equestrian statue of his chancellor forebear, Otto. If that feels slightly self-restraining, it’s because the wholeness v brokenness divide is still everywhere in modern popular culture once you start looking for it. Here thefar-right social media accountswith immaculate classical busts as avatars, the impeccably smooth aesthetics of the iPhone, the flattened masks of the“clean girl” makeup trend; there the rise of broken bodies on the big screen, from Mad Max’s one-armed Furiosa to cleft-lipped lead actors like Tom Burke and Franz Rogowski and Game of Thrones’ “cripples, bastards and broken things”.Clearly, the answer to the question of whether there is a beauty in brokenness is not just one that captured ancient civilisations, but continues to be one of the central cultural dividing lines of our time.Broken: The Power of the Fragment is atPalazzo Strozzi, Florence, 25 September 2026 until 24 January, and at theNational Gallery of Art, Washington, from 13 March to 27 June 2027This article was amended on 29 September 2026. Akhenaten ruled Egypt in the 14th century BC, rather than the 14th century, as appeared in an earlier version.Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsSculptureArtStatuesMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Portuguese House review – picturesque, polite drama of secrets and revelations at a country estate | Movies | The Guardian
