description: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener
Content: Restrained and respectful … Maria de Medeiros and Manolo Solo in The Portuguese House.Photograph: Courtesy of AX1 FilmsView image in fullscreenRestrained and respectful … Maria de Medeiros and Manolo Solo in The Portuguese House.Photograph: Courtesy of AX1 FilmsMoviesReviewThe Portuguese House review – picturesque, polite drama of secrets and revelations at a country estateSpanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardenerCath ClarkeTue 29 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOut of the blue, a woman walks out on her husband. Bags packed and ready to go, at the last moment she crumples up the letter she has written to him and vanishes from their Madrid flat. So begins this drama featuring not one but three characters disappearing without a trace from their lives; it sounds soap opera-ish, but mostly The Portuguese House unfolds as polite elegant drama, told with such rich novelistic detail it often feels like it’s getting into the minds of the characters.Manolo Solo gives an excellent performance as the left-behind husband, Fernando, an introspective mild-mannered geography professor. After his wife’s disappearance, Fernando goes on holiday to Portugal, where he meets a gardener called Manuel. When Manuel drops dead of a heart attack, Fernando decides – like his wife – to leave his old life behind; he assumes Manuel’s identity and takes a job as the gardener at a Portuguese country estate. The owner, Amália (Maria de Medeiros), senses that this intellectual man with glasses and a clumsy way with the loppers is not the man she hired, but doesn’t push it – possibly because she is attracted to him.Like a doorstop paperback, The Portuguese House is an expansive watch, spanning years and going at a gentle pace for nearly two hours. There are more secrets and lies to come – and another person pretending to be someone they are not. That would be a twist too far in another film, but works here in a restrained drama that treats all its characters generously and with sympathy. Though in the end I wondered if it is possibly too respectful, sweeping away difficult hard-to-shift feelings like autumn leaves.The Portuguese House is in UK cinemas from 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSpainEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Child review – jump scares abound in twisty organ transplant fable that keeps horror at its heart | Movies | The Guardian
description: This Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-making
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: This Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-making
Content: How much worse could it get … Child.Photograph: GrimmVisionView image in fullscreenHow much worse could it get … Child.Photograph: GrimmVisionMoviesReviewChild review – jump scares abound in twisty organ transplant fable that keeps horror at its heartThis Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-makingLeslie FelperinTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStippled with first-world guilt about income inequality even between fellow EU member states, this Luxembourg-made horror sprinkles a bit of liberal fairy dust over what is otherwise a pretty straight-up, if twisty, horror setup: a grunting, inarticulate and physically disfigured big baddie stalks the normie protagonists who shouldn’t have come round these impoverished parts. Think Grand Duchy Chainsaw Massacre, though admittedly without any chainsaws. There are sullen locals, a dilapidated farmhouse full of ominous clutter, ill intentions and horrible maiming.The unlucky visitors here are former couple Greg (Malik Zidi) and Anne (Brigitte Urhausen), who are co-parenting little Leo (Leo Todesco), a pre-adolescent who is lying in a hospital bed while waiting for a crucial organ transplant. A little time has to elapse before we learn that control-freak Anne blames likable doctor Greg for Leo’s condition because he took his eyes off the kid for just long enough for him to get hit by a car. But Greg is trying to make it up to her by accompanying his ex on a trip to an unnamed eastern European country (where folks speak Bulgarian) to acquire the organ Leo needs on the black market, their glide path lubricated with lots of cash and pre-arranged bribes to border guards and the like.Heart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroesRead moreUnfortunately, things go very pear-shaped; in fact, they go so wrong we may need a whole other kind of fruit to describe the badness of this shape. Co-writer-director Cyrus Neshvad deliberately toys with audience expectations about survival by violating narrative conventions about point of view, which is really fun. Also impressive is the way he and cinematographer Nikos Welter play with light and colour throughout, shifting the whole palette as soon as the Luxembourgers cross the border, and later using the LED light from a crucial box to cast little pools of first blue and then orange and red light to signify time running out. The performances are mostly held back and buttoned down until it is time to scream in terror. It’s a shame that the initial medical conceit is a little too vague (which organ are they supposed to be collecting?), but there are enough jump scares to give most hearts a jolt.Child is in UK cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsLuxembourgHealthOrgan donationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: April X review – Connor Storrie searches for missing twin in dystopian dream-tech sci-fi thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitative
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: The star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitative
Content: Supermarket sweep under the carpet … Lilly Krug as April and Connor Storrie as Baxter in April X.Photograph: Vertigo Releasing/PAView image in fullscreenSupermarket sweep under the carpet … Lilly Krug as April and Connor Storrie as Baxter in April X.Photograph: Vertigo Releasing/PAMoviesReviewApril X review – Connor Storrie searches for missing twin in dystopian dream-tech sci-fi thrillerThe star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitativeLeslie FelperinTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSketchy in every sense of the word, this sci-fi thriller is set in the not-too-distant future in a dystopian concrete city (actually mostly Bucharest looking like itself), where life is cheap but screenwriting conceits are clearly expensive, given most of the main ones here appear to be borrowed from other movies. Brother-and-sister twins Baxter (Connor Storrie, fromHeated Rivalry) and April (Lilly Krug) are struggling to get by and mooching around the fringes of the criminal world, doing jobs on a spectrum of legality, though nothing especially harmful to themselves or others. He does petty crimes and she makes wigs and sells downloads of her own uncannily clear dreams (a nod to neglected 90s classics Strange Days and Until the End of the World where dream tech played key roles).Unfortunately, Baxter and his screw-up associate Ronny (Tourialay Akbari) fall into debt to and afoul with local kingpin Klein (Serban Pavlu), whose persistent use of Yiddish phrases and general parsimoniousness sets up the characterisation just on the edge of antisemitism. When Baxter cleans out his and April’s joint accounts and still comes up short, someone takes April and her archive of recorded dreams/memories. Suddenly, the action jumps ahead five years in the future and April is both still missing and yet, at a local brothel, all too ubiquitous where it seems she’s been cloned to make numerous sex workers.This nasty spin on human trafficking gets progressively ickier as the last act unfolds, especially as the film both wants us to be repulsed by the situation and seemingly titillated judging by all the shots of Krug, duplicated digitally, having sex with clients or sitting around languidly in lingerie. There’s a bit of jagged editing to make things look cleverer than they are, and lashings of hard-boiled voiceover narration from Storrie. The latter does his best to bring conviction to the material, but this is not a work that will feature prominently in his CV in the years to come.April X is in UK and Irish cinemas from 2 October with an Australian release date yet to be announced.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peak | Prince | The Guardian
description: As a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his genius
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his genius
Content: Prince in 1987.Photograph: Crollalanza/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPrince in 1987.Photograph: Crollalanza/Rex/ShutterstockPrince‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peakAs a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his geniusEthan BeckTue 29 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the early 1980s,Princehad cemented his place as a pop heavyweight with the phenomenal success of his 1999 album, as well as becoming a movie star thanks to Purple Rain. Even when his second film, the old Hollywood throwback Under the Cherry Moon, bombed worldwide in 1986, he notched another massive hit off its soundtrack with Kiss. It didn’t matter if audiences didn’t understand; Prince kept moving forward.That restless spirit propelled Prince’s final masterpiece, 1987’s Sign o’ the Times, as he dabbled with different directions. Anything seemed on the table: maybe he would drop another album with his backing band, The Revolution, or he would explore his feminine alter-ego Camille with a self-titled album. He even, at one point, wanted to put out a triple album, a reasonable response to the vast collection of music that Prince was creating. “Sometimes when people are in a place of transition, they’re distracted,” said John McKie, whose new bookPrince: A Sign o’ the Timesfollows the pop legend’s career through the lens of this classic. “For Prince, he focused on his music.”‘He’d gaze at the stars and go: I’m gonna be up there one day’: Prince by those who knew him best, 10 years after his deathRead moreHis record label pushed back on the triple album, so insteadPrinceput out the kaleidoscopic Sign o’ the Times – which clocked in at 80 minutes across two LPs – and eventually decided against touring the album in the United States. The Purple One’s imperial period can be difficult to nail down, as he rarely gave interviews or even kept collaborators up to date about what he had planned. Even as McKie interviewed more than 100 people about the gestation behind Sign o’ the Times, it wasn’t always easy to understand the headspace Prince was in when he fired his band the Revolution and split up with his fiancee, Susannah Melvoin. “Prince probably would have been a very good poker player because he didn’t give that much away,” said McKie. “If you listen to his music, there are lots of clues. He said it himself: ‘If you want to know me, listen to my music.’”Sign o’ the Times, which turns 40 in March, remains a genre-defying monument in Prince’s discography with a thick layer of funk at the center. It’s the LP where Prince happily dipped into Christian rock with The Cross, built Starfish and Coffee around a jazz chord progression, and casually shared the best power pop song of all time with I Could Never Take the Place of Your Man. But it’s also one of Prince’s most thematically disparate projects: “I want to do it baby all the time,” he sings libidinously, only a few songs before heralding the return of Christ. Few people, it seemed, were as good at compartmentalizing as Prince. “He would be dating two very different women at the same time,” McKie said. “He would record two very different songs on the same day.”Prince’s 50 greatest singles – ranked!Read moreThe first hit from Sign o’ the Times was the title track, where Prince seems to be reciting from the newspaper, touching upon gang violence, the HIV/Aids epidemic, and the possibility of nuclear war, all over an uneasy groove built almost entirely with the Fairlight CMI sampler and synthesizer. He had heardPeter GabrielandKate Bushuse the instrument and wanted in on the fun. Elsewhere, the Linn LM-1 drum machine dictated much of the album’s blocky percussion – Prince reportedly described the party-starting Housequake as having the greatest-sounding kick drum of all time – while he slipped into Camille territory with a zany, high-pitched delivery on a handful of songs. One of them, If I Was Your Girlfriend, McKie believes is in the running for the best song that Prince ever wrote. The dizzying textures seemed designed to confirm that Prince contained multitudes.“Keith Richardsonce said ofMick Jagger, he once described him as a nice bunch of guys – I don’t think it was entirely complimentary,” said McKie. “One of the things that you take from Sign o’ the Times is it’s a nice bunch of Princes.”View image in fullscreenPrince in 1987’s Sign o’ the Times concert film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyPart of Prince wanted to settle down. Nowhere is that clearer than on the tender Forever in My Life. But he also dated voraciously, even before he broke things off with Melvoin, who also spent a brief spell as a vocalist in the Revolution. Their romance guided the omnivorous feelings of Sign o’ the Times, especially on the all-timer slow jam Adore and the hot-and-cold Strange Relationship. “I believe the phrase ‘The one that got away’ could apply here,” said McKie. “Lots of people that loved Prince loved Susannah, and lots of people that loved Prince that I spoke to were quite explicit in saying they wished he’d married her.”Prince had a reputation for being demanding – or difficult, if you are less charitable. Disputes over songwriting credits and payments for his backing band take up a chunk of McKie’s book, while one tour manager describes him as “a very autocratic ruler”. And while his rivalry withMichael Jacksonhas always received ample attention, it seemed that Prince didn’t know how to deal with his contemporaries: his stock answer for meeting someone new was saying: “I know who you are.” At one point, Prince even bristled at collaborating withMiles Davisbecause he couldn’t control what the jazz giant played. (The trumpeter joined Prince onstage at Paisley Park on New Year’s Eve in 1987, only a few months after Sign o’ the Times arrived in stores.) The penultimate track, It’s Gonna Be a Beautiful Night, with its call-and-response grooves, made McKie think of “Prince as a jazz band leader brought up to the modern age.”On this double album, Prince applied a dash of Davis’s spirit, especially when he faced issues in the studio. His hardworking but fast-moving attitude is clearest on a song like The Ballad of Dorothy Parker, where the song’s high frequencies are muted because engineer Susan Rogers made a mistake with a new mixing console. It wasn’t fixed, as Prince believed that many errors were meant to be. Those coincidences reminded McKie of how Davis worked with his bandmates: “He was looking for something different, and sometimes he was known to say ‘play it again’ if someone played a wrong note,” McKie recalled. “Prince was smart enough to acknowledge so-called mistakes and turn them into something.”Prince: A Sign o’ the Times is out now in the UK via Blink Publishing and will be released 13 October in the US by Division BooksExplore more on these topicsPrincePop and rockBiography booksElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world order  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach
Author: Houman Barekat
Headline: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach
Content: An anti-Iraq war march in London, 2003.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenAn anti-Iraq war march in London, 2003.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverPolitics booksReviewThe Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world orderA journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreachHouman BarekatTue 29 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military supremacy; a rules-based global order. As Jones recounts in his new book, these certainties would come crashing down over the next quarter of a century amid a succession of economic failures, foreign policy disasters and political crises.Indeed, “the west” itself – as a shorthand for the US plus the wealthier western European nations – feels almost quaint today, given the increasing unilateralism of the administration in Washington. But in the 2000s it was part of the lexicon, as if the hemisphere were a political actor in its own right. Revisiting the US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, we are reminded not just of their horrific death tolls (totalling half a million, by conservative estimates) but also their total strategic failure; the 2021 evacuation of Kabul airport, Jones writes, was “among the starkest images of American decline yet broadcast to the world”.In addition to destabilising the region, these interventions weakened the foundations of the international legal system. As Jones points out, a precedent was set when Nato bombed Yugoslavia without UN security council authorisation in 1999; the 2003 invasion of Iraq, also without authorisation, further undermined the UN. So when Vladimir Putin subsequently invaded Ukraine on his own dubious pretext, western objections could be dismissed as hypocrisy. Perhaps the most ignominious example of western indifference to the international rule of law was Keir Starmer’s limp assertion that Israel had the “right” to cut off water and electricity to 2 million civilians in Gaza – a war crime – in retaliation for Hamas’s attacks on 7 October 2023.Alongside these geopolitical catastrophes, Jones tells a story of domestic decline, of western economies built on chronic insecurity and precarious employment. In the 2000s, Thatcherite policies pursued by New Labour fleeced the public: “Essential services [were] turned into assets designed to generate returns. Passengers paid more for overcrowded trains. Rivers and seas were fouled while water companies loaded themselves with debt and paid out dividends.” Then came the 2008 financial crisis and the bankers’ bailout, paid for by austerity. In Britain and elsewhere, Jones notes a “correlation between the inability of centrist governments to tackle economic decline in any meaningful way, and the rise of the far right”.double quotation markFor decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideologyThe book is interspersed with snippets of interviews with an assortment of eyewitnesses, journalists, scholars and activists. They include the director of Iraq national museum in Baghdad, a former Lehman Brothers employee, a former head of the Afghan Red Crescent, the Greek economist Yanis Varoufakis, and the conservative commentator Andrew Sullivan, a repentant cheerleader for the Iraq war, who admits: “I was wrong on the major issues, on the morality of it and the practicality of it and the reason for it.”Much of this terrain – Bush and Blair’s wars, the financial crash, the populist surge – has been extensively covered. The average well-informed reader will learn nothing new, but it is bracing to see what was once the news cycle take its place in the sweep of history, and Jones’s focus on free-market fundamentalism provides a compelling through-line. He suggests the second Trump administration, in all its cynical venality, is “the logical endpoint” of that philosophy. And he reminds us that the aggressive privatisation of the Russian economy in the 1990s brought terrible economic hardship which ultimately fuelled Putin’s revanchist nationalism.For decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideology: the prerogatives of the private sector must override the collective interest, and anything less is tantamount to Stalinism. This remains orthodoxy, but the rise to prominence of Zohran Mamdani, the avowedly socialist mayor of New York, offers a glimmer of hope to those who, like Jones, would prefer a society built on “common provision, democratic power, mutual obligation and the recognition that our fates are bound together”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Stations by Louise Kennedy review – a superb follow-up to Trespasses | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphones
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: This tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphones
Content: A London pub in 1982.Photograph: Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA London pub in 1982.Photograph: Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild/Getty ImagesBook of the dayFictionReviewStations by Louise Kennedy review – a superb follow-up to TrespassesThis tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphonesClare ClarkTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouise Kennedy’s first novel,Trespasses, was one of those rare triumphs, a debut that was not only rapturously received by critics but adored by readers around the world. A story of forbidden love set during the Troubles in 1970s Belfast, it was an international bestseller, translated into more than 20 languages. It was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize and scooped debut fiction of the year at the British Book awards. A four-part television adaptation with Gillian Anderson aired last autumn on Channel 4.Inevitably Kennedy found herself lauded as an overnight success – much was made of her 30-year career as a professional chef – but in fact she had been writing short stories for a decade and to considerable acclaim; her first collection, The End of the World Is a Cul de Sac, was published in 2021. Included in that book was Belladonna, the story of Róisín, a young girl from Belfast who moves south with her mother and, ostracised by her new classmates, becomes friendly with the couple who live across the road. Like Briony Tallis in Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the prickly and precociously bright Róisín misinterprets the dynamic of her neighbours’ marriage to disastrous effect.It is a sucker-punch of a story, conjuring in a few restrained pages the violent insecurity and self-absorption of early adolescence. What a joy, then, to rediscover Róisín in the opening pages of Stations, Kennedy’s blisteringly good second novel. It is 1982 and Róisín, still very much the outsider from the north, strikes up a fierce and unexpected friendship with Red, a boy with a reputation for trouble who is “spoken about in giddy whispers at school”. Róisín’s father, a drinker, has moved with his new wife to London. Red’s family is dysfunctional in ways Róisín only vaguely understands, but which come to a head when Red finds himself on the wrong side of the law. Unable to stay, Red bolts to London. It is a year before Róisín, visiting her father for Christmas, finds herself caught up with him once again, the pull he exerts on her impossible to resist.The novel traces the warp and weft of their relationship over the next 25 years. Structured like a sporadically kept diary, clusters of dated entries disrupted by long gaps, it has echoes of David Nicholls’s One Day; but Kennedy’s London is altogether grimmer and more brutal, a city of squats and gas heaters and not enough change for the payphone. Her people are also more damaged, an Irish diaspora fractured by displacement, scarred not only by poverty and violence and addiction but by shame and loss. “Can you not feel it?” Red asks Róisín when, walking through London, they pass the site of the old Millbank prison. “All those wretched lives layered up underneath us.” Kennedy’s émigrés flee the old country, they build new lives, construct new families, but they carry the weight of the past always with them. However far they travel, they can never escape from themselves.double quotation markStations evokes 1980s London with almost hallucinogenic precisionKennedy moved to London herself as a young woman and evokes the 1980s city with almost hallucinogenic precision, but her greater power lies in her remarkable humanity. Her characters are messy, flawed, often shatteringly self-destructive but, mapped with her fierce compassion, they march straight off the page. As a teenager Róisín is bolshy and obstreperous; she is also funny and filthy and generous and agonisingly vulnerable. As she gets older, she gets better – sometimes – at managing herself but she never really changes. The way Kennedy conjures her, we do not want her to.Stations is at its heart a love story, a furious, tender, potty-mouthed paean to loyalty and generosity of spirit. It is also an elegy to a generation of lost Irish boys, a heartbreaking testament to the violence and fear passed down from father to son. In its title, Stations acknowledges the transience of the diasporic experience, the trains and boats and coaches, but, steeped as the book is in an in-the-bone Catholicism (one particularly powerful scene has Róisín unable to bring herself to shake Red’s father’s hand at Mass), it carries too the idea of the Stations of the Cross, the 14 images of Jesus on the day of his Crucifixion.In Trespasses, the teacher Cushla, studying the Stations during the Easter Sunday sermon, reckons Jesus “a ringer for James Taylor”. In Stations, it is tempting to see the elusive and charismatic Red, “loping along in [Róisín’s] father’s coat like an itinerant preacher”, as a Christ figure, offering a kind of redemption through his suffering. Can cycles of anguish or neglect ever be broken? Is love in all its frustrating insufficiency enough to save us? Kennedy’s novel is too subtle and clear-eyed to offer easy answers, but her questions will burn themselves into your heart.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: ‘We got naked and covered ourselves in Vaseline’: Katherine Hubbard on photographing her ailing mother | Photography | The Guardian
description: Over five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: Over five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?
Content: ‘My mum’s completely her own person’ … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (hand to face), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkView image in fullscreen‘My mum’s completely her own person’ … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (hand to face), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkPhotographyInterview‘We got naked and covered ourselves in Vaseline’: Katherine Hubbard on photographing her ailing motherCharlotte JansenOver five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, artist Katherine Hubbard started to sense something was not right with her mother, Antonette Berger. “It was impossible at the time to say what I was noticing, but something was off.”Berger was living alone in Philadelphia, and as restrictions were lifted, Hubbard went to stay with her. Berger was eventually diagnosed with LATE [limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy], a condition which causes symptoms similar to Alzheimer’s, though the decline in memory and day-to-day functioning is slower. The diagnosis was “a painful, drawn-out and confusing process – then a feeling of so much grief, so much loss”, Hubbard explains on Zoom from New York.Finding herself suddenly in the role of a “caretaker under duress”, Hubbard decided to photograph her housebound mother and her environment. “The camera fails us in so many ways,” she says, “and the absurdity with dementia is that I was constantly making lots of images of things that can’t be shown in an image. But I make images because of how they feel, not how they look.”She set up two vintage Polaroid cameras and her equipment at her mother’s apartment in Germantown, and didn’t take it down for five years. The wrenchingly beautiful images became the series The Great Room, published as a book, One Fifty One, named after the house’s street number. The Great Room photographs and installations based on Berger’s apartment are included inHubbard’s solo exhibition at Studio Voltaire, London.Hubbard grew up in Philadelphia, but in a different, “more modest” house than the incredible, maze-like, sprawling setting seen in The Great Room. The apartment that appears in the photographs belongs to a huge, dilapidated building Berger owned and rented out for 40 years. 151 formed an important part of Hubbard’s upbringing and early imaginary – they would regularly visit Berger’s many tenants there, “it was kind of like a community centre, there were always people around, complaining about things breaking”. The title The Great Room references Berger’s own description of the apartment’s main living space.View image in fullscreenThrillingly theatrical … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (snap), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New York“My mum is incredibly headstrong, eccentric, and difficult – she’s completely her own person,” Hubbard says. They completed daily domestic duties together there, and slowly began to pack up and empty out the apartment, so that Berger could move to a care facility.Some of the scenes are thrillingly theatrical: at one point, Hubbard created a stage for her mum with “a set of rotting 1960s mirror doors I found in the garage that I thought were stunning and built them on to stands, so she could roll them around.” Mirrors became an important feature in the images as “a way of never leaving my mum alone in the image, to project myself into the image. If I’m in the image there with her, it changes some of the authority and power dynamics of the camera”. The reflections give a feeling of transition and loss, an image about to disappear – they hold their images in the same space, the way the photograph does, but sometimes give the sense that they are missing each other. It’s a quiet confrontation with the pain of brain disease, of disappearing while being.Magnificent and bristling with tension, Berger often commands the image with authority in majestic light, framed by her grand and rambling home. “Something wonderful happened at some point where we both stopped thinking about the cameras, and we stopped seeing ourselves as an image – the cameras were just present, and the time to make photographs created interruptions into an otherwise brutal, demanding time that was not pleasant.”The camera allowed moments of levity and playfulness into their otherwise gruelling day to day life. “I could ask my mum to engage with me in a way I never would have if I hadn’t been making the photographs.”View image in fullscreen‘Like a performance in darkness’ … Katherine Hubbard, rear pressure slip, 2025.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkThat also included persuading her mother to strip off to make body prints together in the darkroom. “They were weird and hard to make,” Hubbard says. “We would go to the darkroom in the mornings when she had energy. We’d get naked and covered in Vaseline, and Then we’d use our bodies as a printing tool on to photo paper – like a performance in darkness, but it was very choreographed, a lot had to be around her safety getting her on to the floor and on to the paper, and back up again.”The main problem was that Berger “hates Vaseline – she found it suffocating. But when I’d ask her if she didn’t want to do it, she’d get offended and say ‘of course I’ll do it, are you stupid? You think I can’t do it just because I don’t like it!’”Hubbard emphasises that she doesn’t see Berger as a collaborator, and that consent is more complex to navigate with someone with dementia – “her willingness was important, and me being respectful and responsible of who I know her to be, and knowing what her limits are”.The 4x8 ft contact prints represent the physical entanglement of mother and daughters bodies, a private performance in the dark, the texture and movement of their bodies preserved on silver gelatin, while Berger’s inner world was being radically altered and transformed. Made without the intervention of a camera, Hubbard sees them as a “bridge to something more psychic, more energetic” between them than the more traditional representation in the portrait photographs. They convey a sense of freedom, letting go, and trying to hold on, all at once.‘She knows she will forget’: Grief, dementia and motherhood – in picturesRead moreMaking the photographs has affected their relationship in various ways, and at different times, throughout the last five years. Hubbard took over the management of 151, inheriting families of squirrels and raccoons living in the walls, broken pumps in the basement, and a host of other issues. “It was an insane time – I had a lot of anger towards my mum – I felt it was irresponsible not to prepare for old age.”The cameras have helped her come to terms with the anger, the frustration, the loss – and feel a kind of acceptance, and ultimately, love. In the photographs, Hubbard could still see Berger as she’d always been. “I wonder how early the disease really started, when her reality shifted, and I’ll never get the answers.”What does Berger think of the photographs? “She gets a huge amount of strength and sense of value from being part of it, and she trusts me completely. And she’s never had anything but unconditional love for me.”Katherine Hubbard – The Great Room is atStudio Voltaire, London from 7 October until 10 January 2027Explore more on these topicsPhotographyArtExhibitionsDementiaInstallationMemoryinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: No island of strangers: why I’m using art to unite a fractured nation | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Fear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmares
Author: Ekow Eshun
Headline: Fear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmares
Content: Like extras from an Ealing comedy … Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts.Photograph: Jack Elliot Edwards/©  the artist. Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre London.View image in fullscreenLike extras from an Ealing comedy … Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts.Photograph: Jack Elliot Edwards/©  the artist. Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre London.Art and designNo island of strangers: why I’m using art to unite a fractured nationFear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmaresEkow EshunTue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the moral low points of Keir Starmer’s tenure at Downing Street was his “island of strangers” speech, with its rhetorical echoes of Enoch Powell and dispiriting description of a nation fractured by difference. After widespread criticism, Starmer recanted his words, if not the sentiment behind them. Yet his choice of language was a reminder of how the idea of the stranger – representing immigration, but also wider, more inchoate anxieties about otherness and difference – holds such a potent place in Britain today.In fact, from masked anti-migrant protesters on the south coast to xenophobic riots over the summer, from politicians vowing to stop the boats to immigration polling as the No 1 concern among UK voters, it’s probably true to say that fear of the stranger is the totemic issue of our times.Not long after Starmer’s speech, I was appointed curator of the BritishArtShow, which opens in Coventry this week. My thoughts have turned increasingly to the notion of the stranger among us as I’ve worked on the exhibition. The show, developed and produced by Hayward Gallery Touring, is the largest and most significant recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the UK.Founded in 1979, the exhibition takes place every five years, touring across the country to offer a snapshot of the ideas and ambitions of a rising generation of artists born or based in Britain. Previous versions have brought the likes of David Hockney, Bridget Riley and Anish Kapoor to national audiences.This year is the 10th edition and it features a lineup of critically lauded artists including Alvaro Barrington, Lindsey Mendick and recent Turner prize winners Jesse Darling and Jasleen Kaur.Each new iteration prompts the same question: what does the show say about British art? Or, indeed, about Britain? In the context of the globe-spanning fairs, biennales and mega-galleries that make up today’s contemporary art world, the question is possibly antique. Yet an exhibition tasked with addressing recent developments in art will inevitably reveal something about the country in which that work originates. To talk about British art, then, is also to talk about place and belonging. It is to ask who we are as individuals, as communities and as a nation.I’ve chosen to give the latest exhibition a subtitle: A Chorus of Strangers. The name is not a reference to Starmer’s speech, but it does gesture back to another much earlier period in British history also characterised by its antipathy to outsiders.View image in fullscreenMaking the Strangers’ Case … an 1897 depiction of Thomas More pleading for compassion at the 1517 May Day riots.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesOn 30 April 1517, the eve of the annual May Day festival, an angry crowd of more than 1,000 people marched through London protesting at the city’s immigrant population. Xenophobia was rife in Tudor England. Although foreigners, known as “strangers”, made up just 6% of the city’s population, they were often considered a malign presence: “Libertynes, drunkards, murderers, thieves and Conspirators,” in the words of one chronicler.As darkness fell, the mood turned ugly. Thomas More, under-sheriff of London, appealed to the crowd to turn back. But his entreaties went unheard. The mob surged through the streets sacking the shops and houses of French, Italian and Flemish merchants and craftsmen. Only after an army was called out, leading to scores of arrests and over a dozen executions, was order returned.Evil May Day, as the riot came to be known, was not quickly forgotten.In 1591 a new play,Sir Thomas More, told the story of More’s rise and fall, from civic leader to Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII and his subsequent beheading for refusing to accept the king as head of the Church of England. The drama was written collaboratively by several authors. Most prominent among them was William Shakespeare, who revisited More’s encounter with the London mob. In Shakespeare’s telling, More successfully calms the crowd by making “the Strangers’ Case”, a passionate call for empathy in place of the “mountainish inhumanity” of hatred and bigotry.Shakespeare’s scene still feels powerfully relevant. Not just due to the similarity between mob violence then and now, but because the Strangers’ Case is a reminder of how, for hundreds of years, artists have faced times of discord by asserting the value of our shared humanity. With that past in mind, the British Art Show asks: how does art today meet the fears of otherness and difference that emerge in a period of uncertainty and change?View image in fullscreenUnited in protest … Joy Gerrard, March for Palestine, Berlin, 2024.Photograph: courtesy of the artist and Cristea Roberts GalleryLet’s reflect for a moment that the idea of the stranger describes a psychological as well as a social condition. Yes, the stranger denotes a feared outsider. But as the philosopher Julia Kristeva says, we are often “strangers to ourselves”, caught within the mysteries of our psyche. The stranger might be a repressed feeling or a memory that we struggle to acknowledge, its presence curdling our view of the world, turning others into projections of our own anxieties.More and more, it feels as though, when we’re talking about the former, the stranger as outsider, what we’re actually referring to is the latter, the stranger as other, a feeling of unease and disequilibrium; a sense that the times are out of joint, and that instead of all the promises of wealth and ease that the future was supposed to bring, we find ourselves unmoored and lost. As the philosopher Marshall Berman wrote in All That Is Solid Melts into Air: The Experience of Modernity: “To be modern is to find ourselves in an environment that promises us adventure, power, joy, growth, transformation of ourselves and the world – and, at the same time, that threatens to destroy everything we have, everything we know, everything we are.”You can hear echoes of that dread in public polling – seven in 10 people fear the UK is “on the wrong track”, according toMore in Common’s 2025 Shattered Britainreport – and in the despairing labels given by theorists to our current era, such as the New Dark Age and the Age of Unhingement.Yet in uncertain times art can be a beacon. When we enter an exhibition, we leave behind the reductive thinking that only wants to see the world in terms of us versus them. We cross into a realm of complexity, contradiction and creative richness. We take on the point of view of an outsider, seeing the world anew with the eyes of a stranger. “When you are a stranger, you are both in and out. You are there but not really,” writes Ece Temelkuran in Nation of Strangers: Rebuilding Home in the 21st Century. The term stranger signifies “a pure form of curiosity”. It describes “those who are still not poisoned by the fear of the alien”. All those “to whom our time seems too strange to become complicit in its monstrosities”.This sense of openness and discovery is shared by many of the artists in the British Art Show. For example, Accounts, a sculpture by Alex Margo Arden, ties together decommissioned male mannequins from the National Motor Museum with a thick length of rope. The work might gesture to deindustrialisation or exhausted ideas of masculinity.View image in fullscreenVoices raised … a still from Julianknxx’s Shifting/ Spirit/Time.Photograph: © StudioknxxBut it’s hard to look at the men’s florid faces and side-parted hair, like bumptious extras from an Ealing comedy, and not also find something absurd and comic on show. This playfulness reflects Arden’s delight in the small, idiosyncratic private museums dotted around Britain: a favourite of hers is the Museum of Victorian Science in North Yorkshire which it boasts is“Ranked Number 1 Visitor Attraction in the Whitby Area!”. These venues collectively offer a folk history of Britain, based less on fact than storytelling, imagination and what Arden calls the “memories of memories”.Mahtab Hussain’s film Here Is the Brick, made with writer Guy Gunaratne, tells a story of south Asian and Muslim life in Britain over the past half century through a feverish montage of anti-Muslim football chants, family VHS recordings, speeches by Islamophobic politicians, excerpts from old racist TV programmes, and coverage of the 2005 London suicide bombings. The title refers to a brick thrown through the window of an Asian-owned shop that struck the storekeeper in the face, breaking his teeth. Yet the film ends on an optimistic note with a stadium full of Liverpool fans singing in praise of Mo Salah: “If he scores another few, I’ll be a Muslim too.”Other artists explore how we might claim a sense of agency within the disempowering structures of the modern world. In films by Melanie Manchot and Julianknxx, and in Joy Gerrard’s ink drawings of protesting crowds, there is dancing, singing, bodies surging on to the streets: a rejection of a status quo that is so often based on the subjection of the individual to the forces of capital; and an insistence instead on the value of gathering, of raising voices and moving or marching together.Rather than an island separated by difference then, A Chorus of Strangers offers a hymn to possibility. Through the work of the participating artists, the exhibition finds abundant evidence that life might be richer, more wonderfully strange and strangely wonderful if, instead of heeding calls to division, we choose to look at the world through the eyes of others.British Art Show 10is at the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum, Mead Gallery and Coventry University, 2 October to 10 January; then touring to Swansea, Bristol, Sheffield and Newcastle GatesheadExplore more on these topicsArt and designBritish identity and societyExhibitionsSculptureInstallationArtDrawingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there’: Damien Frost’s immaculate queer portraits | Photography | The Guardian
description: The photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat field
Author: Oliver Giles
Headline: The photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat field
Content: Beverly Fabulosity, pictured on her farm in Gungal, New South Wales.Photograph: Damien FrostView image in fullscreenBeverly Fabulosity, pictured on her farm in Gungal, New South Wales.Photograph: Damien FrostPhotography‘You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there’: Damien Frost’s immaculate queer portraitsThe photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat fieldWords byOliver Giles. Pictures by Damien FrostMon 28 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.45 EDTShareOne bright spring day, the photographer Damien Frost arrived at a farm in Gungal, outside Muswellbrook, New South Wales. Goats grazed in a paddock, eucalyptus trees stretched into the brilliant blue sky and a tin shed weathered in the sun. Frost walked into the shed and entered another world.“It’s a drag studio,” says Frost. Lining the walls were dozens of wigs and rails of flamboyant outfits belonging to Beverly Fabulosity. “I’ve never seen anything like it. It was a very Priscillascenario.”Frost grew up in Australia and is now based in London, where for more than a decade he has photographed drag queens and club kids for his acclaimed Night Flowers series. Since late August, he has been back in his home country, commissioned by Newcastle’sNew Annual festivalto photograph night owls in and around the city. These new portraits are being exhibited alongside a selection from Frost’s archive at Watt Space gallery as part of the festival.View image in fullscreenLuke Harris, Blacks Club, Soho.View image in fullscreenJulius Reuben, Soho, 2017.View image in fullscreenMarco Tullio Siviglia, Berlin, 2019.View image in fullscreenOtamere wearing Muriel Nisse, Hackney, 2018.Photograph: Damien FrostThe exhibition is a full-circle moment for Frost, who studied at the University of Newcastle after growing up in Sydney. Returning to Australia has inspired a change in his approach: in London, he meets and photographs his subjects in or around clubs, although his portraits appear so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio. “Coming back to my home country, I wanted to show a little bit of the environment these people are working in,” he says.The locations are a far cry from nightclubs or the catwalks of RuPaul’sDragRace. One person posed near the city’s port against a backdrop of coal trains. Others appear in their homes, on suburban streets, in the Stockton sand dunes. Beverly Fabulosity is pictured in a field wearing a white gown and a towering wig, goats milling around her. “You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there,” says Frost.View image in fullscreenMolly Poppinz at home in lounge room, Lambton, NSW.View image in fullscreenFinlay Ross in the staff room at Creator Incubator, Newcastle, NSW.Photograph: Damien FrostView image in fullscreenBenjamin Frazer McKenzie and ZEAL.H at Stockton sand dunes, NSW.Whether he photographs people on a farm or at a warehouse party, Frost is most interested in how people use fashion, makeup and prosthetics to explore their identity. “I’m not looking for people in fancy dress, I’m looking for people who are expressing something,” he says. Sometimes, this goes beyond experiments with glamour, style or gender. “A lot of the photos I take, the characters can be quite grotesque,” says Frost. “Often, it’s people dressing up as a manifestation of how they feel they’ve been treated … they’re made to feel like a monster, so they reclaim that.”Some of his subjects work for months on a single look they only wear once. “I liken it to Buddhist sand sculptures, where they spend hours and hours on an intricate pattern and just wipe it all off at the end,” says Frost. His photographs immortalise these creations and showcase them to people who might never otherwise encounter them.View image in fullscreenLouisa Magrics in Carrington, NSW.View image in fullscreenJenna Pippin at Wangi Wangi power station, NSW.Looking through his archive, Frost can trace changes in drag culture. Economic pressures have led to the closure ofmore than half the LGBTQ+ venuesin London. On top of that, “not just in drag, but even in artistic practices, social media’s algorithms now influence the direction that people go with their work”, says Frost. This leads to “a lot of people who turn [themselves] into a brand … which they then don’t want to deviate from”.More radical forms of self-expression are still out there, though: “You just have to look a bit harder for them.”Night Flowers: Damien Frostis at Watt Space gallery until 7 November as part of the New Annual festival in Newcastle, NSW

title: Jonathan Anderson mixes Austen romance with chic streetware in Dior’s Paris show | Dior | The Guardian
description: Designer’s latest work takes bold steps away from the fashion house’s brand, creating a show that felt like an event
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Designer’s latest work takes bold steps away from the fashion house’s brand, creating a show that felt like an event
Content: Trees and mist were conjured in the Tuileries Garden for the Dior show.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrees and mist were conjured in the Tuileries Garden for the Dior show.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersDiorJonathan Anderson mixes Austen romance with chic streetware in Dior’s Paris showDesigner’s latest work takes bold steps away from the fashion house’s brand, creating a show that felt like an eventJess Cartner-Morleyin ParisTue 29 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Iwant to land on a vibe.” This was howDiordesigner Jonathan Anderson, one year into what is arguably the biggest job in fashion, summed up his assignment before his latest show. Expounding on chiffon and buttons with the intensity of a barrister delivering a closing speech in the high court, ruffling his hair as if his mind might at any moment explode with ideas, Anderson brings more brainpower to the pursuit of the vibe than the superficial phrasing suggests.View image in fullscreenJonathan Anderson accepting applause after the show.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersThe vibe is coming in to land. This Dior show felt like an event, which is the bar Christian Dior set for his successors back in 1947, when his New Look silhouette made front pages all over the world. Overnight, trees had emerged out of the circular pond in the Tuileries Garden in Paris, and – thanks to the deep pockets of owners LVMH – a magical mist conjured to swirl around them, lending a cinematic grandeur to the slender catwalk spanning the water. (The trees will be replanted elsewhere in the gardens, after the show.)“We are in search of a silhouette,” Anderson explained. The show began and ended with a distinctive shape: a short, kicky skirt in layers of chiffon, the layers catching the light like breaking surf, worn with a soft, short jacket or layers of sheer shirting. He is resistant to being pinned down to one look, though, so in between there were bronze metallic trousers, and luxurious double-breasted coats, and strapless bow-trimmed cocktail dresses tightly frilled as carnation petals.View image in fullscreenMany of the clothes shown were rarefied takes on what is being worn on the chic streets of Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreen“We are in search of a silhouette,” Anderson said.Photograph: Jumeau Alexis/ABACA/Shutterstock“People have a preconceived idea of what Dior should be, and you don’t take the customer from zero to 100 overnight,” he said. His emotional tone is naturally bone-dry, but he is finding a take on “romantic” – a word that is central to Dior, and one that he kept returning to – where he can take that customer somewhere new. His idea of romance, he said, is Jane Austen. Romance, for Anderson, is never going to mean losing his head. If Dior is to get their happy ending, expect plenty of wry asides along the way.“It’s not about, ‘is it wearable or not wearable?’,” he said. “It’s not about, ‘is it going to be worn in the street?’ It’s more about: this is a person, a look, I would love to see in the street.” Nonetheless, many of the clothes were rarefied takes on what is being worn on the chic streets around the Tuileries right now; oversized untucked shirts, sheer fabrics worn in layers, fringed edges, a glimpse of bra, shots of joyful colour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJonathan Anderson delivers high-concept Dior collection that celebrates the sculpturalRead moreThe luxury is in the detail: Murano glass buttons, shawl-collar jackets with the underside of the lapel lined in faux fur, to be glimpsed when a collar is popped. Nuggets of Dior’s long history threaded through the lineup included houndstooth, a Dior classic made unstodgy by being reimagined in sheer chiffon layers, a Barn jacket meets Bar jacket mashup with a corduroy collar, and a revival of zippered sandals from John Galliano’s era at Dior. “This year was about trying to rattle the brand and see what falls out,” Anderson said. “It’s never going to be just one thing, I’d get bored.”Explore more on these topicsDiorLuxury goods sectorParis fashion weekFashion weeksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just look at this monstrosity!’ Inside Britain’s bilious back yard shed wars | Homes | The Guardian
description: The number of luxury sheds and garden rooms has rocketed since the pandemic – fuelled by those wanting an office, a gym or extra living space. Meanwhile, the resentment between neighbours has been rising, too
Author: Emily Retter
Headline: The number of luxury sheds and garden rooms has rocketed since the pandemic – fuelled by those wanting an office, a gym or extra living space. Meanwhile, the resentment between neighbours has been rising, too
Content: Composite: GuardianDesign; deepblue4you;Joe_Potato;Shedwa;UroshPetrovicr;vavlt;O Kemppainen;Aleksandra_Pikalova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: GuardianDesign; deepblue4you;Joe_Potato;Shedwa;UroshPetrovicr;vavlt;O Kemppainen;Aleksandra_Pikalova/Getty ImagesHomes‘Just look at this monstrosity!’ Inside Britain’s bilious back yard shed warsThe number of luxury sheds and garden rooms has rocketed since the pandemic – fuelled by those wanting an office, a gym or extra living space. Meanwhile, the resentment between neighbours has been rising, tooEmily RetterTue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLinda loves her shed. She loves that she can work there rather than in her dining room, which her toddler likes to tear through. She loves its Scandinavian vibe – it’s clad in wood and set on decking at the bottom of her garden. She loves the views of the countryside from the window by her desk. Or she did. Her desk faces the wall now, because she’s too nervous to face her neighbour. She never sits on the decking, either. “What if they see me?” she says. “It’s a horrible feeling.”Linda’s neighbours are unhappy about her shed, or “garden room”, which is actually two rooms. They do not like its size (7.25 metres by 2.74 metres, or 3.5 metres if you include the raised decking) or its position, about 30 metres away from their house. Linda says they have barely spoken since the construction, which is awkward, as the gardens are separated by a low fence.The neighbours say the shed is more than half a metre too tall and too close to their property for it to be a “permitted development”, one that can be built without applying for planning permission. In England and Wales, there is a height cap of 2.5 metres from the ground if any part of the outbuilding falls within 2 metres of a boundary (it is within 1 metre of a boundary in Scotland). If the building is further from the boundary, it can be 3 metres or 4 metres high, depending on the roof type. The council agreed and told Linda she needed to apply for retrospective planning permission. She says it was an “honest mistake” and that she received the wrong guidance from her builders. “I was mortified. I would never have done it intentionally,” she says.Before the build, Linda says, she had a friendly relationship with her neighbours; they would lend each other tools and garden materials. She says she had had an informal conversation with her neighbours about building a garden room in the space and heard no objections. Her neighbours say they were not consulted at all before construction, which took about a month.Linda says she found out the extent of her neighbours’ feelings about her shed only in the paperwork for their planning dispute. They said they could see it from every window of their home and that they felt they had lost all sense of privacy, which had affected their daily lives and mental wellbeing. They also said an estate agent told them it had negatively affected the value of their home.View image in fullscreen‘Planning rules for these outhouses are monumentally complex.’Photograph: stocknshares/Getty ImagesRetrospective planning permission for her shed has been granted, on the condition that a privacy screen and other planting are put up. Was it worth it? Yes, Linda believes, but she says: “I wish we had known to go about it the right way; it would have saved us money and a heck of a lot of effort and time …”The dispute between Linda and her neighbours is just one example of simmering resentment over the increased use of these kinds of outhouses in the UK. The news is regularly peppered with spicy shed disputes – and no social strata is exempt.Pink Floyd’s David Gilmourwas ordered to move a shed in his garden in upmarket Hampstead, north London, last year after it was described as “intrusive” and “overbearing” by neighbours who wanted a retrospective planning application to be refused. It was ordered to be rebuilt further back from the boundary.Part of the reason for these disputes is the growing popularity of outhouses. Simon Rix, a senior planning consultant and a director of Planix.uk, a consultancy company that advises people who want to extend, says he received “a trickle” of clients who wanted to build luxury sheds before the pandemic, but that has “probably gone up tenfold”.As well as home offices, gyms and storage, many are used for habitable living spaces, as the housing crisis continues to stunt home-buying. “Quite a lot of people are coming to me because they want to move into it and let their children live in the main house,” Rix says. He is also seeing more static caravans in gardens for the same reason – these don’t count as a “development” and do not need planning permission if they are housing a family member. “Neighbours get really grumpy, because they can be quite tall and imposing,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘Homeowners often wrongly assume: it’s my garden, I can do what I want.’Photograph: Guido Mieth/Getty ImagesPlanning rules around these outhouses are “monumentally complex”, says Rix, who would like them to be simplified. Both sides regularly misunderstand their rights. “Neighbours frequently assume that if something looks large, blocks a view or sits right on the fence line, it must be illegal. Conversely, homeowners often wrongly assume: ‘It’s my garden, I can do what I want.’ This gap in understanding, combined with the post-pandemic boom, is creating a perfect storm for neighbourhood disputes,” he says.The regulations and rules around erecting outbuildings as part of permitted development vary not only in terms of the height and the proximity to a neighbour’s boundary. They must also be single storey and, in England and Wales, not “forward of the principal elevation” – the front wall of the house facing the highway (in Scotland, there is some provision for a small shed). Outbuildings cannot take up more than 50% of the total garden, either, and listed homes and those in conservation areas and other special sites face different restrictions. According toresearch by Ronseal, more than 40% of Britons are unaware some sheds will require a planning application.double quotation markIt’s so close to the boundary, he climbed on to our picnic table with a tape measureYet even outhouses that meet permitted development heights can loom large and cause tension in tightly packed British gardens. Emma watched her husband creep into their garden under cover of darkness late one night to measure the shed their neighbours were constructing close to the boundary, because it looked so vast. “He climbed on to our picnic table with a tape measure,” she says. “It’s so close to our boundary that it wasn’t a stretch to measure it – he didn’t even need to hang over the fence.”The shed measured under 2.5 metres and the couple had to accept that it was permitted. They felt that mentioning anything to the neighbour would only cause bad feeling, but while they have grown used to the building, which is barely used, they worry about how potential buyers will view it. “The overriding factor is they are small gardens,” says Emma. The plots are around 10 metres by 7 metres. The neighbour mentioned their plans, but “we thought it would be a pod … we didn’t anticipate the sheer size”, she says. “Remaining friends” was most important. “We get on well and didn’t want to rock the boat,” she adds. “But if it was being used as a home office constantly, with phone calls being made and they’re looking back at you, maybe we’d feel differently.”Dr Mike Talbot, a psychotherapist and the CEO of UK Mediation, says the company has noticed a rise in inquiries concerning external structures such as sheds, garden rooms, hot tubs and even trampolines. He believes that councils tend not to intervene and often recommend mediation. Fewer than 10% of inquiries actually reach that stage, though, because while the opposing neighbour is usually the one to call them, they must then approach the shed builder – who generally does not wish to join (or share the £450 cost of the process). He recalls an occasion when a shed window “was mysteriously broken” and things turned nasty: “The shed owner went round and threatened to smash their neighbour’s face in.”However, if mediation takes place, it can be positive. One set of neighbours built a shed to be used as a playroom and office with a window on the neighbour’s side. They had previously had a good relationship, but were “not talking … which is quite common”. (Talbot says “slamming doors or dirty looks in the driveway” are other repercussions.) The compromise was blocking the window and putting up a trellis, which appeased both parties. In another example, an agreement was made concerning the times at which the shed owner’s teenage children could use the space.View image in fullscreenSlamming doors or dirty looks in the driveway are some of the potential repercussions of building a garden shed.Photograph: Ekaterina Demidova/Getty ImagesTalbot believes that people are “more insular” than they used to be and less concerned than previous generations were about getting on with their neighbours. Social media plays a part, too. “We are so much more subject to scrutiny and you know that, if you do something people consider to be out of order, it’s going to be on the local Facebook group,” he says. “Trust is slower to build; we are more cautious of whom we talk to.” But if neighbours build a good relationship, he says, they are less likely to react negatively if a large shed does appear.Dan has a good relationship with his neighbours, so when they approached him to discuss their plans for a structure in their 20-metre garden for a family member to stay in, “I had no problem”, he says. As it would be more than 2.5 metres high and a habitable dwelling, the neighbours had to apply for planning permission. “I looked at the plans and it seemed reasonable,” says Dan.However, issues encountered during construction meant the height increased. When Dan and his partner arrived home from holiday, “I went to our bathroom, looked out of the window and said: ‘You need to come here immediately and look at this monstrosity,’” he says. After an emotional conversation with the neighbours, they agreed to take the height down, but Dan believes it is still about 1.5 metres higher than agreed in the original plans. For the sake of keeping good relations, he has decided not to go to the council and has instead spent about £2,000 on fencing to try to hide the structure.“I did not want to ruin their plans,” he says. “But I did feel emotionally blackmailed.” While he is getting used to it, and continues to chat pleasantly with the neighbours, “when we look out of our living room window, it’s right there. And if someone is stood in that building, they are looking right in at us. It just feels slightly invasive. When people come round and notice it, they go: ‘Oh my God, what?’ They’re shocked.” Dan’s main worry, however, is the impact it may have when he comes to sell his house.Linda, meanwhile, hopes to rebuild relations with her neighbours. “We’re not horrible people, on either side,” she says. “No one has done anything wrong here.” But unlike her shed, which will weather and soften, she knows there is no guarantee of this.Names have been changedDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
