title: Is tech the secret to a more analogue life? How gadgets, apps and tips could actually reduce your screen time | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It’s often thought of as the problem, but what if the right technology could help us switch off and live more in the moment?
Author: Hannah Rochell
Headline: It’s often thought of as the problem, but what if the right technology could help us switch off and live more in the moment?
Content: Take it outside: digital tools can encourage us to spend more time in nature.Photograph: Amar Ghazall/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake it outside: digital tools can encourage us to spend more time in nature.Photograph: Amar Ghazall/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleIs tech the secret to a more analogue life? How gadgets, apps and tips could actually reduce your screen timeIt’s often thought of as the problem, but what if the right technology could help us switch off and live more in the moment?The best screen-free activitiesHannah RochellTue 29 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the continuedbacklash against AIand growing concern about our reliance on screens, an analogue life has never looked so appealing. I haven’t gone so far as to get myself ananalogue bagjust yet, but I have done a relatively complex puzzle and read five physical books this year, which is already two more than in 2025.But it also struck me recently that I have, somewhat conversely, been using digital tools to do a lot of analogue activities. What if tech could help us live more in the presentandreduce our screen time, while benefiting our physical and mental health in the long run?With that in mind, here are six ideas for leading a more analogue life – with a little help from tech.How to lead a more analogue lifeIdentifying birdsongView image in fullscreenCall of the wild: learn to recognise birds by sound.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/GettyI’ve been a birdwatcher since I was nine, but have always struggled to identify calls and songs. While I have a huge stash of bird books, I have never been able to grasp the whimsical descriptions of how they sound, such as “zuz”, “ch-ch-si-si-si” or “tu-reep”. Last year, however, I discovered theMerlin app, which has transformed my hobby into something rather beautiful. The app, which is free and was developed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, lets you record what you hear and then suggests which birds are chirping nearby, using your location as a guide.It turned out that I had been misidentifying wrens, blackcaps, willow warblers and dunnocks as robins for four decades. Now I know what they sound like, I have a better chance of spotting them, which is not always easy with the sometimes elusive blackcap. I like to spend five minutes in the morning and evening sitting still in the garden or by an open window, allowing the app to help me identify and enjoy birdsong. Merlin has also spurred me to take my dogs on more interesting forest walks because the denser the trees, the more interesting the birdsong.Exploring new trailsView image in fullscreenOn the right track: use tech to discover new routes.Photograph: Justin Paget/GettyKeeping an eye on my step count has undoubtedly helped me to be more active, but those who fancy more than my brisk woodland walks may benefit from more than the built-in health app that comes with many smartphones.“I love to useStravaheatmaps to explore new areas. It’s especially useful when I see a trail that looks fun, but don’t know where it leads or if it’s just an animal track,” saysFlora Beverley, an ultramarathon runner and content creator. She adds that heatmaps build confidence because you know roughly where you’ll end up: “It means I can get myself lost on a run and know I can still find my way back. Also, once you’ve used it for a bit, it becomes easy to see the hallmark of ‘fun’ trails – twisty, windy, on a hill, great views – just by looking at the map. Wherever I travel, I always know where the good trails are and can go off-roading.”Getting better at craftsView image in fullscreenStitch by stitch: video guides can help you master a new craft.Photograph: simonapilolla/GettyLast winter I finally learned to knit, thanks to a kit fromWool and the Gang, which I used to make a natty little bonnet. I’ve been meaning to join a knitting club for years, but since this is apparently never going to happen, using the brilliant video tutorials on the brand’s website was the next best thing. Of course, I spent most of my needle time looking at my knitting, not at a screen, but whenever I got stuck, it was like having a friendly, skilled and very young grandmother on hand to help. I would have given up on the project without this visual aid, and it gave me the confidence to make another, much better version of the bonnet when I had finished the first one.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLearning to drumView image in fullscreenStick with it: picking up a new skill, one beat at a time.Photograph: Milan Markovic/GettyI have wanted to learn to play the drums for years, and since I turn 50 next year, now seems like as good a time as ever. I am taking lessons with a real person on their acoustic drum kit, but I have gone digital alongside this both to improve more quickly and to play when my husband is in the room next door watching reruns of House without disturbing him (too much).Mysecondhand electric drum kit(mine was sourced secondhand from my 83-year-old dad’s bandmate, no less) can be played through headphones and attached to my iPhone so I can drum along to songs or, even better, learn from video tutorials on YouTube. Thanks to six years of playing the violin as a child, I am able to read music, so I can get lost in it for hours at a time. Long term, the plan is to progress to my own acoustic kit (advance apologies to my neighbours – I will be considerate) and maybe even start gigging. It doesn’t get more analogue than hitting things with sticks on a stage, after all.Getting the nudge to go outsideFunctional accessories and wearable tech are getting more good looking, with jewellery-style products, such asLoop’s Swarovski earplugsandOura’s rings, which track sleep, steps and heart rate. I’ve never been a fan of smartwatches – is there anything more annoying than the person next to you in a yoga class checking their messages when they should be relaxing into their breath work? – but I do like the subtlety of a ring, particularly since my step count is often out of kilter with my phone because I don’t carry it everywhere with me.For more, read technology expert Samuel Gibbs’s pick of thebest running watchesUnderstanding plant lifeView image in fullscreenKnow your weeds: plant ID apps can help you decide what stays and what goes.Photograph: fermate/GettyKeeping your garden wild is all well and good, but you could end up with some pretty nasty plants popping up – a particular risk for children or pets. I’m far more likely to take my phone outdoors than a hardback book, so thanks to thePictureThisapp, I can more easily distinguish my hemlock water dropwort (deadly) from my wild carrot (not deadly), and even my creeping buttercup (a thug) from my field buttercup (a real beauty). In turn, I am able to spend time doing selective weeding, taking out the plants I really don’t want and keeping those that will benefit the ecosystem (and aesthetics) of my garden, such as the native pussy willow that took up residence this year next to the barbecue.For more, read our roundup of thebest screen-free, calming activitiesHannah Rochell is a journalist who specialises in writing about – and experiencing – a slower, more sustainable lifestyle, which she documents on her SubstackSlowette. This involves everything from switching toeco-friendly cleaning productsand advocating fordehumidifiersinstead of tumble dryers, to shopping exclusively at responsible fashion brands and learning to sewExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterGadgetsAppsHobbiesGardensKnittingCraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: On the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ grows | Whisky | The Guardian
description: Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures
Content: With whisky production paused at Holyrood Distillery in Edinburgh, the copper stills sit idle.Photograph: Holyrood DistilleryView image in fullscreenWith whisky production paused at Holyrood Distillery in Edinburgh, the copper stills sit idle.Photograph: Holyrood DistilleryWhiskyOn the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ growsDemand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closuresPatrick GreenfieldTue 29 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleObscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky. By the time the latest set of warehouses are finished on the former opencast coal mine, Diageo’s 220-hectare (544-acre) maturation campus will be able to store almost 3m casks of Scotch. The drinks multinational needs the space.After a 15-year boom turbocharged by the Covid-19 pandemic, demand for Scotch whisky has slumped around the world. Distilleries have paused production acrossScotlandto avoid adding to the glut of supply, known as a “whisky loch” – the equivalent of a “wine lake”.Last week, the community-owned GlenWyvis Distillery in the Highlands announced it would appoint administrators following sustained financial pressure in the whisky market. On Monday, workers at Cameronbridge, Diageo’s largest distillery, a short drive from Cluny bond, began strike action in opposition to the company’s plans to cut hundreds of jobs across its Scottish operation.Diageo produces about one in three bottles of Scotch globally, including popular brands such as Johnnie Walker. Dozens of Scotland’s 156 active distilleries are rumoured to be up for sale.“Strangely, Scotch has had a really good time since the 2008 financial crisis,” said industry veteran Nick Morgan. “But people have stopped buying at the crazy rates they had been.View image in fullscreen‘People who bought whisky in the pandemic realised they had enough for two or three years.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images“People who bought whisky in the pandemic because they had nothing else to do realised they probably had enough at home for two or three years. There’s increased awareness of health issues, many are choosing to drink less, and booze got very expensive during the good years for the business.”Fluctuations in Scotch whisky’s £5.36bn export market have proven particularly hard to navigate. By law, the drink must be matured for a minimum of three years in an oak cask in Scotland, with high-end speciality Scotch being aged in barrels for up to 40 years. Such lengthy maturation periods, used to create a wide range of flavour profiles from sweet to sulphurous, can make it hard to plan production.DespiteDonald Trump’s decision to remove dutieson Scotch exports to the US after the King and Queen’s state visit to the White House earlier this year, the industry had already suffered a significant hit. The US president’s “liberation day” tariffs in April 2025 resulted ina 15% fall in Scotch exports to the US, according to the Scotch Whisky Association.Demand in France – until recently the largest market by volume – has fallen, while the market in China has never really taken off as hoped. Optimists point to early signs of a tentative recovery, however, withthe industry returning to growthin the first half of this year. Exports to India in particular have surged – but have not yet offset declines elsewhere.A line chart shows Scotch sales growing in India and falling in France, the US and the rest of the UK outside Scotland. Brazil also shows slight growth, but after a large dipThe downturn is by no means limited to Scotch, either. Many drinks manufacturers are experiencing a post-pandemic slump, with five of the biggest publicly listed alcohol producers sitting ona record $22bn of aging spirits, according to the Financial Times.Holyrood Distillery, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat inEdinburgh, is among those to have paused production while its owners wait out the difficult period. Its bulbous copper stills, which would usually be hard at work producing single-malt Scotch, sit idle. Co-founder Rob Carpenter says he does not know when that will change.“Anecdotally, my understanding is that the industry might be producing around a third of its normal level right now,” he said. “No one has a crystal ball, so nobody knows what is going to happen 10 years from now. You try to anticipate where things are going to be. It is a curse of the industry in a sense.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnlike many of its rivals, Holyrood Distillery benefits from tourists visiting the Scottish capital. About 40,000 people each year tour the stone building, which is almost 200 years old and used to support theInnocent railway. The tours account for around half of the company’s current revenue.View image in fullscreenRob Carpenter, Holyrood Distillery co-founderPhotograph: Holyrood Distillery“It is not really that people have stopped drinking spirits,” Carpenter added. “[But] consumers are nervous. We all see what’s happening in the world. There is not a lot of predictability in things right now, and people are just being careful with what they spend their money on. This is a luxury spirit.”The current industry downturn is not new. In the 1980s, the Scotch whisky industry faced a similar mixture of weak demand and chronic oversupply, causing a flurry of distillery closures across Scotland. The rise of Japanese whisky producers, a global economic downturn, and overconfidence from a 1970s boom drove a prolonged bust.Today, few think the latest slump is the beginning of a permanent change in the industry’s fortunes. When Holyrood Distillery opens for tours, visitors file in, scanning through the single malts on the shelves.“Whisky is a waiting game,” said Morgan, who charted Johnnie Walker’s 200-year history in a 2020 book. “If you look at the data on sales, every time you have one of these downturns, it comes back higher. At the moment, the business is in the trough. I can pretty much assure you in five years time, when demand really cranks up again, they’ll find they haven’t got enough whisky, and they’ll have to switch everything on.”Explore more on these topicsWhiskyFood & drink industryScotlandDiageoEdinburghfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Angel Delight croissants?! The autumn food trends hotlist | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: What’s good and what’s going off this autumn in the world of food
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What’s good and what’s going off this autumn in the world of food
Content: Move over minimalism, doilies are back!Photograph: sbossert/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMove over minimalism, doilies are back!Photograph: sbossert/Getty ImagesThe taste matrixAutumn food and drinkAngel Delight croissants?! The autumn food trends hotlistWhat’s good and what’s going off this autumn in the world of foodGurdeep LoyalTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFreshManchesterView image in fullscreenFarm-to-table bistronomy atHigher Ground(pictured above),Layr’shole-in-the-wall tiramisu hatch, Hong Kong dim sum atTai Wu, laminated baked perfection atHalf Dozen Other, understated seasonal exquisiteness atErst. One of the most exciting food cities in the UK right now.Angel Delight croissantsTheevolution of “school cake mania” is now manifesting as unironic “Angel Delight obsession”. See the strawberry Angel Delight croissants at Public & Plants throughout the Midlands, and George Egg’s Guinness Angel Delight.Chilli crisp matured camembertView image in fullscreenCalder Cheesesin Todmorden has created a triple cream Delice de Bourgogne, maturedwithLao Gan Ma chilli crisp – epic!Astragalus rootThe (allegedly) immune system boosting adaptogen (AKA milkvetch) that’s being hailed as the new lion’s mane. All the rage atErewhon, even though it tastes like wet twigs.Pottery diningThe trendiest spots to eat right now are pottery studio-restaurants – artfully pairing hand crafted ceramics and food. Check outFecund Supperclubfrom Will Martin and Kiln in Newcastle.FenugreekView image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Matthew HagueBitter is the new sweet and with it, everyone is cooking with fresh fenugreek and fenugreek seeds. Check out Aktar Islam’s Dahi paneer with fenugreek atOudh, the Georgianchkmerliwith blue fenugreek atKinkally, and the spiced fenugreek baba dessert atAkub by Fadi Kattan(above).Silly crispsSilly crisps, silly snacks – all things silly. The inventive gastronomic reels series fromchef Alex Castaldoof Tonge Tied Hot Sauce that we can’t get enough of.Everything seasoning riffsFromGoat Rodeo Goods’ Spicy Disco Mixwith pink peppercorns and juniper, toM&S’ Everything Greek Seasoningwith oregano and mint, we can’t stop sprinkling everything on everything.Tropical vinegarsView image in fullscreenThe fiery Filipino coconut vinegar Suka Pinakurat is the must-buy pantry ingredient of the season – and makes the tastiest adobos. Also check out Acid League’s mango-jalepino‘living’ ACV dressingand themaple smoked pineapple vinegar(above) from Kai by Matblak.Perennial eatingLiving Rootsby Liz Carlisle and Aubrey Streit Krug has everyone talking. Advocating for permaculture eating from plants that root deeply into the soil and don’t die after one year.Angostura everythingNot just for cocktails. Stir into bolognese, add to tangy salad dressings, use it to enliven buttercream icings and melt into hot chocolates. You even splash it over freshly fried chip shop chips. Yes, really.StaleThe CotswoldsView image in fullscreenTheStudio Nicholsontrenchcoat brigade are all week-ending in Wiltshire’s Nader valley now. See you at the bar ofTeffont House(above) or in the walled garden ofPythouse Kitchen Garden.No added sugarBrown sugar lattes, muscovado brownies, jaggery rice pudding, panela chocolate. Craft and unrefined sugars, rich in molasses, are the flavour superstar of the moment.Dot cakesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cavan Images/AlamyIt’s school cake in apot… stop it. All hail the return of proper lemon drizzle, coffee-walnut and buttery pound cakes heavyhanded on the vanilla.BurrataIt has officially crossed the tipping point from exhilarating to exhausted. Time for oozy autumnal cheeses with mushroomy funk: Stinking Bishop, Epoisse andLa Tur Alta Langa.Double figure coversThe hottest dining spots around the country are seating eight to 10 people. Check outGwenin Machynlleth, Wales,Appalachiain Shoreditch andJuno Omakasein Notting Hill.Smashed everythingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Muhammad Diponegoro/AlamySmashed tacos, smashed burgers, smashed croissants, smashed smash. We’re all for crispy edges, but not all our food being smooshed until it’s paper thin.Brutalist aestheticsView image in fullscreen‘The return of lace doilies, mismatched crockery, and chintzy cushions.’Photograph: Tetra Images/AlamyThe identikit minimal Berlin aesthetic for cafes and restaurants is making way for the return of lace doilies, mismatched crockery and chintzy cushions. Bric-a-brac Boho vibes are back.Ramen snobberySure, hand-pulling your own noodles and making a broth rich in kombu and collagen is delicious, but pimping instant ramen with fried Spam and Kraft cheese slices is all the rage.Predictable picklesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesThe latest humble brag flex for dinner parties is what surprising thing you’ve home pickled:Buddha’s Hand, magnolia petals, crispy bacon, even gummy bears.Low lightWhere only the food is lit and you dine in the dark. We didn’t get dressed up inSimone Rocha for no one in the restaurant to be able to see.Explore more on these topicsAutumn food and drinkThe taste matrixFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Autumn food stars: what to cook, plant and pick now | Food | The Guardian
description: Cook up mushrooms, leeks and foraged chestnuts, pick fruit, sow broad beans for spring and harvest squash
Author: Mark Diacono
Headline: Cook up mushrooms, leeks and foraged chestnuts, pick fruit, sow broad beans for spring and harvest squash
Content: Photograph: Phoebe Pearson / The Guardian, Food Styling - El KempView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Phoebe Pearson / The Guardian, Food Styling - El KempFoodAutumn food stars: what to cook, plant and pick nowCook up mushrooms, leeks and foraged chestnuts, pick fruit, sow broad beans for spring and harvest squashMark DiaconoTue 29 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuinceHard as a baseball and initially unpromising, quince are at their best cooked until beautifully aromatic. To save the torture of peeling (thank you, queen of preservingPam Corbin), poach whole until soft, cool, then discard the core and blitz.LeeksTry cooking these sweet, oniony joys in a moderate oven, wrapped in foil with just a dash of olive oil and a sliced garlic clove per leek, until soft and luscious – about 40 minutes, depending on thickness.AppleOf the thousands of apple varieties, you’ll find only a few in the shops. For those with the best flavour and texture – including Egremont Russet, Worcester Pearmain, and Cox’s Orange Pippin – buy direct or from online suppliers, such asRiverford.SquashAs good as a standard butternut can be,Uchiki Kuri, crown prince and acorn table are a class apart and really worth looking for. Roast unpeeled and deseeded, with a little oil and earthy spices, until soft.Porcini andchanterellesSeptember and October are the best time to pick chanterelles (AKA girolles) and porcini (AKA ceps/penny buns), when warm weather followed by rain makes them most abundant. Take John Wright’sMushrooms: River Cottage Handbookto identify them, or buy fresh fungi online.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Miki LoweChestnutsAutumn doesn’t feel fully here until I’m roasting chestnuts (while silently singing) over an open fire. Cut a cross into the end and cook using a chestnut roaster or dry frying pan, until their scent rises and the skin splits, being careful not to burn them, as they turn bitter easily.ChilliesMost supermarket chillies are within a narrow band of heat, flavour and aroma: order from specialist growers, such asSouth Devon Chilli Farm, and choose from the milder chillies, such as the rich and complex poblano to the super-hots, like Carolina Reaper.In the gardenSowbroad beans knuckle deep for an early crop in spring (Claudia Aquadulce are best in autumn).Harvestsquash by cutting them with a short stalk (it helps prevent rotting) and store somewhere light and cool to ripen for a week or so before storing until ready to use.Pickand ripen any remaining tomatoes on a sunny windowsill or in a paper bag with a banana – the ethylene helps them develop.Dig upand compost any pepper, chilli, tomato and aubergine plants as the first frosts will finish them off.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkGardening adviceFruitNuts and seedsAllotmentsVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for turmeric chicken and cardamom apple tart | Food | The Guardian
description: A rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the meal
Author: Thomasina Miers
Headline: A rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the meal
Content: Thomasina Miers’ turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilli.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilli.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.Thomasina Miers recipesFoodThomasina Miers’ recipes for turmeric chicken and cardamom apple tartA rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the mealThomasina MiersTue 29 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite the back-to-school, back-to-work vibes of September, I also think it’s a time of celebration. There’s the feeling of new things, with apples, corn, walnuts, squash and mushrooms appearing at the markets, and my garden has finally emerged from its drought-induced slumber, as if coming out of a trance – it is greener, more alive, reawakening. There’s still the odd bit of warm weather in which to play, too, so light up the grill, get creative in the kitchen and dance like it’s June again.Grilled turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilliRich Indian spices, sweet onion, garlic and lemon make this marinade stand out when it hits the grill. Serve with a garlicky raita on the side.Prep10 minMarinate30 min+Cook30 minServes4-61kg chickenthighs(about 6), preferably boneless and skin-on2 tsp sea salt1 medium onion,peeled and roughly chopped2 fat garlic cloves,peeled2 red chillies1 tsp ground turmeric2 heaped tsp garam masala1 lemon300g kefir½ tsp chilli powder(optional) – kashmiri for a mild flavour, ancho for a rounded taste and a little heat, cayenne if you like things hot1 handfulfresh coriander, leaves pickedFor the raita½ cucumber1 fat garlic clove,peeled and finely gratedSalt and pepperSeason the chicken thighs generously with salt. Put the onions, garlic, chillies and spices in a food processor, squeeze in the juice of half a lemon and blitz to a paste, scraping down the sides of the bowl a few times as you go. Add a teaspoon of salt and 100g kefir, and blitz again to make a beautiful, ochre-coloured paste. Taste it – I like to add some chilli powder. Slather the marinade all over the chicken thighs and leave for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or for a few hours/overnight in the fridge.Shortly before you’re ready to eat, coarsely grate the cucumber skin and all into a sieve, suspend it over a bowl, and push down to squeeze out any water (the juice is a delicious drink; try it with a little salt and pepper). Mix the squeezed cucumber with the remaining kefir and grated garlic, then season generously.Heat a griddle pan (or barbecue) and chargrill the chicken for six minutes on each side, until the meat is cooked through and the skin is deliciously crisp and golden. Serve scattered with fresh coriander, the remaining half-lemon cut into wedges and the raita.Sugar-burnt cardamom and apple puff tartView image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ sugar-burnt cardamom apple puff tart.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.A crisp, caramelised, scented tart that takes very little time to prepare, but still feels like a proper pudding.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes6-810 green cardamom pods100gsugarSalt5 medium sharp, crispapples(about 450g)Juice of½ lemon40g unsalted butter1320g sheet shop-boughtpuff pastry(preferably all-butter)Plain flour, for dusting1 small egg40g ground almondsStart by making a cardamom sugar. Put the pods in a mortar and bash them a few times with a pestle. Slip off and discard the loosened green sleeves, then bash the remaining black seeds with vigour. Add the sugar and a generous pinch of salt, and bash again to release the cardamom oils and aromatics into the sugar.Quarter and core the apples, then slice into 2-3mm-thick half-moons. As you slice them, toss in a bowl with the lemon juice so they don’t discolour. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Melt the butter in a small pan (or in the microwave). Lay out the pastry on a board. Lightly flour a rolling pin, then roll the pastry so it’s a little larger and a little thinner, but still in a similar rectangular shape. Line a baking tray with baking paper, lay the pastry on top and use a small, sharp knife carefully to mark a 2cm border all around the edge; take care not to cut through the pastry completely. Prick the inside of the border all over with a fork (this will stop it rising in the oven). Whisk the egg with a teaspoon of water, then brush this all over the pastry.Bake for five minutes, then remove and scatter the ground almonds all over the centre of the pastry. Arrange the apple slices in an overlapping pattern on top, then drizzle or brush with the melted butter and sprinkle the lot with the cardamom sugar.Bake for another 20 minutes, then turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for a final 10 minutes, until the apples are browned and caramelised. Leave to cool a little on a rack, then slice and serve with vanilla ice-cream, thick cream, custard or all three.Explore more on these topicsFoodThomasina Miers recipesChickenMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesVegetablesSide dishesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey | Apple | The Guardian
description: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
Content: The Mac mini M6 is a palm-sized powerhouse of a computer.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Mac mini M6 is a palm-sized powerhouse of a computer.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.AppleReviewMac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more priceyApple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouseSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has beenhit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since theM2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIYiMac.View image in fullscreenThe front has two USB-C ports and a headphones socket, making it easy to plug in temporary accessories.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.The mini runs the latestmacOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’sLiquid Glass designthat was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.View image in fullscreenThe power button is on the bottom next to the exhaust vents, which means you have to pick up the Mac mini to press it.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSiri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.SpecificationsProcessor:Apple M6RAM:16, 24 or 32GBStorage:256, 512GB, 1 or 2TB SSDOperating system:macOS 27 Golden GatePorts back:3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb EthernetPorts front:2x USB-C (USB3), headphonesConnectivity:wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, ThreadDimensions:127 x 127 x 50mmWeight:670gSerious M6 speedView image in fullscreenThe back has most of the ports you need, including the rare but welcome 2.5Gb ethernet socket, which can be upgraded to 10GbE if needed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe case is made from 100% recycled aluminium.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact inits report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.PriceThe Mac mini M6 costs from£899(€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.For comparison, theA18 Pro MacBook Neocosts from£699, theM5 MacBook Airstarts at£1,299, the M4 iMac starts at£1,499and the Mac Studio costs from£2,499.VerdictThe Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.The only downside is theRAMageddon-linkedprice hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.Pros:very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.Cons:price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.Explore more on these topicsAppleComputingTechnology sectorreviewsShareReuse this content

title: LV= insurance is ignoring us while our house literally falls apart | Insurance | The Guardian
description: We are living in a collapsing property because of cost-cutting and delays over our subsidence claim
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: We are living in a collapsing property because of cost-cutting and delays over our subsidence claim
Content: A sign showing LV=’s promise, which sounds hollow after years waiting for action after a subsidence claim.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA sign showing LV=’s promise, which sounds hollow after years waiting for action after a subsidence claim.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyConsumer championsInsuranceLV= insurance is ignoring us while our house literally falls apartWe are living in a collapsing property because of cost-cutting and delays over our subsidence claimAnna TimsTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLV= GeneralInsuranceis forcing a family with three young children to live in a collapsing homebecause of cost-cutting and delays.We lodged a claim for subsidence damage to our extension and conservatory in 2023. Instead of authorising the repairs recommended by independent experts,LV=has spent years stalling and proposing inadequate, superficial patching methods.Three years on, significant cracking in the interior walls has caused aradiator to shear away. We have provided proof to LV= but are being ignored while our home literally falls apart around us.Meanwhile, the company has hiked our annual premium from £400 to £2,500. I feel they are penalising us for a claim.KT,LondonSubsidence claims are soaring as repeated droughts cause soil to shrink. Nearby trees accelerate the problem, and you have, on LV=’s advice, had several removed, but to no avail.‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claimsRead moreAn independent surveyor, commissioned by you in May – when you had reached an impasse with the company – concluded that the damaged extension needed underpinning or rebuilding. There was no obvious progress in the case, however.LV= now tells me that it obtained a quote for underpinning last February, although the work wasn’t carried out. It has since acknowledged that the cracks have worsened and a full rebuild is required.It says repairs will begin as soon as the designs and council bureaucracy are complete. The company blames the subsidence and the delay on an eucalyptus tree owned by a neighbour who refuses to remove it.A spokesperson said: “LV= General Insurance takes this claim extremely seriously and we understand and appreciate the frustration at the time it has taken to resolve it. Subsidence claims can be protracted because the most important step is to address the cause of movement, in this case tree removal, before permanent repairs can be undertaken.”LV= says it is reviewing your premium price rise under its complaints procedure.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. title: Saunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to Oslo  | Scandinavia holidays | The Guardian
description: A new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en route
Author: Adam Turner
Headline: A new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en route
Content: The Kallbadhuset (the cold bath house) set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea in Varberg.Photograph: Patrick Kuenne/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Kallbadhuset (the cold bath house) set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea in Varberg.Photograph: Patrick Kuenne/Getty ImagesScandinavia holidaysSaunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to OsloA new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en routeAdam TurnerTue 29 Sep 2026 02.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘This carriage is due for modernisation. Don’t miss the opportunity to experience 90s Germany style,”reads the sign on the door to the dining carriage. The couple inside aren’t missing theirs: they’re taking endless selfies in the clinical pink-and-turquoise carriage that looks like a hospital canteen and smells like cinnamon buns and strong filter coffee.I’m onSnälltåget’siconic red-shelled train, on the Swedish rail company’s new route from Malmö to Oslo – a 6.5-hour journey along Sweden’s picturesque western corridor. Until now, the journey between the two cities involved long bus rides and fragmented train transfers. This direct line is easier and cheaper, with tickets starting at £11 each way. It’s already a hit, shuttling more than 25,000 passengers since launching this summer.I was first seduced by Scandi rail travel a decade ago on a journey from Stockholm to Gothenburg, when I was berthed in a cosy dark-wood cabin and listened to a pianist play in a dining car. This time, starting in Malmö, I will take advantage of the new route to make a series of stops along the country’s western shore.In my view Malmö, across the Øresund Bridge from Copenhagen, is too often overlooked in favour of Stockholm. The southern port city is less polished than the capital and grittier, but its residents seem more outgoing and curious. Within an hour of arriving, I’m invited to drinks by a group of local people – a level of openness I never experienced living in Stockholm.Almost half of the populationis under 35, and 187 nationalities are represented, making it a hotbed of creativity. In the centre of town, theForm/Design Centeroccupies a former 16th-century grain store, now a meeting point and exhibition space for design, crafts and architecture enthusiasts. Then, there areModerna MuseetandMalmö Konsthallmodern art galleries.View image in fullscreenPoints of View by Tony Cragg, a public artwork in Malmö.Photograph: Danita Delimont/AlamyAtMöllevången, or Möllan, a trendy neighbourhood popular with creatives, everybody looks as if they’re at art college, or have just returned from a weekend in Berlin. My friend Rob, who has lived in Malmö for nearly a decade, guides me through Folkets Park, the “people’s park”, pointing out his favourite pizza spot,Far i Hatten, which occupies cute wooden huts. We find a table atAvanearby for a beer on a leafy square dotted with hip restaurants and organic wine bars – it feels like Malmö’s equivalent to London Fields in Hackney. Resisting the urge to continue our purposefully staid bar crawl, we down a nightcap atBar Boboand call it a night.double quotation markFloating on my back, I look up to see a group of Swedish veterans baring all, the building’s mustard shades completing an almost Hockney-esque sceneSnälltåget operates just one direct Oslo-bound train a day, at 6.38am from Malmö Central (plans are in the works to increase this next year), so it’s an early start at a station teeming with families and backpackers with rucksacks the size of fridge-freezers. We soon pass the romanesque towers ofLund Cathedralbefore chugging through pancake-flat yellowing agricultural fields, then skirt Apelviken bay – Varberg’s long, sandy horseshoe beach popular for kitesurfing and surfing.Varberg is Sweden’s equivalent of a coastal British market town. It’s got bunting, cobbled streets, intimate cafes and a weekend market with vendors peddling fresh vegetables, fruit, marmalade, leather belts and socks. It’s also a spa town, which inspired my visit. I was intrigued by its pretty, Moorish-inspiredKallbadhuset(cold bath house), set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea, where for about £8 visitors gain access to segregated men’s and women’s saunas, both with spellbinding sea views. A plunge in the brisk water after the sauna proves the perfect antidote to a 6am start after a bottle of red wine the night before. Floating on my back, I look up to see a group of Swedish veterans sitting on a wooden bench, baring all (it’s a nude bathhouse), the building’s mustard shades completing an almost Hockney-esque scene.View image in fullscreenThe Snälltåget.Photograph: Trygve Finkelsen/AlamyAccording to a sign outside Skarpe Nord – a community-run women’s bathing spot nearby – people have been nude-bathing in Varberg for more than 100 years. Walking along the promenade by a cavernous passage of blasted rocks that resembles a secret pathway from Lord of the Rings, I pass a collection of other designated naked bathing spots. But with the grey weather showing no sign of clearing, my hotel’s spa proves more inviting.In the bowels ofHotell Gästishides a replica of Vladimir Lenin’s favourite bathhouse. The hotel’s owner, Lasse Diding, built the spa as a homage to his idol, inspired by a visit to the original bathhouse in St Petersburg in the 1980s. This slightly eerie space is clad in more than 75,000 cobalt tiles and decorated with candlelit busts of communist leaders.Diding’s interest in the communist movement began during the Vietnam war and never left him. The eccentric entrepreneur is responsible for Varberg’s many visible politically left-leaning monuments – a giant Palestine flag,Hotell Havanna(an ode to revolutionary Cuba) and a statue ofDanuta Danielsson, who became a symbol of solidarity after hitting a marching neo-Nazi with her handbag in Växjö in 1985.The following morning, I hopon the fast train to Gothenburg, a 39-minute ride away. After checking in at the sophisticated, French boudoir-styleHotel Pigalle,just five minutes’ walk from Central station, I wander along Kungsgatan, the city’s modern shopping artery, towards Magasingatan. The area is packed with vintage shops (Ragtime,PopandHumana) and craft stores such asCustomwood, which makes bespoke wooden furniture to order.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSweet treats.Photograph: Gabriella Stroem/Getty ImagesI grab afika(the Swedish tradition of taking a break to drink coffee and indulge in a sweet treat)atDa Matteo, a barn turned cafe spread across three floors. The Scandi-industrial interiors are straight out of a design magazine, as bespectacled folk work away on their laptops. Scents of bread and coffee drift from the in-house bakery and coffee roastery; mybullar(a classic cardamom bun) and a latte cost just under a tenner.double quotation markThe Gothenburg to Oslo leg of the journey is the cinematic climax: lakes widen, trees grow greener and granite canyons appear grander with every kilometreWandering around Slottsskogen park later, I remember why I wanted to move to Gothenburg after a fleeting first visit all those years ago. Sweden’s second-largest city is compact and easy-going. It has a rough-around-the-edges feel like Malmö in places, with the liveability, nature and culture of Stockholm. At its heart is the pretty old town of Haga, which has narrow cobbled streets, inviting wafts of baked goods and the sound of creaky, wooden trams chugging by. And Slottsskogen is my favourite park in Europe. Roughly the size of Hyde Park, it’s home to deer, penguins and Gotland ponies, and exactly the kind of place you can spend long hours strolling without purpose.The Gothenburg to Oslo leg of the journey is the cinematic climax. It starts with rolling green pastures, cows grazing on a riverbank and forests thick with towering conifers beneath a blue summer sky. Then nature really starts showing off: lakes widen, trees grow greener and granite canyons appear grander with every kilometre, drawing excited kids to press their noses against the windows.View image in fullscreenOslo from Vettakollen viewpoint.Photograph: Sean Harrison/AlamyKeen to see it up close, after pulling into Oslo I dump my bags atCitybox, a minimalist hotel a few minutes’ walk from the station, and head north to Sognsvann. This lake and recreational area on the outskirts of the city is the starting point for a circular walk up to Vettakollen, a popular viewpoint. After an easy, 30-minute uphill hike, I reach a rocky mound skirted by pine trees, where families are picnicking. Oslo unfurls in the distance, the urban sprawl of metal and glass stretching to the fjord. For me, this is what makes Scandinavia special: the urban and the natural worlds seamlessly colliding.The trip was provided byVisit Sweden. One-way tickets from Malmö to Oslo withSnälltågetcost from149 Swedish kronor(£11). Double rooms atHotell Gästisfrom£90. Doubles atHotel Pigallefrom£85. Single rooms atCitybox Oslofrom£68Explore more on these topicsScandinavia holidaysRail travelSweden holidaysNorway holidaysEurope holidaysGreen travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pest I’ll never forget: I turned the toaster upside down. A mouse fell out | Homes | The Guardian
description: We tried humane traps, wire wool, hardcore cleaning regimes. Nothing worked. In the end, I wondered if the mice in our house were the real residents, while we were the intruders
Author: Carys Afoko
Headline: We tried humane traps, wire wool, hardcore cleaning regimes. Nothing worked. In the end, I wondered if the mice in our house were the real residents, while we were the intruders
Content: Got any jam?Composite: Guardian design; GlobalP; emilio100;/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGot any jam?Composite: Guardian design; GlobalP; emilio100;/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetHomesThe pest I’ll never forget: I turned the toaster upside down. A mouse fell outWe tried humane traps, wire wool, hardcore cleaning regimes. Nothing worked. In the end, I wondered if the mice in our house were the real residents, while we were the intrudersCarys AfokoTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the happiest years of my 20s were spent in a house-share in east London. Four of us were crammed into a three-bedroom terrace where the dining room had been turned into a bedroom. My housemates were my closest friends. We were young women with the kind of intense-bordering-on-codependent dynamic that becomes unsustainable later in life, when you have long-term partners, pets and children. We lived together, we went out together, in the summer we took our Argos tent to festivals together. We stayed up late discussing love-life and work dilemmas, often crowding round a phone to draft text messages.We were also not particularly clean, which meant our cluttered, chaotic house was the ideal home for mice. At first we told ourselves it was just one mouse we saw running along next to the skirting board or darting behind a sofa. But a quick scan of the internet confirmed our fears that it’s never just one – mice are social creatures, and they were likely in a nest-share similar to our house-share. A female mouse gives birth to a litter of five to eight mice and can be pregnant up to 10 times a year. We read forum posts that claimed mice were doubly incontinent (something I’ve since learned is fake news), and our horror began to grow.As the sightings increased and droppings appeared on the kitchen worktop, we agreed something had to be done. Two of my housemates were vegetarian, so we laid humane traps, with a plan to set the creatures free in the garden or a park. The humane traps did not work. The mice continued to thrive and multiply.Weeks passed and a siege mentality set in. We tentatively agreed it was time to try inhumane traps filled with peanut butter, which mice quite enjoy. We kept the counter tops clean, we checked they weren’t raiding our cupboards. We bought wire wool to plug holes in the skirting board, with mixed results. We were waging war and determined to win.On a rare night alone in the house, I decided to treat myself to some jam on toast. Blaring Beyoncé from my phone, I turned the toaster upside down to empty out the old crumbs. Out dropped a tiny brown mouse. It landed, very startled and very much alive, on the kitchen worktop.I screamed as if I was in a slasher movie, but there was no one to hear me. Meanwhile, the mouse stayed stock-still, staring back at me in terror – or maybe anger. It dawned on me that perhaps it saw me as the intruder, noisy and blundering, disrupting its cosy, carb-filled home. I banged the worktop and it ran away. The evening was ruined. I didn’t approach the toaster for weeks.I do not miss living with mice. Nor do I miss my laissez-faire landlord, who fixed the hole in our roof with tarpaulin and left me and my friends to deal with the infestation alone. But I do miss the chaotic adventures I had living with other women who were too skint and too silly to be proper grownups.I don’t know what happened to the little brown mouse in the toaster. Did she get pushed out of the area by gentrification? Or is she munching on sourdough crumbs left by the house’s new occupants? I wish my old housemate and her many, many descendants well.Explore more on these topicsHomesThe pest I’ll never forgetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: should you water plants less in winter? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Don’t water based on the month or the season – be led by what the plant is actually doing
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Don’t water based on the month or the season – be led by what the plant is actually doing
Content: Photograph: Alexandr Kolesnikov/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alexandr Kolesnikov/Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksLife and styleHouseplant hacks: should you water plants less in winter?Don’t water based on the month or the season – be led by what the plant is actually doingGynelle LeonTue 29 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 05.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheproblemCutting back on watering for winter has become so ingrained that people start rationing by the calendar, giving plants just a fraction of the water they had in summer, because the season changed.The hackThe advice to reduce is because, as light levels drop, most houseplants slow their growth, use less water and dry out more slowly, so watering as you did in summer risks waterlogging the roots and causing rot.The methodWhen we get to October, reduce watering to half or a quarter of what you gave plants in the summer.Houseplant Hacks: can mirrors and foil boost low sunlight?Read moreThe testI reduced watering in two of my own plants last winter. A calathea in a cooler, dimmer room dried out more slowly and needed less watering, exactly as the hack predicts. But a pothos sitting under a grow light in a warm room kept growing and started crisping at the edges and dropping yellow leaves.The verdictThe winter watering rule is not a myth, but it is badly misunderstood. The key is to water according to what the plant is doing, not what the calendar says. Research your plant to see if it has a dormant season and check each plant before you water. Push a finger a couple of inches into the compost, or lift the pot to feel its weight – a bone-dry pot is light, a wet one is heavy.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleHouseplant hacksGardening adviceHouseplantsfeaturesShareReuse this content

Content: 47:48Stateside with Kai and CarterNAZAWhy is Israel so afraid of the film NAZA? We spoke to its directors – Stateside with Kai and CarterWhen NAZA premiered at Venice earlier this month, it sent shockwaves across the globe. Composed of interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers, NAZA is a haunting exposé of the tools that the Israeli military uses to carry out the remote killing of Palestinians in Gaza – including AI, mass surveillance, and devastating airstrikes that kill civilians and raze homes. Now, the Israeli government is treating NAZA like a national security crisis. Benjamin Netanyahu is even pushing for legislation that could strip the film's two directors of their Israeli citizenship. HostCarter Shermanspeaks with the directors of NAZA, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, in one of their first interviews with an American journalist. The film, which was produced by the Guardian, will open in New York this week and soon expand to theaters worldwide. title: Vietnamese government accused of abducting human rights activists  | Cambodia | The Guardian
description: Detained anti-human trafficking campaigners include Tran Hiep, a Vietnamese Australian, not heard from since 18 September
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Detained anti-human trafficking campaigners include Tran Hiep, a Vietnamese Australian, not heard from since 18 September
Content: Tran Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist when he went missing in Cambodia.View image in fullscreenTran Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist when he went missing in Cambodia.CambodiaVietnamese government accused of abducting human rights activistsDetained anti-human trafficking campaigners include Tran Hiep, a Vietnamese Australian, not heard from since 18 SeptemberAustralian Associated Press andTory ShepherdMon 28 Sep 2026 21.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVietnamese authorities have detained three activists, including a Norwegian and an Australian, on what have been described as “fabricated” charges.The Vietnamese government said the three confessed to being members of Viet Tan – a pro-democracy organisation – which it describes as a terrorist group.In a statement, Viet Tan said it “strongly condemns the abduction of two of its members inCambodiaand the fabricated charges issued by the Vietnamese communist authorities to cover up an act of transnational repression”.It is not clear if the third person is a Viet Tan member as well.Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was “making urgent inquiries with Vietnamese authorities to confirm reports that an Australian citizen has been detained” and was giving the family consular assistance.Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Vietnamese Australian democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife, Chloe Dang, after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.Earlier, his wife implored the federal government to find him and bring him home after he failed to board his flight.He had not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”Anthony Albanese said the government was providing consular assistance.“That’s what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we’ll continue to engage directly with the family,” the Australian prime minister said.Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.According to a Vietnamese government statement, they were arrested entering Vietnam from the Cambodian border along with a third person, Thai Cong Truong Son.The statement describes the three Vietnamese-born people as illegal immigrants and says they will be investigated for alleged terrorism and forging identity documents.View image in fullscreenTran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 SeptemberViet Tan says it aims to “overcome dictatorship and build the foundation for a sustainable democracy”, and that it was “committed to peaceful, nonviolent struggle”.“We are convinced that nonviolent means are most effective for generating maximum civic participation,” the organisation said on its website.Human Rights Watchhas previously described Viet Tanas “an opposition political party … which operates openly and lawfully in many countries including Australia, but which Hanoi arbitrarily labels ‘terrorist’”.Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.On 18 September, Human Rights Watch said more than 160 political prisoners were currently locked up in Vietnam, and that activists faced “police harassment, intimidation, surveillance, and interrogation on a daily basis”.Viet Tan urged the Norwegian and Australian authorities to ask for access to the Hiep and Thuan, to “ensure their wellbeing and access to needed medication”.It said the pair had “no intention” of entering Vietnam and the claim they had done so illegally was a “blatant fabrication” to cover up their abduction.“Viet Tan is particularly concerned that To Lam’s police state is using its security apparatus to pursue and repress activists and foreign nationals even beyond Vietnam’s borders,” it said.“Meeting with, exchanging ideas with, and supporting human rights defenders, democracy activists, and civil society is a peaceful form of advocacy to advance freedom, democracy, and human rights in Vietnam.”Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing cooperation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, had earlier described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are longtime human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.Asia Human Rights & Labour Advocates director Phil Robertson labelled it an “unacceptable outrage” and that countries like Australia “continuing business as usual” was not acceptable.“[It] demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia,” he said.Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.“Everything is really uncertain.”The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.Explore more on these topicsCambodiaHuman rightsHuman traffickingAsia PacificActivismVietnamnewsShareReuse this content

title: From One Nation to fossil fuels, Adam Bandt and Bob Brown reveal vision for Greens ahead of leadership showdown  | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: Senior Greens figures say Larissa Waters’ successor must stop Labor approving fossil fuel projects ‘by whatever means’
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: Senior Greens figures say Larissa Waters’ successor must stop Labor approving fossil fuel projects ‘by whatever means’
Content: Adam Bandt, now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said there would be several key climate flashpoints for the next leader with Labor.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenAdam Bandt, now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said there would be several key climate flashpoints for the next leader with Labor.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPAustralian GreensFrom One Nation to fossil fuels, Adam Bandt and Bob Brown reveal vision for Greens ahead of leadership showdownSenior Greens figures say Larissa Waters’ successor must stop Labor approving fossil fuel projects ‘by whatever means’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiTue 29 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Greens leaderAdam Bandtsays the party’s new leadership team, which could be chosen as early as Wednesday, will face mounting pressure to block the Albanese government from approving any new coal and gas projects “by whatever means”.Bandt told Guardian Australia there would be no excuses for the new leader, likely to be elected at a two-day retreat in Sydney which begins on Wednesday, to allow Labor to approve any new fossil fuel development.Three separate tickets have declared an intention to stand for the leadership. On Tuesday, South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Youngannounced she would run for the leadership, while deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, has also announced her intention to run on a joint ticket with Nick McKim as her deputy. On Wednesday morning, senators David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May confirmed they will also stand for leadership positions.Larissa Watersannounced she would step downfrom the Greens’ leadership on Monday night, revealing she has been managing a chronic kidney disease, but that her health had “declined significantly over the course of recent months”. She said while her prognosis for recovery was positive, the pressure of the party’s leadership, including additional travel demands, was detracting from a focus on her health.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereBandt, now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said there would be several key climate flashpoints for the next leader with Labor before the next election, including whether the government would approve Woodside’s Browse gas project near the Scott Reef in northern WA, whether it would allow gas fracking in the Beetaloo basin in the NT and whether datacentres would be permitted to use fracked gas.“In terms of what approach gets taken in parliament, the view from the movement is: look, there’s no excuse now, there’s no parliamentary blocker to stopping new coal and gas mines and to stopping deforestation,” Bandt told Guardian Australia.“Just get it done by whatever means, whatever it takes to make that happen, at whatever style people adopt while they’re in parliament.”Party grandeeBob Brownsaid Waters had been a “splendid” leader, but warned the next leader would have to show they could extract significant reforms from Labor.Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi announce Greens leadership tilt after Larissa Waters’ shock resignationRead more“The next leader has an opportunity to take on not just One Nation but the failures of Labor … It has to be a leader who can take it up with Anthony Albanese and Pauline Hanson,” Brown said.“You need a very, very strong and able negotiator, not just to make incremental changes, but very big changes.”While One Nation has seen its popularity surge in 2026, the Greens voter base has not significantly grown.The party received12.22% of the primary vote in 2025compared with 12.25% in 2022.In 2026, the Australian’s Newspoll showed the primary vote at 13% in August and September. Nine newspapers’ Resolve poll showed the party at a high of 15% in March before dropping to 13% in July and August, and recorded a dip to 11% in September, while Redbridge Group and Accent Research polls in the Financial Review showed the Greens at 14% in June, dropping to 12% in August.Former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather used an open letter to call for the Greens rank and file to elect the new leader, not just MPs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBandt and Brown defended the party’s reach and said the Greens have been cutting through with the public, akin to the surge of support for progressives like the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani.Brown said the Greens “are the antidote to people who despair about politics”.“Under Larissa they have gone up in the polls and I expect that trend to continue, if not escalate. There’ll be surprises between now and 2028, and one of those will be the Greens because they often get taken for granted,” Brown said.Bandt added the progressive moment broadly has grown, pointing to a groundswell of public support for a gas export tax, despite the government abandoning any reforms.As One Nation surges in the polls, why are the Greens being left behind?Read more“Where they decide to go next will be a matter for the Greens party room … the progressive movement is quietly on the march and growing. We saw a big response to the gas tax campaign as it has mobilised over 70,000 people to call for a rethink of the decision to drill for gas off the Scott Reef,” Bandt said.NSW state Greens upper house member, Sue Higginson, said it was harder for her party to cut through the media and against other parties with significant financial backing.“It’s genuinely hard to cut through media narratives, and you’ve got to remember … when you have sort of dark money and dark interests influencing politics and political narratives, that is very hard to push back against.”Higginson said grassroots members expect the party leadership to take both conciliatory and activist approaches to policy.Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensAdam BandtLarissa WatersAustralian politicsBob BrownnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian government concedes no scientific consensus on social media harms for teenagers – but ‘credible risks’ justify ban | Social media ban | The Guardian
description: Commonwealth tells high court its proposed laws to let users opt out of algorithms would ultimately have the same effect as the ban
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Commonwealth tells high court its proposed laws to let users opt out of algorithms would ultimately have the same effect as the ban
Content: The Australian government says the under-16s social media ban has produced ‘substantial practical action’, pointing to nearly 5m accounts being removed in December.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Australian government says the under-16s social media ban has produced ‘substantial practical action’, pointing to nearly 5m accounts being removed in December.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersSocial media banAustralian government concedes no scientific consensus on social media harms for teenagers – but ‘credible risks’ justify banCommonwealth tells high court its proposed laws to let users opt out of algorithms would ultimately have the same effect as the banFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterTue 29 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian government has conceded it implemented the “world-leading” under-16s social media ban before there was scientific consensus on the link between mental health harms and social media use, but argued the “credible risks” of issues such as addictive behaviours and anxiety justify the policy.In its defence against a high court challenge of the ban, the government has also argued its proposeddigital duty of care legislation, allowing users to opt out of social media features such as algorithms, would ultimately have the same effect as the ban, if implemented.US-based platformReddit has challenged the under-16s social media banin the high court as one oftwo cases against the ban, expected to be heard jointly before the end of 2026.Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithmsRead moreIn Reddit’s submission to the court last month, it argued the ban represented a burden on the implied freedom of political communications, while also not addressing the risk of harm.The company pointed to the exclusion of some platforms from the ban, and the design features the ban was aiming to address still available to users without accounts, as well as the reported number of children under 16who have maintained accountsor registered new ones since the ban came into effect in December last year.Reddit pointed to the government’s proposed digital duty of care legislation, stating: “If the commonwealth wishes to address a problem with content to young people, it could address it directly as part of this proposal.”Reddit told the court that “there is no scientific consensus about whether there is a causal link between social media use and particular harms”.In the federal government’s defence, filed on Friday, the Australian government argued the agreed facts in the case identified there were “significant credible risks” of children developing addictive behaviours, disrupted sleep, and worsening depression, anxiety, suicidal behaviours or ideation.“Uncertainty about causation should not delay action to protect young people,” the government’s submission stated.“The existence of credible risks of harm and credible causal pathways between account-related design features and those risks justifies the parliament’s decision to enact a precautionary protective measure before scientific consensus establishes that it will be effective.”The Australian government also argued its proposed digital duty of care legislation would effectively require the features targeted by the ban to not be in operation for under-16s on social media.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Their proper application would require the same action [as the ban]: namely preventing children having accounts or providing children with accounts that do not have any of the [same] features.”The Australian government has claimed in its defence that the ban has already produced “substantial practical action”, pointing to nearly 5m accounts being removed in December last year, with Reddit itself suspending 43,962 accounts between December and March this year.The government hassince boosted the powers of the eSafety commissionerand doubled the fines that can be sought to nearly $100m for non-compliance, as part of measures to attempt to force the platforms to weed out remaining under-16 users.The peak US body for tech companies, NetChoice, is also seeking to be heard in the case, alongside digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). NetChoice members include Meta, Twitch, TikTok, Reddit, Snapchat, X and YouTube – which are all included in the social media ban.Explore more on these topicsSocial media banAustralian politicsSocial media bansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian Essential poll: Coalition’s primary vote sinks to lowest ever as majority support hardline immigration ideas | Essential poll | The Guardian
description: More than half of Australians want to see the country’s migrant intake lowered while One Nation’s primary vote climbs to 25%
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: More than half of Australians want to see the country’s migrant intake lowered while One Nation’s primary vote climbs to 25%
Content: The latest Guardian Essential poll shows Angus Taylor’s opposition is now at its equal-lowest ebb as its primary vote sinks to 22%.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenThe latest Guardian Essential poll shows Angus Taylor’s opposition is now at its equal-lowest ebb as its primary vote sinks to 22%.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPEssential pollGuardian Essential poll: Coalition’s primary vote sinks to lowest ever as majority support hardline immigration ideasMore than half of Australians want to see the country’s migrant intake lowered while One Nation’s primary vote climbs to 25%Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerTue 29 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Coalition has failed to capitalise on growing criticism of Labor, with the opposition stuck at its lowest-ever primary vote in the GuardianEssential poll.The poll also shows more than half of all Australians want immigration cut and have voiced support for hardline enforcement, such as forced deportation.Despite growing scrutiny of Labor’s handling of the economy and inflation, its response to the OpenAI hack, and criticism of the government’s migration plan, the Essential poll found the Coalition’s primary vote sank four pointssince last month, to 22%.Angus Taylor’s Coalition is now at its equal-lowest ebb in the Essential poll, after last month scoring 26%. Labor attracted a primary vote of 29% in September’s poll, up from 26% in August.Australia is talking about migration – but what do people at the centre of the debate have to say?Read moreBut amid a bruising andat times incendiary political brawlon migration, the poll – of 1,022 people last week – returned mixed results. While more Australians see migration as a positive for the country (46%) than see it as a negative (39%), 55% still want the nation’s annual migrant intake lowered.Another 29% want the annual intake to remain the same, while 16% of Australians want more migrants.There is also majority support for someOne Nationand Coalition ideas to curb migration, including forced deportations of people overstaying visas (70% support), greater scrutiny of protection or asylum visas (68%) and preventing most international students bringing their family members here (62%).The proposal by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, to make it harder for temporary migrants to move between different types of visas to extend their stay was backed by 64% of respondents, while 74% backed directing skilled worker visas toward industries with shortages like health or construction.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“This week’s report shows that while there is support to cut the immigration numbers, there is actually growing numbers who see immigration as positive for the nation,” said Peter Lewis, executive director of Essential Media.“The findings suggests it is important not to be dragged into a zero sum game here;
