most people want immigration slowed down with clear rules, rather than to stop it altogether.”Among poll respondents who wanted immigration decreased further, “refugees” and “family members of people living in Australia” were most commonly selected as the categories they wanted cut.While the Coalition is yet to announce its finalised migration policy, Taylor has proposedtying immigration numbers to new housing construction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut 70% of poll respondents said that, even if the government built enough homes and expanded public services to keep pace with population growth, they would still want immigration reduced.“Notably, there was strong support for the government’s suite of measures released earlier this month, but deep concerns about the impact of increased intakes on housing,” Lewis said.Labor this month announced its plan tobring migration in line with its budget forecasts, with Burke proposing changes to working holidaymaker visas, applications for partners and families and stricter monitoring and enforcement of visa overstayers. It came days after One Nation announced plans to slash the number of temporary migrants bymore than 750,000 over three yearsalongside hardline compliance measures.Experts including Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the immigration department, claimed Hanson’s deportation model would cost“many, many billions of dollars”and would shut down aged care homes and construction sites around the country.As federal politics is rocked by the resurgence of One Nation as a genuine third force, the primary votes for major parties are fluctuating month-to-month; in July, Labor’s primary was at 31%, dipping five points in August to 26% then recovering three points this month to 29%.One Nation attracted a 25% primary in this month’s poll, up from 23% in August, while the Greens had a 12% primary – maintaining a consistent figure for several months now.The Greensare expected to elect a new leader on Wednesday, after Larissa Waters stood down for health reasons. Some in the leftwing party have called for a more direct form of leadership and campaigning, to mount a progressive fight against One Nation’s rightwing populism.Explore more on these topicsEssential pollCoalitionAustralian politicsAngus TaylorOne NationAustralian immigration and asylumLabor partynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds detained as student protests across France turn violent | France | The Guardian
description: More than 400 detained as police and students clash over class sizes, exhausting timetables and staff shortages
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: More than 400 detained as police and students clash over class sizes, exhausting timetables and staff shortages
Content: Protesting students outside the Gabriel Guist'hau secondary school in Nantes on Tuesday.Photograph: Loïc Venance/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesting students outside the Gabriel Guist'hau secondary school in Nantes on Tuesday.Photograph: Loïc Venance/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceHundreds detained as student protests across France turn violentMore than 400 detained as police and students clash over class sizes, exhausting timetables and staff shortagesKim Willsherin ParisTue 29 Sep 2026 19.27 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 400 people, most of them children, have been detained in France on Tuesday after teenagers across the country blockaded their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher shortages and long timetables.Interior minister Laurent Nunez told BFM TV: “440 were detained across national territory. We don’t have the final tally yet, but I’m told two-thirds led to police custody.”The education ministry said 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday, out of about 3,700 across the country.The demonstrations began in Paris last week and have since escalated and spread across France. On Tuesday, high school pupils in Lille, northern France, set fire to dustbins and threw bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at police. Officers responded with teargas after protesters vandalised bus shelters and advertising hoardings.View image in fullscreenOn Tuesday, demonstrations and attempted blockades affected several high schools in the Rhône, notably in Lyon, Villeurbanne, Décines-Charpieu and Thizy-les-Bourgs.Photograph: Adrien Pittore/SIPA/Shutterstock“There is nothing that justifies showing up at institutions to demonstrate, masked, with your face disguised, carrying projectiles, and waiting for the intervention of law enforcement just to go after them,” Nunez said, adding that Tuesday’s clashes saw seven instances of hydrochloric acid being thrown at officers. A total of 48 police have been injured during the clashes across the country.There were also confrontations between children and police in Bordeaux, Rennes and Nantes in western France, and Marseille in the south. At the Lamartine lycée, in the north of Paris, students waved placards complaining they had exhausting timetables. One read: “8am-6pm. More hours of lessons than sleep.”In the Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis, mayor Bally Bagayoko joined a protest of hundreds of students at the Lycee Paul-Eluard.Leading students in a rendition of the national anthem, he described the protests as “completely legitimate” and complained that low-income areas received less resources than higher-income ones.When a crowd formed, police carrying riot shields struck the students with batons, Agence France-Presse reported.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators burned rubbish bins in the Lycées du Rhône on Tuesday.Photograph: Adrien Pittore/SIPA/ShutterstockThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said earlier that escalating the demonstrations would be “irresponsible”. He posted on X: “Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students staff or police.”Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), responded to ministers’ instructions to police, posting on X on Monday: “The high school students protesting are harmless. The Lecornu government has ordered a crackdown. This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone. Hands off our youth. Elected officials and France Unbowed activists, step in wherever you can.”View image in fullscreenStudents face police at Baggio high school, Lille, on Tuesday.Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APLecornu, responding on X, called Mélenchon’s intervention an “irresponsible escalation”. “The duty of an elected official of the republic is to protect young people and call for calm. Exploiting their anger for partisan purposes is wrong,” he wrote.He added that Mélenchon’s accusation of racism was “an insult”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStudents blockade the entrance to Hélène Boucher school in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Paoloni Jeremy/Abaca/ShutterstockThe protests came as French unions went on strike over the government’s budget plans, which include €54m in public spending cuts. Many public sector workers stopped work on Tuesday, including an estimated 40% of primary school teachers.Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéene (the high school students’ union) had called for a total blockade of France’s high schools as a parallel action but urged protesters to “remain peaceful”. He said the union was protesting about a “general lack of resources, overcrowded classrooms of sometimes 32-35 students and the shortage of teachers and staff”.He said a circular sent by the interior and the education ministries to the police, telling them to maintain public order outside high schools “with a proportionate use of force”, was a “absolute scandal”.View image in fullscreenStudents join a general protest in Paris on Tuesday against the release of next year’s draft budget.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP“We’re talking about pupils of 15-18 years old and the government’s only response is automatic and institutionalised repression. It’s unacceptable. High school pupils are taking action to demand fairer and more equitable conditions and they’re being met with the BAC [anti-criminal brigade] and the CRS [riot police],” Rani said.He added that some teachers and school staff had stood in front of students to protect them from police. “Those are the images you should be showing,” Rani told BFM TV.View image in fullscreenThe blockaded entrance to Colbert high school, in Paris, on Tuesday.Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/APCaroline Chevé, secretary general of the main teachers’ union the Fédération Syndicale Unitaire (FSU – Unitary Trade Union Federation), who joined protesters at a march in central Paris on Tuesday, said she understood pupils’ frustration. “They’re facing the same challenges as we are. They’re in overcrowded classrooms. Sometimes they don’t have enough teachers because of staffing shortages. They see the same reality as we do, and they’re angry,” Chevé said.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeSchoolsProtestTeacher shortagesSecondary schoolsYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: National Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claims | France | The Guardian
description: President of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenager
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: President of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenager
Content: Jordan Bardella has accused Mediapart of wanting ‘to kill my political career’ and said he would take legal action.Photograph: Blondet Eliot/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJordan Bardella has accused Mediapart of wanting ‘to kill my political career’ and said he would take legal action.Photograph: Blondet Eliot/Abaca/ShutterstockFranceNational Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claimsPresident of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenagerAngelique Chrisafisin ParisTue 29 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member.Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that thereport by the investigative website Mediapartwas false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election.“We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him.Marine Le Pen hails RN senate surge as ‘milestone’ towards French presidencyRead moreJournalists at Mediapart said they had independently authenticated the comments allegedly written between 2013 and 2015, including in email groups and on messaging services. Bardella was aged 17 to 18 at the time and was a member of the party that was then called the Front National.The alleged comments included “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. He is also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”.Mediapart’s investigation has shaken Le Pen’s presidential campaign. Since Le Pen took over the party leadership in 2011, she has sought to detoxify the party image and move it away from its antisemitic past in order to increase its electoral reach.When Le Pen’s father,Jean-Marie Le Pen, co-founded the party in 1972, its ranks included former members of a Waffen SS military unit under Nazi command during the second world war.Pierre Bousquet, a former member of the Waffen SS Charlemagne division, was the party’s treasurer for its first nine years. Another early member had been in the paramilitary militia under Philippe Pétain, the leader of the puppetVichy regimethat collaborated with the Nazis and ensured the deportation of one-quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps, about 76,000 people.In 1987, Jean-Marie Le Pen described the Holocaust as a“mere detail” of the second world war. In the decades that followed he was convicted more than 15 times for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity as he repeated negationist comments, including saying the Nazi occupation was“not particularly inhumane”.Marine Le Pen, who expelled her father from the party in 2015 after he repeated antisemitic comments, has in recent years directly appealed to French Jewish voters. She said her party would protect them, describing the RN as “the best shield for our fellow French citizens of Jewish faith”.View image in fullscreenBardella and Marine Le Pen at a rally in Lievin, northern France, in July.Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APBardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in an attempt to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. In 2023, Bardella told a TV interviewer he did not think Jean-Marie Le Pen was antisemitic, before backtracking on his comments after criticism.The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, responding to the Mediapart investigation, wrote on social media: “To all those with a short memory: antisemitism isn’t an accident in the RN, it’s that party’s history. That’s the real face of the far right.”Aurore Bergé, the minister for equality and against discrimination, said the “antisemitic and conspiracy theory” content of the alleged messages “reminds those who might have forgotten the nature of the far right”.Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the Socialist presidential primary, wrote on social media that no public relations exercise would fundamentally change the RN. “Let us never forget that they all joined a party founded by antisemitic fanatics and out-and-out racists,” he said.Yonathan Arfi, of the CRIF, the umbrella group of French Jewish organisations, toldFranceCulture radio he was “stupefied by the virulence of the antisemitic comments” allegedly made by Bardella. He said that if true, the comments undermined the RN’s claims to have detoxified its image.He asked: “How could a political party leader, having made such sickening comments, reach such a high position in a party that claims to have changed and now fights against the hatred of Jews?”The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, said Bardella, an MEP, should resign from all his political positions. She said: “The man who presents himself today as the biggest defender of Jews … is in reality an obsessional antisemite.”Explore more on these topicsFranceNational RallyMarine Le PenThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We will not be intimidated,’ says Estonian PM after attributing recent arson attack to Russia – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: Kristen Michal says attack ‘against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services’, after Kremlin denies involvement
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Kristen Michal says attack ‘against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services’, after Kremlin denies involvement
Content: 06.08 EDT'We will not be intimidated,' Estonian PM says after attributing recent arson attack to RussiaEstonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by Russia’s denials.Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.We will not be intimidated.”The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing,but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.On the night of 15 August,a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district.Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.On 17 August,two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.On 17–18 September,Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”Share

title: Spain announces plan to ease housing crisis amid outcry over eviction of 87-year-old | Spain | The Guardian
description: Measures, which need to be approved in Congress, include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Measures, which need to be approved in Congress, include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people
Content: People take part in a demonstration in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, where hundreds of people have set up camp to protest against Abascal’s eviction.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople take part in a demonstration in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, where hundreds of people have set up camp to protest against Abascal’s eviction.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPASpainSpain announces plan to ease housing crisis amid outcry over eviction of 87-year-oldMeasures, which need to be approved in Congress, include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable peopleStephen Burgenin BarcelonaTue 29 Sep 2026 10.27 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, aftera public outcryover the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week.Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible.Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028.A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements.View image in fullscreenMaricarmen Abascal attends an event organised by housing activists the day before her scheduled eviction from her home in Madrid.Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMaricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after she was evicted from her Madrid home on Wednesday.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersHundreds of people remained camped out in ⁠one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest againstMaricarmen Abascal’s removal from her homeon a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the ⁠automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree.Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.”She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.”‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisisRead moreThe Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees.“It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.”View image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police near the Puerta del Sol encampment in Madrid.Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to ‌it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners inSpain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.”View image in fullscreenHousing rights protesters remain camped at Puerta del Sol in MadridPhotograph: Mario Mor ³N/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAlberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.”Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction.View image in fullscreenA protester in the encampment at Puerta del Sol. The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress.Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockUnderlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband.Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative.Explore more on these topicsSpainHousingCommunitiesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine  | Estonia | The Guardian
description: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
Content: Margus Tsahkna at a meeting with the Finnish foreign minister, Elina Valtonen (not pictured), on Tuesday.Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPAView image in fullscreenMargus Tsahkna at a meeting with the Finnish foreign minister, Elina Valtonen (not pictured), on Tuesday.Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPAEstoniaEstonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying UkraineEuropean and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in TallinnEurope live – latest updatesJon HenleyEurope correspondent and agenciesTue 29 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia andUkraineafter the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services.Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry.Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said.Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign acrossEuropeaimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said.Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure onRussia. We will not be intimidated.”Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending.Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”.Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”.Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in RussiaRead moreLithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”.The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said.France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media.Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEstoniaRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis
Content: Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (left), the UAE vice-president, and Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince, meeting in Riyadh.Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (left), the UAE vice-president, and Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince, meeting in Riyadh.Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenSaudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in YemenRelations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by SaudisPatrick WintourTue 29 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with theUnited Arab Emiratesover Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.Relations between the UAE andSaudi Arabiain Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen.But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to thenarrow Bab al-Mandab straitagainst pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.The future role of the UAE inYemenwas discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.2:34Why the civil war in Yemen has world governments on edgeNetanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat theHouthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice-president.It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.Following the Houthis’ push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, their forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city, trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front.“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”Yemen mapThe STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi,fled into exileafter the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.The former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provided some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.The STC has urged the Giant Brigades to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.“The UN-recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is, so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”The White House has been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done in the past in Yemen, sometimes to brutal effect.Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.The World Health Organization said 838 people had been killed and 3,643 others injured due to the escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday they published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war was existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis were not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women | World news | The Guardian
description: As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs
Content: Indian women protest in 202 in Uttar Pradesh.Photograph: Anupam Nath/APView image in fullscreenIndian women protest in 202 in Uttar Pradesh.Photograph: Anupam Nath/APThis Is IndiaWorld newsFrom Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on womenAs outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogsDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 29 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 04.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamuiwent viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedlygang-raped in a parkby men posing as police. After, women in Bihartold Outlookhow the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women.Weare the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that womenmight not be safe even inside their own homes.)Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whoselatest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.‘Moral policing’ of the wrong targetView image in fullscreenIndian women commuters board a women-only train carriage.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAWomen, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University havecome out on the streetsdemanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. Arecently published surveyof more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.Another2024 studyfrom India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting onthe molestation videosaid: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an“isolated” incident”.Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations,and was acquittedby a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According toan analysisof 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenThe Indian women’s cricket team triumphed at this year’s Asian games in JapanPhotograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockGolden girls| Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runsto win goldat the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.Moma| A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh,opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Artat the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEC under fire| An explosive Indian Express investigationhas revealedhow two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenThe Ram temple, Uttar Pradesh.Photograph: Press Information Bureau/EPA105An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cashbeing removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenTony Klor showing India, and the rest of the world, the beauty of Satara.Photograph: InstagramTony Klor’scity vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaViolence against women and girlsIndia women's cricket teamnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incident | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man dialled 999 before he and four others were arrested near military base in Gloucestershire, it has emerged
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Man dialled 999 before he and four others were arrested near military base in Gloucestershire, it has emerged
Content: Armed police at a checkpoint near RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenArmed police at a checkpoint near RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUK newsSuspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incidentMan dialled 999 before he and four others were arrested near military base in Gloucestershire, it has emergedVikram DoddandHelena HortonTue 29 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford as part of a terror investigation that prompted fears of an Iran-backed plot called the police to report the incident, it has emerged.The call from the man, in his 20s and from London, was one reason armed police were scrambled to arrest the men, who were with three vans close to the military base used by the US in its attacks on Iran.The Guardian understands that police first on the scene found several barrels in the vans, one of which contained petrol, while the others were empty.An Iranian link to the bizarre events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend is seen as increasingly likely, as the police and security services investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including President Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.It was revealed on Sunday that a farmer driving home from a party at around 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans, and called 999. But why one of the suspects themselves called police is another strand of the complex investigation.News of the call to police by one of the suspects was first reported by the Times.A statement earlier from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons. Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”The mounting view among investigators that Iran was involved was a key reason for Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which was attended by senior police and security officials.Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.The suspects were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. The decision on Monday to bail the men came after examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device.Taylor said of the vans: “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.”Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the dead of night.The vans were marked by the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles.Taylordefended the decision to bail the suspects, saying: “Yesterday we released the five men on police bail. They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday.“I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”Residents were returning home on Tuesday after spending days evacuated from their village.Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, claimed the events were the work of a “foreign actor” but did not provide further details. He said “a lot of people are disturbed” after the release of the suspects from custody. Trump had earlier said he was “surprised” the group had been freed.Speculation has been growing about a connection between the weekend’s incident and Iran. On Monday Taylor said he knew there was “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident”.He added: “But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”In March the British government gave the US permission to use the base for “specific defensive operations into Iran”.The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on the village of Whelford, where the men were arrested.Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.Father Michael Robertson, the priest at the nearby St Thomas Catholic church, told PA: “A lot of parishioners didn’t think they could get to church. Those that came were worried but perfectly happy with the situation.“In fact, quite a lot of Americans who have deployed here actually come to mass and some of the permanently deployed Americans are full members of the parish. We’re quite contented with the situation generally. Obviously, the disruption upsets people.”Additional reporting by Jamie GriersonExplore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Give BrewDog ‘second chance’ says new owner as it invests £50m | BrewDog | The Guardian
description: US cannabis and drinks firm Tilray, which took over in March, says it will improve beers, pubs and working conditions
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: US cannabis and drinks firm Tilray, which took over in March, says it will improve beers, pubs and working conditions
Content: Tilray is working on the launch of new beers while investing in BrewDog’s brewery in Aberdeenshire to improve existing lines.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTilray is working on the launch of new beers while investing in BrewDog’s brewery in Aberdeenshire to improve existing lines.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBrewDogGive BrewDog ‘second chance’ says new owner as it invests £50mUS cannabis and drinks firm Tilray, which took over in March, says it will improve beers, pubs and working conditionsSarah ButlerTue 29 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrewDog’s new owner has urged drinkers to give the ailing brand “a second chance” as it invests more than £50m in improving the company’s beers, pubs and working conditions.The US cannabis and drinks company Tilray bought BrewDogfor £33m in Marchthis year, after the company collapsed into administration after five years of losses and a series of controversies relating to the treatment of workers under the founder James Watt.Some staff accused Watt in 2021 of fostering a “toxic work culture”. He apologised for some of his conduct and left the company in 2024.Tilray’s chief executive, Irwin Simon, said it was listening to BrewDog’s customers and staff and had increased pay this year.He said Tilray was working on the launch of new beers while investing in the company’s brewery in Aberdeenshire to improve the quality and reliability of existing lines, adding that more than £1m of beer that did not meet quality standards had been thrown away.Simon said Tilray was a long-term investor that aimed to grow the company and was also considering buying additional British craft beers for its portfolio. He said Tilray may also consider reviving BrewDog’s closed distillery business if it felt there was a sufficient market in the UK.Administrators said earlier this month that creditors owed about £190m by the collapsed “punk” brewerwould not be paid back in full. However, it is understood that Tilray has picked up the bill on some key suppliers in order to ensure continuity on items such as ingredients.Its deal in March to buy BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars renderedthe shares of more than 200,000 crowdfunding investors worthless.However, these “equity punks” continue to receive benefits, including discounted beer, and some were invited along to ask questions at a relaunch of the brand on Tuesday.One asked why BrewDog beers could not be as cheap as a £2 Bud Light in Wetherspoons. Simon said its craft beers would never be that cheap but added: “We deserve a second chance.”Speaking from BrewDog’s giant bar in Waterloo, central London, with music blaring in the background, the American said: “We are different. We are not a big company like [Budweiser maker] Anheuser-Busch. We are entrepreneurial, nimble and want to connect to consumers.”March’s deal only included 11 of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs. Tilray has since reopened five of those bars and Simon said it was hoping to open more but he said he would only do so in “A locations” and not the “BCD locations” that BrewDog’s owners had previously considered.He said BrewDog could bounce back from the negative publicity it suffered under Watt’s leadership and return to the annual sales of £350m a year, up from about £225m at present, and become profitable again with the right support. He believes it could be worth as much as £2bn in the future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The name of the brand is BrewDog; it is not anyone’s name,” he said. “It is not about one person; it is about a team.”Before a new ad campaign launching next week based around the slogan “choose craft”, Simon said: “What we have to do is perform. What we have to do is what we’re doing here today. Bringing people together and launching campaigns and doing what we say we’re going to do.”Last week the new owners launched an ad campaign that appeared to take shots at Watt, with lines including: “No More Cunning Stunts. Just Great Beer” alongside an image of its Punk IPA and “A Little Less Allegation” alongside its Elvis Juice.Tilray also published a letter outlining its commitment to BrewDog’s future, saying that under its ownership BrewDog would have “sensible working practices, community initiatives and a people-first approach”.It said: “We’re going to take good care of this beloved Scottish craft beer business.”The company has also introduced 24 Tilray-owned American craft beers into BrewDog bars and is planning to produce some of those at BrewDog’s brewery in Scotland.Explore more on these topicsBrewDogFood & drink industryHospitality industryBeerPubsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham gambles on radical progressive plan to help Britain ‘rise again’ | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM accepts some of his plan could be difficult and admits he ‘may pay a political price’
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM accepts some of his plan could be difficult and admits he ‘may pay a political price’
Content: Andy Burnham promised in his speech to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham promised in his speech to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockAndy BurnhamBurnham gambles on radical progressive plan to help Britain ‘rise again’PM accepts some of his plan could be difficult and admits he ‘may pay a political price’Analysis: PM’s promises will take time to come goodKey takeaways from Burnham’s conference speechPippa CrerarPolitical editorTue 29 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has staked his future on a gamble that the public will back radical progressive policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that his agenda will break the mould of the last 40 years and “allow us to rise again”.In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto, acknowledging that he may end up paying the price for creating sharp new dividing lines in politics.“I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”However, while the prime minister said he would try to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living, he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances.“These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,” he told Labour activists.13:38Burnham’s triple lock gamble | Politics Weekly“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down. The approach I am outlining today is the responsible one.”With global economic storm clouds gathering and Labour dropping behind Reform UK in one poll this week, Burnham was determined to leave his audience in the conference hall in Liverpool, and at home, some hope.During his hour-long speech, in which he paused several times after being overcome with emotion at mentioning the death of his father, he said he wanted to show the UK was “something worth saving, worth fighting for”.He said: “I believe the plan I have outlined today will not just hold us together, it will allow us to rise again.“Today we draw a line on a decade of division. We stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down. And we put the country on a new path.”Burnham promised to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong, saying it was time to admit “Brexit hasn’t given us control” and that it was a handbrake on growth.In his strongest hint yet that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he said he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship with the bloc at the reset summit this autumn.Options could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, the customs union or single market, or even reversing Brexit in its entirety.2:20Andy Burnham fights tears as he speaks of his dad at Labour conference – video“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” he said. “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a high level of growth and prosperity for Britain.”While public attitudes towards leaving the EU have shifted over time, Burnham’s shift away from Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines will still be a big political gamble in seats such as his own, Makerfield, which voted for Brexit.Burnham confirmed he wouldend the pensions triple lockshould Labour win the next election and use the savings tofund a national care servicein England that would be free at the point of use.He plans to break the link between wage growth and pensions and promised instead a rise based on inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, which he claimed would still leave millions of pensioners better off.He said pensioners would benefit from the new care system – which would be expected to follow the Scottish system in covering care costs but not accommodation – and a promise to exempt them from income tax.Burnham suggested that care workers were “invisible to the political class” but he told them: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”As well as a promise to fix the broken system, the prime minister’s words will be interpreted as a sign he is preparing to carve out migrant care workers from Shabana Mahmood’s immigration measures.View image in fullscreenMembers of the cabinet watch Burnham’s speech.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAIn another commitment to a long-held belief, Burnham also confirmed he would put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto, announcing a cross-party national commission to consider options to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation.“We can’t succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times,” he said. “It is always in my mind that I’m the seventh prime minister in 10 years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled | John CraceRead more“We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on 30% of the vote or less.”Burnham said it was the drive of his government for every person to feel greater control over the basics of life and renew faith that systems could work for them.He said the common wealth of Britain, its homes, energy, water and care, had been stripped out and sold for profit. “The wealth we had created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few,” he said.“The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said in remarks that drew a standing ovation.Burnham promised two new pieces of legislation later this year, including a leasehold reform bill that would put curbs on charges for homes.“The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” he said. “This is the break we are making with the flawed thinking of the last 40 years. Not seeing housing only as a market with winners and losers, but as an essential everyone needs for a good life.”View image in fullscreenBurnham addresses his audience in Liverpool.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press/ShutterstockHe said a water bill would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on state-owned water companies, which was a “symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain”. There will be new curbs on bosses and pay and new powers for mayors over water systems.He also confirmed thecreation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid, while ministers will speed up the breaking of the link between energy prices and the international gas market.The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “Burnham wants to take Britain back to the 1970s – a time of more government control, more trade union control and no economic growth. There is a reason our country took a different course after that decade.“Nothing Burnham announced today will do anything to fix Britain’s long-term problems. He had no plan to fix our stagnant economy. No plan to fund defence. No plan to sort out the spiralling welfare bill beyond more government schemes.”Reform UK’s Nigel Farage said: “By potentially scrapping the triple lock, Andy Burnham will abdicate his responsibility to British pensioners. Instead of cutting our bloated benefits bill, stopping migrants from accessing benefits, or slashing foreign aid, he’s considering launching an offensive against our elderly.”Labour MPs responded with relief and enthusiasm to Burnham’s conference address, which the prime minister wrote almost entirely alone, with more than one describing it as the speech of their political lifetimes.However, there were words of caution from some ministers and Downing Street insiders, who will be more interested in how the speech goes down with the wider public at home than in the room.“I don’t want to be negative, but we’ve got to be realistic,” one cabinet minister said. “We just don’t know what’s going to happen with the economic headwinds. But if anybody can get us through it, Andy can.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabour conference 2026LabourLabour conferenceSocial careElectoral reformBrexitnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham says he would put PR in Labour manifesto and scrap triple lock to fund social care – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: PM, in first speech to party conference as leader, insists his plans are a ‘good deal’ for older people
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: PM, in first speech to party conference as leader, insists his plans are a ‘good deal’ for older people
Content: 10.55 EDTBurnham's conference speech - snap verdictParty conference speeches by a leader are rather weird and antiquated constructions. There is almost no other time in the year when a PM, or an opposition leader, gives a speech uninterrupted for an hour or so. Some are great, some are mediocre, but normally even the better speakers tend to lose the audience halfway through as they rattle through second-order issues included to keep an interest group happy.Andy Burnham’s speech today was a rare exception. Because it was emotionally engaging, because it was laced with anger and it felt like a speech 15 years in the making, because it had a coherent argument, because it was quite colloquial, and perhaps because Burnham was not standing at a lectern, this was much more interesting and watchable than these speeches usually are. Normally, 40 minutes in, you are desperate for it to end. I would have happily listened to Burnham for another half an hour.On substance, it was strong – but perhaps not quite as bold as Burnham maintains. His ambitions on social care are in the best traditions of “Go Big” (see8.40am) and Burnham has shown himself to be a politician confident of his ability to turn public opinion on a big, difficult issue (getting rid of the triple lock). It was bold and inspiring. But whether it turns out to be effective remains to be seen, and if Burnham fails to win this argument, he has got time to trim, or back down.On PR and Europe, he also staked out brave positions that will attract considerable opposition – not just out in the country, but from some inLabourtoo. But here he was a bit less specific than on social care and pensions. He implied PR would be in the Labour manifesto, but he just said he would fight the election on a proposal“to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts”, which implied something less ambitious than PR – the alternative vote, perhaps, or PR for an elected Lords? – might end up to be the only option he thinks he can sell to the PLP.And, on Europe, Burnham implied that he will open a conversation on rejoining. But he was not explicit about that, and then he started talking about “consensus” – which sounded naive because there no subject in British life on which consensus seems less possible than Brexit. One colleague has a theory that Burnham wrote the speech planning to end with a flourish saying rejoining would be an option (like Keir Starmer saying “nobody is ruling out remain”in his 2018 speech) – only to drop the wording at the last minute. There was definitely a bit of a hiatus at the end where the speech had been building up to a big reveal. (See3.10pm.)Still, this speech was daring, moving and – potentially – transformational. Burnham has had a good week, and today it got better.Andy Burnham giving his speech.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianShareUpdated at12.42 EDT

title: Burnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures – but his promises will take time to come good | Labour conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: PM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next election
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: PM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next election
Content: 2:20Andy Burnham fights tears as he speaks of his dad at Labour conference – videoLabour conference 2026AnalysisBurnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures – but his promises will take time to come goodJessica ElgotDeputy political editorPM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next electionKey takeaways from Andy Burnham’s conference speechTue 29 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.06 EDTShareHope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again.Just forget about the last two years, after the party won a historic majority but where the mood never matched the achievement. Now, as conference delegates and MPs filed out of the hall after AndyBurnham’s first speech as prime minister, it was close to euphoria. Where the hell have you been all our lives? What have we been doing – when you were right there all along?That feeling rarely lasts: Burnham himself warned he would make choices that would be a harsh comedown from thisLabourhigh. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country.In his sights are some of the most untouchable topics in British politics: social care, the triple lock, Brexit, public control of water and council homes and changing the voting system.Burnham wrote the speech almost entirely alone, working on it until the very last minute. Cabinet ministers have been full of tales of how often meetings overrun with the new prime minister, clearing their diaries for the extra half an hour, because of his desire to chew the fat, to understand, to argue, to persuade.Close friends saw the speech just the night before, as Burnham reworked it. But strategists in No 10 were very clear that the new prime minister did need to introduce himself, his story, to the country that barely knows him.Each judicious choice of an anecdote from his past drew on his personal history to explain his desire to make fundamental change. The home in Old Roan in Merseyside bought by his grandmother Kitty, which gave his family security that the younger generation cannot now experience: sold, he explained, to pay for Kitty’s care, which he will promise future generations will never happen under a new national care service. The care of his dad, Roy, who died two weeks ago, and his promise to his care workers that he would elevate their profession.Burnham was overcome with emotion at the moment he spoke about his father, pausing for so long it caused one member of the audience to cry out: “You can do it Andy.” They want to back him, they want to believe.Unusually for a conference speech, Burnham did not use the speech to attack his opponents. There were no reference to either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage. But one of the loudest cheers came from the crowd as Burnham drew the dividing line with the right in the starkest terms on public ownership.“The British right talk about ‘taking back control’. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said, the reddest of red meat to a jubilant Labour crowd.Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled | John CraceRead moreSo, was it Burnham – and Labour – unleashed? No, because the prime minister is still constrained by his own party manifesto and the state of the public finances. “I would love to go quicker,” he said. “But I have to be honest about what the country can afford.”His most radical promises are promises deferred. The party will overhaul the triple lock by 2030, the national care service can only be paid for if the party ditches its tax pledges, it can only explore a customs union, the single market, even rejoining, outside the manifesto’s “red lines”.Even at this most unitedLabour conferencethe party has seen in two decades, there remains a proud Labour tradition – pessimism. And there are causes for concern, which creep in when cabinet minsters are at their most candid. The first is the impatience of the country for change – and that being told to wait will not be enough.People, they say, are suffering now. The budget will need to show that any sparse funds that remain must be delivered to giving people relief from everyday costs.“People need to start feeling actual benefits next year. We have got less time than we might think,” one cabinet minister said.The second is a fear that Labour is not speaking to a broad enough base, no matter the elevation in Liverpool. Though there has been a discernible “Burnham bounce”, the polls are volatile. A YouGov poll on the eve of Burnham’s speech put Reform UK back in first place by a tiny margin.Labour is reuniting a progressive coalition with a divided right, which is an advantage but which is unlikely to put them in majority territory. There are few cabinet ministers who are so frustrated with the constraints of their own legacy manifesto that they want to swap that for the constraints of a Lib Dem manifesto. There is no sign of revival yet in Wales or Scotland, so crucial to a Labour majority government.When the dust clears and Labour strategists pick over the bodies of the sacred cows that Burnham promised to slay in his speech, many will probably wonder why he didn’t choose an easier life.But perhaps now Burnham has waited this long to be prime minister – and watched so many others squander the office – he knows he has no choice but to tool up for the fight.Explore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026Andy BurnhamLabour conferenceLabourSocial careElectoral reformHealth policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back
Author: Cecilia Nowell
Headline: ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back
Content: ‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 December 2025.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreen‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 December 2025.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APLos Angeles‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming backCecilia NowellTue 29 Sep 2026 19.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering theLos Angelesneighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home.“Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday.Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower.Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LARead more“I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said.Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next.“Yellow 2120”made headlines last yearwhen he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months.In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns.“He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson toldthe Orange County Registerat the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute.
