Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.”After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at leasttwo 500-plus-pound black bearssought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings aregrowing more common. In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455.This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters,told the Guardianthat human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population isestimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000, with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesWildlifeAnimalsCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas charged with assaulting an officer | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Garcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive away
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Garcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive away
Content: Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a food delivery driver, after he was shot by a federal immigration agent, in Austin, Texas, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Austin Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenWilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a food delivery driver, after he was shot by a federal immigration agent, in Austin, Texas, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Austin Police/ReutersUS immigrationVenezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas charged with assaulting an officerGarcés Pérez, who was shot in his car by agents, is accused of striking officer with side mirror while trying to drive awayAssociated PressTue 29 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 21.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal prosecutors on Tuesday announced an assault charge against a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent inTexas, accusing the man of striking an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint. Garcés Pérez, whose attorney has said still has a bullet lodged in his back from the 20 September shooting, made an initial court appearance in anAustinfederal court on Tuesday, according to the US attorney’s office in the western district of Texas.Venezuelan shot by ICE in Austin needs surgery to avoid losing feeling in body, supporters sayRead moreA nine-page affidavit from a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent amounts to the government’s fullest public account to date of the shooting in the Texas capital, which has set off protests and outrage from Democrats over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The document includes photos taken from body-worn cameras but no video was released, and the complaint did not say whether the agent allegedly struck by the side mirror sustained any injuries.The accusations against Garcés Pérez were reminiscent of previous claims made by immigration agents after high-profile shootings, in which officers have similarly accused drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, those allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, and have renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.Garcés Pérez was in the custody of US marshals after being removed from a federal detention center in south Texas, according to court documents filed by federal prosecutors. Separately, Garcés Pérez’s attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop his removal from the US.If convicted, Garcés Pérez faces up to 20 years in prison.An attorney for Garcés Pérez declined to immediately comment on Tuesday. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Department of Justice.According to an affidavit signed by a DHS agent, officers first saw Garcés Pérez’s car parked outside a restaurant with its emergency flashers on. They decided to pull him over after conducting a database check that showed the car was registered to Garcés Pérez, who had a final order of removal from the US.The agents said that they turned on their lights to execute the stop, but in the same filing, Garcés Pérez told investigators that an unmarked SUV followed him and then abruptly cut him off on the side of the road.Garcés Pérez, who was making a DoorDash delivery, provided his driver’s license through a crack in the window, but ignored agents’ requests to step out of the car, the complaint said. Garcés Pérez told investigators that he declined to exit because he had asked for officers to wait to apprehend him until his wife could come retrieve his car. Court documents describe the interaction as initially conversational, with a tone that was “pleasant and not aggressive”.About a minute later, according to court records, Garcés Pérez “abruptly” closed the window and drove off. One of the officers, who is referred to only by his initials, was struck in his torso with the driver’s side mirror when Garcés Pérez tried to drive away, the documents say.The unnamed officer who shot Garcés Pérez wasn’t wearing a body camera. The other officer involved in the chase was wearing a camera, but only caught up to the chase after Garcés Pérez had been shot, according to the affidavit.ICE has previously said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September.The affidavit included screenshots from previously unreleased body-worn camera footage of the officer’s initial interactions with ICE agents. The first of three photos appear to show the officer standing in front of Garcés Pérez’s driver’s door mirror; the second shows the officer resting his hands on the hood and side of Garcés Pérez’s car, with the mirror close to or touching the officer’s abdomen; and the third shows the car pulling away.The Austin police department last week released video from its officers but that footage did not show the shooting or the moment that Garcés Pérez allegedly tried driving away.The affidavit includes Garcés Pérez providing his account to federal investigators, which paints a contrasting picture of the lead-up to the shooting than what federal prosecutors described.According to the affidavit, Garcés Pérez said that a law enforcement SUV struck his car after a brief chase and caused it to spin before an agent opened fire, shooting him in the back. By contrast, US attorney Justin R Simmons said in a statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol”.Garcés Pérez entered the US in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under Joe Biden that allowed immigrants to make appointments with US authorities to be considered for asylum.Donald Trumpended the program on his first day in office.Garcés Pérez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garcés Pérez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.The shooting occurred amid a surge in ICE enforcement across the US during Trump’s second term. ICE reported more than 50,000 monthly arrests in July and August – a first for the agency.Immigration officers have come under intense scrutiny for shootings that have occurred since Trump took office in January 2025 – at least 10 of which have been fatal. On a few occasions, federal law enforcement has charged the person shot by immigration officers with assault.A woman shot several times by border patrol officers in Chicago and a man shot in the leg by an ICE agent in Minneapolis were both accused of assaulting officers, but in both cases the charges were dropped. The ICE officer in Minneapolis has since been charged with lying about getting assaulted before shooting the man in the leg.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsTexasAustinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Reported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotation
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Reported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotation
Content: Reuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenReuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO documentReported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotationDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 29 Sep 2026 06.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic is telling investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, according to reports, as it prepares for a potential $2tn (£1.5tn) flotation.The warning inside the startup’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be made public, was reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. It follows the company’scall for a slowdownin breakneck development of the technology – a warningechoed by rivals.The prospectus – a document outlining a company’s finances, growth plans and risk profile ahead of a share listing – is said to warn that AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”.“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further ⁠increase the risk that our models cause harm,” the developer of the Claude chatbot reportedly said, adding the potential for a model to be aware it was being tested created a “significant limitation” on Anthropic’s ability to assess model safety.Anthropic declined to comment.Companies preparing to go public routinely report on risks ranging from safety issues to regulatory concerns but warnings about a product causing human extinction reflect heightened concern about such a consequential technology.The reported prospectus admission follows a surge in debate about the existential risk question, triggered this month when an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon,resigned warning that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.A senior safety researcher at Anthropic then posted their agreement on X, claiming there was a more than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”.Some experts have criticised the existential risk warnings, saying they are unverifiable and unscientific. However, there are growing examples of unsanctioned behaviour by the technology, including OpenAI agents – autonomous systems that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention – hacking dozens of third-party organisations including theAI startup Hugging FaceandAustralia’s universal healthcare system.OpenAI announced on Monday it hadcancelled the releaseof its newest model because of safety concerns. It said the GPT-6.1 Astra model showed higher levels of deception and performed poorly on tests for alignment, the term for ensuring a model adheres to human values and goals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors, compared with 48 pages to describe its business.Anthropic is reportedly seeking a valuation of more than $2tn, compared with the$1.8tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingInternet IPOsIPOsInternetShareReuse this content

title: US ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationship | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: It marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationship
Content: Cows are shown from a Quebec dairy farm in Monceau, Canada, on 10 September 2026. The US and Canada have long clashed over the northern neighbor’s aims to protect its dairy industry from foreign competition.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCows are shown from a Quebec dairy farm in Monceau, Canada, on 10 September 2026. The US and Canada have long clashed over the northern neighbor’s aims to protect its dairy industry from foreign competition.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockTrump tariffsUS ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationshipIt marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationshipAssociated PressTue 29 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS-Canadarelations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early on Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1bn worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880bn worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors. But it marks another ratcheting up ofDonald Trump’s second-term trade war with the US’s longtime ally and trading partner.The import ban “certainly won’t do anything to help the trade tensions between the United States and Canada’,’ said trade attorney Patrick Childress, a partner at Holland + Knight and a former US trade official.‘It’s just getting worse’: anger in Maine over Trump’s trade war with close neighbor CanadaRead moreThe latest sparring began over the summer when Trump reached back to a Great Depression law to impose 50% tariffs on about $20bn worth of Canadian imports, charging that Canada discriminates against US dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly counterpunched with tariffs of 15%, 25% or 50%, matching US imports dollar for dollar.To punish Canada for retaliating against his tariffs, Trump decided to ban a list of Canadian products, effective 12.01 am Eastern time Tuesday.The economic impact is likely to be minimal. Childress noted that the products on the banned list were already facing Trump’s tariffs. “For a lot of these goods, the 50% was already acting as a de facto ban by making importation from Canada into the United States uneconomical,″ he said.Jacob Jensen, director of trade policy at the center-right American Action Forum thinktank, calculates that the ban would cover $967m worth of Canadian imports, based on 2025 numbers. Of that, 87% would be alcoholic beverages that the US targeted because of some Canadian provinces responding to Trump’s provocations by banning US booze from store shelves.Also banned are some dairy products – including the milk byproduct whey. The two countries have long clashed over Canada’s attempts to protect its dairy industry from foreign competition by imposing hefty tariffs once dairy imports have exceeded a quota.The ban also covers motorcycles. Bombardier Recreational Products (BRP) in Quebec confirmed that its three-wheel Can-Am Spyder and Canyon motorcycles “will be excluded from importation into the US’’. But BRP said the impact would probably not be felt until next year because it has completed most production and shipments for the current season.“This marks yet another escalation in the trade war that may result in further retaliation on the Canadian side,” Jensen said. He expects Canadian exporters and US importers “impacted by these bans will be highly motivated’’ to demand that trade officials on both sides find some way to reach a “resolution of this whole ordeal’’.The impasse imperils efforts to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a North American trade pact Trump pressured the US’s neighbors into accepting in his first term and which he once declared “the most modern, up-to-date, and balanced trade agreement in the history of our country’’.The deal allowed most goods to cross North American borders duty free. But since returning to the White House last year, Trump has announced a series of tariffs that have clouded the future of trade in the region.Trump has directed most of his ire at Canada. He is openly seeking to pull Canadian manufacturing south. And he has inflamed public opinion in Canada by repeatedly suggesting that the country become the US’s 51st state.The Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, came to power last year on a promise to stand up to Trump. In addition to retaliating against Trump tariffs, Carney has sought to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States, which last year accounted for more than 70% of Canadian exports.“There is now a price to be paid for access to the United States market,” Carney said earlier this month. Carney has embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsUS economyCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpTariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: On the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ grows | Whisky | The Guardian
description: Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures
Content: With whisky production paused at Holyrood Distillery in Edinburgh, the copper stills sit idle.Photograph: Holyrood DistilleryView image in fullscreenWith whisky production paused at Holyrood Distillery in Edinburgh, the copper stills sit idle.Photograph: Holyrood DistilleryWhiskyOn the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ growsDemand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closuresPatrick GreenfieldTue 29 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleObscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky. By the time the latest set of warehouses are finished on the former opencast coal mine, Diageo’s 220-hectare (544-acre) maturation campus will be able to store almost 3m casks of Scotch. The drinks multinational needs the space.After a 15-year boom turbocharged by the Covid-19 pandemic, demand for Scotch whisky has slumped around the world. Distilleries have paused production acrossScotlandto avoid adding to the glut of supply, known as a “whisky loch” – the equivalent of a “wine lake”.Last week, the community-owned GlenWyvis Distillery in the Highlands announced it would appoint administrators following sustained financial pressure in the whisky market. On Monday, workers at Cameronbridge, Diageo’s largest distillery, a short drive from Cluny bond, began strike action in opposition to the company’s plans to cut hundreds of jobs across its Scottish operation.Diageo produces about one in three bottles of Scotch globally, including popular brands such as Johnnie Walker. Dozens of Scotland’s 156 active distilleries are rumoured to be up for sale.“Strangely, Scotch has had a really good time since the 2008 financial crisis,” said industry veteran Nick Morgan. “But people have stopped buying at the crazy rates they had been.View image in fullscreen‘People who bought whisky in the pandemic realised they had enough for two or three years.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images“People who bought whisky in the pandemic because they had nothing else to do realised they probably had enough at home for two or three years. There’s increased awareness of health issues, many are choosing to drink less, and booze got very expensive during the good years for the business.”Fluctuations in Scotch whisky’s £5.36bn export market have proven particularly hard to navigate. By law, the drink must be matured for a minimum of three years in an oak cask in Scotland, with high-end speciality Scotch being aged in barrels for up to 40 years. Such lengthy maturation periods, used to create a wide range of flavour profiles from sweet to sulphurous, can make it hard to plan production.DespiteDonald Trump’s decision to remove dutieson Scotch exports to the US after the King and Queen’s state visit to the White House earlier this year, the industry had already suffered a significant hit. The US president’s “liberation day” tariffs in April 2025 resulted ina 15% fall in Scotch exports to the US, according to the Scotch Whisky Association.Demand in France – until recently the largest market by volume – has fallen, while the market in China has never really taken off as hoped. Optimists point to early signs of a tentative recovery, however, withthe industry returning to growthin the first half of this year. Exports to India in particular have surged – but have not yet offset declines elsewhere.A line chart shows Scotch sales growing in India and falling in France, the US and the rest of the UK outside Scotland. Brazil also shows slight growth, but after a large dipThe downturn is by no means limited to Scotch, either. Many drinks manufacturers are experiencing a post-pandemic slump, with five of the biggest publicly listed alcohol producers sitting ona record $22bn of aging spirits, according to the Financial Times.Holyrood Distillery, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat inEdinburgh, is among those to have paused production while its owners wait out the difficult period. Its bulbous copper stills, which would usually be hard at work producing single-malt Scotch, sit idle. Co-founder Rob Carpenter says he does not know when that will change.“Anecdotally, my understanding is that the industry might be producing around a third of its normal level right now,” he said. “No one has a crystal ball, so nobody knows what is going to happen 10 years from now. You try to anticipate where things are going to be. It is a curse of the industry in a sense.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnlike many of its rivals, Holyrood Distillery benefits from tourists visiting the Scottish capital. About 40,000 people each year tour the stone building, which is almost 200 years old and used to support theInnocent railway. The tours account for around half of the company’s current revenue.View image in fullscreenRob Carpenter, Holyrood Distillery co-founderPhotograph: Holyrood Distillery“It is not really that people have stopped drinking spirits,” Carpenter added. “[But] consumers are nervous. We all see what’s happening in the world. There is not a lot of predictability in things right now, and people are just being careful with what they spend their money on. This is a luxury spirit.”The current industry downturn is not new. In the 1980s, the Scotch whisky industry faced a similar mixture of weak demand and chronic oversupply, causing a flurry of distillery closures across Scotland. The rise of Japanese whisky producers, a global economic downturn, and overconfidence from a 1970s boom drove a prolonged bust.Today, few think the latest slump is the beginning of a permanent change in the industry’s fortunes. When Holyrood Distillery opens for tours, visitors file in, scanning through the single malts on the shelves.“Whisky is a waiting game,” said Morgan, who charted Johnnie Walker’s 200-year history in a 2020 book. “If you look at the data on sales, every time you have one of these downturns, it comes back higher. At the moment, the business is in the trough. I can pretty much assure you in five years time, when demand really cranks up again, they’ll find they haven’t got enough whisky, and they’ll have to switch everything on.”Explore more on these topicsWhiskyFood & drink industryScotlandDiageoEdinburghfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?
Content: Manchester City celebrate winning the Premier League in 2018. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters after the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City celebrate winning the Premier League in 2018. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters after the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersManchester CitySham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severeJonathan WilsonHow can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTShareHow bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation thatManchester Cityhad been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.Manchester City’s ‘sham’ seasons: how they fared and who was in chargeRead moreCity continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that thePremier LeagueBoard and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.View image in fullscreenThe Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19.Photograph: Carl Recine/ReutersThe verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’Read moreHaving been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFinancesPremier LeagueFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: MLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall? | MLB | The Guardian
description: As the postseason starts with the wildcard round, our writers pick the dark horses, likely winners and the high seeds at risk of going out early
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: As the postseason starts with the wildcard round, our writers pick the dark horses, likely winners and the high seeds at risk of going out early
Content: Shohei Ohtani, Jacob Misiorowski and Junior Caminero will all play a big part in this year’s playoffs.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)View image in fullscreenShohei Ohtani, Jacob Misiorowski and Junior Caminero will all play a big part in this year’s playoffs.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)MLBMLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall?As the postseason starts with the wildcard round, our writers pick the dark horses, likely winners and the high seeds at risk of going out earlyBryan Armen Graham,Alex KirshnerandDavid LengelTue 29 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeam who will most be missed from the playoffsTheMariners. The only active MLB team to have never appeared in a World Seriescame within a single winof ending that hoodoo last October and appeared poised to go one stage further in 2026. Instead, their 76-86 clunker feels like a wasted chance for a lineup featuring Julio Rodríguez, Cal Raleigh and Randy Arozarena.BAGThePiratescould have brought real verve to the postseason with a healthy Konnor Griffin at shortstop and Paul Skenes on the mound. Sadly the team dug too deep a hole in August and, in usual Pirate fashion, didn’t give themselves a chance.AKThat has to be theOrioles, which meansPete Alonso’s F-David Stearns tourwon’t see the bright lights of the postseason. The Mets’ president of baseball operations, one with almost all the money in the world at his disposal, who didn’t offer a contract to Alonso – who hit 43 home runs, arguably the second-best season of his career – is finally off the hook. That is, at least until a would-be 2027 season. Too bad.DLHigh seed at risk of going out earlyThe American League’s No 2 seed is an 85-win division champion with a plus-11 run differential who FanGraphs suggestswas closer to a .500 ball club. TheGuardianshave the pitching to thrive in close games, but a lineup without a 20-homer batter leaves them little room for error.BAGJustin Verlander leaves field in tears with daughter after final start of 21-year careerRead moreTheDodgersare finally going to face the consequences that come with age, variance, and having had to play an extra 31 games over the prior two postseasons. They still have no big weaknesses, but their lineup is old (the average age on their roster is 31, making them the oldest team in MLB) and has occasionally looked the part this year.AKIf you needed a team to squeak out a single run under pressure against great playoff pitching, that’s not theYankeeswithAaron Judge in the lineup. Without him, against some superb Red Sox hurlers, the swing-and-a-miss Bronx Bombers have even less of a chance of putting runs on the board. They could find themselves bronzing in Cancún sooner rather than later.DLDark horse to winIt seems odd to call a team with baseball’sbest offenseanddefensea dark horse, butthe Cubs’ leaky relief pitching makes them one. Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman give Chicago plenty of ways to win games. If the bullpen can keep the ball in the park, they could go far.BAGTheRayswill always have a dark-horse feel, even in a year when they win the AL East. Pitching could be the difference here: whether injured starter Shane McClanahan returns at some point or not, the deadline acquisition of Freddy Peralta from the Mets ensures rotation depth that will serve this club well.AKHow can a team with 98 wins be a dark horse? When they don’t hit for power, get on base less than the Rockies, and their ability to score is a little better than middle of the road. They play in a condom-covered dump in front of some of the leanest crowds in the league. An inspiring, title-like set up? Nope, and theRaysare dark horses because few fans know they even exist. Pragmatic as they come though; they can pitch and Kevin Cash can manage. The AL can’t handle them, and the Dodgers are vulnerable.DLPlayer to watch …Tarik Skubal arrives in October as the centerpiece of baseball’s most formidable rotation, with a potential record-setting free agency ahead. Every start will be judged against theimposing price the Dodgers paidto acquire him in their bid for a rare third straight title.BAGTampa Bay’sChandler Simpsonis a throwback, a defense, speed and batting average-heavy corner outfielder who’s made a place for himself despite lacking the power that makes most great modern hitters. In a lineup with a lot of thump, Simpson’s slap hitting offers a bit of variety.AKSticking to my Rays theme, it’sJunior Caminero. The Dominican gets no recognition, or at least not enough, despite crushing close to 90 home runs in two years, while also hitting for average. He’s making strides every season and he’s only 23. At some point the third baseman is going to be very expensive, so who knows how long he’ll remain on the Gulf. At the moment, he’s the straw that stirs Tampa’s tipple, and now Caminero has the spotlight.DLMost important factor this postseason/offseasonThe labor talks. The collective bargaining agreement expires on 1 December and MLB’s salary-cap proposal remains at odds with the players’ intractable position. A lockout could freeze the hot-stove market while a prolonged dispute could torpedo the 2027 season entirely. Whatever happens on the field, the most important baseball story after the Fall Classic will unfold across a bargaining table.BAGThe lack of great teams in the American League.The Rays may be a great team, but is anyone else in the Junior Circuit? MLB’s three best teams – the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves – are all in the NL, and I’d probably prefer the Cubs over any team in the AL at the moment, too. The AL has a true “anyone’s ballgame” feel. You could imagine this league producing a trulyweirdpennant winner.AKThepostseason CBA negotiationsmay not bring us world peace, but hopefully they will create a new rule that bans teams with .500 records or worse from winning a division, or reaching the playoffs via a wildcard spot. The team with the best above-.500 record not to qualify for the playoffs, regardless of league, will replace that team, and the sub-.500 bums will not be allowed to complain AT ALL. And God forbid the Astros win the 2026 World Series, I will pull whatever is left of my hair out. Who’s with me?DLNLCSDodgers over Brewers.BAGBrewers over Dodgers.AKBrewers over Dodgers.DLALCSRays over White Sox.BAGRays over White Sox.AKRays over Guardians.DLYour World Series winners will be …View image in fullscreenThe Dodgers celebrate last year’s title. Will they repeat?Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesThe Rays will put the ball in play, run the basepaths aggressively and make the Dodgers earn their outs. But a rotation of Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow gives the Dodgers four starters capable of shutting down the Rays’ contact-heavy lineup, while the incandescent Shohei Ohtani supplies the power capable of turning any close game with one swing of the bat. Milwaukee and Tampa Bay may grade out better analytically, but the smell test clearly favors theDodgersto become only the third franchise to win three consecutive World Series crowns.BAGTheBrewerswill finally get the right October mixture this year. They have the same deep lineup as usual, with no real stars but also no weaknesses. Jacob Misiorowski gives them a rotation trump card that they haven’t had since CC Sabathia’s brief run in Milwaukee after the 2008 trade deadline. And they have the necessary high-leverage relievers (Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby) to feel good about any game that’s still competitive after six innings.AKIn many ways the Brewers and Rays are mirror images of each other, especially when it comes to their contract-based approaches to baseball. They are also similar in the way that absolutely nobody except their fans wants to see such a matchup. The Brewers have the overwhelming ace in Misiorowski, but theRayshave more pitching depth. They’re also due to win, with the owners detesting this matchup which proves lower payroll teamscanwin it all. And at precisely the wrong time.DLExplore more on these topicsMLBTampa Bay RaysNew York YankeesLos Angeles DodgersMilwaukee BrewersCleveland GuardiansHouston AstrosfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ferrari say team has ‘made its choices’ and there’s no vacancy for Christian Horner | Ferrari | The Guardian
description: Marque reaffirmed its commitment to Fred Vasseur after Christian Horner had expressed interest in joining Ferrari
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Marque reaffirmed its commitment to Fred Vasseur after Christian Horner had expressed interest in joining Ferrari
Content: Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner told the Times leading Ferrari would be his ‘dream’ job.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFormer Red Bull team principal Christian Horner told the Times leading Ferrari would be his ‘dream’ job.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockFerrariFerrari say team has ‘made its choices’ and there’s no vacancy for Christian HornerMarque reaffirms commitment to Fred VasseurHorner had expressed interest in joining FerrariGiles RichardsTue 29 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFerrari have reaffirmed their backing for their team principal, Fred Vasseur, in an effort to end speculation thatChristian Hornerwas being considered as a potential replacement for the Frenchman.Horner gave aninterview in the Times last weekin which he stated that leading Ferrari would be his “dream” job and the only one he would consider without having part-ownership of the team. His comments provoked debate that he could replace Vasseur, given the Scuderia’s underperformance this season.Lando Norris targeted by online abuse after calling for Franco Colapinto banRead moreOn Tuesday,Ferraritook the unusual step of holding an unscheduled media call in an effort to close down the chatter, with the team’s chief communication officer, Maria Conti, speaking on behalf of the chair, John Elkann, and the chief executive officer, Benedetto Vigna.“Ferrari’s position is clear, has not changed, and Ferrari has made its choices already. We have confidence, full confidence, in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so,” she said.“Everybody, they are still ­creating a lot of different stories around Fred and this is not useful. We do not intend to fuel speculation or ­comment on assumptions coming from outside the company.“It is not just related to the story in the Times of Mr Horner but in general, there was other speculation also.”Ferrari had hoped the new ­regulations this season would ­present a chance to once more compete for the title but while they are second in the constructors’ championship they are 160 points off the leaders, Mercedes.Vasseur, who joined the team in 2023 and had his contract extended in July of last year, made it clear after the last round in Baku that speculation about his future was not helping the team. “We are not working in the perfect serenity,” he said. “But it is what it is, it’s not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job – that everybody knows – everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team.”Conti noted that Horner’s interest in the position was indicative of the enduring appeal of Ferrari. “Ferrari has always attracted extraordinary interest, and it is only natural that many professionals aspire to be part of it,” she said. “It is a reflection of the strength of what Ferrari really represents.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElsewhere on Tuesday Aston Martin confirmed their driver lineup for 2027 will remain the same with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. Alonso’s decision to remain in F1 ends conjecture that the 46-year-old double world champion was contemplating retirement from the sport as Aston Martin endure a dismal season with an underperforming car and engine. Next year will be Alonso’s 24thtfull season in F1.“It took me a little bit of time to make my decision. But now I have things very clear on my mind,” he said. “I will retire from F1 … But not yet. I still feel fast and motivated and a huge passion for F1 and for the sport. It is my life.”Explore more on these topicsFerrariChristian HornerFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: American exodus: why do so many US NHL stars want out of Canada? | NHL | The Guardian
description: Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respect
Author: Colin Horgan
Headline: Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respect
Content: Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck is one of several American players who sought moves out of Canadian markets this offseason.Photograph: Panayiota Good/NHLI/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWinnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck is one of several American players who sought moves out of Canadian markets this offseason.Photograph: Panayiota Good/NHLI/Getty ImagesNHLAmerican exodus: why do so many US NHL stars want out of Canada?Players across the league are leaving their teams up north to return home. It’s prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respectColin HorganTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in September 1925, Frederick Wilson, sports editor at the Globe, explained the fear among hockey fans that Canadian teams might not be able to compete for players against the new US teams like New York or Boston that were entering the pro league. “Will it be a matter of money?” Wilson headlined his piece. And for about a century, money was the recurrent nexus of the Canadian hockey panic, proven by franchise departures and depleted buying power.At the time, Wilson reassured everyone that, no matter the big US cash, everyone on the ice would be Canadian anyway. “It will be some years before the [US] will be in a position to furnish players,” he wrote. He was right about that. It took a long time for the US to catch up to Canada in on-ice talent. But now that it has, should we expect Americans to want to play anywhere else than the US? For 100 years Canada has worried that the US would just buy all the best hockey players. But now it makes its own and, as the newNHLseason gets underway on Tuesday night, they want to go home.Alex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the oppositeRead moreIt’s difficult to pinpoint where this all started. But the general feeling, given the timing, is that something happened around this year’s Olympics that prompted US-born players to turn their backs on Canada. Maybe it started earlier, in 2025, afterthe 4 Nations Face-Off. Or maybe it was just in the wind, given the new geopolitical tensions between the two countries. In any event, as the 2026-27 NHL season kicks off Tuesday, the divide is back – or at least seems to have deepened.Quinn Hughes was the first to jump, leaving Vancouver for Minnesota last December after making it clear he wouldn’t re-sign. In April, Jim Rutherford, the Canucks’ president of hockey operations,was blunt about what underpinned it. “Some people think Quinn left here because the team wasn’t any good. He was leaving anyway,” Rutherford said, pointing to Matthew Tkachuk, who had left Calgary in 2022. “He wanted to go back to the US, and he went.” And, Rutherford noted, Hughes wouldn’t be the last.Rutherford was right. As the 2025-26 season ended, Tkachuk’s brother, Brady, captain of the Ottawa Senators, asked to go. Sure enough, he got his wish and landed in Florida with his brother. “Blood is thicker than water, and let’s just say that his father and his brother got in his kitchen,” Senators owner Michael Andlauersaid earlier this month. “Ultimately, the decision was made to go and play with his brother. It’s a decision that was out of our control to a certain degree.”Detroit’s now-former captain Dylan Larkin also wants out. And while it’s a US city he’s leaving, his reported potential destinations don’t include any Canadian teams – including the one who’s been asking about him for a while, Montreal, who have plenty of cap space and an exciting young roster built on fresh contract extensions. But it’s all moot. According to TSN, Larkinwon’t considerany Canadian team at all.View image in fullscreenMatthew Tkachuk, left, and Brady Tkachuk both left Canadian teams to play for the Florida Panthers.Photograph: Charles Krupa/APWhich brings us to Connor Hellebuyck, whose story is a little more complicated. Last month, the Winnipeg Jets goaltenderrevealedhe’d requested to be traded “several months” earlier. It came as a surprise. When Hellebuyck signed a seven-year contract worth $59.5m in 2023,he saidthat he was “ready to be a Jet for life and bring a Cup to this city”. But things changed. For one thing, the Jets have faltered and a Cup looks unlikely soon. Then there were the Olympics. Hellebuyck wasn’t the only reason the US beat Canada in the gold-medal game, but he was a big one (he made 41 saves) – good enough, anyway, for Donald Trump to award Hellebuyck the Presidential Medal of Freedom. That, and theWhite House visitthat came with it, soured some fans and, according to Hellebuyck, led to threats and online abuse aimed at his family.Hellebuyck is reportedly open to a competitive US team, and talks with Buffalo stalled over Winnipeg’s asking price. It’sbeen suggestedthat Hellebuyck would accept a move to Edmonton or Montreal, so it’s possible he’s swayed less by anti-Canada bias than he is by wanting to win, but who knows? For now, he’s beensuspendedfor failing to report to training camp, and will sit in limbo – presumably somewhere between Manitoba and his home state of Michigan – until it’s resolved.In fairness, none of these players has publicly decried Canada. There are legitimate reasons to go, including family ties and better tax rates. Nor is it a universal exit. Toronto Maple Leafs captain Auston Matthews is staying put for now, likely influenced by the team’s management overhaul and offseason additions. Ultimately, these are hockey players. They have the right to play where they want, contract allowing.But rights and respect are two different things, and that second one is tricky. Rutherford’s prediction echoed throughout the summer because it plucked a chord deep in the Canadian psyche. For a long time, the problem seemed to be one of money. But money problems can be fixed – and largely were. Since the salary cap was introduced in 2005, Canadian teams have been able to move and manipulate the numbers to compete with their US peers.But what they can’t manufacture is desire. “You have to want to play for Ottawa,” Andlauer said of Tkachuk’s departure. Lots of players still do want to play in Canada. The worry now is that the best American ones don’t.Explore more on these topicsNHLUS sportsIce hockeyUSA ice hockey teamCanada ice hockey teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man Czechia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane strikes steered England to a 2-0 Nations League win against Czechia, who had Pavel Sulc sent off in the first half
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane strikes steered England to a 2-0 Nations League win against Czechia, who had Pavel Sulc sent off in the first half
Content: Harry Kane (left) celebrates with Anthony Gordon after scoring England’s second goal against Czechia in Prague.Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane (left) celebrates with Anthony Gordon after scoring England’s second goal against Czechia in Prague.Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPANations LeagueGordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man CzechiaDavid Hytnerat the Fortuna ArenaTue 29 Sep 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnybody can lose to Spain. But whenEngland did so at Wembley on Saturday, it served to turn up the temperature for this trip to Czechia. England have form for finding it difficult at this compact stadium. Remember the European Championship qualifierhere in 2019 when they lost 2-1?It was not easy at first. Thomas Tuchel shuffled his pack, making the surprise decision to start Jude Bellingham among the substitutes. It was all a little angsty andCzechia, for whom this is the dawn of a new era under the Spaniard Santi Denia after their World Cup wipeout, dared to dream of another upset.Czechia 0-2 England: Nations League football – as it happenedRead moreThen everything changed. It was a rash challenge in the 23rd minute by Pavel Sulc on Elliot Anderson, late and high, albeit nothing overtly nasty. The referee, Umut Meler, showed the Czechia midfielder a yellow card and on we went. Yet the VAR was not happy and when Meler was called to the pitchside monitor, everybody knew what was coming next.It was a red card to disfigure the contest but Tuchel was not complaining. His players made the most of the decision to get theirNations Leaguecampaign up and running with the standout moment being provided by Tuchel’s headline selection.Trent Alexander-Arnold was in from the cold at the outset for only his second appearance under Tuchel; the first was as a substitute against Andorra in the summer of last year. It was the Real Madrid player who helped to unlock the stalemate at the beginning of the second half, his whipped cross made to measure for Anthony Gordon.Harry Kane added the second with his 87thEnglandgoal and, after all the focus on England’s defensive vulnerability, there was the bonus for Tuchel of a first clean sheet in seven matches. The team had conceded 13 times in the previous six. It did not start particularly well. By the end, it was a stroll.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane fires home to double England’s lead with his 87th goal for the national team.Photograph: Javier García/ShutterstockThe inclusion of Alexander-Arnold at right-back was the ­wildcard. Any team with him in it feels more nuanced and it meant Tuchel retained only Marc Guéhi from the back four against Spain. Ezri Konsa and Nico O’Reilly had minor injuries. With Trevoh Chalobah in central defence and Lewis Hall at left-back, it was a completely untested unit.England lacked cohesion at the outset. There were errors from them and it was easy to fret about their lack of care on the ball; the looseness of some of the passing. They were a little open at the back. Czechia were the better team until the sending-off.England could highlight the moment on 16 minutes when Gordon took a fizzed pass from Myles Lewis-Skelly and crossed low for Morgan Rogers. The man who came in for Bellingham spun and sent a shot against the inside of the far post. But Czechia had flickers. Sulc almost got in after Anderson misjudged a high ball. Lukas Cerv hit a sweet volley past the post. Sulc choose the wrong option when well-placed and was crowded out by Guéhi and Chalobah.View image in fullscreenPavel Sulc (left) is shown a red card by Halil Meler for a foul on Elliot Anderson.Photograph: Slávek Růta/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe red card was devastating for Sulc, and not only because he did not have to jump into the tackle. It was in a non-threatening area of the pitch for Czechia. He overstretched in an effort to win the ball and it did not feel crazily excessive in terms of the force. There was no outrage from the England players around Anderson. At the monitor, though, Meler concluded that it ticked the boxes for an upgrade to red. As always, it looked worse on the slow-motion replays.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCzechia felt their attacking ambition evaporate. England came to dominate the ball. What could they do with it? Not much before the ­interval. Kane took another incisive pass from Lewis-Skelly and extended Matej Kovar in the 45th minute but that was about it.Tuchel finished the first half in an almighty funk at the fourth official after a decision had gone against Bukayo Saka. The manager reset at the interval, sending on Eberechi Eze for Lewis-Skelly – who was booked on 35 minutes – and going to a 4-1-4-1. Lewis-Skelly had lunged in on Cerv, whose screams could be heard up in the press box. The Czechs wanted a red card to even things up. It was not that bad but Tuchel could not take any chances.View image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon plants his astute second-half header, from Trent Alexander-Arnold’s cross, into the corner of the net.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesEngland got the breakthrough almost immediately and it was one for the Alexander-Arnold lovers. When Czechia coughed up the ball cheaply, he chased it down on the right, turned and did what he does. The pinged cross had a low trajectory and it bounced once before sitting up for Gordon, whose headed conversion was marked by precision. It was deserved reward for Gordon, who was quick and urgent; the player most likely to spark England.England relaxed. They were good thereafter. Hall began to surge up the line. He shot inches wide after getting a pass back from Gordon while he watched Ladislav Krejci turn a low cross from him against the far post. The Kane goal was inevitable and it came when he drilled a loose ball into the far corner after a break into the box by Rogers.Tuchel got Alex Scott on for his debut and he did well. Ditto Rio ­Ngumoha, who also came off the bench. England might have scored more with Kovar making a particularly fine save to deny Eze. Next up for them is Croatia away on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueCzechiaEnglandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at Infantino | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Aleksander Ceferin condemned FFE and Balogun affair, and told club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to Fifa
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Aleksander Ceferin condemned FFE and Balogun affair, and told club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to Fifa
Content: The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferinin (right), has launched a scathing takedown of Gianni Infantino’s conduct.Photograph: Mark Pain/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferinin (right), has launched a scathing takedown of Gianni Infantino’s conduct.Photograph: Mark Pain/AlamyUefa‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at InfantinoAleksander Ceferin condemns FFE and Balogun affairTells club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to FifaNick Amesin CopenhagenTue 29 Sep 2026 15.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has attacked his embattled Fifa counterpartGianni Infantinoin a scathing takedown of the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and other recent scandals, saying “the emperor is naked” and declaring “it is time to say ‘enough’”.In a pointed address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin did not mention Infantino by name but made clear his view that Fifa’s leadership must change. He drew on the event’s location, Copenhagen, to make a comparison to Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes inassessing Infantino’s conduct, making clear reference to the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump and last summer’s FolarinBalogun affair along with the FFE scheme.Fifa accuses Uefa of ‘harassment’ and ‘misinformation’ in push against InfantinoRead more“An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see,” Ceferin said. “His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities.“Selling part of football’s future does not become development because you call it development. Putting afait accompliin front of national associations does not become democratisation because you call it democratisation, however big the cheque is. And secrecy does not become consultation because you call it consultation.”Ceferin suggested to the ­hundreds of club representatives present that ­Infantino’s behaviour would not be tolerated at one of their organisations. “Imagine one of your senior executives secretly negotiating away control of your club’s crown jewels,” he said. “You didn’t know. Your board didn’t know. Your players and fans didn’t know. And by the time you find out, the deal is almost done. What would your board do?“Imagine that he creates a peace prize for a political leader, without his own board having any say over its creation or its recipient. Then, that same political leader calls during the biggest competition in the world to complain about a decision on the pitch. The rules say one thing. The phone rings. Then the decision changes.“How many times would this have to happen at your club before the board says: ‘enough’? I think it is time to say ‘enough’. No office, no title and no amount of power gives anyone the right to sell the future of football.”The ongoing war of words between football’s biggest governing bodies had already intensified on Tuesday when Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency,urging a US court to reject Uefa’s requestto receive documents for use in a planned criminal complaint against Infantino.Senior figures within Uefa remain adamant that a candidate to oppose Infantino in theFifaelection next March must be found before the 18 November deadline for nominations. The EFC chair, Nasser al-Khelaifi, has been mooted in the past as a future contender but conclusively ruled himself out of the Fifa presidency in the Danish capital.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I have zero interest in Fifa, zero agenda or ambition to be there,” al-Khelaifi said. “I don’t think I’m the right guy for this position. I’m enjoying what I’m doing, having fun. Fifa, not for me.”Al-Khelaifi has designs on expanding the scope of his own organisation. In his speech to the general assembly he said “now is the time to create World Football Clubs”, explicitly stating that a representative body including those beyond Europe should be formed. “We are more than proud and happy if we can help and contribute outside of Europe for our colleagues from different clubs in the world,” he said later.Explore more on these topicsUefaFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senate passes bipartisan Protect College Sports Act amid ‘chaos’ in industry | College sports | The Guardian
description: The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill on Monday that would regulate college sports amid athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill on Monday that would regulate college sports amid athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers
Content: College sports are a huge industry in the US.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenCollege sports are a huge industry in the US.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersCollege sportsSenate passes bipartisan Protect College Sports Act amid ‘chaos’ in industryCollege sports have been upended by athlete paymentsCritics say legislation does not go far enoughAssociated PressTue 29 Sep 2026 07.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill on Monday thatwould regulate college sports, an attempt to end “chaos” in an industry that has been upended by skyrocketing athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers between schools.The overwhelming 77-22 vote to pass the Protect College Sports Act is the strongest effort yet by Congress to set national regulations governing payments to college athletes for their name, image and likeness and how often they can transfer. It would give the NCAA new authority over those rules and limited antitrust protections to enforce them.The bill is the product of years of Senate negotiations that intensified after a lawsuit settlement uprooted the college sports landscape by allowing colleges to pay their players. The legislation, which would still have to pass the House, would codify the settlement into law but also establish new guardrails around the system in an attempt to rein in the runaway costs for colleges.“It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and only Congress can fix it,” said Republican Texas senator Ted Cruz, who negotiated the bill with a Democratic senator, Washington’s Maria Cantwell.Donald Trump praised the bill in a social media post after the late-night passage. “This is a really big deal,” he said. “It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves.”The bill’s backers – more than 70 senators from both parties – say it aims to curtail constant litigation and uncertainty across college sports for athletes, schools and fans. It would also give hundreds of thousands of athletes new health and labor protections.40 years on, did Proposition 48 protect US college sports – or punish Black athletes?Read moreBut critics say the bill doesn’t do enough to protect athletes or curtail the enormous sums of money flowing to coaches, colleges and conferences.“This is a bill that essentially ensconces a system of exploitation, and it doesn’t fix the broader problems,” said Connecticut senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat who has worked with labor and civil rights groups to rally opposition to the bill.The bill’s future is still unclear. It could face an uphill battle in the House, which failed repeatedly over the last year to get a different version to the floor and is in recess until after the November elections. Lawmakers will have to start over in the next Congress if the bill doesn’t pass both chambers by the end of the year.College sports have been reeling in the wake of the 2025 court settlement allowing colleges to directly pay players for their name, image and likeness. The fallout has reshaped the industry and led to football roster payrolls that can exceed $40m.View image in fullscreenCollege football generates huge revenues.Photograph: Tom Jones/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe bill would codify the court settlement, including a revenue cap that allows schools to share up to $21.5m in revenue with their players. The legislation would more than double that amount for some schools, allowing up to an additional $27.5m in payments through a retention fund – a change that helped win the support of the two largest conferences, the Big Ten and Southeastern Conference.To help schools raise more revenue, the bill would give schools and conferences the option of pooling their TV media rights.The legislation also aims to stabilize the NCAA transfer portal that has led to players constantly switching teams. It would restrict player transfers to one “free” move over five years without sitting out a year, with some exceptions, and also would restrict players to five years of total eligibility.The proposed eligibility limit comes amid backlash to schools that have increasingly pushed boundaries, including LSU’s now-canceled plans to place players on the roster who had participated in NFL training camps.The bill also would restrict coaches from leaving their schools during the season, force schools that want to switch conferences to spend three years as an independent and prevent conferences from growing larger than 20 programs – an effort to prevent so-called “superleagues” from taking over sports.Some Democrats say the bill wouldn’t do enough to limit the big money in college sports.The legislation “places a cap on the students’ cut of the revenues, but there are no caps on coaches’ salaries or on the size of donations to athletic programs,” Murphy said last week.Groups including the NAACP, the Congressional Black Caucus and AFL-CIO have also opposed the bill, in part, because it leaves unresolved whether athletes should be considered employees with the ability to collectively bargain.All four Black Democrats in the Senate – Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Angela Alsobrooks – have opposed the bill.Booker, who played football at Stanford in the late 1980s on a scholarship, noted the “outsized role” that Black athletes play in college sports. He said it wasn’t until college athletes were able to begin to win cases in court that the power started to shift, “and now the NCAA is coming here to the United States Senate, asking for sweeping powers” to exempt antitrust laws.“We know who this bill is protecting,” Booker said.Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsCollege footballCollege basketballUS politicsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: USWNT roster: Ashley Sanchez earns the call for friendlies v Spain | USA women's football team | The Guardian
description: The NWSL’s top scorer returns to the national team after yeas on the periphery for games against the current World Cup champions
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The NWSL’s top scorer returns to the national team after yeas on the periphery for games against the current World Cup champions
Content: Ashley Sanchez last appeared for the US in a 2024 friendly v Argentina.Photograph: Joe Robbins/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAshley Sanchez last appeared for the US in a 2024 friendly v Argentina.Photograph: Joe Robbins/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUSA women's football teamUSWNT roster: Ashley Sanchez earns the call for friendlies v SpainSanchez, NWSL’s top scorer, returns after years awayNaomi Girma called up despite injury absence for ChelseaMallory Swanson earns recall after Olympic heroicsJeff RueterTue 29 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaomi Girma and Sam Coffey are returning to the United States women’s national team, with their pair of WSL standouts named in Emma Hayes’ squad for October’s friendlies against defending World Cup champion Spain.NWSL top scorer Ashley Sanchez has also earned a recall on the back of her MVP-caliber performance with the North Carolina Courage. Sanchez has already set an league record for goals in a season by an American player, already up to 20 in 26 matches. With another goal, Sanchez will break Temwa Chawinga’s overall scoring record. An attacking midfielder, Sanchez’s most recent cap came in October 2024, in a friendly against Argentina early in Hayes’ tenure.Hayes largely leaned on established members of her core for the 26-player squad, adding four uncapped players on the back of strong seasons in the NWSL.“While we are very much looking forward to playing the World Cup champions, I keep coming back to the journey that we are all on together,” said Hayes. “This camp will be about reestablishing connections after a long break, looking at a few players who haven’t been with us this cycle, and putting on the best performances we can in front of packed stadiums.”‘A lot of people counted me out’: Ashley Sanchez on goal records, grit and potential USWNT returnRead moreAshley Sanchez gets the callSanchez’s recall has been a hot topic in NWSL circles as the playmaker continues a career year. A member of the 2023 Women’s World Cup squad, Sanchez failed to get on the field that summer and has since been a peripheral figure as positional alternatives like Lavelle, Jaedyn Shaw, and Croix Bethune have been preferred by Hayes.Sanchez’ recall may help explain the absence of Shaw, whose brace over the weekend brought her to nine goals for Gotham this season. Shaw has been a regular part of the national team setup following the last World Cup, with 17 caps earned in the explorational 2024 and 16 more caps since the start of 2025.The question this window, and in subsequent ones, is how much of Sanchez’s stellar performance with North Carolina will carry over with the national team. The Courage’s team is built to cater to her strengths, allowing her to serve as chief facilitator as well as the team’s primary scoring threat. Hayes’ team already has plenty of players who are comfortable with those responsibilities, and while no team can ever have too many decisive game-breaking options in the final third, it’ll be up to the coaching staff and Sanchez to find the right way to maximize her considerable threat.View image in fullscreenMallory Swanson was in camp with the US earlier this year but did not appear v Brazil.Photograph: Jess Stiles/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockSwanson returnsAlso among those selected is Mallory Swanson, who was involved in the team’s June camp but who didn’t see the field in two contentious friendlies against Brazil. Her last cap for the national team was her goal-scoring, gold medal-winning showing in the 2024 Olympic final. Swanson has appeared in just one of the struggling Chicago Stars’ five most recent games as she works back from injury and the birth of her daughter late last year, but earned Hayes’ faith while co-headlining the Olympic team with fellow “Triple Espresso” front-liners Trinity Rodman and Sophia Wilson – both also selected for the October friendlies.USA exit U-20 World Cup on penalties as tournament’s timing draws criticismRead moreGirma called up despite injury absencesAll eight defenders selected have made at least seven appearances for the USWNT, including young options like Kennedy Wesley, Gisele Thompson, and Lilly Reale. Girma’s return should help refine the team’s play in the defensive third and give a vital primary focal point in possession sequences, as Girma often leads the team in touches whenever available. However, she will be lacking in match fitness, having not appeared for Chelsea due to injury since early September.Emily Fox, Tierna Davidson, Tara Rudd, and Avery Patterson round out the options along the backline.View image in fullscreenSam Coffey has returned to form after injury with Man City.Photograph: Davide Elias/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe usual suspects in midfieldCoffey will offer similar stability at the base of midfield, giving Hayes all of her most leaned-upon options for this window. Lindsey Heaps arrives with 178 caps to her name, having been in and out of availability since joining expansion Denver Summit this summer. Claire Hutton and Lily Yohannes have emerged as regular contributors since the Olympics, while Rose Lavelle remains in fine form for Gotham. Notably, the team listed Swanson among the midfielders and Sanchez among the forwards.Rodman, Swanson, and Wilson are again the attackers in focus, but Alyssa Thompson will look to fortify her case to be Hayes’ starting left winger. The Los Angeles native played matchwinner over the weekend against Arsenal and complements Wilson and Rodman well, moving upfield with decisiveness and showing equal willingness to bait defenders into opening space for her teammates as she is to set up her own shot. Emma Sears and Michelle Cooper offer strong alternatives on the right wing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOlivia Moultrie’s injury leaves the USWNT with a thinning midfield pool ahead of the World CupRead moreThe newcomersJordan Silkowitz could earn her first cap in goal on the back of a strong season. The Bay FC goalkeeper ranks second in the NWSL with 10.4 goals prevented, a metric which compares her conceded goals to post-shot expected goals faced, and leads all NWSL goalkeepers in minutes played without misplaying a cross. She’ll vie for minutes against two of Hayes’ most trusted options in goal, Phallon Tullis-Joyce of Manchester United and Claudia Dickey of the Seattle Reign.The sole newcomer among the midfield septet is Evelyn Shores, who primarily features for Angel City as a left back. The 21-year-old is a threat to create chances with both chipped crosses and her corner kicks, and gives Hayes a needed extra option down the left flank.Two forwards could earn their debuts this window, too. Pietra Tordin has been electric in her second season with the Portland Thorns, with seven goals and nine assists in 2,086 minutes. Her partnership with Wilson has come together quickly, with Tordin benefitting from the additional focus Wilson commands from opponents.
