Trinity Byars also arrives without a senior cap to date, with the 23-year-old having scored 10 goals in just over 1,000 minutes for San Diego.The United States will play their first game against Spain in Washington DC on 10 October, before playing a second friendly on 13 October in Philadelphia.Full USWNT rosterGoalkeepers: Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign), Jordan Silkowitz (Bay FC), Phallon Tullis- Joyce (Manchester United)Defenders: Tierna Davidson (Gotham FC), Emily Fox (Arsenal), Naomi Girma (Chelsea), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash), Lilly Reale (Boston Legacy), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit), Gisele Thompson (Angel City), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave)Midfielders: Sam Coffey (Manchester City), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit), Claire Hutton (Bay FC), Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC), Evelyn Shores (Angel City), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes)Forwards: Trinity Byars (San Diego Wave), Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit), Emma Sears (Racing Louisville), Ashley Sanchez (North Carolina Courage), Pietra Tordin (Portland Thorns), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns)Explore more on these topicsUSA women's football teamUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bears’ 38-year-old backup Case Keenum rolls back the years to ground Eagles | NFL | The Guardian
description: Case Keenum passed for two touchdowns in his first start in almost three years, and the Chicago Bears shut down Jalen Hurts and the Philadelphia Eagles
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Case Keenum passed for two touchdowns in his first start in almost three years, and the Chicago Bears shut down Jalen Hurts and the Philadelphia Eagles
Content: Case Keenum celebrates a touchdown during his team’s victory over the Eagles.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCase Keenum celebrates a touchdown during his team’s victory over the Eagles.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesNFLBears’ 38-year-old backup Case Keenum rolls back the years to ground EaglesPhiladelphia Eagles 7–27 Chicago BearsKeenum throws for two TDs and rushes for anotherAssociated PressMon 28 Sep 2026 23.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCase Keenum passed for two touchdowns in his first start in almost three years, and the Chicago Bears shut down Jalen Hurts and thePhiladelphia Eaglesfor a 27-7 victory on Monday night.Stepping in for Caleb Williams, Keenum was 24 for 34 for 247 yards. He also scored his first rushing touchdown since 2019 on a one-yard plunge with 7:19 left, capping a 13-play drive that took more than eight minutes off the clock.Giants trade for Vikings quarterback JJ McCarthy with Jaxson Dart ruled out for seasonRead moreIt was the 38-year-old’s first action since he started for Houston in a 36-22 loss to Cleveland on Christmas Eve 2023. Williams was sidelined by a right hamstring injury for Monday’s game, and Tyson Bagent backed up Keenum after he cleared the NFL’s concussion protocol on Sunday.“I really don’t have any words, there’s so much emotion,” Keenum said after the game. “Man, these guys I play with in this locker room are incredible … It was so much fun … Just an incredible opportunity, I love this city. This Texas boy loves Chicago. It’s a cool spot.”Keenum played Monday’s game with his children in the stands, something he said was a special experience.“We kept it exciting for them, I’m going to have fun watching the game with them tomorrow on the couch, or probably just Bluey,” said Keenum. “It’s so special, I love my family.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueKalif Raymond had six receptions for 90 yards and a touchdown as Chicago (2-1) bounced back after an ugly 9-3 loss to Minnesota in Week 2.Philadelphia (2-1) turned the ball over three times and failed to record a takeaway for the third consecutive game to begin the season. Hurts was 16 for 25 for 153 yards with an interception, and Saquon Barkley rushed for 82 yards on 15 carries.Keenum capped Chicago’s first drive witha shovel pass to Luther Burdenfor an eight-yard touchdown, and he connected with a wide-open Raymond on a 41-yard touchdown in the second half.Trailing 7-0, Hurts drove Philadelphia deep into Chicago territory in the second quarter before he absorbed a late hit by linebacker D’Marco Jackson along the sideline. Hurts was pulled off the field to be checked for a concussion, and backup Andy Dalton was intercepted by rookie Dillon Thieneman in the back of the end zone.Hurts returned and scored on a quarterback sneak as time expired in the first half, but Chicago controlled the final two periods as they closed out their victory.The Bears are Keenum’s eighth NFL franchise, and he is in his 14th season in the league.Explore more on these topicsNFLChicago BearsPhiladelphia EaglesUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City guilty over Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contracts | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City breached Premier League financial rules by creating ‘sham’ contracts to help inflate revenue and reduce costs by more than £900m over a nine-year period, an independent commission found
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Manchester City breached Premier League financial rules by creating ‘sham’ contracts to help inflate revenue and reduce costs by more than £900m over a nine-year period, an independent commission found
Content: A number of options are on the table for Manchester City regarding sanctions, including the stripping of titles, financial penalties and points deductions.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA number of options are on the table for Manchester City regarding sanctions, including the stripping of titles, financial penalties and points deductions.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesManchester CityManchester City guilty over Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contractsCommission: club broke rules over nine-season periodCity will appeal against verdict before Friday deadlineMatt Hughes,Will UnwinandPaul MacInnesTue 29 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Premier League has confirmedManchester Cityhave been found guilty of all charges of breaching its financial rules over a nine-year period, with the club found to have boosted their income by a staggering amount of more than £900m.In a bombshell announcement thePremier Leaguerevealed an independent commission had found City guilty of arranging “sham ­contracts” with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs, and of filing inaccurate accounts to hide the true state of their finances, which if accurately reported would have led to significant breaches of Premier League and Uefa spending limits.Manchester City’s ‘sham’ seasons: how they fared and who was in chargeRead moreThe club were also found to have entered into “sham” image rights deals with players and the then manager Roberto Mancini to artificially inflate their earnings.City have said they will appeal by Friday’s deadline “on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. Their chief executive, ­Ferran Soriano, said in a video sent to employees that the decision was based on a “Premier League conspiracy theory”.The appeal is expected to run alongside a sanctions hearing presided over by the independent commission, with the Premier League eager to conclude matters as quickly as possible.The extraordinary scale of what Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, has described as City’s “financial doping” has sent shock waves throughout the world of ­football, leaving executives at other Premier League clubs stunned.The Premier League’s chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case “as the most significant in Premier League history”. It seems inevitable it will lead to an unprecedented punishment, including in all probability a points deduction that will condemn City to relegation.Although there is no direct precedent given the scale of City’s offences, Everton’s 10-point penalty for breaching profitability and sustainability rules by £19.5m over a period ending with the 2021-22 season was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5m the club overspent.The commission made damning comments regarding the behaviour of City witnesses during the hearings. “Evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects,” it wrote, arguing that some witnesses had given evidence “they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”.Graphic showing Manchester City’s ‘sham’ commercial dealsCity were found to have operated a “disguised funding scheme” worth £830.6m over nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, and to have hidden costs by a further £70m. In addition the club have been found guilty of multiple breaches of failing to cooperate with the Premier League and act in good faith. The commission concluded the club had made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the investigation.The Premier League published a redacted 40-page “core decision” from the independent commission, which has taken almost two years to produce after a 42-day hearing that concluded in December 2024.The league said: “The independent commission found City arranged ‘sham’ commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.View image in fullscreenManchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano leaving the European Football Clubs board meeting in Copenhagen.Photograph: PA Video/PA“As part of the scheme, further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a ‘sham’ circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.“The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900m during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The consequence of this, as the commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.ADUG bought City on behalf of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan for £200m in 2008, with the new owners making an immediate impact by paying £32.5m to sign the Brazilian superstar Robinho from Real Madrid. That was the start of a spending spree City struggled to afford from their existing revenues, with the independent commission concluding that the only way to match the owners’ ambitions for the club was for ADUG to “provide very significant funds by way of equity contribution”.The commission report states that in 2010 City devised a scheme whereby sponsors would pay a “base sum” and ADUG would pay a “tagged sum”, despite the base sum being the only true revenue. The recorded sponsorship fee would be the total of them both.City’s lawyers claimed that the “tagged sum” was a loan by the Abu Dhabi government on liabilities on sponsorship fees. The commission rejected that argument.Manchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’Read moreThe judgment is a huge victory for the Premier League and Masters. Despite the commission demonstrating that City breached Uefa’s spending limits there appears little prospect of Uefa’s case being revisited because there is a five-year statute of limitations on its disciplinary proceedings. Uefa’s punishment of City in relation to alleged financial fair play breaches waslargely overturned in 2020by the court of arbitration for sport, which found “most of the alleged breaches were either not established or time-barred”.Masters said: “The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade. It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City.”He said in relation to sanctions: “Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans.”Other Premier League clubs are surprised City have not reached an agreed sanction with the Premier League, given the judgment, but City continue to deny wrongdoing. “Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today,” the club said. “The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Switzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after Hendry’s early red card | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Ricardo Rodríguez’s free-kick after Jack Hendry’s 11th-minute dismissal inspired Switzerland to a 3-0 Nations League victory against Scotland
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Ricardo Rodríguez’s free-kick after Jack Hendry’s 11th-minute dismissal inspired Switzerland to a 3-0 Nations League victory against Scotland
Content: Ricardo Rodríguez curls home Switzerland’s 12th-minute opener.Photograph: Alan Rennie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRicardo Rodríguez curls home Switzerland’s 12th-minute opener.Photograph: Alan Rennie/ShutterstockNations LeagueSwitzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after Hendry’s early red cardEwan Murrayat Hampden ParkTue 29 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwitzerland have responded exceptionally well after allegations ofcapers involving vaccination certificatesthat threatened to overshadow this international window. Make that six points out of six for Murat Yakin’s stylish team. Switzerland look comfortably capable of breezing out of Group B1 in the Nations League. They have not even played at home yet. Granit who?Sébastien Pocognoli, conversely, has been left to ponder one step forward and umpteen back.Scotland’s second half in Sloveniaat the ­weekend provided hope to the new manager and a supporter base who want to enter a brave new world. Age old, troublesome flaws remain.Scotland 0-3 Switzerland, Spain 4-1 Croatia, and more: Nations League – liveRead moreJack Hendry’s red card meantScotlandplayed almost 80 minutes of this encounter with 10 men. They were, however, outclassed in every department. Scottish patterns of play were not immediately obvious. The upcoming trip to North Macedonia carries importance as Pocognoli seeks to win hearts and minds. This was all pretty grim for anyone of a Scotland persuasion.“The red card of Jack is all of our red card,” said Pocognoli. “We stay together. We put this moment in our DNA today and hopefully it can be helpful for the future.”Scottish expectancy heading into a World Cup where theysubsequently took tedium to new levelsfeels a long time ago. They have scored only once in five games. Impotence can only concern Scotland’s Belgian manager, whose bow at Hampden Park was over as a contest long before full-time. A penny for the thoughts of Steve Clarke, Pocognoli’s immediate predecessor and a coach much-maligned in certain quarters. Were Clarke in charge of this ragged display, the public response would have been ferocious.Judgment of Pocognoli on this occasion requires appropriate context.Switzerlandhad control of the early exchanges without creating anything until a slick move saw Dan Ndoye sent through on goal from the halfway line. It was quickly apparent ­Hendry did not have the pace to halt his ­opponent. Initially, the referee Nenad Minakovic booked Hendry and awarded a penalty for the clear pull on Ndoye which ­toppled the Swiss forward. Following a video assistant referee check that was unnecessarily lengthy, the official corrected his decision to a free-kick and sending off. Up stepped Ricardo Rodríguez to crack the ball beyond Angus Gunn from 19 yards.Pocognoli’s immediate response was to withdraw Kieron Bowie, one of two strikers. The introduction of ­Stephen Welsh retained Scotland’s three-man backline. A noticeably subdued Hampden crowd feared a long evening. This is, after all, a Switzerland team that followed up a strong World Cup performance with a comfortable win in North Macedonia on Saturday.John McGinn appealed in vain for a penalty after claiming he was held at a Scotland corner. The blunt truth is Scotland have needed more from McGinn than the seeking or winning of fouls for some time.McGinn’s Aston Villa teammate Johan ­Manzambi was unsurprisingly lively; he fired just wide of Gunn’s right-hand post moments after a delicious cross that found no Swiss takers. With half an hour played, the Scots were gasping for air against opponents who looked physically and technically superior. When in possession, far too much of the hosts’ play was sideways or backwards. Gunn denied Ndoye nine minutes before the break.View image in fullscreenNico Elvedi celebrates after doubling Switzerland’s lead from close range in the second half.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAThe half ended with a yellow card for Pocognoli, who protested a little too vociferously after McGinn was fouled. All the episode did was sum up Scottish frustration. There had been needle in the game but the coherent football had been played by those in red.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManzambi had irritated the home support by embellishing fouls and entering into a verbal spat with Oli McBurnie. His play, though, was a compelling watch. Manzambi’s movement unnerved Scotland. His willingness to drop deep or wide to get involved in the game emphasised his versatility. His touch and dribbling ability set him apart; all at the age of 20. Scotland’s lack of anything approaching such emerging talent is glaring.Switzerland’s second came from a more unlikely source. Scotland only partially cleared a corner, with the ball funnelled wide right to Ndoye. The cross was pacy and low, with the central defender Nico Elvedi striding forward to flick home. Two nil was a more appropriate reflection of events to that point.Pocognoli now made a triple change. McBurnie’s 18th cap had passed without the ending of his international scoring wait. As on Saturday, the alterations were like-for-like in positional nature. ­Pocognoli’s level of tactical flexibility remains open to question. Yakin withdrew ­Manzambi, in what could be classed as a humanitarian act towards Scotland.Not that Switzerland had stopped dishing out punishment. The ­closing stages resembled an attack ­versus defence training exercise. A third from the Swiss was inevitable as they toyed with the Scots.Gunn was pitifully weak in attempting to deal with Zeki ­Amdouni’s strike, which flew into the roof of the Scotland net via the goalkeeper. Cue a mass exodus from the stands. Pocognoli has been served a strong, painful reminder of the scale of task he chose to inherit.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueScotlandSwitzerlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League roundup: Lamine Yamal sinks Croatia in Spain’s World Cup homecoming | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Lamine Yamal scored two goals and set up another as Spain hammered Croatia 4-1 in the Nations League in their first home game since lifting the World Cup
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lamine Yamal scored two goals and set up another as Spain hammered Croatia 4-1 in the Nations League in their first home game since lifting the World Cup
Content: Lamine Yamal’s two goals against Croatia helped Spain extend their unbeaten run to 40 matches.Photograph: Joaquin Corchero/AFP7/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLamine Yamal’s two goals against Croatia helped Spain extend their unbeaten run to 40 matches.Photograph: Joaquin Corchero/AFP7/ShutterstockNations LeagueNations League roundup: Lamine Yamal sinks Croatia in Spain’s World Cup homecomingTeenager scores twice in 4-1 win to boost Ballon d’Or caseSlovenia beat North Macedonia; Faroe Islands hold MoldovaAgenciesTue 29 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLamine Yamal scored two goals and set up another asSpainhammeredCroatia4-1 on Tuesday in theNations Leaguein their first home game since lifting the World Cup.Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring within two minutesagainst England in Saturday’s Wembley winand took just 75 seconds to do so against Slaven Bilic’s side in Andalusia. The teenager’s left-footed finish took his tally of international goals to nine in 36 appearances.Switzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after Hendry’s early red cardRead moreJust before the half-hour mark, the visitors equalised through Dion Beljo’s header as the 6ft 4in attacker headed home from an Ivan Perisic cross.Two minutes later the hosts restored their lead as Marc Pubill fired home a header from a pinpoint Lamine Yamal cross before provider turned scorer again on 63 minutes, beating Barcelona teammate andCroatiagoalkeeper Dominik Livakovic at his near post. With fewer than two minutes to play Athletic Bilbao’s Nico Williams notched up a fourth for Spain with a crisp dribble and finish.La Roja next play Czechia on Saturday in Group A3.Lamine Yamal’s contribution strengthened his case for the Ballon d’Or, with voting having closed on Monday and the winner announced on 26 October.Spain’s captain, Rodri, showed off the World Cup trophy before kick-off at the packed Estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán, being handed it by Sevilla legend Jesús Navas, a winner withSpainin 2010.“We were very excited to bring the cup here,” Lamine Yamal said. “To be able to win the game and bring it home is great.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Group B1,SloveniabeatNorth Macedonia2-0 with goals from Sandi Lovric and Aljosa Matko.Moldovawere held to a 1-1 draw at home to theFaroe IslandsandSlovakiabeatKazakhstan2-1, whileIcelandwere 3-0 winners inLuxembourgandEstoniadrew 1-1 inBulgaria.FinlandandBelarusplayed to a scoreless draw in Helsinki.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueSpainCroatiaSloveniaNorth MacedoniaMoldovaFaroe IslandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone dropped by England after not hitting ‘expected’ level | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Lexi Potter, the Chelsea midfielder, has received her first senior England call-up for the Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Greece
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Lexi Potter, the Chelsea midfielder, has received her first senior England call-up for the Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Greece
Content: Chloe Kelly (left) and Ella Toone have played key roles in England’s run of three consecutive major tournament finals.Photograph: Daniel Chesterton/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChloe Kelly (left) and Ella Toone have played key roles in England’s run of three consecutive major tournament finals.Photograph: Daniel Chesterton/Offside/Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamChloe Kelly and Ella Toone dropped by England after not hitting ‘expected’ levelChelsea’s Lexi Potter gets first call-up to face GreeceLeah Williamson back after injury for World Cup playoffTom GarryTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElla Toone and Chloe Kelly have been dropped from England’s squad because of their performance levels bySarina Wiegman, who has given a first call-up to the 20-year-old ­Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter.Toone and Kelly have played key roles in England’s run of three consecutive major tournament finals but Wiegman made clear on Tuesday, when announcing her selection for the Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Greece, that she wants to see more from them for their clubs.“The main reason is that I think the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch,” Wiegman said. The head coach “still believes in them” but said: “We expect a bit more and we know they can bring more. That was the message.“There is also competition going on. It’s about talent, it’s about playing minutes and it’s about the ­competition going on. I hope they can step up and show what they can do.Quick GuideEngland squadShowGoalkeepers: Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool), Anna Moorhouse (Manchester City on loan from Orlando Pride)Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Niamh Charles (Manchester City), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Lucia Kendall (Aston Villa), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)Forwards: Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Lauren James (Chelsea), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I’m convinced they can do better, I think they are convinced about that, too. I think they took the feedback in a good and in a positive way but it’s hard to take at the same time of course; it’s not a nice message. I hope they respond to it really well. We will support them and of course they get the support at club, too. I hope they come back even better than they were before.”Neither Toone nor Kelly has scored or provided an assist in the Women’s Super League this season, although Toone did score in ­Manchester United’s 10-1 League Cup victory against the second-tier side ­Sheffield United last week, after she had been left out of their draw at Arsenal. Toone has started three of United’s four WSL games. Kelly has started one of Arsenal’s league matches, their ­Champions League win against Køge and made three WSL substitute appearances.There was also no place for the Chelsea forward Aggie Beever‑Jones. Wiegman has called up the uncapped 18-year-old midfielder Erica Meg ­Parkinson and the London City Lionesses winger Freya Godfrey, and there is a return after injury for the captain, Leah Williamson.There had been growing calls for the inclusion of Potter this term after her strong form for Chelsea, ­including her starring role in the1-0 victory against Arsenalon Sunday. “She’s grown a lot,” Wiegman said.“Last season we kept a close eye on her because she was getting into the squad and playing really well. But I think she’s started the season so well. Her performances have really impressed us so she really deserves this call-up.“She’s shown at Chelsea that she can start against any team. The last game I thought she did very well against a top Arsenal [team]. What I’ve seen from her is that she comes out on the pitch and no matter who she plays against, she’s just going to play and she’s comfortable. I hope to see that next week.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Lionesses face Greece in the first leg at the Pankritio Stadium in Heraklion, Crete on Friday 9 ­October before the return at Leicester’s King Power ­Stadium the following ­Tuesday, needing victory to reach the second decisive round of the ­playoffs in December.England are having to contest the playoffs despite winning five of six matches in their qualifying group, having missed out on top spot to the world champions, Spain, based on the head-to-head record from their meetings in April and June, in repeats of the 2023 World Cup final.England will be heavily fancied to progress to next summer’s finals in Brazil.That tournament could be ­Wiegman’s last with England because her contract expires after the World Cup. She gave little away when asked about any contract discussions.“We have regular conversa­tions together, and we talk about the future at moments, but at this point I’m just focusing on Greece. We want to get through and qualify for the World Cup. Of course I talk to Mark [­Bullingham], every two weeks, and we speak about what’s ­happening now, what’s in the future, but there’s nothing new.”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamSarina WiegmanWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa sack manager Natalia Arroyo with club second-bottom of WSL | Aston Villa Women | The Guardian
description: Aston Villa have sacked their women’s manager Natalia Arroyo with the side second-bottom of the Women’s Super League with two points from four matches
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Aston Villa have sacked their women’s manager Natalia Arroyo with the side second-bottom of the Women’s Super League with two points from four matches
Content: Natalia Arroyo’s Aston Villa ended last season with four successive defeats and the poor form has continued.Photograph: Elli Birch/WSL Football/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNatalia Arroyo’s Aston Villa ended last season with four successive defeats and the poor form has continued.Photograph: Elli Birch/WSL Football/Getty ImagesAston Villa WomenAston Villa sack manager Natalia Arroyo with club second-bottom of WSLVilla have two points from first four league matchesArroyo took charge of women’s side in January 2025Suzanne WrackTue 29 Sep 2026 04.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAston Villa have sacked Natalia Arroyo as their women’s manager, with the side winless and second-bottom of the Women’s Super League.Arroyo was let go on Monday night, after Villa endured a 4-0 defeat at Tottenham on Sunday. It was a second loss in their opening four games of the season, with a 4-1 defeat by Manchester City sandwiched between 1-1 draws with Chelsea and Brighton, with performances largely poor.Arroyo was appointed in January 2025, signing a three-and-a-half-year contract with the club. The former Barcelona and Espanyol player, who spent time as a journalist before focusing on her coaching career, joined Villa following four impressive years in charge at Real Sociedad where she guided the club to a second-place finish in the 2021-22 season and a Copa de la Reina final in her final campaign.Graphic showing Aston Villa bottom of the Women’s Super League table for the period in which Natalia Arroyo was their managerThe 40-year-old replaced Shaun Goater, who took temporary charge following Robert de Pauw’s departureamid allegations over remarks he had made to players. Villa had only two wins from their first 12 WSL games when Arroyo took charge. Five consecutive league defeats followed as the team adapted to the new manager and they won their remaining five games to finish sixth.Villa finished ninth in Arroyo’s first full campaign, with 20 points from 22 games, but a poor run of form and four successive defeats blighted the end of the season. “Everyone at Aston Villa would like to thank Natalia for her efforts and wish her all the best in her future endeavours,” the club said in a statement.Villa have confirmed that Brian Sørensen, the women’s technical adviser, will take temporary charge of the team, including for their Subway Players Cup tie against Newcastle on Wednesday. Sørensen joined Villa as technical adviser in March, following his exit from Everton in February after four years with the Merseyside club.Explore more on these topicsAston Villa WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Goodison Gazza’ Billy Kenny: ‘The only time I’ve had peace was when I was locked up’ | Everton | The Guardian
description: Everton’s great lost talent of the 90s tells Donald McRae about the drinking culture that enveloped him as a teenager, his time in jail, struggles with depression and how he got clean
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Everton’s great lost talent of the 90s tells Donald McRae about the drinking culture that enveloped him as a teenager, his time in jail, struggles with depression and how he got clean
Content: ‘If my idols tell me to have a drink I’ll have a drink. I was always drunk from then on,’ says Billy Kenny of his time at Everton.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘If my idols tell me to have a drink I’ll have a drink. I was always drunk from then on,’ says Billy Kenny of his time at Everton.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEvertonInterview‘Goodison Gazza’ Billy Kenny: ‘The only time I’ve had peace was when I was locked up’Donald McRaeEverton’s great lost talent of the 90s explains the drinking culture that enveloped him as a teenager, his time in jail, struggles with depression and how he got cleanTue 29 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Iwas just a kid and no one was there for me,” Billy Kenny says as he wipes away the tears of hurt and regret on a September afternoon in Liverpool. “I’m angry withEvertonfor not looking after me.“Listen, I’m no angel. I’ve played my part, but there are other people who played their part in the demise of Billy Kenny. So I’m still bitter and frustrated today, at the age of 53. It wasan absolute waste of talent.”‘I had no love for myself … now I have peace’: former Ireland rugby player Ryan Caldwell’s journey back from the edgeRead moreKenny used to be one of the most promising young footballers in England, pursued by Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, Kenny Dalglish at Liverpool and Howard Kendall at Everton. He chose his beloved Everton and for a few fleeting months his extraordinary talent shimmered – most memorably during a man‑of‑the-match performance against Liverpool at Goodison Park in December 1992.His teammate Peter Beardsley called him “the Goodison Gazza” in an eerily prophetic comparison. Kenny played once for England’s under-21s in March 1993, but his ravaging fall echoes the addictions and troubles of Paul Gascoigne.Kenny discovered cocaine in the early hours of the morning after his greatest game, when he had just turned 19. A cocaine habit spiralled out of control very quickly and he retired from professional football two years later. He had played 23 games for Everton, four for Oldham and two for Barrow. Kenny struggled as an addict for years and ended up in prison.“I’m clean now,” he says. “I’ve been off the drink and drugs, since my ma died 15 years ago.” Kenny looks up. “It’s my ma’s birthday today. I came off the drugs the day of her funeral and she’s given me the strength to stay sober. I just couldn’t do it while she was alive and that’s what kills me.”Kenny breaks down twice during our interview, but he tells his story with raw force. He was besotted with Everton, but now the club haunts him. “I ended up being a product of Howard Kendall’s environment,” he says. “For years and years I carried all the blame, but there was no help at all.”He thinks of Michael Branch,another former Everton playerwho also wound up in jail. “I spoke to Michael last year and he said at Finch Farm [Everton’s training ground] there are 17 people you can speak to about mental health – whether it’s problems with drink, drugs, your family, your girlfriend. There was no one for me.”How would life have turned out for Kenny if he had been a gifted player today? “I wouldn’t be talking about misery. I would be talking about glory days and winning for Everton. I feel as though it’s been stolen from me and the fans have been robbed of me as well.”View image in fullscreenBilly Kenny played 17 league games for Everton despite his talent and retired from professional football at the age of 21.Photograph: Action Images/ReutersKenny’s movingnew book, written by the Guardian’s Jamie Fahey, who grew up on the same streets in Liverpool, is a penetrating and, yes, sobering depiction of a period in English football when drink addled so many young men. Thecomplex figure of Kendalllies at the broken heart of this story.“It’s bittersweet when I’m talking about Howard, because I grew up loving the fella,” he says of Kendall, who formed an unforgettable midfield with Colin Harvey and Alan Ball before becoming one of the most successful managers in Everton’s history. “Even today, I’ve got no hatred. He had his own troubles, didn’t he? Where does his alcoholism come from?”Kenny, at first, hated drinking: “I couldn’t stand it. My dad never touched drugs his whole life, but he would have a couple of pints on a Saturday night. I’d be in bed and my dad would come tell me how good I played for Everton reserves. I had to chase him out because I didn’t like the smell of the ale.“I then played with my idols in the Everton first team. Kendall always wanted us to go to the Sefton [a pub near the training ground] for a bevvy. As a first-team player I had to go. It was the same forNeville Southall, who never drank.Pat Nevinand Andy Hinchcliffe, too. They’d drop off all the pissed lads at the end. Kendall should have said: ‘Billy, you’re 18, go home.’“The second time, with the senior pros, I stood with Nevin and the other non-drinkers. But I’ve gone over to the lads with my pint of blackcurrant and lemonade and they’re all laughing at me. A very senior player said: ‘You’d better have a shandy, son, because [Kendall] will sell you if you don’t drink.’“The next time I dropped my guard, on the ale, and when I got home my head was spinning, spewing up all over my ma’s house. My ma laughed the first time. They really thought I was in a safe place. But I was with a load of alcoholics.“I don’t care who reads it because I’ve carried this for years. I was just a kid, made up, playing with my idols. If my idols tell me to have a drink I’ll have a drink. I was always drunk from then on.”In his book, Kenny says “it seemed as though most of the first‑team set-up lived for the booze”.He describes to me how, for away games, “the first thing on the coach would be the crates of lager and chablis [for Kendall]. On one of my early away games, down to London, I wasn’t really drinking. [On the journey back to Liverpool after the game] I sat in the front with [the assistant manager] Colin Harvey, who I loved. Colin had my best interests at heart and we talked football while they were drinking in the back.double quotation markI started to adore the drugs, the birds and the music more than I needed Everton“We came off the M57 and I’m thinking: ‘Where are we going?’ It’s half 11 [at night] and the coach pulls into the Paradox nightclub. That was Kendall, taking us to the biggest nightclub in Liverpool.”In January 1993, Kenny did well against Vinnie Jones and the hard men of Wimbledon as Everton won away. He injured his ankle, but he writes: “Kendall told me I’d played a blinder. He said the lads were made up with me and how it would be a real shame if I missed out on the Chinese and a few drinks. I could always put ice on my ankle in the restaurant. Then the killer line: ‘You’ll feel much better after a couple of drinks, lad.’”Five months later, struggling with injury, Kenny lost himself in cocaine and ecstasy: “I started to adore the drugs, the birds and the music more than I needed Everton.”His compulsive personality led to “three-day benders”, skipping training and disappearing from football. What would Kenny say to Kendall if his manager were alive today? “I’d say: ‘Howard, you should have looked after me. I shouldn’t have been made to feel I had to drink to play for your team.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Everton terminated his contract in 1994 Kenny felt abandoned. “I needed help. I needed support. Empathy. Guidance. I received none of it.”He explains: “Everton sent me to the Priory in Cheshire. But I’m 19 and in group therapy with 60‑year‑old alcoholics who’ve been hiding bottles of scotch in the garden. I couldn’t relate to none of it. They put me in there for two months. Colin Harvey and Paul Power came to see me every day, to get me fit, but Everton were only doing that to sell me.”Manchester City tried to sign Kenny, but Everton wanted a prohibitive £1m transfer fee. “They’d already done a deal with Oldham behind my back so I got no signing-on fee,” Kenny says. “That’s Everton for you. It’s a badly run club and that still carries on today.”At Oldham, who were managed by Joe Royle, another former Everton favourite, Kenny felt motivated to try again. But everything fell apart when Royle left – to manage Everton.View image in fullscreenBilly Kenny says he is getting ‘three or four good days a week’ after 25 years without one.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAt 21, Kenny’s football life was over. The years passed in a drugged-up maze and he was sentenced to nine months in prison – six for drink-driving and three for missing the original trial. “I did five months and got myself in the gym, played five-a-side. No drugs, no drink. In a crazy way the only time I’ve had peace in my life was when I was locked up.”Kenny was fortunate to escape a 14-month sentence a few years later “because someone was growing cannabis in my house when I was away”. He says: “I had to take the rap for that, but I was lucky. The judge was an Evertonian and I got a suspended sentence. I didn’t want to go to jail then because my ma was dying.”double quotation markI’d have been perfect for Fergie. He loved me and I loved it at UnitedAt his mother’s wake, Kenny left his pint on the counter and walked out of the pub. He swore, in her memory, he would never resort to drugs again. He tells me he has kept his promise but “I still get depression”, adding: “I can have a great morning, take the dog out, do an hour on the bags, come home, eat lovely food, and it’s back. But I don’t go round the pub. I don’t phone anyone for drugs. I let it take its toll.”Kenny’s weathered face brightens. “I’m getting three or four good days a week now where for 25 years I didn’t have one fucking good day. I was either sitting in my house crying or I’d be out, off my head. Now the depression can knock all it wants. I’ve learned to live with it.”Should he have chosen Manchester United or Liverpool instead of Everton? Both clubs were keen to sign Kenny as a teenager – with Liverpool arranging for him to travel to and from Wembley with the first-team squad for the1988 FA Cup finalwhen he was 14. “I think about this all the time. As much as I loved the Liverpool staff and the way they treated me, it was out of the question. I’m a born Evertonian. But Man United? I went to United for six weeks in the summer holidays and I saw how Fergie got rid of Kevin Moran, Paul McGrath, Norman Whiteside, Bryan Robson and, later, Lee Sharpe. He wouldn’t stand for any drinking or lack of discipline.Rob Smyth: The Joy of Six: football’s lost talentsRead more“I’d have been perfect for Fergie. He loved me and I loved it at United. But I’ve given my life to Everton and if I had to do it again I’d probably still go to Everton because I loved the fans. I’m one of them.”We can see Everton’s new stadium from where we sit and Kenny confirms he has been back to watch the club he once loved so much. “All these ex-players who’re connected to Everton are manufactured Evertonians. I went to the Chelsea game [last season] and it was the same faces, doing the same thing. That’s why our club isn’t moving forwards. Get rid of the dead wood.“The only legends are the fans. I absolutely love Evertonians and I’m made up when the team does well for them. But that’s it. I just see Everton as the club who never looked after me.”The Goodison Gazza is published by Reach on 8 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: England can take vital lessons from worst defeats into Rugby World Cup, says Johnson | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Martin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at the Rugby World Cup in Australia next year
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: Martin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at the Rugby World Cup in Australia next year
Content: Martin Johnson believes some of England’s most painful defeats, such as their 42-21 loss to Ireland at Twickenham, will help them.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMartin Johnson believes some of England’s most painful defeats, such as their 42-21 loss to Ireland at Twickenham, will help them.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersEngland rugby union teamEngland can take vital lessons from worst defeats into Rugby World Cup, says JohnsonFormer captain says losses can benefit team next yearJohnson refuses to comment on Henry Pollock hypeLuke McLaughlinTue 29 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Johnson believes England’s most painful defeats under Steve Borthwick can benefit them at theRugby World Cupin Australia next year.England endured some disastrous moments during the Six Nations this year, most notably the42-21 defeat by Ireland at Twickenham, and finished the tournament with a solitary win against Wales. Summer Nations Championship fixtures began with an away defeat by the world champions, South Africa, before victories against Fiji and Argentina.Why England are yet to reap rewards of £264m deal with Rugby World Cup only a year away | Gerard MeagherRead moreWith a year until the tournament – England’s opener is scheduled for 2 October against Tonga in Brisbane – Johnson acknowledged the Six Nations was “up and down” under Borthwick but said vital lessons must be taken from the defeats.“The bad experiences, the losing, it’s not wasted experience,” said Johnson, who captained England to the Rugby World Cup in 2003, and was head coach from 2008 to 2011. “You always want to win and they’re horrible at the time, but it shouldn’t be a wasted experience. All experience, good or bad, should go into your memory bank as a player.“The emotional side: ‘We can’t let this happen again because it’s too painful,’ and the technical side: ‘This is why it happened … We now have that as a memory, as something to use.’ All your experiences go in that memory bank. You try to delete the emotional hurt of them, but sometimes that’s quite good to have there.”Speaking as patron of theJoe Humphries Memorial Trust, which is calling for everyone in sport to get free, life-saving sudden cardiac arrest training duringSADS week, Johnson said England’s concluding Six Nationsdefeat by Francein March was “one of the best games of rugby I’ve ever watched”.Regarding England’s prospects of matching the fearsome French and South African forward packs in Australia next year, he said: “I think we’re starting to develop some guys, front row, back row. The back five has probably been our strongest area in the last couple of years.View image in fullscreenJamie Osborne on his way to scoring Ireland’s fifth try against England at Twickenham in this year’s Six Nations.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA“If everyone’s fit you’ve got some pretty good depth there. It would be great to go to the tournament with all those guys firing. You’re going to need them at some point, the way the game is now, guys coming off benches is vitally important.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAsked if he sees parts of himself in the powerful Saracens lock, George Martin, Johnson said: “I think he’d give me a good kicking. He is a presence, isn’t he, when he’s there? I remember watching him ramming an All-Black through the ruck and into the No 9. That was a beautiful piece of rugby.”On whetherHenry Pollock’s ability justifies the considerable hype, meanwhile, Johnson said of the Northampton and England back-rower: “I don’t get involved in the Henry Pollock chats that go on. I always say for any young player, if you just keep improving and getting yourself to be a world-class player, that’s always a good thing. That’s what you need to do. Get yourself into the position where you’re a top-drawer player, and when they talk about the best in the world, your name gets mentioned. That’s never a bad place to be.”Regarding the buildup to the tournament next year and increasing interest in the media, the former Leicester second-row said: “You always get asked about it as a player, and it used to annoy me a bit … most things annoyed me a bit, really. But it does start to loom and these [Nations Championship and Six Nations] games are all part of your collective memory, as a team and a player.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamMartin JohnsonSteve BorthwickRugby World Cup 2027Rugby World CupSix Nations 2026Rugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tuchel praises Alexander-Arnold for ‘decisive’ display on England return | Nations League | The Guardian
description: The head coach said after Alexander-Arnold set up England’s opener in the 2-0 win against Czechia: ‘We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this’
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The head coach said after Alexander-Arnold set up England’s opener in the 2-0 win against Czechia: ‘We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this’
Content: Thomas Tuchel said Trent Alexander-Arnold had a ‘good performance overall’ in the win against Czechia.Photograph: Slávek Růta/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said Trent Alexander-Arnold had a ‘good performance overall’ in the win against Czechia.Photograph: Slávek Růta/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNations LeagueTuchel praises Alexander-Arnold for ‘decisive’ display on England return‘We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this’Alexander-Arnold set up opener in 2-0 win over CzechiaJacob Steinbergat the Fortuna ArenaTue 29 Sep 2026 18.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel praised Trent ­Alexander-Arnold after the right-back impressed on his first England appearance since June 2025.Alexander-Arnold, who has a point to prove after missing out on a World Cup spot, was one of the big positives as Tuchel’s side recovered from their defeat to Spain by recording acomfortable 2-0 win away to Czechiain the Nations League on Tuesday.Alexander-Arnold proves his worth to England with trademark assist against CzechiaRead moreThe Real Madrid defender shone in possession, particularly after the Czechs lost Pavel Sulc to a red card at 0-0, and helpedEnglandtake the lead when he crossed for Anthony Gordon to score early in the second half.“We never doubted that he can produce these kind of assists,” Tuchel said. “I think the second half the position, a bit of a deeper position, suited him more than the higher position in the first half. Overall, I think we had a good and professional performance. Of course the red card is such a heavy influence in the game.“We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this, because he’s very secure on the ball and can be decisive with his crosses. He did this solid defending and one decisive action that helped us score, so a good performance overall.”Jude Bellingham started on the bench but the midfielder wore the captain’s armband after replacing Harry Kane during the closing stages. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup,” Tuchel said. “It is always a reward and always an honour. If you’re the captain at the end of these matches you can for sure be the permanent captain.“He loves to be with us at the moment. We had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts to say: ‘Let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that. But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland moved clear with a late goal from Kane and are second in Group A3 after Spain’s 4-1 win over Croatia. Next up is a trip to ­Croatia on Saturday. Tuchel hopes that the ­Manchester City left-back Nico O’Reilly will return from injury.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueThomas TuchelTrent Alexander-ArnoldEnglandCzechianewsShareReuse this content

title: Czechia 0-2 England: Nations League football – as it happened | Nations League | The Guardian
description: The excellent Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane gave England a comfortable win against 10-man Czechia
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: The excellent Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane gave England a comfortable win against 10-man Czechia
Content: 4h ago16.59 EDTDavid HytnerMatch report: Czechia 0-2 EnglandAnybody can lose to Spain. But whenEnglanddid so at Wembley on Saturday, it served to turn the temperature up on on this trip to Czechia, where England have form for finding it difficult. Remember the European championship qualifier here in 2019 when they lost 2-1?It was not easy at first. Thomas Tuchel shuffled his pack, making the surprise decision to start Jude Bellingham among the substitutes. It was all a little angsty andCzechia, for whom this is the start of a new era under the Spaniard Santi Denia after their World Cup wash-out, dared to dream about another upset.Then everything changed. It was a rash challenge in the 23rd minute by Pavel Sulc on Elliot Anderson, late and high, albeit nothing overtly nasty. The referee, Umut Meler, showed theCzechiamidfielder a yellow card and on we went. Yet the video assistant referee was not happy and when Meler was called to the monitor, everybody knew what was coming next.Gordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man CzechiaRead moreShare

title: Manchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’ | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Ferran Soriano has said the guilty verdicts against the club for breaches of financial rules are based on ‘a single false accusation’
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Ferran Soriano has said the guilty verdicts against the club for breaches of financial rules are based on ‘a single false accusation’
Content: From left to right: Khaldoon al-Mubarak, Pep Guardiola, Ferran Soriano and Txiki Begiristain celebrate winning the 2023-24 Premier League.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Khaldoon al-Mubarak, Pep Guardiola, Ferran Soriano and Txiki Begiristain celebrate winning the 2023-24 Premier League.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityManchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’Soriano: the case is based on ‘a single false accusation’Club to appeal after verdict on more than 100 chargesWill UnwinTue 29 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, has said the guilty verdicts against the club for breaches of financial rules are based on “a single false accusation” and a “Premier League conspiracy theory”, as he maintained City’s innocence.It was confirmed on Tuesday that City, according to an independent panel, had artificially inflated revenue andreduced costs by more than £900mover a nine-year period through “sham” sponsorship deals, which were mainly funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club. In a video sent to City staff after confirmation of the guilty verdict on more than 100 charges, Soriano said the club would appeal and fight the case.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester City guilty over Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contractsRead more“The wholePremier Leaguecase against us is based on a single false accusation – that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi,” Soriano said. “This is just not true. Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner.”City must await to hear the sanctions they will receive at a further hearing of the independent commission but the club remain confident of overturning the original decision.“Every other false charge that has been thrown at us comes from that simple, central and completely false accusation. Surprisingly for us and our lawyers after nearly two years the commission has issued an opinion that supports the Premier League’s conspiracy theory.“To do so, the opinion had to ignore the extensive evidence provided by the club in order to reach a conclusion that is clearly wrong. Our lawyers will now file an appeal that sets out the opinion contains clear, material errors of law, principle and fact and that it is unsafe.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Wayne Rooney says Manchester City should not be stripped of titles for rules breach | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The former striker, part of the Manchester United team which finished behind City in 2011-12, said: ‘I wouldn’t feel comfortable … I don’t think we deserved it’
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: The former striker, part of the Manchester United team which finished behind City in 2011-12, said: ‘I wouldn’t feel comfortable … I don’t think we deserved it’
Content: Wayne Rooney said Manchester City should be put ‘in the lowest league they can go in’ for breaching Premier League financial rules.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenWayne Rooney said Manchester City should be put ‘in the lowest league they can go in’ for breaching Premier League financial rules.Photograph: John Walton/PAManchester CityWayne Rooney says Manchester City should not be stripped of titles for rules breach‘I wouldn’t feel comfortable … I don’t think we deserved it’Manchester United finished second to City in 2011-12Will UnwinTue 29 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWayne Rooney does not believe it would be appropriate forManchester Cityto be stripped of titles for breaching Premier League financial rules, even if it gave him another Premier League winner’s medal, as that would be unfair of the City players and staff whose endeavours secured success.City are waiting to find out what sanctions they will face after beingfound guilty of more than a hundred charges, with an array of potential punishments on the table. Rooney was part of the United squad in 2011-12 that finished second to City on goal difference after Sergio Agüero’s last-minute winner secured the Premier League trophy for Roberto Mancini’s side on the final day.Manchester City found guilty on all Premier League charges over rule breachesRead moreCity continue to deny any wrongdoing and are confident of overturning the verdict on appeal.“I wouldn’t feel comfortable about accepting anotherPremier Leaguemedal if I’m being honest, because I don’t think we deserve it,” Rooney said on the Stick to United podcast. “We didn’t do enough ‌that season to win the league. I’m thinking as their players, they’re doing everything they can to win the Premier League title and in their minds they’ve done it. And if that happened to me, if all of a sudden Manchester ⁠United have been doing the same and I’m getting my Premier League medals taken away from me, I’d be absolutely devastated.”Rooney would still want City punished if they are ultimately guilty of wrongdoing. “I’d put them in the lowest league they can go in and then put restrictions on them in terms of how much money they can spend for the next three or four seasons,” the former England captain said.Javier Tebas, the La Liga president and a longtime critic of City, wants the punishment to fit the crime. “We’re trying to make football sustainable ‌and clean across all competitions,” he said at the Peak Performance + Health Summit in London. “As many ‌clubs are saying, titles were lost that shouldn’t have been lost to other clubs. What has happened is very important, and we hope it marks ‌a turning point, not just for the Premier League.“The Manchester City case has implications across Europe. There should be a punishment that sets an example. Breaking them [the rules] for more than 10 years ... is very serious. The punishment should therefore be severe, not only to set an example, but because the rules were broken.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityWayne RooneyManchester UnitedPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Reported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotation
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Reported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotation
Content: Reuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenReuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO documentReported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotationDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 29 Sep 2026 06.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic is telling investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, according to reports, as it prepares for a potential $2tn (£1.5tn) flotation.The warning inside the startup’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be made public, was reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. It follows the company’scall for a slowdownin breakneck development of the technology – a warningechoed by rivals.The prospectus – a document outlining a company’s finances, growth plans and risk profile ahead of a share listing – is said to warn that AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”.“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further ⁠increase the risk that our models cause harm,” the developer of the Claude chatbot reportedly said, adding the potential for a model to be aware it was being tested created a “significant limitation” on Anthropic’s ability to assess model safety.Anthropic declined to comment.Companies preparing to go public routinely report on risks ranging from safety issues to regulatory concerns but warnings about a product causing human extinction reflect heightened concern about such a consequential technology.The reported prospectus admission follows a surge in debate about the existential risk question, triggered this month when an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon,resigned warning that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.A senior safety researcher at Anthropic then posted their agreement on X, claiming there was a more than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”.Some experts have criticised the existential risk warnings, saying they are unverifiable and unscientific. However, there are growing examples of unsanctioned behaviour by the technology, including OpenAI agents – autonomous systems that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention – hacking dozens of third-party organisations including theAI startup Hugging FaceandAustralia’s universal healthcare system.OpenAI announced on Monday it hadcancelled the releaseof its newest model because of safety concerns. It said the GPT-6.1 Astra model showed higher levels of deception and performed poorly on tests for alignment, the term for ensuring a model adheres to human values and goals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors, compared with 48 pages to describe its business.Anthropic is reportedly seeking a valuation of more than $2tn, compared with the$1.8tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingInternet IPOsIPOsInternetShareReuse this content

title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey | Apple | The Guardian
description: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
Content: The Mac mini M6 is a palm-sized powerhouse of a computer.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Mac mini M6 is a palm-sized powerhouse of a computer.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.AppleReviewMac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more priceyApple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouseSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has beenhit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since theM2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIYiMac.View image in fullscreenThe front has two USB-C ports and a headphones socket, making it easy to plug in temporary accessories.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.The mini runs the latestmacOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’sLiquid Glass designthat was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.View image in fullscreenThe power button is on the bottom next to the exhaust vents, which means you have to pick up the Mac mini to press it.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSiri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.SpecificationsProcessor:Apple M6RAM:16, 24 or 32GBStorage:256, 512GB, 1 or 2TB SSDOperating system:macOS 27 Golden GatePorts back:3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb EthernetPorts front:2x USB-C (USB3), headphonesConnectivity:wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, ThreadDimensions:127 x 127 x 50mmWeight:670gSerious M6 speedView image in fullscreenThe back has most of the ports you need, including the rare but welcome 2.5Gb ethernet socket, which can be upgraded to 10GbE if needed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe case is made from 100% recycled aluminium.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact inits report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.PriceThe Mac mini M6 costs from£899(€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.For comparison, theA18 Pro MacBook Neocosts from£699, theM5 MacBook Airstarts at£1,299, the M4 iMac starts at£1,499and the Mac Studio costs from£2,499.VerdictThe Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.The only downside is theRAMageddon-linkedprice hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.Pros:very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.Cons:price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.Explore more on these topicsAppleComputingTechnology sectorreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests | Facial recognition | The Guardian
description: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert
Content: More than half a million faces were scanned in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the trial.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than half a million faces were scanned in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the trial.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesFacial recognitionTrial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrestsFreedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alertPhoebe Davis andDaniel BoffeyTue 29 Sep 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests.More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British TransportPolice(BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders.A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive.Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations. British Transport Police said that since the extension there had been three positive confirmed alerts of people who were subsequently confirmed to be complying with sexual harm prevention orders or other imposed court conditions.Met to expand use of live facial recognition into central London by ChristmasRead moreWhen Transport for London announced its support for the extension of the trial, it said LFR technology “will target and identify people on police watchlists at key stations chosen for maximum impact” and would “specifically tackle violence against women and girls, whose travel behaviours are shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”.Fraser Sampson, a former biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner for the UK, said the police needed to show that the use of the technology was proportionate. “There many variables and all need to align: the choice of location, times of day, make up of the watchlist and likelihood of people being present and many more.”Sampson, who is now a non-executive director of Facewatch, a company that operates facial recognition systems in shops, added: “We know the technology works, but using it in supermarkets to deter shoplifters and prevent attacks on staff is very different from deploying it to catch people on a public transport network.“Success in a shop means no such people coming in. Success for the police trying to catch people means people being caught. In that respect the trial doesn’t appear to have been very fruitful.“Everything depends on the police watchlists; if you’re not on a watchlist, the live FRT cameras do not ‘see’ you and they don’t retain your image in the same way as CCTV cameras.“However, they are processing special category personal data and the technology must be used in a way that is appropriate, proportionate and necessary. It’s for the police to show how any deployment meets those criteria and – as the ICO [information commissioner’s office] has recently reported – for their oversight boards to hold them firmly to account in doing so.”More than half of police forces inEnglandand Wales have now deployed LFR on British streets, according to an analysis by Liberty Investigates.The Metropolitan police and London mayor’s office announced this summer that fixed LFR cameras would be installed in the capital’s West End. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has since confirmed the technology will be used on the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street.A recent report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights, which called on the government to introduce a law to address the threat of artificial intelligence to human rights, identified the rollout of live facial recognition technology as a “particularly clear example of risk”.Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Labour MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “Live facial recognition technologies are a serious invasion of our privacy.
