title: Stop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence | Garrison Lovely | The Guardian
description: The industry is engaged in a perverse quest to replace humans. We cannot cede the best tools available to the other side
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The industry is engaged in a perverse quest to replace humans. We cannot cede the best tools available to the other side
Content: ‘Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table.’Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table.’Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Stop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescenceGarrison LovelyThe industry is engaged in a perverse quest to replace humans. We cannot cede the best tools available to the other sideTue 29 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTShareIdon’t need to tell you that people hate AI. The list of grievances is long: slop, cheating, bias, enfeeblement, electricity bills, environmental destruction, exploitation, theft, cybercrime, doom. But resistance to the technology has often taken the form of shaming people for personally using it, with precious little organizing against the companies building the machines. This is perplexing, given that those companies are attempting to render us obsolete.The executives may contest this framing, offering some bromides about how AI will augment human work or how we’ll simply find new jobs to do. But their clear goals are to create systems that so clearly surpass our abilities that we will have little hope of competing.OpenAIdefinesits north star of artificial general intelligence (AGI) as “a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work”. And the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei,writes: “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.”The industry’s ultimate ambition, what it calls AGI, is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. These systems would be able to do any work a human could do from a remote desk – leaving livelihoods safe to the extent a human touch is preferred, a physical presence is required, or the jobs themselves are legally protected.It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed HusseinRead moreYou may doubt that the industry will ever succeed in its perverse quest, but we should agree that it shouldn’t even be allowed to try.We shouldfreezefrontier AI development – that is, the effort to build AGI, andonly resumethe work when there is strong public buy-in and broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably.But realizing this commonsense ideal will require us to get organized enough to overcome the richest industry in history. And that means changing the way we think about AI.In many corners of the internet, especially on the left, people pride themselves on never touching the stuff – while simultaneously making bold, deeply mistaken claims about its nature and capabilities.I understand the reluctance to give these companies your money, your data, your attention. But using what is increasingly an indispensable technology is not an endorsement of the industry building it, any more so than using Instagram to advocate for aggressive regulations on social media would be an endorsement of Mark Zuckerberg’s toxic empire.Moreover, the people using AI are going to outcompete the ones who don’t, bending the world in their preferred direction, while forming a deeper understanding of the technology itself. Bosses will use Claude Code to replace workers, while the leftist policy analyst Matt Bruenig ishavingit build a publicly accessible, automatically updating database of National Labor Relations Board decisions. If you’re serious about your mission, you should use whichever tools work best.Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table. Sixty-nine active members of Congresshave publicly usedterms like artificial superintelligence, the Singularity and AI existential risk. If certain techies are the only people willing to acknowledge that the technology’s capabilities have dramatically improved and could pose a species-level threat in the future, that’s who concerned policymakers will disproportionately listen to.The left’s lack of engagement here is a real loss. Even non-leftists recognize it. Joshua Achiam, then OpenAI’s chief futurist,declared: “The left has completely abdicated their role in this discussion. A decade from now, this will be understood on the left to have been a generational mistake; perhaps even more than merely generational.”Dean Ball, who led the authorship of Trump’s AI action plan before becoming an executive at OpenAI,declared: “Joshua is right.”You may be suspicious of political adversaries wishing you were more present in the arena, but they recognize that – on the technology’s current course – this is an all-hands-on-deck situation. Indeed, we all need to reckon with the industry’s race to replace us, but we especially need – and especially don’t have – the left. We need organizers. We need people who can’t help but think about power to teach the ones who never learned to. We need ambition. We need people who believe that better worlds are possible.The popularity of stigmatizing individual AI usage has been a gift to the industry, fracturing would-be opponents and activating our identities as consumers. BP had to pay an ad agency topopularizethe “carbon footprint” to shift the blame for climate change to individuals. When we think as consumers, the goal becomes minimizing our own complicity. We should instead think as citizens: how do we democratically govern this technology in the public interest?Right now, AI is being governed by unelected, unaccountable tech billionaires, subject to intense pressures from shareholders and the Trump administration. To have any hope of changing this intolerable status quo, we’ll need to build a movement powerful enough to defeat the richest industry in history.How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios | Toby WalshRead moreIn March, when I finished writingObsolete, the book this piece draws from, I predicted:It won’t be easy, but the ingredients are there for a mass movement unlike any the world has ever seen. Everyone has a stake in how AI develops – a reality that will become increasingly indisputable as the technology eats ever more of the world.Since then, the dangers have appeared faster than I expected, but public awareness has grown even faster – making me feel more optimistic than ever. The AI story was never going to have a happy ending without deep and sustained engagement from the world, not just the tiny handful of people racing to build our replacements.The big question is whether we can channel this new wave of concern into effective advocacy. Personally, I think the most promising place to start is atIrreplaceable.org. (I serve on the non-profit board and am donating my share of the book’s royalties to Irreplaceable.) Founded by veterans of the climate movement, Irreplaceable aims to meet people where they are, organize their anger into political power, and build a coalition strong enough to win democratic control over AI. The non-profit is organizing anational walkoutto Freeze AI on 20 October. Anyone can join one near them or host their own.I have no illusions that a day of walkouts will solve our AI problems. But it will bring together people with shared concerns, and some of them will become the friendships that sustain successful movements. Most of all, we’ll need to keep our eye on the ball: the companies trying to render us obsolete, not the friends and neighbors using their products.Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist, the author ofObsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It(Nation Books, 29 September), and the co-host of the podcastOrganize Against the MachineExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionActivismProtest (US)ProtestComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: How Senate Democrats can stop Trump from stealing the midterms | David Walbert | The Guardian
description: Republicans could lean on congressional procedure to defy the will of voters. But if they try that, the Senate has a clear way to fight back
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Republicans could lean on congressional procedure to defy the will of voters. But if they try that, the Senate has a clear way to fight back
Content: ‘If Trump and his allies try to steal the House, Senate Democrats can retaliate in kind.’Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAView image in fullscreen‘If Trump and his allies try to steal the House, Senate Democrats can retaliate in kind.’Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAOpinionUS midterm elections 2026How Senate Democrats can stop Trump from stealing the midtermsDavid WalbertRepublicans could lean on congressional procedure to defy the will of voters. But if they try that, the Senate has a clear way to fight backTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTShareHaving lost hismail-in ballot case, Donald Trump will probably resort to ever more extreme ways to try to hold a Republican Congress in November’s elections.His last-ditch effort to count Joe Biden out in 2020 was for Republicans to “investigate” states Biden narrowly won; proclaim fabricated allegations of “stolen elections” to be true; and then reassign those states’ electoral votes to Trump. I havepreviously describedhow that same playbook could be used to try to steal the midterms if a Democratic margin of victory in the House is relatively narrow.Less discussed, however, has been what SenateDemocratscould do to stop the danger.The potential threats are extensive.Article I of the constitution makes each chamber of Congress the “Judge of the Elections [and] Returns … of its own Members”. No matter who state officials or courts say won, Congress has the final word on who will be seated.That gives Trump a potential path to corrupt the congressional election – create confusion and doubt about close elections, challenge the results, and have the members of the House decide congressional election contests to determine who will be seated. His electoral vote scam was stopped in 2020 when the attorney general and other officials refused to join his effort, but they’ve been succeeded by people loyal to Trump, not the law.There have been hundreds of congressional election contests in the country’s history, beginning with the very first Congress in 1789, and they are very different from the 62 election cases Trump and his Republican allies brought and lost in 2020. They lost those cases because they were decided by judges operating under rules of evidence that don’t allow conspiracy theories, unproven allegations and bogus “expert” opinions, but that kind of sham “evidence” could drive congressional decisions determined by politics, not facts.The US supreme court issued a fragile win for voting rights – the real test comes later | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreFor the scheme to work in the midterms,Republicanswould have to have an initial majority in the House when the new Congress is seated on 3 January 2027, since that initial majority will control who else is seated.When the current Congress ends on that date, all now-seated representatives lose their status as members of Congress. Furthermore, candidates who win election in November don’t become representatives simply because of the election returns. They become members of Congress only after they take theoath of office required by the constitution.It’s at that juncture where the danger lies, and the problem has been discussed bylawyers, writers and punditssince it was raised in the Guardian.Federal law requires the clerk of the current House to “make a roll of the Representatives-elect”, and persons on that roll are sworn in as the initial members of the new Congress.Jeffrey Toobinand others, such as the retiredjudge Michael Luttig, are concerned that Republicans could appoint a loyal clerk – a “GOP toady”, in Toobin’s words – who would prepare a fraudulent list of representatives-elect.Some commentatorsdismiss that threat, believing the law is so clear the judiciary would not let the roll be subverted by politics or a corrupt clerk. Maybe I’ve tried too many cases, including at the supreme court, where what looked white and black became gray, but I’m afraid those who feel the law is so clear are overly optimistic. They also underestimate the heavy hand of politics in such litigation.In my bookStealing Elections, American Style, I point out that for 150 years, beginning with the 1876 Tilden-Hayes presidential election, “[p]artisan affiliation has been a near-perfect predictor of Supreme Court justices’ votes in cases that involved a presidential candidate’s claim to the office”. I am quite sure that same “rule of decision” would weigh on the scales if the current supreme court were called on to decide a case that would determine which party controls the next Congress.In my mind, the statute that directs the clerk to prepare the roll of eligible representatives-elect gives Republicans room to argue about who should be included without resorting to a crooked clerk. The law states that candidates should be listed only if their “credentials show that they were regularly elected in accordance with the laws of their states respectfully, or the laws of the United States”.What should the clerk do with candidates who receive the largest number of votes, according to the latest returns, but who face ongoing disputes over election fraud – in other words, disputes over whether they were “regularly elected in accordance with” state and federal law? What if the election is in doubt because of a pending congressional election contest under article I? Could such a candidate’s credentials show they were elected in accordance with the law, since it’s up to Congress to make that decision where there is a contest?The scenarios get uglier if red states are complicit.While no secretaries of state complied with Trump’s demands to falsify the vote in 2020, there were plenty of legislators willing to do so, and some local election officials said the election should not be certified. Since then, election deniers havegained more state and county offices, in addition to the hardcore election deniers and Trump loyalists who now hold many election-related positions with federal agencies.With thesupreme court’s rulingon Friday, the Department of Homeland Security will be preparing lists of “approved” citizen voters in at least 27 states. Election officials loyal to Trump could parrot his inevitable claims of vote fraud, bolstered by disparities between the county’s lists and the notoriously inaccurate DHS lists.Would it be illegal for them to refuse to certify a Democratic win because of those disparities? Probably, but it would add uncertainly, confusion and chaos – perennial Trump favorites – and give cover to Republicans demanding a congressional election contest to decide the winner.Moreover, without a “credentialed” winner before 3 January, the clerk couldn’t add an apparent winner to the roll under the explicit terms of the statute.An even uglier case would involve federal agents seizing ballots from one or two Democratic precincts. Many judges would issue injunctions to stop that, but others might not.How the supreme court would rule on an emergency petition is unknown. The justices have ruled for Trump in dubious cases and split 5-4 and 6-3 in cases that should have been unanimous rulings against Trump.Further confounding the problem, a complicit state or county might acquiesce in a federal seizure and even concede the presence of fraud in order to delay certification of a Democratic win. Again, some haveargued that the law prohibits this possibility, but the law is not so certain with today’s supreme court.One final example shows just how complicated and unpredictable the legal-political landscape can be.The current Trump-controlled House could have expedited or preliminary votes on pending election contests and rule in favor of enough Republicans to keep their initial majority in the new Congress. The clerk is an officer of the House and does not have discretion to ignore a congressional directive because he disagrees with it. He would be have to prepare the roll according to the House’s direction.While the current Congress can’t dictate to the next Congress how to rule in election contests for its members, it wouldn’t be doing that. The current Congress would “only” be dictating to its clerk how he should actnowwhen the clerk is subject to its control.double quotation markWhat appears to be a Democratic House majority after the election may not be when initial representatives-elect are sworn in on 3 JanuaryIn short, what appears to be a Democratic House majority after the election may not be when initial representatives-elect are sworn in on 3 January.But what has not been considered by those who have addressed this conundrum is the role the Senate could play. It could be crucial in preventing Republicans from stealing the House.Unlike the House, where all members’ terms end on 3 January, the Senate is a continuing body, and the 65 currently seated senators who are not up for election now will retain the full authority of their office on 3 January.Because of that,the Senate will be under the control of the Democratic party when it convenes on 3 January regardless of the election. Of the 65 senators carrying over, 32 are Democrats, plus the two independents (Bernie Sanders and Angus King) who caucus with them, but only 31 Republicans will carry over.That assures Democrats an initial 34-31 advantage in the Senate. Normally, that advantage would just be momentary if the Democrats don’t capture the Senate in November, but this will be anything but a normal year if Republicans try to take the House with bogus election challenges.If Trump and his allies try to steal the House, Senate Democrats can retaliate in kind and guarantee their control of that chamber, regardless of the election outcome, by refusing to seat a few Republicans who had close elections. Their claims of fraud can mimic Republican claims in the House.Democratic senators would have to play very serious hardball to do this, but if Republicans are subverting House elections, what would they have to lose?Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change | Kathryn SikkinkRead moreThe battle would come to a head in the Senate when newly elected senators are called up to take the oath of office and be seated. The vice-president in his constitutional role as president of the Senate customarily handles that procedure. But Vance would be stopped cold if a seated Democrat challenged a Republican senator-elect.Riddick’s Senate procedure is the authoritative compendium of Senate procedures and precedents, and itaddresses this exact scenario:double quotation markAfter the name of a Senator-elect is called, while the question of swearing him in is pending the consideration of a resolution to refer his credentials to a committee and to deny him the right to take his oath of office in the meantime is privileged andtakes precedence over swearing him in…What if Vance tried to ignore Senate procedure by ruling the motion out of order and attempting to administer the oath to a challenged senator? Vance has the authority to make procedural rulings, but his authority is strictly limited by the will of the Senate. Democrats have the right to challenge his ruling immediately, and their appeal would be determined by the currently seated Democratic majority.A filibuster by the Republican minority is a possible reaction to this process, but the Senate would remain under control of the Democratic majority.Will the United States sink to this level, where Congress will be determined by a political standoff between the House and Senate? There have been serious credentials fights before, but nothing this extreme has happened outside of civil war-era elections.To be sure, all of this would have been an impossible fantasy just a few years ago, but very little is inconceivable with Trump in the White House and in control of the Republican party. Trump is willing to destroy the country’s hold on democracy and fair elections to retain power.We can only hope the prospect of a doomsday standoff between the House and Senate over the true election winners would make enough Republicans forgo trying to steal the House.David F Walbert has litigated dozens of election cases, including landmark cases before the supreme court, taught constitutional law, testified before Congress on voting legislation, and most recently authoredStealing Elections, American Style, published by Bloomsbury on 3 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS CongressTrump administrationRepublicansDemocratsUS politicsHouse of RepresentativescommentShareReuse this content

title: Scarlett Johansson swears by magnesium. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep? | Melissa Davey | The Guardian
description: Experts cite inconsistent evidence for supplementing with the essential mineral – and warn taking magnesium without a deficiency has risks
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Experts cite inconsistent evidence for supplementing with the essential mineral – and warn taking magnesium without a deficiency has risks
Content: There are not enough consistent, strong findings to show strong cause and effect between magnesium supplementation and better sleep, dietitians say.Illustration: Guardian Design/Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere are not enough consistent, strong findings to show strong cause and effect between magnesium supplementation and better sleep, dietitians say.Illustration: Guardian Design/Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralHealth & wellbeingScarlett Johansson swears by magnesium. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep?Melissa DaveyExperts cite inconsistent evidence for supplementing with the essential mineral – and warn taking magnesium without a deficiency has risksRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 29 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 18.35 EDTShareDanielle Shine says her Instagram inbox was filled with questions after Scarlett Johansson was quotedin the Daily Mailand other publications recently saying she takes magnesium to improve her digestion and sleep.“I know that everybody is taking magnesium now. It’s so helpful,” the actorreportedly told beauty publicationByrdie.Shine, a dietician, says celebrity endorsement of supplements is persuasive and always leads to an uptick in questions.The ‘sleepy girl mocktail’ is just making dry January all the more unbearableRead more“The general sentiment was, ‘If she [Johansson] takes magnesium and says it works for her, then maybe I should be taking it too,’” Shine says.But celebrity andinfluencer endorsementaside, what does the evidence say?Magnesium is importantMagnesium is an essential mineral that the body needs for blood pressure regulation, bone health and many other important functions. Because the body doesn’t produce it, diet is critical, with nuts, seeds, legumes, leafy greens and brown rice among good sources.But magnesium deficiency is not common in Australia, and is more likely in people with certain conditions such as diabetes or bowel disease. Despite this, it is promoted widely as a good supplement anybody can take for a range of conditions.Limited evidence for sleepShine says some studies have reported improvements in certain aspects of sleep when taking magnesium supplements, “but the findings are inconsistent”.“Studies are generally small, short-term and use different forms and doses of magnesium, which makes it difficult to draw firm conclusions about whether supplementation reliably improves sleep,” she says.Sports dietitian Dr Evangeline Mantzioris says another difficulty is studies measure sleep quality differently, with some examining sleep duration, time taken to fall asleep, or depth of sleep. But there are not enough consistent, strong findings to show strong cause and effect, she says.If someone was struggling with sleep, “We would want to look at sleep hygiene first, such as lights and devices off, and no caffeine,” she says, along with stress and other factors.What about digestion and gut health?Shine says some forms of supplemental magnesium draw water into the intestine, and this has a laxative effect. The British Dietetic Association names magnesium oxide as anevidence-based treatment optionfor adults with constipation.Mantzioris says people who exercise regularly need to be careful of this, because taken wrongly, magnesium can cause nausea, abdominal cramping and diarrhoea.This is because intense exercise jolts the intestines while diverting blood away from them, making the gut extra sensitive to magnesium and giving a laxative double-whammy effect.“We always say in sports that you don’t want to take magnesium when you know you’re going to be out training the next day,” she says.Can magnesium help exercise recovery?Magnesium is important for metabolism and muscle contraction, Shine says, “but its role in these processes doesn’t mean that supplementation will improve recovery”, including from muscle pain and damage.“The Australian Institute of Sport classifies magnesium as aGroup Csupplement, a category where the scientific evidence doesn’t support a benefit among athletes or is insufficient to draw firm conclusions,” she says.There’s alsono good evidencemagnesium supplementation prevents muscle cramps, Mantzioris says. While soaking in a warm magnesium salt bath may bring relief, it ismore likely the warm waterrather than the magnesium doing the heavy lifting.Will it calm my nerves?Shine says marketing of magnesium products exploits it being “essential” to calming the nervous system, with suggestions supplementation is also essential to preventing and treating stress and anxiety.“Magnesium is involved in processes including nerve transmission and regulation of neuronal activity, helping nerves communicate throughout the body,” she says.“However, there’s no strong evidence that magnesium supplementation provides broad benefits for nervous-system function.”Mantzioris says supplement companies play on people’s real-life stressors and “they capture our fear that we might be deficient in something, and try to sell that this might explain why we’re stressed or tired”.“But the reason many of us are stressed and tired isbecause we work too much, which magnesium can’t fix.”Magnesium is the latest buzzy supplement. Can it help with anxiety?Read moreThose with a genuine deficiency may benefitPeople at risk of deficiency or worriedcan see a doctorwho can order a blood test and recommend the best way to increase intake. There is alsono strong evidenceto show that routine oral magnesium supplementation during pregnancy is beneficial.Taking magnesium in the absence of a known deficiency has some risks, Shine says.“Very high doses can cause toxicity, including low blood pressure, breathing problems, abnormal heart rhythms and, in severe cases, cardiac arrest,” she says.Melissa Davey is Guardian Australia’s medical editorAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: The Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunity | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/PAView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/PAOpinionManchester CityThe Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunityJonathan LiewWhen transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealthTue 29 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.52 EDTShareThe cache of leaked emails and documents that would eventuallylead to the crisis in which Manchester Cityare now embroiled waspublished by Der Spiegel in 2018, and often it was the tone of the club’s communications that was as startling as their content. Of City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a trusted adviser to the royal family of the United Arab Emirates,it was said that he would“rather spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue [Uefa] for the next 10 years” than accept a fine.In the same tranche of documents,City lawyer Simon Cliff assertsthat “Uefa doesn’t respond to anything other than aggression”, and threatens the governing body of European football – who were pursuing City over alleged financial irregularities at the time – with “the destruction of their rules and organisation”.All of which feels like a rather extreme way of ensuring that your football club has the right tosign Jack Rodwell from Everton. And, yes, this is one of those stories in which the deeply serious and the deeply trivial, the universal and the parochial, are not always easy to tell apart. From a safe distance, the news that one of English football’s most successful clubshas been found guilty of more than 100charges of financial irregularity, including “sham” payments totalling around £900m, may feel like so much so-what, a thicket of sporting arcana that even devoted fans occasionally struggle to parse. But, of course, the City case goes deeper than one club, one league, even one sport. Fundamentally, it is a parable of power.After all, this is not simply a football club but a beloved cultural asset that happens to be majority-owned by the billionaire Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the UAE and brother of the president. Since the Premier League announced thecharges against City in 2023, the case has been discussed not merely at boardroom level but at a diplomatic level. Just last month,Bloomberg reported UAE officialswarning that an adverse verdict against City could threaten billions in Emirati investment in the UK.Bilateral trade between the countriesnudged above £25bn in 2025.Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney RonayRead moreAnd perhaps the logical starting point here is to observe just how ridiculous it is that this country’s foreign relations are effectively being negotiated in a football tribunal. That the UK’s clean-energy transition is somehow contingent on whether a panel decides whetherRoberto Mancini’s coaching contractwas fair or not. This was one of the reasons why it was such a bad idea for the Premier League to allow entire states to invest in football clubs. Over time it was inevitable that questions of sporting merit and integrity would become entangled with questions of diplomacy and hard power; that footballing warfare would increasingly come to resemble the real thing.We caught a glimpse of this in the bellicose statement City releasedin response on Tuesday evening, obliquely questioning the Premier League’s ability “to behave as an independent, impartial and fair- minded regulator, free from partisan influence”. In 2024, in a separate case against the Premier League, City tried to discredit the league’s basic governance model, arguing that the two-thirds majority required for motions to pass represented “the tyranny of the majority”, which gives you a good idea of what Abu Dhabi thinks of basic democracy.View image in fullscreenVincent Kompany lifts the Premier League trophy as Manchester City win the title after drawing 0-0 with Huddersfield Town at the Etihad Stadium, Manchester, 6 May 2018.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAt this point we should probably recall that this is a football club majority-owned by a country that, according to the UN’s own reports, is defying arms embargos inSudanandLibya, and that, according to Human Rights Watch, is responsible for widespread acts of political repression and rights abuses. From the years of warlike rhetoric, veiled threats, legal challenges and poisonous off-record briefings, City’s approach appears to consist, in part, of discrediting the very idea that anyone is fit to regulate it.In one respect, this stems from a genuine belief that football’s financial regulations – largely nonexistent in the decade after the Premier League’s foundation in 1992 – were designed to protect elite wealth while extinguishing new-money challengers such as City and the Chelsea of Roman Abramovich. But to follow this thread to its logical conclusion is essentially an argument for a world in which there are no legitimate checks on power – where you can do what you want, however you want, for as long as you want, for whatever purpose you want; where the only meaningful rules of the game are power and leverage; where you would rather destroy your enemies than accept even the slightest curb on your volition.And, of course, there is little sense in singling out City or Abu Dhabi here. From City and the Saudi-run Newcastle United to the opaque private-equity funds that now run most of their rivals, the top end of English football is essentially owned by bored men given more money than they can possibly know what to do with and more power than it is ever advisable to invest in a single human being.For Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia you might just as easily read Jeff Bezos, part of a consortium thatnow owns almost 40% of Liverpool FC. Or Meta, or Elon Musk, or Benjamin Netanyahu, or Donald Trump: an entire class of men who recognise no authority beyond their own, for whom politics and business and sport and culture are essentially the same basic substance – a game to be brought to heel by any means necessary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is the broader significance of the City verdict, beyond the interminable debate over whether the club should be forcibly relegated, stripped of titles and trophies. In a world where the UN is neutered, where transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, it offers an alternative vision to a world increasingly aligned along axes of brute power and wealth. It articulates the increasingly outmoded idea that there is a shared set of values and rules by which all must abide.And clearly this case is not over yet. City continue to deny any wrongdoing. Doubtless there will be appeals upon appeals, perhaps even ending in the high court many years hence. Doubtless there are diplomatic representations to be made, high-level deals to be brokered, realpolitik to be waged. After all, geopolitics, like football, is very much a results business.But it is in the interests not just of City’s rivals and not just of football itself, but of everyone with an interest in the rule of law that they do not succeed.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? In an earlier version, the caption below the picture of Vincent Kompany raising the Premier League trophy said Manchester City had beaten Huddersfield Town. In fact, the match was a 0-0 draw.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityOpinionFinancesFinancial fair playUnited Arab EmiratesUefaPremier LeagueFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: To the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button? | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guy, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guy, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Nigel Farage at a Reform UK press conference in Kirkcaldy, 15 January 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage at a Reform UK press conference in Kirkcaldy, 15 January 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionNigel FarageTo the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button?Marina HydeThe Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guyTue 29 Sep 2026 07.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTShareAnother week, another chance for Nigel Farage to demonstrate his literally hysterical leadership inabilities. For a guy who supposedly valorises the wartime British spirit, Nigel would genuinely have had to have been interned during that conflict on account of his serial predilection for spreading panic and unverified information at any given chance. The weekendincident near RAF Fairfordwas simply the latest in a long line of occasions that make you suspect the poster on the wall at Reform HQ reads simply: “Lose Cool and Start Shitposting.”Despite its popularity now, the famous “Keep Calm and Carry On” poster from the second world war was almost certainly never displayed in that conflict. Although more than 2m copies of it were printed, it was in factheld in reservein case a really serious crisis hit. Which, when you consider even the blitz apparently didn’t clear the bar, it is almost impossible to conceive of in our era where comparatively minuscule incidents force certain party leaders into more than 24 hours of madly irresponsible and emotional online incontinence.Many of you may find you have a low tolerance for shrieks of “We have the right to know absolutely everything, immediately!” from a congenitally secretive guy who notoriously declined to declare the £5m he was given from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and, since that weird “gift” has been uncovered, has been in a prolonged tantrum that has caused him to snap at any attempts to discover more about what might have motivated it. “None of your business,” ran one particularly ill-judged attempt by Farage to put the issue to bed. “What’s it got to do with you?”I do find my finger hovering over the “What’s it got to do with you?’ button with increasing regularity when Farage appears on screen to insert himself into moments of obviously active sensitivity. The clearly nuanced and potentially complex Fairford investigation – still ongoing, despite the release on bail of the five men arrested – was a case in point, although on Monday Nigel did attempt to set it out in a madly precipitous video on what he called “the Fairford plot”, captioned: “Fairford proves my pointon Iran and the IRGC.” Does it? OK, thanks Jack Ryan.Anyone who judges that this intemperate psychological liability should have access to the nuclear codes and other top-level information must have a subconscious wish for their answer to the question “where do you see yourself in five years’ time?” to be “living in Britain’s catacombs and distilling drinking water from my own urine”. It’s unclear whether a Prime Minister Farage would just bottle everything or shoot first and ask questions later, but the most likely metaphorical outcome in any given scenario may well be him shooting the wrong person first, then refusing to answer questions later.Furthermore, as always with Nigel, it’s worth highlighting his insistence on rising to only the occasions from which he feels he might personally benefit. And so it is that he will have an awful lot to say about the horrific murder ofHenry Nowak, but nothing or next to about those of Jo Cox or Sarah Everard. Whatever may or may not have happened at Fairford feeds into what we have to call, with heavy irony, his two-tier approach to public life. After all, for a guy who supposedly worries about illegal activity that could bear the hallmarks of foreign sponsorship, Farage strangely didn’t have a lot to say about the Ukrainian and Romanian nationals who were recruited via a Russian-speaking pseudonymous Telegram user tocommit arsonon property connected to Keir Starmer and on a car he had previously owned, back when Starmer was prime minister. Even after they were found guilty, the Reform leader didn’t seem to find this sort of darkly intriguing activity worthy of comment. Things he did find worthy of comment that same month included disputes over flying the St George’s cross flag andAI scam videos.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDon’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John HarrisRead moreThe thing about attaining the very highest office in the land is that you have to be prime minister of all the things, all the time. It is difficult to see how someone as cynically selective as Farage could somehow become the sort of leader able to speak for a nation. Or, just as importantly, the sort of leader able to realise when it’s time to shut up for a nation.Far more troubling still is the gathering sense that Farage is too mentally weak for the role, and would go to pieces in very short order once plunged into the realities of life in Downing Street. Perhaps hisdeclining poll ratingsmean worrying may be unnecessary. But he’s increasingly a set of walking psychological red flags: emotional, quick to temper, incapable of rising above the self-serving.Amazing that there is apsychological screening testto determine whether you are up to appearing on a reality TV show these days, but you could ascend to the office of prime minister without submitting to anything similar. At least 20% of would-be Big Brother contestants are deemed mentally unfit to participate during the casting process each year. And looking at the five main party leaders this week, you’d think a similar percentage had the potential to absolutely implode were they to enter the Downing Street house. Perhaps our politics needs new duty-of-care guidelines, so that the office of British prime minister is psychologically guardrailed to the same level as, say, a dating show like Love is Blind.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist. Her new book is What a Time to Be Alive! To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may applyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Britons are not ageing healthily – we need to learn from countries that have made it a priority | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Although we’re living longer, the data on healthy life expectancy in the UK isn’t good. Andy Burnham must reverse this trend to protect the NHS and social care, says public health academic Prof Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Although we’re living longer, the data on healthy life expectancy in the UK isn’t good. Andy Burnham must reverse this trend to protect the NHS and social care, says public health academic Prof Devi Sridhar
Content: ‘It’s about our diet, as well as regular movement of the muscles we need to stay functionally independent each day.’Photograph: Cultura RM/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s about our diet, as well as regular movement of the muscles we need to stay functionally independent each day.’Photograph: Cultura RM/AlamyOpinionHealth policyBritons are not ageing healthily – we need to learn from countries that have made it a priorityDevi SridharAlthough we’re living longer, the data on healthy life expectancy in the UK isn’t good. Andy Burnham must reverse this trend to protect the NHS and social careProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh, and the author of How Not to Die (Too Soon)Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTShareThe prime minister has put forwardhis bold proposalfor a universal, NHS-style social care service. In doing so, Andy Burnham has put the spotlight back on one of the major challenges facing almost everywhere in the world: how to manage thedemographic changeslinked to an ageing society.It’s an important discussion. But what if government didn’t just look at how to care for people in their later years and instead spent real political capital on policies to help people live longer independently, and in good health? The data isn’t pretty on this. While the trend over the past half-century in almost all countries has been for people to live longer,healthylife expectancy has been consistently falling.Thelatest figuresfrom the Office for National Statistics show that in 2022-24, healthy life expectancy at birth was just 60.7 years for men (77% of life) and 60.9 years for women (73%) across the UK, despitelifeexpectancy being 79.1 years for men and 83.0 years for women.In Scotlandit is even worse: for 2022-24, healthy life expectancy at birth was 59.1 for men and 59.4 for women, numbers that continue to decline.The data points to a major problem in ageing societies: that a growing number of the years we have gained in life expectancy are being spent with reduced independence, limited health conditions or in disability. This has huge ramifications for social care. Without anything changing in these trends, more older people in poor health means more people dependent on their loved ones, the private sector and the state for care – and a higher burden on an already struggling NHS.As a public health expert, my question is: how much of this shift is preventable? We know there is enormous variation in how people age. Some of it is down to luck, but it is also about staying active and socially connected to a community, and about larger social policies. For me, a key UK government planning objective, across all sectors, should be to increase the number of healthy years of life.Healthy ageing is largely about what happens in our 40s, 50s and 60s. It’s about effective prevention and early management of conditions such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and cancer. It’s about our diet, as well as the regular movement of the muscles we need to stay functionally independent each day – to be able to take stairs, go out to the shops, use the toilet or take a shower. It is inextricably linked to the quality of the environments in which people live, such as whether they have access to green space, social connection, public transport, housing and employment. We know the factors that lead to living longer, healthier lives: I’ve writtenan entire bookabout the evidence base on population-level health.View image in fullscreen‘We know the factors that lead to longer, healthier lives.’Photograph: Peter Cripps/AlamyThere are countries that have already recognised this demographic shift and made healthy ageing a priority. In Japan, thehealthy life expectancy extension planaims to increase years lived well by more than three years by 2040, to at least 75 for men and women. This goal is linked to wider reforms to employment, healthcare and social welfare. Japan has also pioneered community-based integrated care to facilitate older people staying in their own homes and communities for as long as possible.Singapore has had initiatives for“successful ageing” since 2015, involving initiatives across health, social welfare, employment and infrastructure. Building on that, in 2023 the governmentlaunched further measurestargeting health, housing and transport policy, with the explicit aim of helping older people remain active, socially connected and supported in their communities. Singapore and Japan now lead the global rankings for total life expectancy and for healthy life expectancy.Burnham has much to learn from their planning in this area. Any debate on the future funding and organisation of social care needs to consider not only the financial challenges of providing the best care for an ageing population, but also how we collectively reduce the number of people who reach a point of dependency that could be avoided in the first place.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe success of an ageing society should be measured not only on how it collectively shoulders the burden of dependency, but also on how well it extends the years in which people can live independently and well. If Burnham is serious about the social care agenda, that is the long-term question we should be asking now: not simply how we will care for people when they become dependent, but how we will create the conditions that allow more people to remain healthy for longer.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh, and the author ofHow Not to Die (Too Soon)Explore more on these topicsHealth policyOpinionSocial careOlder peopleHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: As AI models go rogue, do you still trust OpenAI and Anthropic to stop them? I don’t and neither should you | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: The need for independent regulation grows more obvious by the day. We must keep this tech in check before it’s too late, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: The need for independent regulation grows more obvious by the day. We must keep this tech in check before it’s too late, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: The OpenAIapp and the company’s CEO, Sam Altman.Photograph: Rokas Tenys/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe OpenAIapp and the company’s CEO, Sam Altman.Photograph: Rokas Tenys/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)As AI models go rogue, do you still trust OpenAI and Anthropic to stop them? I don’t and neither should youChris Stokel-WalkerThe need for independent regulation grows more obvious by the day. We must keep this tech in check before it’s too lateOpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testingTue 29 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.32 EDTShareFool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Fool me more than 16,000 times – asOpenAI agents didto a UN public data hub while repeatedly trying to find its way around the UN’s cyber-blocks – and perhaps it’s time to admit the system we have for keeping AI agents under control isn’t working particularly well.The news about AI systems cropping up in places they shouldn’t sounds alarming. Though the description of these as “hacks” is perhaps overstating things, AI has exploited issues in IT systems that humans simply haven’t got around to finding. It’s also important to note that we shouldn’t be worried that the machines have suddenly become sentient and decided torebel against humanity. There is not enough evidence to suggest that’s what is happening. The systems are simply following instructions and trying to complete the tasks they have been given, even if they’re sometimes finding unintended ways around obstacles to do so.But we ought to be very concerned about the fact the AI companies we’re meant to trust to keep their models in check seem unable to do so. Worse than that, they don’t seem to know what their products are even doing.The scale of the problem is staggering. In June, an OpenAI research agent given the job of looking up public medicine spending data inAustraliawas repeatedly blocked by a Medicare statistics portal. OpenAI’s model found a way around the blocks, gaining unauthorised access and secreting away the documents. It took until August for OpenAI to discover what had happened. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said the company had taken “way too long” to tell his government, and it’s very hard to disagree with him.OpenAI has sincepublisheda reporting framework for model “misalignment”, along with six more examples of its AI committing troubling behaviour from the previous six months. The firm acknowledged that its previous disclosures were “ad hoc and less frequent than ideal”, and said evidence about AI safety needs to be checked by people outside the companies building the models.This isn’t just an OpenAI problem, which makes it all the more worrying.Anthropicfound three incidents in which its Claude models got unauthorised access to real third-party systems after reviewing about 141,000 model transcripts. It only found a fourth, dating back to January, after collating a dossier for an independent investigation.Googleconfirmed that Gemini had accessed systems belonging to three real companies during testing. Another OpenAI agentused DNS– the system that acts as the internet’s address book, turning web addresses into machine readable forms – to reach an outside chatbot despite internet restrictions. Another published a researcher’sGitHubtoken – an access password – while trying to cheat on a mathematical proof, despite twice being told to stop. And research agents posted 53 user images to external hosting sites.Other agents accessed census data using credentials found online, copied the US Securities and Exchange Commission information elsewhere and apparently tried unsuccessfully tobreak into a US Department of Education website. OpenAI says it has notified dozens of third parties affected by its agents, and that its review of past activity is still ongoing.These haphazard, post-hoc discoveries of major incursions into companies and organisations’ IT systems are not the right way to police a technology as powerful as AI. We learned a while back not to leave air crash investigations solely to Boeing or Airbus. Now we need to be less naive about AI.Last week, at the UN general assembly, the AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury launched theIndependent AI Evaluation Foundation(IAEF) with $10m in philanthropic backing. Its immediate focus is education, but the important idea is to turn independent AI evaluation into an actual profession: people and organisations with the skills, infrastructure and standards to test these systems without having a financial stake in whether they pass. Because right now, a company can report an incident, investigate it, announce whatever mitigations it’s made and move on.The IAEF is a welcome intervention but it can’t fix the problem on its own. It can’t compel OpenAI or Anthropic to hand over logs, preserve evidence or tell a government that one of its systems has crossed a line. And its $10m is chump change beside companies such asAnthropic, which is lining up a proposed public listing that has been discussed at a valuation of about $2tn. But it is infrastructure we should be building on, and which politicians should press the case for.Governments need to agree to common rules that compel companies to disclose serious AI incidents and near misses, and to do so quickly. They need to make them open up their books to external evaluators rather than relying on the goodwill or whims of the companies themselves. And the findings should be shared so we can learn from every incident. The labs should help design those rules but they shouldn’t have the final say until they have earned our trust.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd money complicates things: while OpenAI has postponed its IPO until at least 2027 amid the safety concerns, it seems that Anthropic’s flotation is still going full steam ahead. There are billions – potentially trillions – of dollars riding on how these companies and their products are perceived. We created independent auditors and accident investigators in other industries because we understood that good intentions don’t remove real conflicts of interest.The labs can and should keep building better fences. But when a model manages to gets over one, they shouldn’t be the only ones allowed to decide what happens next. Because so far they’ve shown themselves to be uniquely unqualified to do so.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingOpenAIAnthropicData and computer securityHackscommentShareReuse this content

title: A leftwing victory in Berlin shows people want freedom, and liberals cannot deliver it | Eva von Redecker | The Guardian
description: Die Linke’s surge was propelled by a compelling promise: for voters to have the freedom to stay in their city. This is how to fight back against the far right, says writer and philosopher Eva von Redecker
Author: Eva von Redecker
Headline: Die Linke’s surge was propelled by a compelling promise: for voters to have the freedom to stay in their city. This is how to fight back against the far right, says writer and philosopher Eva von Redecker
Content: Die Linke’s top candidate, Elif Eralp (with flowers) during a meeting of its Berlin state branch on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDie Linke’s top candidate, Elif Eralp (with flowers) during a meeting of its Berlin state branch on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionGermanyA leftwing victory in Berlin shows people want freedom, and liberals cannot deliver itEva von RedeckerDie Linke’s surge was propelled by a compelling promise: for voters to have the freedom to stay in their city. This is how to fight back against the far rightTue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.26 EDTShareThe German leftwing party Die Linkewon the state elections in Berlinon 20 September. It’s unclear whether the party will be able to form a coalition, appoint its lead candidate Elif Eralpas mayor, and follow through on her core campaign promise: to socialise the housing stock of the city’s biggest real-estate companies. A barrage of accusations started to circulate immediately after the results came in. Even by the standards of present-day polarisation, the pitch was extreme.On the basis of one leaked chat andone rapper’s performance, the party was described as schmoozing with criminal clans andendangering the lives of Berlin Jews. Accusations of antisemitism prompted the Greens and the SPD – potential coalition partners – to question any potential cooperation, while “alt-right” opinion-makers suggested that “Hamas and Hezbollah” hadwon the elections, or that the German Democratic Republic (the old East Germany) was about to come back. Alice Weidel of the rightwing AfDallegedthat Die Linke intended to “shoot the rich”.Our liberal capitalist orders are designed to protect property. Touch one bit of it, and the whole thing is apparently on fire. And yet, nerves aren’t always this raw. The current flare-ups reveal a deep crisis. Sober-sounding commentators have pointed out that the accusations against Die Linke are simply a strategy to stop the socialisation agenda. But that account of moral panic as deliberate strategy can hardly explain everything. Why do so many people want to believe the smear campaigns, especially while the simultaneous wins for the AfD are swiftly normalised?The frenzy becomes less surprising once we understand the way in which liberalism is under pressure, and how that pressure predisposes the saner political forces to look like freedom’s foes. Freedom is the core of liberalism. It is freedom of a particular kind: individual freedom. It lets you do whatever you want as long as you don’t violate the freedom of others or, crucially, their property. The analogy between freedom and property runs deep: my entitlement to do whatever I want is derived from ownership of the self. I am my own quasi-property, and in that capacity I face other self-owners and rely on the state to adjudicate between us.This balance, between personal freedom and the freedom of all others, is already precarious , but in the face of the global crises we face now, it is especially under strain. Liberalism cannot govern economic inequality or ecological disaster, except by pitting the individual freedom of future or far-away others against the freedom of the currently privileged. Without democratic pride in our collective ability to rule our shared fate, the resulting policies look like sacrifice with no upside – I lose the (however hypothetical) freedom to own a row of houses, or I lose the freedom to drive a car, but even if I got public housing or public transport in turn, that wouldn’t register as compensation. After all, I cannot do whatever I want with those.View image in fullscreenThe “time for a change” demonstration in Berlin, 12 September 2026, in which more than 100 organisations took part.Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/ShutterstockReason might be on the side of anti-discrimination, social distancing or electric vehicles, but freedom kicks on the other side. It isn’t full liberal freedom any more, which would have to regard other people as a limit, but its unhinged, ultra-possessive part.The right offers quasi-property (or “phantom possession”, as I like to call it) to satisfy its voters: it defends traditional gender roles, the family, freedom of speech and the nation as though they were things to own. “Take back your country” was acore campaign sloganof the AfD. It alludes to the “great replacement” myth, according to which white populations are in the process of being replaced by people who are not. This plot weaves together several possessive entitlements: white citizens should “own” their country; the country and its men should “own” female reproductive powers to increase the domestic birthrate. And migrants aren’t even seen as capable of moving by their own will, but are imported by a woke or Jewish cabal, and now need to be removed by “remigration”.While such racist discourse is more associated with rural areas, “phantom possession” can suddenly override concern for fellow migrant citizens in Berlin, too. Any wrong step by the Left will suffice for the political middle to succumb to its own generalised property panic. Shaken by the success of the AfD, disoriented by a future that liberalism effectively cannot rule, challenged by emancipatory claims of various groups, and struggling to defend Israel’s crimes, much of the so-called centre also breaks the liberal pact that is founded on equality.In what some German Jews describe as “paternalistic philosemitism”, centrist pundits exceed the concern to fight antisemitism where it happens. Instead, they prop up an idea of absolute victimisation and defend it at all costs. They defend German “memory culture” as if it were their private asset. Consequently, Die Linke – just as human rights organisations, anti-zionist Jews, pro-Palestinian demonstrators and anyone perceived as vaguely “Arab” – is cast in the role of ruthless plunderer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBerlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma AydemirRead moreHow Die Linke – and itspromise to socialise some private housing– will weather this particular campaign is still unknown. But whatever happens, it has to continue to navigate a fractured political map. Like all emancipatory efforts at present, its potential Berlin mayoralty is up against unhinged claims, and faces objective problems that require real change.Which is why the left cannot win within the liberal script. It can only win with a compelling formulation of freedom that points beyond the current impasse. Like Zohran Mamdani in New York, Die Linke has understood this. It has not only promised an abstract right, but literally the freedom to stay in one’s city, one’s neighbourhood, one’s flat. And this freedom can scale up: against displacement, genocide and the ecological doom that threatens our ability to remain on planet Earth.The German left urgently needs to find a way to translate such an agenda to the countryside, where parts of the white population have fallen for fascist myths. Which non-toxic freedom could repair their lost sense of place? And above all, how can we guarantee the freedom to stay for the migrant communities who arethreatened with deportationby the AfD? Where this fails, even the most basic liberal achievement of human rights is lost. And definitely not because of socialised housing.Eva von Redecker is a philosopher and nonfiction writer. She is the author ofThe Freedom to StayDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
