title: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire  | Movies | The Guardian
description: One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film
Content: Moments to enjoy … Tom Cruise (Digger Rockwell) in Digger, directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenMoments to enjoy … Tom Cruise (Digger Rockwell) in Digger, directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesReviewDigger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satireOne man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory filmPeter BradshawTue 29 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnew movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican directorAlejandro González Iñárrituis always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played byTom Cruisewith a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played byJohn Goodman, with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.View image in fullscreenCranky … John Goodman as President Compson in Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Entertainment Inc/PABut wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, including nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. As withAdam McKay’s Don’t Look Up, there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection. Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump’s greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?Digger is out on 2 October in Australia, the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsComedy filmsAlejandro González IñárrituTom CruiseRiz AhmedJohn GoodmanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We got naked and covered ourselves in Vaseline’: Katherine Hubbard on photographing her ailing mother | Photography | The Guardian
description: Over five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: Over five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?
Content: ‘My mum’s completely her own person’ … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (hand to face), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkView image in fullscreen‘My mum’s completely her own person’ … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (hand to face), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkPhotographyInterview‘We got naked and covered ourselves in Vaseline’: Katherine Hubbard on photographing her ailing motherCharlotte JansenOver five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, artist Katherine Hubbard started to sense something was not right with her mother, Antonette Berger. “It was impossible at the time to say what I was noticing, but something was off.”Berger was living alone in Philadelphia, and as restrictions were lifted, Hubbard went to stay with her. Berger was eventually diagnosed with LATE [limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy], a condition which causes symptoms similar to Alzheimer’s, though the decline in memory and day-to-day functioning is slower. The diagnosis was “a painful, drawn-out and confusing process – then a feeling of so much grief, so much loss”, Hubbard explains on Zoom from New York.Finding herself suddenly in the role of a “caretaker under duress”, Hubbard decided to photograph her housebound mother and her environment. “The camera fails us in so many ways,” she says, “and the absurdity with dementia is that I was constantly making lots of images of things that can’t be shown in an image. But I make images because of how they feel, not how they look.”She set up two vintage Polaroid cameras and her equipment at her mother’s apartment in Germantown, and didn’t take it down for five years. The wrenchingly beautiful images became the series The Great Room, published as a book, One Fifty One, named after the house’s street number. The Great Room photographs and installations based on Berger’s apartment are included inHubbard’s solo exhibition at Studio Voltaire, London.Hubbard grew up in Philadelphia, but in a different, “more modest” house than the incredible, maze-like, sprawling setting seen in The Great Room. The apartment that appears in the photographs belongs to a huge, dilapidated building Berger owned and rented out for 40 years. 151 formed an important part of Hubbard’s upbringing and early imaginary – they would regularly visit Berger’s many tenants there, “it was kind of like a community centre, there were always people around, complaining about things breaking”. The title The Great Room references Berger’s own description of the apartment’s main living space.View image in fullscreenThrillingly theatrical … Katherine Hubbard, one fifty one (snap), 2022.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New York“My mum is incredibly headstrong, eccentric, and difficult – she’s completely her own person,” Hubbard says. They completed daily domestic duties together there, and slowly began to pack up and empty out the apartment, so that Berger could move to a care facility.Some of the scenes are thrillingly theatrical: at one point, Hubbard created a stage for her mum with “a set of rotting 1960s mirror doors I found in the garage that I thought were stunning and built them on to stands, so she could roll them around.” Mirrors became an important feature in the images as “a way of never leaving my mum alone in the image, to project myself into the image. If I’m in the image there with her, it changes some of the authority and power dynamics of the camera”. The reflections give a feeling of transition and loss, an image about to disappear – they hold their images in the same space, the way the photograph does, but sometimes give the sense that they are missing each other. It’s a quiet confrontation with the pain of brain disease, of disappearing while being.Magnificent and bristling with tension, Berger often commands the image with authority in majestic light, framed by her grand and rambling home. “Something wonderful happened at some point where we both stopped thinking about the cameras, and we stopped seeing ourselves as an image – the cameras were just present, and the time to make photographs created interruptions into an otherwise brutal, demanding time that was not pleasant.”The camera allowed moments of levity and playfulness into their otherwise gruelling day to day life. “I could ask my mum to engage with me in a way I never would have if I hadn’t been making the photographs.”View image in fullscreen‘Like a performance in darkness’ … Katherine Hubbard, rear pressure slip, 2025.Photograph: © Courtesy of Katherine Hubbard, the artist; and Company Gallery, New YorkThat also included persuading her mother to strip off to make body prints together in the darkroom. “They were weird and hard to make,” Hubbard says. “We would go to the darkroom in the mornings when she had energy. We’d get naked and covered in Vaseline, and Then we’d use our bodies as a printing tool on to photo paper – like a performance in darkness, but it was very choreographed, a lot had to be around her safety getting her on to the floor and on to the paper, and back up again.”The main problem was that Berger “hates Vaseline – she found it suffocating. But when I’d ask her if she didn’t want to do it, she’d get offended and say ‘of course I’ll do it, are you stupid? You think I can’t do it just because I don’t like it!’”Hubbard emphasises that she doesn’t see Berger as a collaborator, and that consent is more complex to navigate with someone with dementia – “her willingness was important, and me being respectful and responsible of who I know her to be, and knowing what her limits are”.The 4x8 ft contact prints represent the physical entanglement of mother and daughters bodies, a private performance in the dark, the texture and movement of their bodies preserved on silver gelatin, while Berger’s inner world was being radically altered and transformed. Made without the intervention of a camera, Hubbard sees them as a “bridge to something more psychic, more energetic” between them than the more traditional representation in the portrait photographs. They convey a sense of freedom, letting go, and trying to hold on, all at once.‘She knows she will forget’: Grief, dementia and motherhood – in picturesRead moreMaking the photographs has affected their relationship in various ways, and at different times, throughout the last five years. Hubbard took over the management of 151, inheriting families of squirrels and raccoons living in the walls, broken pumps in the basement, and a host of other issues. “It was an insane time – I had a lot of anger towards my mum – I felt it was irresponsible not to prepare for old age.”The cameras have helped her come to terms with the anger, the frustration, the loss – and feel a kind of acceptance, and ultimately, love. In the photographs, Hubbard could still see Berger as she’d always been. “I wonder how early the disease really started, when her reality shifted, and I’ll never get the answers.”What does Berger think of the photographs? “She gets a huge amount of strength and sense of value from being part of it, and she trusts me completely. And she’s never had anything but unconditional love for me.”Katherine Hubbard – The Great Room is atStudio Voltaire, London from 7 October until 10 January 2027Explore more on these topicsPhotographyArtExhibitionsDementiaInstallationMemoryinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re broken | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: From a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasures
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: From a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasures
Content: Less of the lip … a fragment of a statue of 14th-century BC ruler Akhenaten.Photograph: © The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Art Resource/Scala, FirenzeView image in fullscreenLess of the lip … a fragment of a statue of 14th-century BC ruler Akhenaten.Photograph: © The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Art Resource/Scala, FirenzeExhibitions‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re brokenFrom a pharoah’s pouting and almost kissable lips to a Mussolini with a hole in the head, a new exhibition is exploring how some ancient fragments speak more profoundly than fully intact treasuresPhilip OltermannTue 29 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nose of Cleopatra VII was supposed to have been so beautiful that it changed the course of history: if it had been shorter, French philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote, “the whole face of the earth would have changed”. A visit to the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence, however, will leave you convinced that Cleo’s conk was only the second most stunning feature to ever grace the face of an Egyptian pharaoh. Among the more than 80 objects on display at an exhibition that opened last week is an astonishingly lifelike sculpture showing off the lips of Akhenaten, from the 14th century BC: a seagull shape resting on a pillow of lush flesh, at once both stern and sensuous, almost uncomfortably kissable.It was Thomas Aquinas who first came up with the theory that we perceive things to be beautiful when they are intact and whole, but the Akhenaten sculpture is so striking precisely because it has a major blemish. Like all the objects shown in Florence, it is only a fragment: a shard of polished limestone found in the dumps south of the Great Aten Temple in the city of el-Amarna, showing only the ruler’s nose and mouth.View image in fullscreenHeads up … fragments of sculptures that feature in the Broken show.Photograph: Roberto Serra/Iguana Press/Getty Images“One of the unique qualities of fragments is that they focus your attention on details,” says CD Dickerson, an expert in Renaissance and baroque art. “You wouldn’t have considered the subtle way that the lip has been crisply carved in this stone if it had been part of a bigger statue with a bunch of other features. Fragments make you think about objects in a different way.”Entitled Broken: The Power of Fragments, the show that Dickerson has co-curated for the Palazzo Strozzi and the National Gallery ofArtin Washington DC, explores why people throughout history have gone to great lengths to damage or destroy carefully crafted sculptures and statues. But along the way, it raises an even more intriguing question: why it is that some works of art have a more powerful emotional pull in a broken state than when whole?Many of the objects shown here speak of fault lines in history. There is a decapitated lifesize statue of a kneeling prior from Romainmôtier in Switzerland, likely beheaded during the iconoclastic frenzy of the Protestant Reformation. The dismembered left foot and right hand of King Louis XIV are all that remains of an equestrian monument to the French royal after the revolution rolled across Paris’s Place Vendôme and put up a guillotine instead. Modernist sculptor Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini was adorned with a simple bullet through the forehead after the fall of the fascist regime.The vandals were following an age-old tradition, says co-curator Andrew Sears. “Across the ancient world it was a common practice during regime changes or religious transformations to destroy images of the previous one because it was believed that the images contained some kind of life force of the ruler.”In some cases, these defaced sculptures would stay on as a deterrent. “They were made to be displayed in that way,” says Sears. A 19AD bust representing Germanicus, heir to Tiberius, had its nose expertly hacked off, upper earlobes cut and forehead adorned with a cross by Christians who protested against the deification of Roman emperors. The past, we are reassured, was a foreign country with cruel rituals.View image in fullscreenFallen fascist … Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini, 1923.Photograph: Collezione Carlo EleuteriBroken starts to get more surprising and interesting where it explores brokenness as more than a result of historical fractures. A section called Sculpting the Fragment opens with an intriguingdogūfigurine from ancient Japan. Little is known about these small, fired-clay statuettes with bulging coffee-bean eyes other than that they have been found in pieces all over burial sites in Japan.Current research indicates that the function ofdogūfigurines may have been akin to modern-day birthday pinatas: smashed to celebrate not just the end of the old but also the start of the new. “It’s very clear that the culture was to make these sculptures to intentionally break them, and for communities to share pieces with each other,” says Dickerson. “Our contemporary perception of ancient cultures being more violent is not always accurate.”Dickerson and Sears’ rummage through the darker corners of museum storage rooms has yielded little evidence of Aquinas’s equation of breakage with ugliness. Often, the opposite held true. From the early 15th-century Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, they present a statue of a reclining figure that was intentionally decapitated, as part of a campaign to rebuild a temple. Modelling their approach on the ruinous state of their surroundings, the Mexica seem to have understood completion to be unattainable. A broken artwork was proper because it revealed the true state of the world.View image in fullscreenThe Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed jeans … Michelangelo’s Model of a Nude Woman, from around 1533.Photograph: © Photo Giusti Claudio Firenze/Archivio Fotografico, Fondazione Casa BuonarrotiWe may think of the cult of ruined buildings and broken statues as an obsession of the Romantics, of the paintings of Caspar David Friedrich or the “colossal wreck” ofPercy Shelley’s Ozymandias. But Dickerson says ruin lust was already embedded in the art and literature of the Renaissance from the 13th century onwards. One of the most striking displays in Florence is a Michelangelo terracotta model of a headless and armless woman. Dated around 1533, it looks damaged but isn’t. Instead, it was the Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed grunge-wash jeans: recent technical analysis of the torso’s breakage points suggests Michelangelo deliberately sculpted a fragment, in homage to the awe-inspiring antiquities that were being excavated in Rome at the time.View image in fullscreenBroken bodies on the big screen … Charlize Theron (on knees) in 2015’s Mad Max: Fury Road.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyThe exhibition culminates with contemporary artistic takes on broken sculptures, such as a Louise Bourgeois foot in a leg brace and German artist Julius von Bismarck’s collapsable equestrian statue of his chancellor forebear, Otto. If that feels slightly self-restraining, it’s because the wholeness v brokenness divide is still everywhere in modern popular culture once you start looking for it. Here thefar-right social media accountswith immaculate classical busts as avatars, the impeccably smooth aesthetics of the iPhone, the flattened masks of the“clean girl” makeup trend; there the rise of broken bodies on the big screen, from Mad Max’s one-armed Furiosa to cleft-lipped lead actors like Tom Burke and Franz Rogowski and Game of Thrones’ “cripples, bastards and broken things”.Clearly, the answer to the question of whether there is a beauty in brokenness is not just one that captured ancient civilisations, but continues to be one of the central cultural dividing lines of our time.Broken: The Power of the Fragment is atPalazzo Strozzi, Florence, 25 September 2026 until 24 January, and at theNational Gallery of Art, Washington, from 13 March to 27 June 2027This article was amended on 29 September 2026. Akhenaten ruled Egypt in the 14th century BC, rather than the 14th century, as appeared in an earlier version.Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsSculptureArtStatuesMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It was a ghost town of three people. So how did Luckenbach rival Nashville as the heartland of country music? | Country | The Guardian
description: In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American life
Content: Hondo Crouch in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonView image in fullscreenHondo Crouch in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonCountryIt was a ghost town of three people. So how did Luckenbach rival Nashville as the heartland of country music?In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American lifeLauren SneadeTue 29 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 1973, the US country singer Jerry Jeff Walker was in the middle of nowhere, recording his soon-to-be-classic album ¡Viva Terlingua!. A crowd was packed to the rafters in an old dancehall 70 miles west of Austin, in Luckenbach,Texas. An extension lead ran from the hall to a recording truck outside. After everyone had gone home that night, Walker stood in the street and said to Hondo Crouch, Luckenbach’s self-appointed mayor: “I wonder what we just did.”View image in fullscreenJerry Jeff Walker, left, and Hondo Crouch, right, in Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonWhen Crouch had bought the town two years prior, its population was just three people – and according to the most recent census in 2021, it’s back at the same number. But in the 1970s, this ramshackle town thrived as Walker and his peers headed there, and Luckenbach became one of the most improbable yet important centres for country music.Hondo Crouch, who died 50 years ago this month, was a goat-rancher, writer and champion swimmer. A contradiction of white hair and a mischievous, boyish face he’d sing Mexicanrancheras– ranch songs – wherever he went. His business card read “Imagineer, authorised distributor”. In 1971, he clubbed together with two friends to buy Luckenbach, which had become a ghost town since its creation in the late 1800s and its population high in 1904. They paid $30,000 for an old dancehall, general store, bar and a few outhouses. With Crouch as the town’s self-appointed mayor, the Luckenbach Dance Hall became a gathering place for outlaw country musicians; a freer, rural alternative to Nashville.Country star Gary P Nunn remembers him as a “pied piper”, leading musicians and eccentrics to a simpler life. In Walker’s case, Crouch’s daughter Becky Patterson met him at an open-mic night, and brought him back to the family ranch. “He had on these little Coke bottle blue glasses,” Patterson remembers, “and Hondo said, ‘I knew he was a musician because he asked for seconds and ate so much. He was starving!’”View image in fullscreenHondo Crouch, left, and Gary P Nunn.Photograph: Becky PattersonAt the time, Nashville’s country industry was chasing the urbane, pop-friendly sound of countrypolitan, heard in stars like Patsy Cline and Charlie Rich. Musicians like Walker andWillie Nelsonwere tired of being told to clean the rust out of their music, and wanted their steel guitars and fiddles back. Going up into the country, they found Luckenbach, Texas.Away from the eye of studio producers, ¡Viva Terlingua! sounded like the communal, unpolished life it celebrated. Gary P Nunn’s song London Homesick Blues appears on the record and Nunn spent that summer in Luckenbach sleeping in a teepee with his wife and baby. “My wife didn’t think much of it, everyone else was staying in hotels,” he chuckles. “But Jerry Jeff used to say you can’t get that magic in the studio.”The atmosphere in the dancehall is palpable: you can hear crickets during the lulls between the crowd’s stamping and hooting. Two years later, ¡Viva Terlingua! even reached space when the song Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother was played to wake the Apollo–Soyuz astronauts in July 1975.Rolling Stone covered the ¡Viva Terlingua! sessions, which drew hippies from across the country. By the mid-70s, the life expectancy of Luckenbach road signs was reportedly about four hours; visitors stole them so frequently that the highway department stopped replacing them.View image in fullscreenInterior of rustic bar in Luckenbach, Texas, US.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesBut a haunt for hippies and country fans was catapulted to even greater renown when in 1977, Waylon Jennings released Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love). Guy Clark, who had been involved in ¡Viva Terlingua!, had told Nashville songwriters Bobby Emmons and Chips Moman about Crouch. They wrote the song the next morning. Willie Nelson joined Waylon on the final chorus and the song hankers after leaving metropolitan riches for a simpler life in Luckenbach: “Baby, let’s sell your diamond ring / buy some boots and faded jeans, and go away.”That yearning for rural life resonated so much that the song spent six weeks at No 1 on the country chart, then crossed over to pop radio. “It was like the whole world were like, where’s this Luckenbach, Texas?”, Nunn says. Folk came by the busload to get back to basics. Willie Nelson famously lost a game of dominoes against the town’s elderly champions, and returned in 1995 to host his Fourth of July Picnic festival in Luckenbach for five years running.There is a “picking tree” at Luckenbach, where country musicians have passed guitars around since Crouch’s day. Contemporary star and Yellowstone actor Ryan Bingham honed his trade there and organised an annual festival, The Western, in the hall. Kit Patterson, Crouch’s grandson, remembers Bingham and other musicians sitting round the picker circle. “It was this beautiful, intimate moment around the fire, reliving life before all the fame.”Crouch’s family still runs Luckenbach through Luckenbach Texas, Inc. Protecting its name has meant taking legal action, including against a whisky brand trying to piggyback on the town’s cultural capital. “Lawsuits are the antithesis of what Luckenbach is about,” says Kit, the company’s president. “But at the same time, if the integrity of what Luckenbach is isn’t protected, it becomes diluted.”View image in fullscreenHondo Crouch, self-appointed mayor, Luckenbach, Texas.Photograph: Becky PattersonCrouch preached a kind of backyard mysticism – a characteristically American devotion to ordinary things. In surviving footage filmed outside the hall he twinkles at the camera, “I love this town. I love every rotten board in it.” He liked to say Luckenbach had a bigger moon than any other town, and he says as much on Walker’s 1977 album A Man Must Carry On, also recorded in Luckenbach. On Luckenbach Moon, Crouch crows his poem over a stumbling guitar line.double quotation markWe try to tell folks who come by here to look at our townWhat a big, mean moon we haveBut nobody’ll believe it.Elsewhere on the record, poet Charles John Quarto remembers Crouch as “like some song you can’t unlearn” and Walker sings My Buddy: “I miss the way your eyes saw things upon the land … the grey days I miss you most of all.”‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generationRead moreCrouch never heard A Man Must Carry On or Waylon Jennings’s hit. He died suddenly of a heart attack on 27 September 1976. When Patterson phoned Walker to tell him her father had died, he dropped the receiver and never came back to the call. The church overflowed at Crouch’s funeral. Willie Nelson arrived but didn’t get out of his truck, unwilling to draw attention from Crouch.I asked his youngest daughter, Cris Crouch Graham, whether the moon really was bigger in Luckenbach. She laughed. “The moon’s the same moon as everywhere else. But he made it bigger, and so it is.”Explore more on these topicsCountryTexasWillie NelsonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No island of strangers: why I’m using art to unite a fractured nation | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Fear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmares
Author: Ekow Eshun
Headline: Fear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmares
Content: Like extras from an Ealing comedy … Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts.Photograph: Jack Elliot Edwards/©  the artist. Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre London.View image in fullscreenLike extras from an Ealing comedy … Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts.Photograph: Jack Elliot Edwards/©  the artist. Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre London.Art and designNo island of strangers: why I’m using art to unite a fractured nationFear of outsiders is the defining issue of our times. But is it actually our own selves we’re scared of? And could art hold the answers? Here, the British Art Show’s curator reveals why he’s exploring our deepest dreams and nightmaresEkow EshunTue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the moral low points of Keir Starmer’s tenure at Downing Street was his “island of strangers” speech, with its rhetorical echoes of Enoch Powell and dispiriting description of a nation fractured by difference. After widespread criticism, Starmer recanted his words, if not the sentiment behind them. Yet his choice of language was a reminder of how the idea of the stranger – representing immigration, but also wider, more inchoate anxieties about otherness and difference – holds such a potent place in Britain today.In fact, from masked anti-migrant protesters on the south coast to xenophobic riots over the summer, from politicians vowing to stop the boats to immigration polling as the No 1 concern among UK voters, it’s probably true to say that fear of the stranger is the totemic issue of our times.Not long after Starmer’s speech, I was appointed curator of the BritishArtShow, which opens in Coventry this week. My thoughts have turned increasingly to the notion of the stranger among us as I’ve worked on the exhibition. The show, developed and produced by Hayward Gallery Touring, is the largest and most significant recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the UK.Founded in 1979, the exhibition takes place every five years, touring across the country to offer a snapshot of the ideas and ambitions of a rising generation of artists born or based in Britain. Previous versions have brought the likes of David Hockney, Bridget Riley and Anish Kapoor to national audiences.This year is the 10th edition and it features a lineup of critically lauded artists including Alvaro Barrington, Lindsey Mendick and recent Turner prize winners Jesse Darling and Jasleen Kaur.Each new iteration prompts the same question: what does the show say about British art? Or, indeed, about Britain? In the context of the globe-spanning fairs, biennales and mega-galleries that make up today’s contemporary art world, the question is possibly antique. Yet an exhibition tasked with addressing recent developments in art will inevitably reveal something about the country in which that work originates. To talk about British art, then, is also to talk about place and belonging. It is to ask who we are as individuals, as communities and as a nation.I’ve chosen to give the latest exhibition a subtitle: A Chorus of Strangers. The name is not a reference to Starmer’s speech, but it does gesture back to another much earlier period in British history also characterised by its antipathy to outsiders.View image in fullscreenMaking the Strangers’ Case … an 1897 depiction of Thomas More pleading for compassion at the 1517 May Day riots.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesOn 30 April 1517, the eve of the annual May Day festival, an angry crowd of more than 1,000 people marched through London protesting at the city’s immigrant population. Xenophobia was rife in Tudor England. Although foreigners, known as “strangers”, made up just 6% of the city’s population, they were often considered a malign presence: “Libertynes, drunkards, murderers, thieves and Conspirators,” in the words of one chronicler.As darkness fell, the mood turned ugly. Thomas More, under-sheriff of London, appealed to the crowd to turn back. But his entreaties went unheard. The mob surged through the streets sacking the shops and houses of French, Italian and Flemish merchants and craftsmen. Only after an army was called out, leading to scores of arrests and over a dozen executions, was order returned.Evil May Day, as the riot came to be known, was not quickly forgotten.In 1591 a new play,Sir Thomas More, told the story of More’s rise and fall, from civic leader to Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII and his subsequent beheading for refusing to accept the king as head of the Church of England. The drama was written collaboratively by several authors. Most prominent among them was William Shakespeare, who revisited More’s encounter with the London mob. In Shakespeare’s telling, More successfully calms the crowd by making “the Strangers’ Case”, a passionate call for empathy in place of the “mountainish inhumanity” of hatred and bigotry.Shakespeare’s scene still feels powerfully relevant. Not just due to the similarity between mob violence then and now, but because the Strangers’ Case is a reminder of how, for hundreds of years, artists have faced times of discord by asserting the value of our shared humanity. With that past in mind, the British Art Show asks: how does art today meet the fears of otherness and difference that emerge in a period of uncertainty and change?View image in fullscreenUnited in protest … Joy Gerrard, March for Palestine, Berlin, 2024.Photograph: courtesy of the artist and Cristea Roberts GalleryLet’s reflect for a moment that the idea of the stranger describes a psychological as well as a social condition. Yes, the stranger denotes a feared outsider. But as the philosopher Julia Kristeva says, we are often “strangers to ourselves”, caught within the mysteries of our psyche. The stranger might be a repressed feeling or a memory that we struggle to acknowledge, its presence curdling our view of the world, turning others into projections of our own anxieties.More and more, it feels as though, when we’re talking about the former, the stranger as outsider, what we’re actually referring to is the latter, the stranger as other, a feeling of unease and disequilibrium; a sense that the times are out of joint, and that instead of all the promises of wealth and ease that the future was supposed to bring, we find ourselves unmoored and lost. As the philosopher Marshall Berman wrote in All That Is Solid Melts into Air: The Experience of Modernity: “To be modern is to find ourselves in an environment that promises us adventure, power, joy, growth, transformation of ourselves and the world – and, at the same time, that threatens to destroy everything we have, everything we know, everything we are.”You can hear echoes of that dread in public polling – seven in 10 people fear the UK is “on the wrong track”, according toMore in Common’s 2025 Shattered Britainreport – and in the despairing labels given by theorists to our current era, such as the New Dark Age and the Age of Unhingement.Yet in uncertain times art can be a beacon. When we enter an exhibition, we leave behind the reductive thinking that only wants to see the world in terms of us versus them. We cross into a realm of complexity, contradiction and creative richness. We take on the point of view of an outsider, seeing the world anew with the eyes of a stranger. “When you are a stranger, you are both in and out. You are there but not really,” writes Ece Temelkuran in Nation of Strangers: Rebuilding Home in the 21st Century. The term stranger signifies “a pure form of curiosity”. It describes “those who are still not poisoned by the fear of the alien”. All those “to whom our time seems too strange to become complicit in its monstrosities”.This sense of openness and discovery is shared by many of the artists in the British Art Show. For example, Accounts, a sculpture by Alex Margo Arden, ties together decommissioned male mannequins from the National Motor Museum with a thick length of rope. The work might gesture to deindustrialisation or exhausted ideas of masculinity.View image in fullscreenVoices raised … a still from Julianknxx’s Shifting/ Spirit/Time.Photograph: © StudioknxxBut it’s hard to look at the men’s florid faces and side-parted hair, like bumptious extras from an Ealing comedy, and not also find something absurd and comic on show. This playfulness reflects Arden’s delight in the small, idiosyncratic private museums dotted around Britain: a favourite of hers is the Museum of Victorian Science in North Yorkshire which it boasts is“Ranked Number 1 Visitor Attraction in the Whitby Area!”. These venues collectively offer a folk history of Britain, based less on fact than storytelling, imagination and what Arden calls the “memories of memories”.Mahtab Hussain’s film Here Is the Brick, made with writer Guy Gunaratne, tells a story of south Asian and Muslim life in Britain over the past half century through a feverish montage of anti-Muslim football chants, family VHS recordings, speeches by Islamophobic politicians, excerpts from old racist TV programmes, and coverage of the 2005 London suicide bombings. The title refers to a brick thrown through the window of an Asian-owned shop that struck the storekeeper in the face, breaking his teeth. Yet the film ends on an optimistic note with a stadium full of Liverpool fans singing in praise of Mo Salah: “If he scores another few, I’ll be a Muslim too.”Other artists explore how we might claim a sense of agency within the disempowering structures of the modern world. In films by Melanie Manchot and Julianknxx, and in Joy Gerrard’s ink drawings of protesting crowds, there is dancing, singing, bodies surging on to the streets: a rejection of a status quo that is so often based on the subjection of the individual to the forces of capital; and an insistence instead on the value of gathering, of raising voices and moving or marching together.Rather than an island separated by difference then, A Chorus of Strangers offers a hymn to possibility. Through the work of the participating artists, the exhibition finds abundant evidence that life might be richer, more wonderfully strange and strangely wonderful if, instead of heeding calls to division, we choose to look at the world through the eyes of others.British Art Show 10is at the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum, Mead Gallery and Coventry University, 2 October to 10 January; then touring to Swansea, Bristol, Sheffield and Newcastle GatesheadExplore more on these topicsArt and designBritish identity and societyExhibitionsSculptureInstallationArtDrawingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peak | Prince | The Guardian
description: As a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his genius
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his genius
Content: Prince in 1987.Photograph: Crollalanza/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPrince in 1987.Photograph: Crollalanza/Rex/ShutterstockPrince‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peakAs a new book on the Paisley Park polymath is released, author John McKie explains why Prince’s 1987 album is the ultimate showcase of his geniusEthan BeckTue 29 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the early 1980s,Princehad cemented his place as a pop heavyweight with the phenomenal success of his 1999 album, as well as becoming a movie star thanks to Purple Rain. Even when his second film, the old Hollywood throwback Under the Cherry Moon, bombed worldwide in 1986, he notched another massive hit off its soundtrack with Kiss. It didn’t matter if audiences didn’t understand; Prince kept moving forward.That restless spirit propelled Prince’s final masterpiece, 1987’s Sign o’ the Times, as he dabbled with different directions. Anything seemed on the table: maybe he would drop another album with his backing band, The Revolution, or he would explore his feminine alter-ego Camille with a self-titled album. He even, at one point, wanted to put out a triple album, a reasonable response to the vast collection of music that Prince was creating. “Sometimes when people are in a place of transition, they’re distracted,” said John McKie, whose new bookPrince: A Sign o’ the Timesfollows the pop legend’s career through the lens of this classic. “For Prince, he focused on his music.”‘He’d gaze at the stars and go: I’m gonna be up there one day’: Prince by those who knew him best, 10 years after his deathRead moreHis record label pushed back on the triple album, so insteadPrinceput out the kaleidoscopic Sign o’ the Times – which clocked in at 80 minutes across two LPs – and eventually decided against touring the album in the United States. The Purple One’s imperial period can be difficult to nail down, as he rarely gave interviews or even kept collaborators up to date about what he had planned. Even as McKie interviewed more than 100 people about the gestation behind Sign o’ the Times, it wasn’t always easy to understand the headspace Prince was in when he fired his band the Revolution and split up with his fiancee, Susannah Melvoin. “Prince probably would have been a very good poker player because he didn’t give that much away,” said McKie. “If you listen to his music, there are lots of clues. He said it himself: ‘If you want to know me, listen to my music.’”Sign o’ the Times, which turns 40 in March, remains a genre-defying monument in Prince’s discography with a thick layer of funk at the center. It’s the LP where Prince happily dipped into Christian rock with The Cross, built Starfish and Coffee around a jazz chord progression, and casually shared the best power pop song of all time with I Could Never Take the Place of Your Man. But it’s also one of Prince’s most thematically disparate projects: “I want to do it baby all the time,” he sings libidinously, only a few songs before heralding the return of Christ. Few people, it seemed, were as good at compartmentalizing as Prince. “He would be dating two very different women at the same time,” McKie said. “He would record two very different songs on the same day.”Prince’s 50 greatest singles – ranked!Read moreThe first hit from Sign o’ the Times was the title track, where Prince seems to be reciting from the newspaper, touching upon gang violence, the HIV/Aids epidemic, and the possibility of nuclear war, all over an uneasy groove built almost entirely with the Fairlight CMI sampler and synthesizer. He had heardPeter GabrielandKate Bushuse the instrument and wanted in on the fun. Elsewhere, the Linn LM-1 drum machine dictated much of the album’s blocky percussion – Prince reportedly described the party-starting Housequake as having the greatest-sounding kick drum of all time – while he slipped into Camille territory with a zany, high-pitched delivery on a handful of songs. One of them, If I Was Your Girlfriend, McKie believes is in the running for the best song that Prince ever wrote. The dizzying textures seemed designed to confirm that Prince contained multitudes.“Keith Richardsonce said ofMick Jagger, he once described him as a nice bunch of guys – I don’t think it was entirely complimentary,” said McKie. “One of the things that you take from Sign o’ the Times is it’s a nice bunch of Princes.”View image in fullscreenPrince in 1987’s Sign o’ the Times concert film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyPart of Prince wanted to settle down. Nowhere is that clearer than on the tender Forever in My Life. But he also dated voraciously, even before he broke things off with Melvoin, who also spent a brief spell as a vocalist in the Revolution. Their romance guided the omnivorous feelings of Sign o’ the Times, especially on the all-timer slow jam Adore and the hot-and-cold Strange Relationship. “I believe the phrase ‘The one that got away’ could apply here,” said McKie. “Lots of people that loved Prince loved Susannah, and lots of people that loved Prince that I spoke to were quite explicit in saying they wished he’d married her.”Prince had a reputation for being demanding – or difficult, if you are less charitable. Disputes over songwriting credits and payments for his backing band take up a chunk of McKie’s book, while one tour manager describes him as “a very autocratic ruler”. And while his rivalry withMichael Jacksonhas always received ample attention, it seemed that Prince didn’t know how to deal with his contemporaries: his stock answer for meeting someone new was saying: “I know who you are.” At one point, Prince even bristled at collaborating withMiles Davisbecause he couldn’t control what the jazz giant played. (The trumpeter joined Prince onstage at Paisley Park on New Year’s Eve in 1987, only a few months after Sign o’ the Times arrived in stores.) The penultimate track, It’s Gonna Be a Beautiful Night, with its call-and-response grooves, made McKie think of “Prince as a jazz band leader brought up to the modern age.”On this double album, Prince applied a dash of Davis’s spirit, especially when he faced issues in the studio. His hardworking but fast-moving attitude is clearest on a song like The Ballad of Dorothy Parker, where the song’s high frequencies are muted because engineer Susan Rogers made a mistake with a new mixing console. It wasn’t fixed, as Prince believed that many errors were meant to be. Those coincidences reminded McKie of how Davis worked with his bandmates: “He was looking for something different, and sometimes he was known to say ‘play it again’ if someone played a wrong note,” McKie recalled. “Prince was smart enough to acknowledge so-called mistakes and turn them into something.”Prince: A Sign o’ the Times is out now in the UK via Blink Publishing and will be released 13 October in the US by Division BooksExplore more on these topicsPrincePop and rockBiography booksElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: JMW Turner’s ‘great love letter’ to Rome makes brief return to city before UK auction | JMW Turner | The Guardian
description: Rome, From Mount Aventine will also visit Hong Kong and New York before it is expected to sell for record price
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Rome, From Mount Aventine will also visit Hong Kong and New York before it is expected to sell for record price
Content: JMW Turner’s Rome, from Mount Aventine is still on its original canvas and in its original frame.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APView image in fullscreenJMW Turner’s Rome, from Mount Aventine is still on its original canvas and in its original frame.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APJMW TurnerJMW Turner’s ‘great love letter’ to Rome makes brief return to city before UK auctionRome, From Mount Aventine will also visit Hong Kong and New York before it is expected to sell for record priceAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 29 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAJMW Turnerpainting of Rome that has been described as his “great love letter” to the city and has fleetingly returned there after almost 200 years is expected to set a new record when it goes up for sale in December.One of the few works by Turner that remains in private ownership, Rome, From Mount Aventine will be on display at Palazzo Rondinini in central Rome from Tuesday to Thursday.The painting will then be shown in Hong Kong and New York before being transported back to London where it is expected to fetch £50m when auctioned by Sotheby’s on 9 December.The masterpiece was last bought in 2014 when a private collectorpaid £30.3m, making it the most expensive painting by the artist ever sold to date.The golden-hued work, which depicts Rome’s Tiber River as seen from the Aventine Hill, is still on its original canvas and in its original frame. Furthermore, it has never been relined or restored, with marks made by Turner’s palette knife and brushes still visible, as well as his fingerprints from when he would have picked the canvas up to move it around his studio.“Because it’s unlined, the surface of the picture is extraordinarily well preserved,” Julian Gascoigne, a senior specialist at Sotheby’s London, told reporters in Rome. “You can see all the delicate glazes of translucent paint that he’s built up over successive painting sessions that give the picture this extraordinary sense of light and depth and glow. You can see the teeth of the brush and the scrape of the palette knife in a way that is not really seen in almost any other work by the artist.”View image in fullscreenJulian Gascoigne (left) and Mario Tavella of Sotheby’s at a press conference in Rome.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersThe painting has exchanged hands only twice since it was commissioned by Hugh Andrew Johnstone Munro of Novar, an amateur British artist who accompanied Turner on his sketching tours, in the late 1820s.Turner began the work in Rome and completed it in London, where it was displayed for the first time at the Royal Academy to mixed reviews in 1836.The painting remained in Munro’s estate until 1878, when it was bought by Archibald Primrose, the 5th Earl of Rosebery and a prominent 19th-century British prime minister, as a wedding gift for his bride, Hannah de Rothschild.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTurner first visited Rome in 1819 and then again in the late 1820s, when he was part of a thriving community of artists, sculptors, writers and poets based in the area of the Spanish Steps.Turner, who died in 1851, produced several paintings of the city. “However, this is the only painting by the artist of Rome as it looked during his time,” Gascoigne said. “Every other painting he did of Rome was an evocation of a bygone age. But this is the only portrait of the city. In many ways, it’s his great love letter to the city that inspired him throughout his life.”Mario Tavella, the chair of Sotheby’sEurope, said he hoped the painting would be bought by a public museum “where it could be admired by everyone”.Explore more on these topicsJMW TurnerPaintingArtItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one night | Gisèle Pelicot | The Guardian
description: Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall
Content: ‘Act of witnessing’: the play is based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Act of witnessing’: the play is based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAGisèle Pelicot‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one nightFour-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County HallHelena HortonTue 29 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA play based on the trial of the men who drugged and rapedGisèle Pelicotwill come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast.The four-hour production ofThe Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicothas been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution.“I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.”Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks.Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once. That allows you to call up the best of people who are available for a short commitment. I really can’t wait to announce the company. It is, I think, 27 actors all in all.”The play was created byMilo Rauand Servane Dècle. The Swiss director and playwright Rau is known for adapting court cases for the stage, including the Moscow trial of the Russian punks Pussy Riot and the trial of the Romanian despot Nicolae Ceaușescu.Pelicot became internationally recognised after she waived her right to anonymity to ensure a public trial of her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, who, for almost a decade from 2011,drugged her unconscious and invited dozens of men from an internet forum to rape her. Her husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison in December 2024 and guilty verdicts were returned for all 51 accused men. She wanted the story to be public, saying “shame must change sides”.“We do it one time only in each city,” said Rau. “It is more of a political act really, than a play.”“It is a harsh watch,” said Dècle, “but people stay for the whole time. We let them come in and out if they want, but very few do. Even Gisèle Pelicot herself came to watch in New York. That was amazing. She said, ‘The actress was doing better than I did on trial.’”Journalists covering the trial gave Rau and Dècle thousands of pages of their notebooks, and the play is based on what was said in court.“Everyone wanted to share with us,” said Rau. “It became a trial of our society, of the patriarchy. And we have toured it in at least 15 different countries, in different languages, some I barely understand myself, and the audience still understands the play. Sadly it is a universal experience. It would be better for humanity if this was just a French experience.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you,” said Fall.The large majority of the audience has been female, Dècle said. “I wish more men would see it. The very interesting thing about this whole affair is you can really dive into who these male perpetrators were.”Fall said: “Pelicot represents so much for everybody, especially women; resilience and courage and a radical joy for me that she triumphed and lives on. She’s in love and lives her life. That is two fingers up to the patriarchy and I think that is really empowering for us women. This piece and her story is not just about the specifics about her story and sexual assault.”She agreed to the play, the writers said, because she wanted to keep the conversation that was started by her trial going. “We always say she opened the door, and we just keep it open,” said Rau.Explore more on these topicsGisèle PelicotFranceGisèle Pelicot rape trialTheatreMilo RauPolitical theatreEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there’: Damien Frost’s immaculate queer portraits | Photography | The Guardian
description: The photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat field
Author: Oliver Giles
Headline: The photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat field
Content: Beverly Fabulosity, pictured on her farm in Gungal, New South Wales.Photograph: Damien FrostView image in fullscreenBeverly Fabulosity, pictured on her farm in Gungal, New South Wales.Photograph: Damien FrostPhotography‘You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there’: Damien Frost’s immaculate queer portraitsThe photographer’s photos are so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio – not behind a London nightclub or in an Australian goat fieldWords byOliver Giles. Pictures by Damien FrostMon 28 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.45 EDTShareOne bright spring day, the photographer Damien Frost arrived at a farm in Gungal, outside Muswellbrook, New South Wales. Goats grazed in a paddock, eucalyptus trees stretched into the brilliant blue sky and a tin shed weathered in the sun. Frost walked into the shed and entered another world.“It’s a drag studio,” says Frost. Lining the walls were dozens of wigs and rails of flamboyant outfits belonging to Beverly Fabulosity. “I’ve never seen anything like it. It was a very Priscillascenario.”Frost grew up in Australia and is now based in London, where for more than a decade he has photographed drag queens and club kids for his acclaimed Night Flowers series. Since late August, he has been back in his home country, commissioned by Newcastle’sNew Annual festivalto photograph night owls in and around the city. These new portraits are being exhibited alongside a selection from Frost’s archive at Watt Space gallery as part of the festival.View image in fullscreenLuke Harris, Blacks Club, Soho.View image in fullscreenJulius Reuben, Soho, 2017.View image in fullscreenMarco Tullio Siviglia, Berlin, 2019.View image in fullscreenOtamere wearing Muriel Nisse, Hackney, 2018.Photograph: Damien FrostThe exhibition is a full-circle moment for Frost, who studied at the University of Newcastle after growing up in Sydney. Returning to Australia has inspired a change in his approach: in London, he meets and photographs his subjects in or around clubs, although his portraits appear so meticulously staged that viewers often assume they were taken in a studio. “Coming back to my home country, I wanted to show a little bit of the environment these people are working in,” he says.The locations are a far cry from nightclubs or the catwalks of RuPaul’sDragRace. One person posed near the city’s port against a backdrop of coal trains. Others appear in their homes, on suburban streets, in the Stockton sand dunes. Beverly Fabulosity is pictured in a field wearing a white gown and a towering wig, goats milling around her. “You’ve got to be pretty tough to be a drag queen out there,” says Frost.View image in fullscreenMolly Poppinz at home in lounge room, Lambton, NSW.View image in fullscreenFinlay Ross in the staff room at Creator Incubator, Newcastle, NSW.Photograph: Damien FrostView image in fullscreenBenjamin Frazer McKenzie and ZEAL.H at Stockton sand dunes, NSW.Whether he photographs people on a farm or at a warehouse party, Frost is most interested in how people use fashion, makeup and prosthetics to explore their identity. “I’m not looking for people in fancy dress, I’m looking for people who are expressing something,” he says. Sometimes, this goes beyond experiments with glamour, style or gender. “A lot of the photos I take, the characters can be quite grotesque,” says Frost. “Often, it’s people dressing up as a manifestation of how they feel they’ve been treated … they’re made to feel like a monster, so they reclaim that.”Some of his subjects work for months on a single look they only wear once. “I liken it to Buddhist sand sculptures, where they spend hours and hours on an intricate pattern and just wipe it all off at the end,” says Frost. His photographs immortalise these creations and showcase them to people who might never otherwise encounter them.View image in fullscreenLouisa Magrics in Carrington, NSW.View image in fullscreenJenna Pippin at Wangi Wangi power station, NSW.Looking through his archive, Frost can trace changes in drag culture. Economic pressures have led to the closure ofmore than half the LGBTQ+ venuesin London. On top of that, “not just in drag, but even in artistic practices, social media’s algorithms now influence the direction that people go with their work”, says Frost. This leads to “a lot of people who turn [themselves] into a brand … which they then don’t want to deviate from”.More radical forms of self-expression are still out there, though: “You just have to look a bit harder for them.”Night Flowers: Damien Frostis at Watt Space gallery until 7 November as part of the New Annual festival in Newcastle, NSW

title: Stations by Louise Kennedy review – a superb follow-up to Trespasses | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphones
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: This tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphones
Content: A London pub in 1982.Photograph: Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA London pub in 1982.Photograph: Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild/Getty ImagesBook of the dayFictionReviewStations by Louise Kennedy review – a superb follow-up to TrespassesThis tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphonesClare ClarkTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouise Kennedy’s first novel,Trespasses, was one of those rare triumphs, a debut that was not only rapturously received by critics but adored by readers around the world. A story of forbidden love set during the Troubles in 1970s Belfast, it was an international bestseller, translated into more than 20 languages. It was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize and scooped debut fiction of the year at the British Book awards. A four-part television adaptation with Gillian Anderson aired last autumn on Channel 4.Inevitably Kennedy found herself lauded as an overnight success – much was made of her 30-year career as a professional chef – but in fact she had been writing short stories for a decade and to considerable acclaim; her first collection, The End of the World Is a Cul de Sac, was published in 2021. Included in that book was Belladonna, the story of Róisín, a young girl from Belfast who moves south with her mother and, ostracised by her new classmates, becomes friendly with the couple who live across the road. Like Briony Tallis in Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the prickly and precociously bright Róisín misinterprets the dynamic of her neighbours’ marriage to disastrous effect.It is a sucker-punch of a story, conjuring in a few restrained pages the violent insecurity and self-absorption of early adolescence. What a joy, then, to rediscover Róisín in the opening pages of Stations, Kennedy’s blisteringly good second novel. It is 1982 and Róisín, still very much the outsider from the north, strikes up a fierce and unexpected friendship with Red, a boy with a reputation for trouble who is “spoken about in giddy whispers at school”. Róisín’s father, a drinker, has moved with his new wife to London. Red’s family is dysfunctional in ways Róisín only vaguely understands, but which come to a head when Red finds himself on the wrong side of the law. Unable to stay, Red bolts to London. It is a year before Róisín, visiting her father for Christmas, finds herself caught up with him once again, the pull he exerts on her impossible to resist.The novel traces the warp and weft of their relationship over the next 25 years. Structured like a sporadically kept diary, clusters of dated entries disrupted by long gaps, it has echoes of David Nicholls’s One Day; but Kennedy’s London is altogether grimmer and more brutal, a city of squats and gas heaters and not enough change for the payphone. Her people are also more damaged, an Irish diaspora fractured by displacement, scarred not only by poverty and violence and addiction but by shame and loss. “Can you not feel it?” Red asks Róisín when, walking through London, they pass the site of the old Millbank prison. “All those wretched lives layered up underneath us.” Kennedy’s émigrés flee the old country, they build new lives, construct new families, but they carry the weight of the past always with them. However far they travel, they can never escape from themselves.double quotation markStations evokes 1980s London with almost hallucinogenic precisionKennedy moved to London herself as a young woman and evokes the 1980s city with almost hallucinogenic precision, but her greater power lies in her remarkable humanity. Her characters are messy, flawed, often shatteringly self-destructive but, mapped with her fierce compassion, they march straight off the page. As a teenager Róisín is bolshy and obstreperous; she is also funny and filthy and generous and agonisingly vulnerable. As she gets older, she gets better – sometimes – at managing herself but she never really changes. The way Kennedy conjures her, we do not want her to.Stations is at its heart a love story, a furious, tender, potty-mouthed paean to loyalty and generosity of spirit. It is also an elegy to a generation of lost Irish boys, a heartbreaking testament to the violence and fear passed down from father to son. In its title, Stations acknowledges the transience of the diasporic experience, the trains and boats and coaches, but, steeped as the book is in an in-the-bone Catholicism (one particularly powerful scene has Róisín unable to bring herself to shake Red’s father’s hand at Mass), it carries too the idea of the Stations of the Cross, the 14 images of Jesus on the day of his Crucifixion.In Trespasses, the teacher Cushla, studying the Stations during the Easter Sunday sermon, reckons Jesus “a ringer for James Taylor”. In Stations, it is tempting to see the elusive and charismatic Red, “loping along in [Róisín’s] father’s coat like an itinerant preacher”, as a Christ figure, offering a kind of redemption through his suffering. Can cycles of anguish or neglect ever be broken? Is love in all its frustrating insufficiency enough to save us? Kennedy’s novel is too subtle and clear-eyed to offer easy answers, but her questions will burn themselves into your heart.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world order  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach
Author: Houman Barekat
Headline: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach
Content: An anti-Iraq war march in London, 2003.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenAn anti-Iraq war march in London, 2003.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverPolitics booksReviewThe Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world orderA journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreachHouman BarekatTue 29 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military supremacy; a rules-based global order. As Jones recounts in his new book, these certainties would come crashing down over the next quarter of a century amid a succession of economic failures, foreign policy disasters and political crises.Indeed, “the west” itself – as a shorthand for the US plus the wealthier western European nations – feels almost quaint today, given the increasing unilateralism of the administration in Washington. But in the 2000s it was part of the lexicon, as if the hemisphere were a political actor in its own right. Revisiting the US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, we are reminded not just of their horrific death tolls (totalling half a million, by conservative estimates) but also their total strategic failure; the 2021 evacuation of Kabul airport, Jones writes, was “among the starkest images of American decline yet broadcast to the world”.In addition to destabilising the region, these interventions weakened the foundations of the international legal system. As Jones points out, a precedent was set when Nato bombed Yugoslavia without UN security council authorisation in 1999; the 2003 invasion of Iraq, also without authorisation, further undermined the UN. So when Vladimir Putin subsequently invaded Ukraine on his own dubious pretext, western objections could be dismissed as hypocrisy. Perhaps the most ignominious example of western indifference to the international rule of law was Keir Starmer’s limp assertion that Israel had the “right” to cut off water and electricity to 2 million civilians in Gaza – a war crime – in retaliation for Hamas’s attacks on 7 October 2023.Alongside these geopolitical catastrophes, Jones tells a story of domestic decline, of western economies built on chronic insecurity and precarious employment. In the 2000s, Thatcherite policies pursued by New Labour fleeced the public: “Essential services [were] turned into assets designed to generate returns. Passengers paid more for overcrowded trains. Rivers and seas were fouled while water companies loaded themselves with debt and paid out dividends.” Then came the 2008 financial crisis and the bankers’ bailout, paid for by austerity. In Britain and elsewhere, Jones notes a “correlation between the inability of centrist governments to tackle economic decline in any meaningful way, and the rise of the far right”.double quotation markFor decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideologyThe book is interspersed with snippets of interviews with an assortment of eyewitnesses, journalists, scholars and activists. They include the director of Iraq national museum in Baghdad, a former Lehman Brothers employee, a former head of the Afghan Red Crescent, the Greek economist Yanis Varoufakis, and the conservative commentator Andrew Sullivan, a repentant cheerleader for the Iraq war, who admits: “I was wrong on the major issues, on the morality of it and the practicality of it and the reason for it.”Much of this terrain – Bush and Blair’s wars, the financial crash, the populist surge – has been extensively covered. The average well-informed reader will learn nothing new, but it is bracing to see what was once the news cycle take its place in the sweep of history, and Jones’s focus on free-market fundamentalism provides a compelling through-line. He suggests the second Trump administration, in all its cynical venality, is “the logical endpoint” of that philosophy. And he reminds us that the aggressive privatisation of the Russian economy in the 1990s brought terrible economic hardship which ultimately fuelled Putin’s revanchist nationalism.For decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideology: the prerogatives of the private sector must override the collective interest, and anything less is tantamount to Stalinism. This remains orthodoxy, but the rise to prominence of Zohran Mamdani, the avowedly socialist mayor of New York, offers a glimmer of hope to those who, like Jones, would prefer a society built on “common provision, democratic power, mutual obligation and the recognition that our fates are bound together”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
