title: Child review – jump scares abound in twisty organ transplant fable that keeps horror at its heart | Movies | The Guardian
description: This Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-making
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: This Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-making
Content: How much worse could it get … Child.Photograph: GrimmVisionView image in fullscreenHow much worse could it get … Child.Photograph: GrimmVisionMoviesReviewChild review – jump scares abound in twisty organ transplant fable that keeps horror at its heartThis Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-makingLeslie FelperinTue 29 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStippled with first-world guilt about income inequality even between fellow EU member states, this Luxembourg-made horror sprinkles a bit of liberal fairy dust over what is otherwise a pretty straight-up, if twisty, horror setup: a grunting, inarticulate and physically disfigured big baddie stalks the normie protagonists who shouldn’t have come round these impoverished parts. Think Grand Duchy Chainsaw Massacre, though admittedly without any chainsaws. There are sullen locals, a dilapidated farmhouse full of ominous clutter, ill intentions and horrible maiming.The unlucky visitors here are former couple Greg (Malik Zidi) and Anne (Brigitte Urhausen), who are co-parenting little Leo (Leo Todesco), a pre-adolescent who is lying in a hospital bed while waiting for a crucial organ transplant. A little time has to elapse before we learn that control-freak Anne blames likable doctor Greg for Leo’s condition because he took his eyes off the kid for just long enough for him to get hit by a car. But Greg is trying to make it up to her by accompanying his ex on a trip to an unnamed eastern European country (where folks speak Bulgarian) to acquire the organ Leo needs on the black market, their glide path lubricated with lots of cash and pre-arranged bribes to border guards and the like.Heart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroesRead moreUnfortunately, things go very pear-shaped; in fact, they go so wrong we may need a whole other kind of fruit to describe the badness of this shape. Co-writer-director Cyrus Neshvad deliberately toys with audience expectations about survival by violating narrative conventions about point of view, which is really fun. Also impressive is the way he and cinematographer Nikos Welter play with light and colour throughout, shifting the whole palette as soon as the Luxembourgers cross the border, and later using the LED light from a crucial box to cast little pools of first blue and then orange and red light to signify time running out. The performances are mostly held back and buttoned down until it is time to scream in terror. It’s a shame that the initial medical conceit is a little too vague (which organ are they supposed to be collecting?), but there are enough jump scares to give most hearts a jolt.Child is in UK cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsLuxembourgHealthOrgan donationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Portuguese House review – picturesque, polite drama of secrets and revelations at a country estate | Movies | The Guardian
description: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener
Content: Restrained and respectful … Maria de Medeiros and Manolo Solo in The Portuguese House.Photograph: Courtesy of AX1 FilmsView image in fullscreenRestrained and respectful … Maria de Medeiros and Manolo Solo in The Portuguese House.Photograph: Courtesy of AX1 FilmsMoviesReviewThe Portuguese House review – picturesque, polite drama of secrets and revelations at a country estateSpanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardenerCath ClarkeTue 29 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOut of the blue, a woman walks out on her husband. Bags packed and ready to go, at the last moment she crumples up the letter she has written to him and vanishes from their Madrid flat. So begins this drama featuring not one but three characters disappearing without a trace from their lives; it sounds soap opera-ish, but mostly The Portuguese House unfolds as polite elegant drama, told with such rich novelistic detail it often feels like it’s getting into the minds of the characters.Manolo Solo gives an excellent performance as the left-behind husband, Fernando, an introspective mild-mannered geography professor. After his wife’s disappearance, Fernando goes on holiday to Portugal, where he meets a gardener called Manuel. When Manuel drops dead of a heart attack, Fernando decides – like his wife – to leave his old life behind; he assumes Manuel’s identity and takes a job as the gardener at a Portuguese country estate. The owner, Amália (Maria de Medeiros), senses that this intellectual man with glasses and a clumsy way with the loppers is not the man she hired, but doesn’t push it – possibly because she is attracted to him.Like a doorstop paperback, The Portuguese House is an expansive watch, spanning years and going at a gentle pace for nearly two hours. There are more secrets and lies to come – and another person pretending to be someone they are not. That would be a twist too far in another film, but works here in a restrained drama that treats all its characters generously and with sympathy. Though in the end I wondered if it is possibly too respectful, sweeping away difficult hard-to-shift feelings like autumn leaves.The Portuguese House is in UK cinemas from 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSpainEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: April X review – Connor Storrie searches for missing twin in dystopian dream-tech sci-fi thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitative
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: The star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitative
Content: Supermarket sweep under the carpet … Lilly Krug as April and Connor Storrie as Baxter in April X.Photograph: Vertigo Releasing/PAView image in fullscreenSupermarket sweep under the carpet … Lilly Krug as April and Connor Storrie as Baxter in April X.Photograph: Vertigo Releasing/PAMoviesReviewApril X review – Connor Storrie searches for missing twin in dystopian dream-tech sci-fi thrillerThe star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitativeLeslie FelperinTue 29 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSketchy in every sense of the word, this sci-fi thriller is set in the not-too-distant future in a dystopian concrete city (actually mostly Bucharest looking like itself), where life is cheap but screenwriting conceits are clearly expensive, given most of the main ones here appear to be borrowed from other movies. Brother-and-sister twins Baxter (Connor Storrie, fromHeated Rivalry) and April (Lilly Krug) are struggling to get by and mooching around the fringes of the criminal world, doing jobs on a spectrum of legality, though nothing especially harmful to themselves or others. He does petty crimes and she makes wigs and sells downloads of her own uncannily clear dreams (a nod to neglected 90s classics Strange Days and Until the End of the World where dream tech played key roles).Unfortunately, Baxter and his screw-up associate Ronny (Tourialay Akbari) fall into debt to and afoul with local kingpin Klein (Serban Pavlu), whose persistent use of Yiddish phrases and general parsimoniousness sets up the characterisation just on the edge of antisemitism. When Baxter cleans out his and April’s joint accounts and still comes up short, someone takes April and her archive of recorded dreams/memories. Suddenly, the action jumps ahead five years in the future and April is both still missing and yet, at a local brothel, all too ubiquitous where it seems she’s been cloned to make numerous sex workers.This nasty spin on human trafficking gets progressively ickier as the last act unfolds, especially as the film both wants us to be repulsed by the situation and seemingly titillated judging by all the shots of Krug, duplicated digitally, having sex with clients or sitting around languidly in lingerie. There’s a bit of jagged editing to make things look cleverer than they are, and lashings of hard-boiled voiceover narration from Storrie. The latter does his best to bring conviction to the material, but this is not a work that will feature prominently in his CV in the years to come.April X is in UK and Irish cinemas from 2 October with an Australian release date yet to be announced.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Saunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to Oslo  | Scandinavia holidays | The Guardian
description: A new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en route
Author: Adam Turner
Headline: A new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en route
Content: The Kallbadhuset (the cold bath house) set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea in Varberg.Photograph: Patrick Kuenne/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Kallbadhuset (the cold bath house) set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea in Varberg.Photograph: Patrick Kuenne/Getty ImagesScandinavia holidaysSaunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to OsloA new direct train service connects the far south of Sweden to the Norwegian capital in just over six hours, with the option of stopping off in the seaside town of Varberg or lively Gothenburg en routeAdam TurnerTue 29 Sep 2026 02.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 02.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘This carriage is due for modernisation. Don’t miss the opportunity to experience 90s Germany style,”reads the sign on the door to the dining carriage. The couple inside aren’t missing theirs: they’re taking endless selfies in the clinical pink-and-turquoise carriage that looks like a hospital canteen and smells like cinnamon buns and strong filter coffee.I’m onSnälltåget’siconic red-shelled train, on the Swedish rail company’s new route from Malmö to Oslo – a 6.5-hour journey along Sweden’s picturesque western corridor. Until now, the journey between the two cities involved long bus rides and fragmented train transfers. This direct line is easier and cheaper, with tickets starting at £11 each way. It’s already a hit, shuttling more than 25,000 passengers since launching this summer.I was first seduced by Scandi rail travel a decade ago on a journey from Stockholm to Gothenburg, when I was berthed in a cosy dark-wood cabin and listened to a pianist play in a dining car. This time, starting in Malmö, I will take advantage of the new route to make a series of stops along the country’s western shore.In my view Malmö, across the Øresund Bridge from Copenhagen, is too often overlooked in favour of Stockholm. The southern port city is less polished than the capital and grittier, but its residents seem more outgoing and curious. Within an hour of arriving, I’m invited to drinks by a group of local people – a level of openness I never experienced living in Stockholm.Almost half of the populationis under 35, and 187 nationalities are represented, making it a hotbed of creativity. In the centre of town, theForm/Design Centeroccupies a former 16th-century grain store, now a meeting point and exhibition space for design, crafts and architecture enthusiasts. Then, there areModerna MuseetandMalmö Konsthallmodern art galleries.View image in fullscreenPoints of View by Tony Cragg, a public artwork in Malmö.Photograph: Danita Delimont/AlamyAtMöllevången, or Möllan, a trendy neighbourhood popular with creatives, everybody looks as if they’re at art college, or have just returned from a weekend in Berlin. My friend Rob, who has lived in Malmö for nearly a decade, guides me through Folkets Park, the “people’s park”, pointing out his favourite pizza spot,Far i Hatten, which occupies cute wooden huts. We find a table atAvanearby for a beer on a leafy square dotted with hip restaurants and organic wine bars – it feels like Malmö’s equivalent to London Fields in Hackney. Resisting the urge to continue our purposefully staid bar crawl, we down a nightcap atBar Boboand call it a night.double quotation markFloating on my back, I look up to see a group of Swedish veterans baring all, the building’s mustard shades completing an almost Hockney-esque sceneSnälltåget operates just one direct Oslo-bound train a day, at 6.38am from Malmö Central (plans are in the works to increase this next year), so it’s an early start at a station teeming with families and backpackers with rucksacks the size of fridge-freezers. We soon pass the romanesque towers ofLund Cathedralbefore chugging through pancake-flat yellowing agricultural fields, then skirt Apelviken bay – Varberg’s long, sandy horseshoe beach popular for kitesurfing and surfing.Varberg is Sweden’s equivalent of a coastal British market town. It’s got bunting, cobbled streets, intimate cafes and a weekend market with vendors peddling fresh vegetables, fruit, marmalade, leather belts and socks. It’s also a spa town, which inspired my visit. I was intrigued by its pretty, Moorish-inspiredKallbadhuset(cold bath house), set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea, where for about £8 visitors gain access to segregated men’s and women’s saunas, both with spellbinding sea views. A plunge in the brisk water after the sauna proves the perfect antidote to a 6am start after a bottle of red wine the night before. Floating on my back, I look up to see a group of Swedish veterans sitting on a wooden bench, baring all (it’s a nude bathhouse), the building’s mustard shades completing an almost Hockney-esque scene.View image in fullscreenThe Snälltåget.Photograph: Trygve Finkelsen/AlamyAccording to a sign outside Skarpe Nord – a community-run women’s bathing spot nearby – people have been nude-bathing in Varberg for more than 100 years. Walking along the promenade by a cavernous passage of blasted rocks that resembles a secret pathway from Lord of the Rings, I pass a collection of other designated naked bathing spots. But with the grey weather showing no sign of clearing, my hotel’s spa proves more inviting.In the bowels ofHotell Gästishides a replica of Vladimir Lenin’s favourite bathhouse. The hotel’s owner, Lasse Diding, built the spa as a homage to his idol, inspired by a visit to the original bathhouse in St Petersburg in the 1980s. This slightly eerie space is clad in more than 75,000 cobalt tiles and decorated with candlelit busts of communist leaders.Diding’s interest in the communist movement began during the Vietnam war and never left him. The eccentric entrepreneur is responsible for Varberg’s many visible politically left-leaning monuments – a giant Palestine flag,Hotell Havanna(an ode to revolutionary Cuba) and a statue ofDanuta Danielsson, who became a symbol of solidarity after hitting a marching neo-Nazi with her handbag in Växjö in 1985.The following morning, I hopon the fast train to Gothenburg, a 39-minute ride away. After checking in at the sophisticated, French boudoir-styleHotel Pigalle,just five minutes’ walk from Central station, I wander along Kungsgatan, the city’s modern shopping artery, towards Magasingatan. The area is packed with vintage shops (Ragtime,PopandHumana) and craft stores such asCustomwood, which makes bespoke wooden furniture to order.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSweet treats.Photograph: Gabriella Stroem/Getty ImagesI grab afika(the Swedish tradition of taking a break to drink coffee and indulge in a sweet treat)atDa Matteo, a barn turned cafe spread across three floors. The Scandi-industrial interiors are straight out of a design magazine, as bespectacled folk work away on their laptops. Scents of bread and coffee drift from the in-house bakery and coffee roastery; mybullar(a classic cardamom bun) and a latte cost just under a tenner.double quotation markThe Gothenburg to Oslo leg of the journey is the cinematic climax: lakes widen, trees grow greener and granite canyons appear grander with every kilometreWandering around Slottsskogen park later, I remember why I wanted to move to Gothenburg after a fleeting first visit all those years ago. Sweden’s second-largest city is compact and easy-going. It has a rough-around-the-edges feel like Malmö in places, with the liveability, nature and culture of Stockholm. At its heart is the pretty old town of Haga, which has narrow cobbled streets, inviting wafts of baked goods and the sound of creaky, wooden trams chugging by. And Slottsskogen is my favourite park in Europe. Roughly the size of Hyde Park, it’s home to deer, penguins and Gotland ponies, and exactly the kind of place you can spend long hours strolling without purpose.The Gothenburg to Oslo leg of the journey is the cinematic climax. It starts with rolling green pastures, cows grazing on a riverbank and forests thick with towering conifers beneath a blue summer sky. Then nature really starts showing off: lakes widen, trees grow greener and granite canyons appear grander with every kilometre, drawing excited kids to press their noses against the windows.View image in fullscreenOslo from Vettakollen viewpoint.Photograph: Sean Harrison/AlamyKeen to see it up close, after pulling into Oslo I dump my bags atCitybox, a minimalist hotel a few minutes’ walk from the station, and head north to Sognsvann. This lake and recreational area on the outskirts of the city is the starting point for a circular walk up to Vettakollen, a popular viewpoint. After an easy, 30-minute uphill hike, I reach a rocky mound skirted by pine trees, where families are picnicking. Oslo unfurls in the distance, the urban sprawl of metal and glass stretching to the fjord. For me, this is what makes Scandinavia special: the urban and the natural worlds seamlessly colliding.The trip was provided byVisit Sweden. title: Stop press: why are garlic presses so out of fashion? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?
Content: Sometimes, a press can helpful, especially if the garlic is going in a sauce, stew or braise.Photograph: JoeGough/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenSometimes, a press can helpful, especially if the garlic is going in a sauce, stew or braise.Photograph: JoeGough/Getty Images/iStockphotoKitchen aideChefsStop press: why are garlic presses so out of fashion?It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?Anna BerrillTue 29 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy are garlic presses suddenly a no-no? Recipes nowstipulate gratinginstead, but who wants lumps of garlic in theirdinner?Sally, by emailPeople sure do love to hate on the garlic press, not that that’s anything new: in her aptly titled essayGarlic Presses Are Utterly Useless, Elizabeth David called them “both ridiculous and pathetic”, whileAnthony Bourdainwrote in Kitchen Confidential: “I don’t know what that junk is that squeezes out the ends of those things, but it ain’t garlic.” Fighting talk, indeed.Christina Soteriou, recipe writer at Ottolenghi Inc and author ofBig Veg Energy, however, takes a more balanced approach: “A garlic press is not necessarily a no-no, and there can definitely be a time and a place for it,” she says. “It’s definitely quicker [than chopping], but I’d use it only when said garlic is going into a sauce, stew or braise.” Which is to say, in a dish where those lumps that concern Sally will cook down and dissolve almost entirely.For Jenny Chandler, author ofThe Capsule Kitchen, meanwhile, there’s no “abhorrence and disgust at the idea of anybody using a garlic press, it just seems to add extra work to your cooking”. First, you’ve got to fumble around in a drawer to find it, then “half the garlic just squeezes up around the sides of the press, so I’ve got to do it twice to get all the garlic out”. That’s especially irksome given that Chandler is more often than not crushing multiple cloves. “So, in the time it takes me to locate my press and load it with, say, four cloves, I could have just crushed them with a bit of salt on a board under a heavy blade,” she says. And you’ll sure need extra time for cleaning the damned thing, Chandler adds: “That’s an absolute pain.”Soteriou usually minces her garlic with flaky sea salt “for the absolute best garlic flavour”, otherwise she “almost always” uses a Microplane grater or pestle and mortar. “The flavour is more consistent and mellow,” she explains. “Without getting too science-y, a pestle gently breaks down the garlic cells and releases a rounder, more even flavour, whereas a garlic press gives a slightly more bitter and uneven flavour because of how the cells are sharply broken down.” A Microplane falls somewhere between the two, and of course doing that by hand can be a sticky business. “People think a garlic press stops you from getting garlicky fingertips,” Chandler says, but there’s another solution: “When I worked on a boat many years ago, the owner gave me a bar ofstainless-steel soap, which turned out to be miraculous at getting rid of garlic smells.” The sulphur compounds in garlic bind to the metal molecules and wash away under water, and the same works if you brush those garlicky digits against a stainless-steel sink.As with most things in life, Sally should just do her, though Soteriou does suggest sticking to one rule: “A garlic press for anything that’s going to be slow-cooked, and a Microplane, pestle and mortar, or minced for anything where it will be raw or cooked very quickly.” Just “never, ever buy ready-crushed garlic”, Chandler says. “That’s another business altogether and it tastes awful.”Got a culinary dilemma? title: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for turmeric chicken and cardamom apple tart | Food | The Guardian
description: A rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the meal
Author: Thomasina Miers
Headline: A rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the meal
Content: Thomasina Miers’ turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilli.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilli.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.Thomasina Miers recipesFoodThomasina Miers’ recipes for turmeric chicken and cardamom apple tartA rich and sweet chicken main and a punchy tart to round off the mealThomasina MiersTue 29 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite the back-to-school, back-to-work vibes of September, I also think it’s a time of celebration. There’s the feeling of new things, with apples, corn, walnuts, squash and mushrooms appearing at the markets, and my garden has finally emerged from its drought-induced slumber, as if coming out of a trance – it is greener, more alive, reawakening. There’s still the odd bit of warm weather in which to play, too, so light up the grill, get creative in the kitchen and dance like it’s June again.Grilled turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilliRich Indian spices, sweet onion, garlic and lemon make this marinade stand out when it hits the grill. Serve with a garlicky raita on the side.Prep10 minMarinate30 min+Cook30 minServes4-61kg chickenthighs(about 6), preferably boneless and skin-on2 tsp sea salt1 medium onion,peeled and roughly chopped2 fat garlic cloves,peeled2 red chillies1 tsp ground turmeric2 heaped tsp garam masala1 lemon300g kefir½ tsp chilli powder(optional) – kashmiri for a mild flavour, ancho for a rounded taste and a little heat, cayenne if you like things hot1 handfulfresh coriander, leaves pickedFor the raita½ cucumber1 fat garlic clove,peeled and finely gratedSalt and pepperSeason the chicken thighs generously with salt. Put the onions, garlic, chillies and spices in a food processor, squeeze in the juice of half a lemon and blitz to a paste, scraping down the sides of the bowl a few times as you go. Add a teaspoon of salt and 100g kefir, and blitz again to make a beautiful, ochre-coloured paste. Taste it – I like to add some chilli powder. Slather the marinade all over the chicken thighs and leave for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or for a few hours/overnight in the fridge.Shortly before you’re ready to eat, coarsely grate the cucumber skin and all into a sieve, suspend it over a bowl, and push down to squeeze out any water (the juice is a delicious drink; try it with a little salt and pepper). Mix the squeezed cucumber with the remaining kefir and grated garlic, then season generously.Heat a griddle pan (or barbecue) and chargrill the chicken for six minutes on each side, until the meat is cooked through and the skin is deliciously crisp and golden. Serve scattered with fresh coriander, the remaining half-lemon cut into wedges and the raita.Sugar-burnt cardamom and apple puff tartView image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ sugar-burnt cardamom apple puff tart.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.A crisp, caramelised, scented tart that takes very little time to prepare, but still feels like a proper pudding.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes6-810 green cardamom pods100gsugarSalt5 medium sharp, crispapples(about 450g)Juice of½ lemon40g unsalted butter1320g sheet shop-boughtpuff pastry(preferably all-butter)Plain flour, for dusting1 small egg40g ground almondsStart by making a cardamom sugar. Put the pods in a mortar and bash them a few times with a pestle. Slip off and discard the loosened green sleeves, then bash the remaining black seeds with vigour. Add the sugar and a generous pinch of salt, and bash again to release the cardamom oils and aromatics into the sugar.Quarter and core the apples, then slice into 2-3mm-thick half-moons. As you slice them, toss in a bowl with the lemon juice so they don’t discolour. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Melt the butter in a small pan (or in the microwave). Lay out the pastry on a board. Lightly flour a rolling pin, then roll the pastry so it’s a little larger and a little thinner, but still in a similar rectangular shape. Line a baking tray with baking paper, lay the pastry on top and use a small, sharp knife carefully to mark a 2cm border all around the edge; take care not to cut through the pastry completely. Prick the inside of the border all over with a fork (this will stop it rising in the oven). Whisk the egg with a teaspoon of water, then brush this all over the pastry.Bake for five minutes, then remove and scatter the ground almonds all over the centre of the pastry. Arrange the apple slices in an overlapping pattern on top, then drizzle or brush with the melted butter and sprinkle the lot with the cardamom sugar.Bake for another 20 minutes, then turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for a final 10 minutes, until the apples are browned and caramelised. Leave to cool a little on a rack, then slice and serve with vanilla ice-cream, thick cream, custard or all three.Explore more on these topicsFoodThomasina Miers recipesChickenMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesVegetablesSide dishesrecipesShareReuse this content
